News.title: Kemi Badenoch vows to cut screentime in schools with return to pen-and-paper learning under Tory plan
News.content:
Next

SCHOOLS would be forced to ditch laptops and bring back textbooks under a Tory plan to drastically cut screentime during lessons.

Kemi Badenoch will today outline proposals to do away with electronic devices in most classrooms and return to pen-and-paper learning.



She will warn that Britain has “sleepwalked” into an unhealthy situation where the majority of pupils use screens during lessons.

The Tory leader is pledging to axe devices altogether for under-5s amid concerns of the impact in their cognitive development.



Primary schools would be told to only give kids screens when absolutely necessary – like computer class – while secondary pupils would be limited to two hours each day.

Health experts have warned of the impact on excessive screen use for youngsters, including weakening their attention spans.



Ms Badenoch is also concerned that pupils are becoming overly reliant on artificial intelligence which is “lowering educational standards”.

She will today pledge to divert part of an existing £950million government “EdTech” budget for laptops and instead commit £250million for physical textbooks.

Shadow Education Secretary Laura Trott said last night: “We have sleepwalked into a situation where nearly a million children spend almost every lesson on a screen, while medical professionals warn of the damage excessive screen time can do to children’s health, development and learning.

“I want to slash screen use in classrooms and set a new norm where screens are no longer the default.



“Everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards.”

Most kids are already compelled to hand their mobile phones into schools during the day.

Some headteachers are already shunning laptops in favour of traditional methods.

This year top fee-paying school Winchester scrapped screens entirely from their lessons amid fears they were too distracting for the pupils.

Dr Rebecca Foljambe, founder of Health Professionals for Safer Screens, said last night: “We have become excessively preoccupied with why children are on screens.



“Although content is important, this distracts from the fact that daily screen time can profoundly affect a child’s health, whatever they are watching or doing.”

News.title: Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies in hospital aged 80 after notorious reign as Guadalajara Cartel boss
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

‘THE GODFATHER’ Mexican drug lord Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo dies in hospital aged 80 after notorious reign as Guadalajara Cartel boss







Next

A NOTORIOUS Mexican drug lord who founded the Guadalajara Cartel has died aged 80.

Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, dubbed “The Boss of Bosses”, died in hospital on Sunday after he reportedly suffered multiple organ failures.



He was rushed to a medical centre from his Puente Grande prison cell alongside a heavy security team including air support.

Authorities have not disclosed his official cause of death yet.



The narcotics kingpin was widely considered one of the biggest smugglers in the world.

He was credited with building alliances between criminal groups in Colombia and his own Mexican cartel.

Gallardo was convicted of killing a US drug-enforcement agent in 1985 – solidifying his name in history as one of the country’s most infamous traffickers.

His Guadalajara Cartel swept over the Mexican drug scene in the 1980s at the peak of the cocaine boom.

The foundations of the illegal drug network he helped pioneer still endure to this day.

He has been in jail in 1989.



The security ministry in Jalisco, where he was being held, said: “After remaining under observation with a guarded prognosis, he died on November 15 at the medical facility.”

His health had spiralled in recent years – blighted by issues including high blood pressure, diabetes and deafness.

In 2022, then-Mexican president Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador said he was “in very poor health”.



A judge granted him house arrest, but technical problems with electronic ankle monitoring prevented his transfer.

Gallardo was from Sinaloa, where he was born on January 8, 1946.

His 1985 conviction came after he murdered US narcotics agent Camarena Salazar, who was kidnapped and tortured.

News.title: Burnham set to insist his Brexit reversal plot will be welcomed by his constituents in Makerfield
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham will tonight insist his Brexit reversal plot will be welcomed by his constituents in Makerfield who overwhelmingly voted Leave.

The PM has previously sparked anger with claims nobody believed in the current “hard” deal with Europe during the 2016 referendum.



This week, he will use a summit to lock in EU deals set to increase youth immigration and to make Britain contribute more cash.

In a speech at Mansion House tonight, the PM will say: “It’s like the Emperor’s new clothes — where no-one is prepared to say the obvious truth.



“The Brexit we were given has not worked.

“We have lost more than we gained.”

He will say his new terms will bring the Brexit deal “closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016”.

He also stressed the deal will have to pass the “Makerfield test” and improve people’s lives.

But Makerfield voted to leave the EU by 65 per cent in 2016.

Pro-Brexit group Stay Out said: “He won that seat promising not to undo Brexit and has since said his ultimate goal is to take Britain back in.”



Mr Burnham will rule out rejoining the single market, customs union, or reviving freedom of movement this Parliament.

News.title: Labour’s benefits overhaul under fire as it’s revealed welfare bill will still be surging after next election
News.content:
Next

LABOUR’S benefits overhaul was under fire last night as ministers admitted the bill would still be surging beyond the next election.

Welfare Secretary Pat McFadden refused to guarantee reductions in this parliamentary term – while government czar Alan Milburn said it could take 10 years for spending to start falling.



Mr Milburn will tomorrow present his long-awaited plan to get a near-million jobless youngsters off the dole and into work.

He yesterday said he would recommend slashing benefits for some younger claimants to pay for employment support.



The ex-Health Secretary also urged ministers to scrap the system of GPs signing people off sick and to slow down hikes to the youth minimum wage.

Andy Burnham is expected to adopt his demands, teeing up a showdown with left-wing Labour MPs who oppose benefit cuts and are threatening rebellion.



But even with the changes, Mr Milburn warned they would not deliver spending reductions for at least a decade.

Taxpayers are currently footing an annual £145billion working age welfare bill that is projected to keep rising every year.

Asked if he would make progress reducing this before the next election, Mr McFadden said: “Look I can’t say that, we upgrade benefits every year and I think that’s important to keep people up with the cost of living.

“These are some of the poorest people in the country and the best way to get the benefits bill down is exactly with the long term reset that we are talking about.”



Reform’s Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick told The Sun: “We can’t afford to waste 10 years before we fix the youth jobs crisis.

“Radical action is needed now to cut taxes on jobs, end poor quality university courses and boost apprenticeships. Burnham doesn’t have any time to waste.”

Mr McFadden also drew criticism from bosses who said that Labour’s tax hikes have made it harder to hire youngsters.

The London Chamber of Commerce said: “The Government will not tackle the NEET crisis while continuing to make it more difficult and more expensive for businesses to employ people.

“The fundamental reset Pat McFadden has described must include reducing hiring costs and ensuring our education system gives young people the skills businesses need, rather than tweaks to the edges of the welfare system.”

News.title: How a harmonious start to Burnham’s time in No10 could start to shift as three rebellions are brewing
News.content:
POLITICS FIX How a harmonious start to Burnham’s time in No10 could start to shift as three rebellions are brewing







Next

ANDY Burnham is about to discover that those Labour MPs who installed him in No10 are a hard group to please.

While they have largely behaved themselves during his first few months in power, this could be the week where discord starts to break out.



There are three potential rebellions brewing that the PM will be looking to head off.

The first could blow tomorrow when the long-awaited welfare report by Alan Milburn is finally published.



Ministers are due to adopt recommendations to cut benefits for jobless young people and use that money to fund more employment support.

While this sounds sensible to many voters, Labour left-wingers have already vowed to reject any kind of reductions.

Downing Street has spent months rolling the pitch for tomorrow’s moment and will be hoping to dampen the flames of mutiny as much as possible.

Lessons from Sir Keir Starmer‘s doomed welfare overhaul have been learned and Mr Burnham will be hoping to weather the inevitable row.

A second crunch is looming over the Rosebank oil field, which the party’s eco-minded MPs are dead against.

After ministers approved the Jackdaw gas field that begins piping energy into homes today, more than 75 rebels are telling the PM any further North Sea drilling would be a line crossed.



But the party is divided on the issue, and many MPs are ferociously in favour of extracting more homegrown resources to power British industry.

Take Henry Tufnell, who told me last night: “We cannot and should not turn our backs on those industrial communities that have powered this country for generations.”

Finally, Mr Burnham is flying into the mother-of-all spats on Friday when he heads to Brussels to meet EU leaders.

He is seeking closer ties with the bloc to smooth trade frictions, but will fire the starting gun on a massive watering down of Brexit.

The PM will give us more of a hint of his plan in a speech tonight, but we know he is keen on freedom of movement and even rejoining entirely at some point.



While this is music to the ears of many left-wingers, his MPs in Leave-voting seats are less than impressed.

After a relatively harmonious start to his time in No10, things could be about to get a whole lot more restless.

News.title: Fury as 75 Labour MPs join oil drilling revolt against Burnham ‘putting thousands of British jobs at risk’
News.content:
YOU FUELS! Fury as 75 Labour MPs join oil drilling revolt against Burnham ‘putting thousands of British jobs at risk’







Next

ANDY Burnham was under pressure last night after more than 75 Labour left-wingers staged a revolt to stop new oil drilling.

The PM and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh were battling to stare down a fresh push to halt extraction at the Rosebank field in the North Sea.



The eco-rebels are warning Mr Burnham’s credentials as a climate campaigner will be in tatters should it be approved.

It comes as gas will today begin heating UK homes after Labour green-lit the nearby Jackdaw field after public pressure on energy bills.



Ms Fahnbulleh admitted supplies would heat millions of homes this winter and were a “boost for energy security”.

She is said to be more sceptical of Rosebank and is facing fevered demands from colleagues to kibosh it.



Industry bosses, however, are urging the Government to grant approval, saying it would safeguard thousands of jobs.

The move could also generate £1.4billion in tax by 2029, North Sea operator Adura says.

Reform’s Richard Tice said: “The Rosebank rebellion risks killing thousands of well-paid British jobs and tanking our energy industry.

“Eco-zealot Labour MPs are once again holding the country to ransom and sabotaging a critical national project. It would be an act of gross negligence for Burnham to abandon the national interest and capitulate to these nutters.”



Labour MP Henry Tufnell also spoke up for Rosebank.

He said: “We are drifting towards a reliance on foreign imports and an economic orthodoxy that couldn’t care less about manufacturing.

“We cannot turn our backs on the industrial communities that have powered this country for generations.”

News.title: Jensen Huang ‘plotting Nvidia comeback’ just days after resigning over ‘Chinese spy’ scandal as fresh probe launched
News.content:
Next

NVIDIA’S ousted CEO Jensen Huang is plotting a sensational comeback to the firm just days after resigning over his suspected Chinese spy mistress scandal, reports say.

The tech titan‘s closest allies in Silicon Valley are putting together a “war room” to have him reinstated as the AI chip-making giant’s boss.



Huang stepped down as CEO on Thursday amid claims he had extramarital flings with a suspected Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees.

He has now discussed with his inner circle the possibility of returning, sources close to the matter told the Financial Times.



This is despite Nvidia currently being in the middle of an independent probe into Huang’s alleged behaviour which sparked a full-blown company crisis.

One of his close aides told the outlet they were bringing together a “war room” of top Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return to power.

They are reportedly looking to the White House and Donald Trump for support.

The source said: “Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen.”



They also claimed Huang was supporting the potential coup.

This is not the only reported movement backing Huang’s return.

A petition to have him reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO snowballed in momentum over the weekend.



Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk has supported the public letter calling for the chip-maker’s board to “Bring Jensen Back”.

Huang continues to exert significant sway over his most loyal employees – some of whom have spoken up and publicly demanded his return.

Efforts from the Huangites to bring him back are likely to face pushback from Washington.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shake-up” in leadership at Nvidia following the ousted leader’s dramatic exit.

The White House has also demanded the board respond within 10 days to allegations Nvidia allowed chips to be funnelled illicitly to China to “goose their revenues and their earnings”.



Interim boss of the AI giant, Colette Kress, is now facing mounting pressure.

Huang’s dramatic fall from grace has wiped $200billion off the company’s value this week.

The leather jacket-loving casanova, who founded Nvidia more than three decades ago, resigned on Thursday amid the spiralling scandal.

He admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, 49, last week – who US intelligence services believe is a Chinese spy.

Reports then emerged he had secret flings with top Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, and another unnamed woman.



Huang is set to appear before Congress to answer questions related to national security and his relationship with Alice.

The FBI has also launched an investigation into him.

Meanwhile, the White House has come under fire for not properly assessing claims Huang was romantically involved with a suspected Chinese spy, despite being briefed on the situation months before it emerged.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The former Nvidia CEO was a pivotal figure in balancing China-US relations amid the deepening AI race.

He pushed for Washington to greenlight critical AI chip sales to Beijing.

News.title: Chippy’s epic ‘Codzilla’ meal challenge features 3ft piece of fish weighing 5lbs and a HUGE cash prize if you finish it
News.content:
Next

A CHIPPY has launched a “Codzilla” meal challenge — featuring a 3ft piece of fish weighing at least 5lb.

Andreas Matheou gives entrants 30 minutes to eat the fillet along with five portions of chips, pickled eggs, onions and gherkins and unlimited curry sauce and mushy peas.



Two out of 23 people have so far managed to finish the gargantuan £60 dish at Marino Fish Bar in ­Sittingbourne, Kent, meaning they get it for free plus a £100 prize — but both were competitive eaters.

Andreas, 40, describes his shop on Facebook as the “home of Codzilla, the world’s biggest battered cod”.



The dad of three had previously sold it as a meal for six before a customer suggested he should launch it as an eating challenge to drum up trade.

He said: “It’s really helping. It’s gone crazy.

“People come from all over the UK to try to finish the lot.

“I’m getting a lot more youngsters coming in and wanting to eat fish, which was my main goal.”



He added: “We want to keep the British tradition alive.”

Marino Fish Bar was started by Andreas’ grandad in 1966 in Margate, before his dad moved it to Sittingbourne 30 years ago.

He took the shop over six years ago, and after feeling Gen Z weren’t coming in, tried to think of new ways to attract younger customers.

They tried introducing burgers and kebabs, but he ideally wanted them ordering the classic cod.

News.title: Cut national insurance for under-25s to create jobs, Milburn report to say
News.content:
National Insurance (NI) paid by businesses on workers aged under 25 should be gradually lowered to encourage companies to create jobs for young people, a major review of youth unemployment will say.

A report by former Labour minister Alan Milburn will suggest the government should reduce NI costs over five years for people aged between 21 and 24 years old, starting in retail and hospitality.

Under Sir Keir Starmer, the government raised NI for firms. Milburn will say the number of young people not in employment, education or training - known as Neets - was not started by the NI rise.

But shadow work and pensions secretary, Helen Whately, said the government should "just stop doing the taxing".

The independent report, which has been in the works for a year and will be published on Tuesday, will also make recommendations on reducing the UK's benefits bill.

Milburn has said the government spends Â£22bn a year supporting young people who are economically inactive. There are nearly one million so-called Neets aged between 16 and 24 in the UK, according to data from the Office for National Statistics.

He will recommend that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide Universal Credit or personal independence payment (Pip), which is the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Milburn wants the government to provide a legal guarantee of a job, training or employment support. Those who refuse to take up help could lose their benefits.

Milburn is also expected to say that helping young people develop skills is pointless if there are no jobs available for them.

The former health secretary will recommend doubling the threshold at which businesses start paying NI for 21 to 24-year-olds from Â£5,000 to Â£10,000.

But he will say this should only be done "when fiscal conditions allow".

Immediately axing NI for 21 to 24-year-olds would cost Â£5.1bn, according to research by the Resolution Foundation, a left-leaning think tank.

Milburn is set to say that given the UK's fiscal position, an immediate across-the-board cut in employer NI is not the best use of several billions of pounds of public money.

News.title: Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says
News.content:
A discussion over a staggered age of consent is to take place, the work and pensions secretary has said, as the government faces calls to change the law following the case against Russell Brand.

Speaking to the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Pat McFadden said that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" have emerged this week.

A woman who alleges she was raped by jailed comedian Brand when she was 16 is now campaigning to see the law changed so that relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal.

Questions over a staggered age of consent have "been raised and will be discussed" McFadden said, adding: "[I] can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."

Adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, under UK law.

Mia Latter, who has waived her right to anonymity, told the Sunday Times that she wants the age of consent to be staggered.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

At Southwark Crown Court on Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half-years imprisonment after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one allegation of attempted indecent assault.

Latter said she was 16 when she met the comedian, then 30. She told the Sunday Times: "I think people were so struck by my story because of the age difference and the clear imbalance [in power].

"I don't want to criminalise teenagers having sex with each other.

"If you're between the ages of 16 and 18, it seems reasonable that you can have relationships with each other, and [teenagers] are always going to.

"But...if you're in your thirties, forties and fifties and you're trying to have a relationship with someone under the age of 18, it [should be] a criminal offence."

Latter told the Sunday Times the CPS decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings.

She told the paper she was "devastated" by the decision and that police had said they didn't want the trial "to become 'the Alice show'", a reference to her pseudonym in the stories published in 2023.

It is understood the Met Police has apologised for the language officers used in a meeting with Latter about her case.

A Met spokesperson said: "This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence."

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, said bringing in a staggered age of consent was about addressing a "power imbalance" in relationships involving 16 and 17 year-olds and adults. She urged ministers to commit to such a change.

Stone, a child protection social worker, told the BBC that 16 and 17 year-olds were seen as children in "every single framework of the law" and "we don't believe [they are] old enough to consent to having sex with much older adults".

Close the Consent Gap is proposing that 16 year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Further allegations of sexual misconduct in the entertainment industry came in the same week Brand was convicted.

ITV News and the Guardian published a story alleging that comedian David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Other women alleged inappropriate behaviour when he was a judge at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

The Metropolitan Police said on Friday it has launched an investigation into Walliams over reports of "alleged serious sexual offences", after the ITV News and the Guardian story. The Met said that the allegations it is investigating are separate from those reported by ITV and the Guardian but that it was "also proactively reviewing that reporting".

Speaking to Sky News, the work and pensions secretary said: "I do think that between Russell Brand, David Walliams, what's been put out there, people are looking at these issues in a new light."

News.title: Prince Harry praises war veterans on surprise visit to Ukraine
News.content:
That included an innovation for Mykhailo Damaskin, a Ukrainian air assault forces veteran, who was so seriously injured in fighting in Kherson he was never expected to walk again.

In an experimental treatment he had a spinal cord stimulator implanted in his back, which allows him to walk, but has to be re-charged every 12 hours. He cannot feel his feet and controls his steps using his eyes.

He needs to be plugged in and charged up to be able to move - and jokes that he is "like a demo model of a Tesla".

"My goal is to go to the Invictus Games. I promised my father before he was killed that I'd be part of the team to represent Ukraine internationally.

"I'll prove to every guy with spinal cord injuries that life goes on after injury," said Mykhailo.

At the Superhumans Center Prince Harry sat at the bedside of Konstiantyn Vlasenko, who was airlifted from the front line by a drone last month in a rescue that was a first of its kind.

He had been alone for more than 200 days and had stayed at his position, despite losing both his feet.

In a moving encounter, Prince Harry told him he represented the spirit of resilience of Ukraine.

And he described the injured veterans as "role models", promising his audience: "The rest of the world will continue to support you."

Along with all the determination, it was an inescapably poignant sight too, with so many families and children at the medical facility visiting the growing numbers of badly injured war casualties.

News.title: UK will have 'voice' but no vote on EU food rules in Brexit reset
News.content:
The UK will have a "voice in the room" but no vote on European Union food policies as part of a so-called "Brexit reset" to reduce red tape, EU relations minister Hamish Falconer has told the BBC.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham hopes to agree a deal at a summit on Friday but critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker" but not a rule maker.

Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules and said the deal could help bring down prices for shoppers.

The reset would not involve any upfront payments, Falconer added, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.

Falconer said it was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements.

"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.

The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.

The reset means they will be dismantled.

In September, the Conservative Party said it was "raising the alarm" over the government's planned reset, saying it would leave British consumers and businesses "dangerously exposed, with no input on how regulations are made or power to reject them".

Both the Conservatives and Reform have said they would undo the planned reset if they were in power.

News.title: Trident submarine returns home after record-breaking undersea patrol
News.content:
A Royal Navy submarine carrying Trident nuclear missiles has returned to its Scottish base after a record-breaking 217 days spent submerged on patrol.

The 140-strong crew of HMS Vengeance have spent the tour in almost total isolation beneath the surface after setting out from Faslane, near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 12 April.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting was at HM Naval Base Clyde to welcome them home after the longest undersea deployment at sea for a British vessel.

The typical patrol length for the UK's Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines has more than doubled in recent years, with six-month durations now routine due to a shortage of seaworthy vessels.

Crew members could be seen standing on HMS Vengeance as it travelled up Gare Loch earlier, accompanied by some smaller Naval support vessels and tug boats.

The vessel was encrusted in marine growth and some of its sound-absorbing tiles were missing.

HMS Vengeance was expected back at Faslane last weekend, but that was reported to have been delayed, external when the submarine replacing it on patrol had to return to base to fix a technical fault.

The head of the navy, First Sea Lord Gen Sir Gwyn Jenkins, praised the dedication of submariners in keeping Nato safe at a conference last week in Oslo, but said the UK must do better at maintaining the fleet.

News.title: Man and woman die and four arrested after police pursuit crash in Leeds
News.content:
Two people have been killed after their car was hit by a vehicle fleeing from police in Leeds.

West Yorkshire Police said it happened at 00:44 GMT, when a blue BMW 123D failed to stop for officers in Gelderd Road and then crashed into a white Volkswagen Scirocco.

The driver of the Volkswagen, a 22-year-old man, died at the scene. His passenger, a woman, 23, died later in hospital. Both were from York.

The occupants of the BMW, a 39-year-old man from Harrogate, two boys aged 16 and 17 and a 16-year-old girl, have been arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving.

The 39-year-old is also being held on suspicion of driving while over the prescribed limit for cannabis, the force confirmed.

The teenagers in the BMW were taken to hospital for treatment to injuries that were not considered life-threatening.

A spokesperson for West Yorkshire Police said a referral had been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), which confirmed it had started an investigation.

News.title: Cancer 'sponge' tests could be offered to more people with bad indigestion
News.content:
It's thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. This collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it's gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

The cells can then by analysed.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."

However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.

The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.

Final recommendations by NICE will be made in the new year.

News.title: Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison, his wife confirms on podcast
News.content:
Russell Brand has been transferred to a category C prison, his wife Laura has confirmed, in her first public comments since his jailing.

On Monday, the comedian was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Over the weekend, Brand was transferred from category B HMP Wandsworth in London to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, which houses men convicted of sexual offences.

Laura Brand returned to the couple's podcast on Sunday, saying that she had spoken to her husband in prison and he "is OK and is praying". Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

HMP Littlehey, a category C training prison, is one of the largest prisons in Europe for men convicted of sexual offences.

It held more than 1,200 prisoners as of January 2025, according to data from the Independent Monitoring Board.

Before Brand's move to the prison, a source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" at HMP Wandsworth and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing.

A member of staff at Wandsworth said there had been "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival, with some slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. They added that there had also been some anger displayed about his crimes.

Staff at other prisons told the BBC Brand's fame, combined with the nature of his crimes, could make him a target for other inmates.

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can seen sitting on a sofa in what looks like a conservatory. She is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

News.title: I had to explain to my teacher what a young carer was - we need more support
News.content:
Neraya is only 15 but cannot remember a time when she was not a carer for her two sisters.

She is among the young carers crying out for what they have called crucial support, with Neraya saying she has even had to explain what she does to her teachers.

On Monday, the Welsh government will publish a national strategy for unpaid carers, which will have seven priorities including earlier recognition and mental health support.

Neraya, from Bridgend, said people in her position wanted the chance of "a childhood of our own".

Carers Wales said the strategy looked positive in parts, but it was "disappointed" manifesto promises would be excluded and raised questions over how it will be funded.

There are an estimated 5.8 million unpaid carers in the UK, external, 170,000 of whom are young.

The 2021 Census said this included about 120,000 carers, aged five to 17 in England and 8,200 in Wales.

Scottish government recognised there were 42,050 unpaid carers identified in the 2021-22 Carers Census.

Neraya's sisters have varying needs and she helps with practical things such as helping them get ready for school, as well as emotional support, and said there was a lack of understanding about the sacrifices young carers make.

"There's not the understanding that you might not have been able to go somewhere because we had some sort of problem within the household because my sister was ill and I'm worrying about my sister, that kind of thing," she said.

Neraya said she used to get "picked on" because people did not know what was happening with her siblings and others tended to assume they were just "naughty".

Once, in primary school, she said she was called to stand in front of her class and explain what she did because "teachers themselves didn't understand what it was".

Being a carer does not take away from her life, she said, but having support and being made to feel "valid" would give people like her "the chance to have a... childhood of our own at the same time".

The Welsh government said its strategy would focus on seven priority areas, shaped by conversations with carers with the aim of improving early recognition, access to support and respite, and better information on their rights.

It also indicated more support for mental health and wellbeing.

News.title: Tories pledge to halt screen-based school exams and cut coursework
News.content:
The Conservatives have promised to halt screen-based exams and cut coursework in a bid to limit the use of AI by schoolchildren in England if the party returns to power.

The party has also pledged to develop new guidelines so that laptops and tablets are not the "default in classrooms".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott cited recent warnings from clinicians that excessive screen time could be damaging children's health, adding that "everything in schools must be safe for children and improve standards".

The government is currently developing new screen-time guidance for children and has previously said it would consult on the safety of AI in schools.

The vast majority of school exams in the UK are pen and paper based. Under the previous government led by Sir Keir Starmer, exam regulator Ofqual launched a consultation last year, external on the introduction of on-screen exams.

But it emphasised that pen and paper would "remain central" and that the most widely taken subjects would not be moving to digital assessments for the "foreseeable future".

In their announcement on Sunday, the Tories said they would "put a stop" to the introduction of screen-based exams, and require screen time for secondary pupils to be limited to no more than two hours a day.

The party said it would also minimise the amount of coursework in school assessments to avoid lowering educational standards "by allowing children to become overly reliant on the use of generative AI platforms".

Under the plans, primary schools would be required to keep screen use to a minimum and only use screens where necessary, such as in computing lessons.

News.title: Eleven officers convicted of crimes still on Police Scotland payroll, chief confirms
News.content:
Eleven officers who have been convicted of crimes - including eight who have been violent towards women and girls - are still on the Police Scotland pay roll.

In a letter, external to the Scottish Parliament's justice committee, Chief Constable Jo Farrell said there were other cases with "incontrovertible evidence" against officers, but they cannot be sacked quickly enough.

Farrell also said the Â£4.5m annual cost of the 80 officers who are currently suspended was down to "sluggish" conduct arrangements, as well as the time necessary for cases to go through courts.

She described the state of affairs as "intolerable" and called for a modernisation of the police conduct regime.

The revelation follows a number of high-profile cases of police officers who have been exposed as rapists this year alone.

Derek McNee, Campbell Petrie, Carmichael John Williamson and Cameron Ross have all been convicted and are no longer on the payroll.

Meanwhile, Alan Greer, who was named as a violent serial rapist by a BBC investigation, took his own life in May after police raided his home.

It also emerged last month that 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.

News.title: Minister backs legal right to job support for young people
News.content:
The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.

Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".

McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.

But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers.

It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.

His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade.

However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year.

Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.

He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness.

How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted.

Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service.

News.title: Sea of phones at Christmas event prompts backlash
News.content:
When BBC London uploaded a video, external of the Carnaby Street Christmas lights being switched on last week, the comments section filled with thousands of people reacting to what they saw.

But, it wasn't the bright lights or the pretty fireworks that they were reacting to, it was the sea of spectators filming on their phones.

"Remember when we used to look at stuff directly with our eyes? Those were the good old days," said one comment. Another simply said: "It's such a sad sad sight."

Former EastEnders actress Natalie Cassidy commented: "Why is this piece not mentioning the fact that no-one is looking through their eyes at this beautiful display? It's really scary and depressing."

Many of the comments questioned why people would film the fireworks rather than watch them in real life, with one saying: "Nice to see everyone living in the moment, there's a 90% chance they will never watch the video again too."

News.title: Schoolboy imposter subjected ex-professor and wife to 'terrifying ordeal'
News.content:
An imposter who made headlines around the world for posing as a school pupil in while in his 30s has appeared in court and admitted hiding in the home of his former university professor before subjecting him to a "terrifying ordeal".

Brian MacKinnon targeted Prof Brian Whiting, 87, as he lay in bed with his wife, the day after a BBC docudrama on his ruse was broadcast.

My Old School chronicled MacKinnon's return to Bearsden Academy, as Brandon Lee, a 16-year-old who had supposedly just moved to Scotland from Canada.

MacKinnon hatched the plan so he could pursue his dream of becoming a doctor having been thrown out of Glasgow University, when Prof Whiting was dean of the medical school.

News.title: Man dies after being hit by ambulance
News.content:
A man has died after being struck by an ambulance transporting a patient near Sunderland, police have said.

Northumbria Police said the crash occurred on the A19, between the junctions for the A1018 and A690, shortly after 02:00 GMT.

The ambulance was travelling on the northbound carriageway and did not have its blue lights on when it hit the man, who was in his 30s and died at the scene.

Neither the patient nor their partner who were travelling in the ambulance were injured in the collision, while the vehicle's driver, a man in his 40s, was also not hurt and remained at the scene to assist police with their inquiries.

The North East Ambulance Service (NEAS) said the patient in the ambulance and their partner were transferred to another ambulance.

Officers from Northumbria Police's roads unit have launched an investigation into the collision.

Sgt Ben Rutherford said: "Our thoughts are firmly with the family and loved ones of the man who has tragically died following this collision.

"We will continue to support them in any way that we can at this incredibly difficult time."

Anyone with CCTV or dashcam footage of the incident itself or the moments leading up to the collision has been urged to contact the force.

Rutherford said anyone with information, no matter how insignificant it may seem, "could prove key to our investigation and help provide answers for the man's loved ones".

News.title: Ex-Met Police inspector lied about wife's death in Barbados hotel room, BBC learns
News.content:
An inquest in the UK later found that Rebekah's organs had been inexplicably "chopped up" into small pieces by a pathologist in Barbados.

This served no medical purpose and destroyed vital evidence, according to a UK pathologist who examined her body after it had been repatriated.

The inquest also established that key toxicology and histology tests - to look for signs of disease, injury or other changes in the body - were not conducted.

The coroner, Andrew Harris, said this raised the prospect of "deliberate concealment or obstruction of further investigation".

He also said that while bloodstains on bedclothes may be consistent with vomiting, he could not accept the cause of death determined by Barbadian authorities, aspiration pneumonitis - inflammation of the lungs - and delivered an open verdict.

He concluded that Rebekah's death likely involved intoxication and said unlawful killing could not be ruled out.

The inquest did not, however, consider Arter's alleged sexual exploitation of several other women whose cases he had investigated, to be within its scope.

Police in Barbados have previously said no marks of violence were found on Rebekah's body and there was nothing to suggest anything untoward - adding that they did not order toxicology tests because they believed she died from natural causes.

A week after Rebekah died, Arter flew back to the UK where he was arrested at Heathrow in connection with alleged sexual offences against another woman whose case he had investigated as a police officer in 2010. He was found dead in Wandsworth prison three days later.

In response to the BBC, Metropolitan Police Commander Simon Messinger said: "Our thoughts at this time remain with Rebekah Arter's family, who understandably have questions about the circumstances of her death.

"We would urge any victim survivors of rape and sexual offences - no matter how long ago a crime may have occurred - to reach out."

Elliot says his two young children will never know their grandmother.

"My daughter, my son - they're never gonna actually have any memories of her," he says.

"For the rest of my life, I'm never going to know how she's passed away."

News.title: ‘Sponge on a string’ oesophageal cancer test endorsed for NHS roll-out
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thousands of people in England at increased risk of oesophageal cancer could be offered an innovative seven-minute test on the NHS.

The "sponge on a string" technique checks for Barrett’s oesophagus, a condition that occurs when stomach acid damages the lining of the food pipe.

In some individuals, cells may grow abnormally and eventually develop into oesophageal cancer.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) has recommended two tests – Cytosponge and EndoSign – for NHS deployment under new draft guidance.

Tested during pilot schemes, the non-sedative technology can be administered in GP surgeries, local pharmacies and community diagnostic centres.

The patient swallows a small capsule attached to a string, which dissolves inside the stomach to release a small sponge.

open image in gallery A Cytosponge test, one of those used to help diagnose oesophageal cancer. ( PA Media )

Pulled out using the string after a few minutes, the sponge collects cell samples from the oesophageal lining for analysis in a laboratory.

The complete process takes approximately seven minutes.

Nice said its committee found patients prefer the sponge on a string test to endoscopy, which involves a thin tube with a camera at the end being passed through the throat.

More than 9,000 people a year are diagnosed with oesophageal cancer in the UK.

It is often diagnosed late, when it is harder to treat.

According to Nice, Barrett’s oesophagus impacts around 1 to 2 per cent of adults, and is common among those who have long-term acid reflux.

Most people do not go on to develop cancer, but the tests also offer a way for them to monitor their condition.

Professor Jonathan Benger, chief executive of Nice, said: “Oesophageal cancer is very difficult to treat when it is diagnosed at a later stage, so identifying people sooner is really important.

“For people with persistent acid reflux and other risk factors, there is an increased chance of developing Barrett’s oesophagus, which can increase their risk of oesophageal cancer.

“Capsule sponge tests offer a quick and less invasive way to detect concerning changes associated with oesophageal cancer or Barrett’s oesophagus, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

“This new technology has the potential to make testing easier for patients, while helping the NHS focus valuable endoscopy capacity on those who need it most.”

Professor Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: “The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people’s symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it’s fantastic it is now being considered for roll-out across the country.

“Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients – reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage.”

The recommendation is the first to be issued by Nice under the National HealthTech Access Programme.

The initiative was designed to identify cutting-edge technology and devices and assess whether they should be used routinely on the health service.

Thomas Slater, director of healthtech at Nice, said the recommendation “is an important milestone” and “a real example of what we want it to achieve for patients and the NHS”.

“Capsule sponge tests show how innovative health technologies can improve people’s experience of care and help the NHS use its resources more effectively,” he added.

“This is just the beginning. We want the programme to support consistent adoption of high-impact technologies across the country, ensuring they deliver benefits for patients and value for taxpayers.”

News.title: Shock report finds AI-generated child sex abuse images soar 8,400% in two years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

AI-generated child sexual abuse imagery has escalated by more than 8,400 per cent over a two-year timeframe, according to international research.

The global investigation revealed that documented cases worldwide grew by upwards of 395,300 between 2023 and 2025.

Academics also calculated that over 300 million children across the globe suffer at least one instance of technology-facilitated sexual exploitation or abuse annually.

Furthermore, approximately one in four young people can expect to face some form of online abuse prior to turning 18.

The statistics were compiled as part of a major international project involving Scottish experts from the Childlight Global Child Safety Institute, based at the University of Edinburgh.

Childlight highlighted that referrals of AI-generated abuse material provided by technology firms to the US-based National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children surged from approximately 4,700 in 2023 to more than 400,000 in 2025.

The material includes “deepfakes”, which are created using so-called “nudify apps”, where the face of a real child can be digitally placed onto sexually explicit images in a realistic manner within seconds.

Although the images may be fake, researchers said the harm to children is very real, with images sometimes used to blackmail children, demanding money or more images.

Researchers said the problem affects ordinary people as well as high-profile celebrities.

However, the study cautioned that changes in detection and reporting may have contributed to the dramatic increase.

Professor Debi Fry, Childlight’s global director of data at Edinburgh University, said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning.

“These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.”

She added: “While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.”

Childlight’s new international study also warned that serious gaps in government data are hampering prevention efforts to protect children.

Of 103 countries and areas examined across the three regions, the group said only 22 had representative survey data covering both offline and technology-facilitated abuse.

According to Childlight, children with disabilities, Indigenous children, migrants, those in humanitarian settings, very young children and children abused within their families are particularly underrepresented.

In response, Childlight is urging governments to treat sexual exploitation and abuse as a preventable public health issue, invest in reliable and consistent measurement, and use evidence to strengthen protection, support survivors and prevent harm before it occurs.

The institute is also calling for stronger technology-sector accountability, laws that keep pace with emerging threats and prevention efforts beginning earlier in childhood.

Childlight chief executive Paul Stanfield said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk.

“What remains invisible risks remaining unaddressed. We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature.”

Mr Stanfield, there is “nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse”.

He added: “With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.”

Despite the challenges, the report highlighted encouraging progress, with several countries strengthening online safety legislation, improving detection and focusing more on prevention.

With better intelligence, coordinated action and sustained investment, researchers said governments have an opportunity to protect hundreds of millions of children and help create a safer future.

The findings are contained in the group’s 2026 Into the Light Index, which was unveiled at a global summit involving representatives from more than 100 governments on ending violence against children on Monday.

News.title: Young Brits spending more on side hustles to beat cost-of-living crisis
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Younger Britons are investing in new technology to expand their secondary businesses, as those aged under 30 look to bolster their earnings amid cost-of-living pressures, according to new data.

Currys’ business division recorded a sharp increase in sales of portable card readers used by small firms to take payments. The retailer reported a 150 per cent year-to-date rise in purchases of devices from Square and SumUp compared to the same period last year.

Sales of Starlink terminals – compact devices offering satellite internet connection – also climbed 93 per cent year-on-year.

The company said the figures show people elevating their side ventures and properly equipping themselves.

Currys chief services officer Dean Kramer said: “A side hustle used to mean a bit of extra cash at the weekend.

“What we’re seeing now is people setting up properly – taking payments, getting online in places they couldn’t before and generally making a small operation look professional.”

Currys reported a 150 per cent increase in sales over the year-to-date, compared with the same period a year ago, for machines from brands SumUp and Square

Side hustles typically refer to activities that generate cash in addition to people’s main job and popularity has boomed in recent years as people tap into online marketplaces and social media content.

Currys said this was particularly the case for under-30s who are doing so to bolster their income streams.

Its survey of 2,000 UK adults found that a quarter of Britons have an additional income stream to give them more breathing space.

This rises to 43 per cent of under-30s, and 30 per cent for millennials.

Among the most popular side hustles are online selling and reselling, content creation and social media influencing, and selling crafts and handmade goods, the survey found.

Economic pressures were a key driver of activity with a quarter saying they started their venture specifically to help cover rising living costs, while a third said they wanted to have more disposable income.

Some 38 per cent of respondents said cost-of-living pressures had led them to put more time and effort into their side hustle, averaging seven hours a week.

In last month’s Budget, the chancellor pledged to triple the trade allowance – the amount you can earn from a new venture tax-free – from £1,000 to £3,000, and bring in a new allowance to cover a year of living costs for young entrepreneurs.

The government said the move was set to make it easier to earn money from a side hustle.

News.title: Digital financial products used as ‘weapons of abuse’ against women and girls
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Nearly one in five (19%) teenage girls and young women aged 16 to 24 have experienced economic abuse from a current or ex-partner through a digital financial product in recent months, a report indicates.

Charity Surviving Economic Abuse (SEA), which published the research, said digital financial abuse is a “hidden” form of harm.

Economic abuse can happen as part of domestic abuse. It may include someone controlling another person’s access to their own money, running up debts without their consent or knowledge, or controlling their access to a job.

Digital ways of managing money can make everyday life simpler for many people, but SEA warned that, in the wrong hands, abusers are using them as a “weapon”.

SEA said abusers are exploiting banking apps, online payments and digital credit to control people, cause financial damage and prevent people from leaving a relationship.

As digital financial products become increasingly relied on in everyday life and organisations adopt AI (artificial intelligence), SEA is calling for urgent action to prevent perpetrators from exploiting these technologies as tools of economic abuse.

Ipsos UK surveyed more than 1,990 women and girls aged 16 to 24 across the UK in March, among whom 19% had experienced economic abuse through the misuse of a digital financial product from their current or ex-partner in the past 12 months.

The survey for SEA found that in the previous 12 months, 12% of girls and women aged 16 to 24 had experienced a current or ex-partner preventing them from having log-in information, such as passwords for online banking.

And 12% experienced an abuser controlling their digital wallets.

One in 14 (7%) said an abuser had taken out credit in their name without their consent or because they were scared to refuse, including from buy now pay later lenders.

Of those who had experienced economic abuse in the past 12 months, 43% had experienced financial difficulty as a result and 17% had to borrow money to cover essential items or bills.

Half (50%) said that the economic abuse had negative impacts on their mental health, such as anxiety, depression, panic attacks, self-harm or suicidal thoughts.

Around a third (36%) said the economic abuse prevented them from leaving a relationship with the abuser.

Digital options can also provide routes to support, SEA said.

More than half (55%) of teenage girls and young women said they had learned about economic abuse through a digital source, such as social media, internet searches and AI chatbots.

Nearly a third (31%) of young victim-survivors said they had used digital sources to seek information, help or advice.

SEA said it is encouraging financial services providers to work with young victim-survivors and economic abuse experts to help remove opportunities for domestic abusers to exploit digital financial products and to help build in protections.

Sam Smethers, chief executive of Surviving Economic Abuse, said: “This research clearly shows that, in a perpetrator’s hands, digital financial products are weapons of abuse.”

She said abuse must be tackled “where it happens, including through the digital financial products young women use every day”.

Ms Smethers said: “An app becomes surveillance, a digital bank account becomes a means of cutting off a survivor’s money, and a coerced buy now pay later loan becomes a route into crippling debt.

“This hidden online harm devastates the lives of one in five young women, robbing their financial independence and ability to take control of their future.

“AI is now used routinely by financial services and by young people themselves, posing both opportunities as well as risks.

“Young women’s safety must not be an afterthought, leaving perpetrators free to exploit digital financial products to cause harm.”

Ms Smethers said spotting the signs of economic abuse, financial independence and how to manage money fairly in a relationship must be at the heart of financial education.

She added: “We also want to see financial services firms working with survivors and experts to design out abuse of digital financial products and build in protections.”

Minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Satvir Kaur, said: “Economic abuse can rob young women and girls of their independence and opportunities, with consequences that can last long after a relationship has ended.

“This report shines an important light on a type of abuse that too often goes unrecognised and can take many forms, from controlling someone’s money to their choices, to their future.

“This Government has set the unprecedented ambition to halve violence against women and girls in a decade.

“Through our Enough campaign, we are working with partners across society, including the banking sector, to help people recognise the signs of economic abuse, challenge abusive behaviour and support victims to access the help they need and deserve.

“We are also rolling out domestic abuse protection orders across England and Wales, which protect victims from all forms of domestic abuse, including economic abuse, and help hold perpetrators to account.”

People who are experiencing abuse can get support from charities, banking providers and the police.

Some banks and other places on high streets offer “safe spaces” in branches for people experiencing economic and domestic abuse.

TSB also offers a “flee fund” to help domestic abuse victim-survivors pay for essentials.

Meanwhile, Nationwide Building Society has an online tool to help domestic abuse survivors to discreetly access support.

The “safe space” tool can be accessed through a link at the bottom of the Nationwide.co.uk webpage and gives people access to support information, emergency contacts and domestic abuse resources.

News.title: Special portrait of Andy Burnham to feature on front page of Big Issue
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A special portrait of the Prime Minister is being featured in the Big Issue to mark his pledge to end rough sleeping.

The portrait is by Shepard Fairey, whose Hope painting of Barack Obama helped visually define his first presidential campaign in the US.

Mr Fairey’s portrait of Andy Burnham includes the word “home” to mark the Prime Minister’s pledge.

open image in gallery The Big Issue cover has been drawn by Shepard Fairey (Big Issue/PA) ( PA Media )

It captures the moment Mr Burnham donned a red Big Issue tabard to sell copies of the magazine in Manchester in 2023, when he was mayor of Greater Manchester.

The portrait will be published on the front cover of the Big Issue this week as well as being shown in the Saatchi Gallery in London for its six-month street culture exhibition Beyond The Streets.

Mr Fairey said: “The thread that runs through all my work is a push for justice. This portrait reminds us of the pledge Burnham made.

“Politicians often want people to forget to hold them accountable for the promises they’ve made. That is harder to do when a symbol of that promise is in thousands of people’s hands.

open image in gallery Shepard Fairey pictured in 2023 (Alamy/PA)

“I’m overjoyed that this work, showing that the Prime Minister cares about vulnerable people, will be out in the public sphere. What I wanted to convey was simply warmth and a reminder that he has actually been out on the streets promoting and selling the Big Issue, even before he was Prime Minister.”

Mr Burnham told the Big Issue: “Coming in as Prime Minister, I was very clear, I don’t think anyone should sleep rough in this country.

“I’m not going to be naive. I can offer people a route off the streets, but not everybody will take it.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham speaking to service users during a visit to a homeless charity in central London (Ian Vogler/Daily Mirror/PA) ( PA Wire )

“What I can say though is, I can ask every council as part of the funding we’ve given to provide an offer to everyone.

“And that’s what we’re confident of now.

“Big Issue knows better than anybody. You get a surge of sentiment around rough sleeping later in the year, for really great reasons, but when you hit the earlier months of the new year it falls away.

“What I’m saying today is that the public money won’t fall away. That’s the only way to do it.

“Stop-start is not fair to the organisations that are out there working with rough sleepers. This is a fixable problem and it’s about a national effort to fix it.”

The exhibition is being held at the London gallery until May 2027, dedicated to six decades of art, activism and street culture.

News.title: Reports of AI-generated child sex abuse images soar 8,400%, Scottish group finds
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Researchers said the problem affects ordinary people as well as high-profile celebrities.

However, the study cautioned that changes in detection and reporting may have contributed to the dramatic increase.

Professor Debi Fry, Childlight’s global director of data at Edinburgh University, said: “The speed at which artificial intelligence is changing the threat to children is deeply concerning.

“These figures show an extraordinary rise in reports of AI-generated child sexual abuse material in just two years.”

She added: “While improved detection and reporting may explain some of that increase, the findings underline why governments and technology companies must act urgently to understand and prevent these emerging forms of abuse and remove material rapidly.”

Childlight’s new international study also warned that serious gaps in government data are hampering prevention efforts to protect children.

Of 103 countries and areas examined across the three regions, the group said only 22 had representative survey data covering both offline and technology-facilitated abuse.

According to Childlight, children with disabilities, Indigenous children, migrants, those in humanitarian settings, very young children and children abused within their families are particularly underrepresented.

In response, Childlight is urging governments to treat sexual exploitation and abuse as a preventable public health issue, invest in reliable and consistent measurement, and use evidence to strengthen protection, support survivors and prevent harm before it occurs.

open image in gallery Professor Debi Fry, Childlight’s global director of data at Edinburgh University, is unveiling the group’s new international research at a global ministerial summit in the Philippines on Monday (Childlight/PA)

The institute is also calling for stronger technology-sector accountability, laws that keep pace with emerging threats and prevention efforts beginning earlier in childhood.

Childlight chief executive Paul Stanfield said: “Millions of children are being subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse, yet governments are too often working with an incomplete picture of where harm is happening and who is most at risk.

“What remains invisible risks remaining unaddressed. We cannot effectively prevent abuse or protect children without understanding its true scale and nature.”

Mr Stanfield, there is “nothing inevitable about child sexual exploitation and abuse”.

He added: “With sustained leadership and international collaboration, we can prevent harm, intervene earlier and give millions more children the safe childhoods they deserve.”

Despite the challenges, the report highlighted encouraging progress, with several countries strengthening online safety legislation, improving detection and focusing more on prevention.

With better intelligence, coordinated action and sustained investment, researchers said governments have an opportunity to protect hundreds of millions of children and help create a safer future.

The findings are contained in the group’s 2026 Into the Light Index, which was unveiled at a global summit involving representatives from more than 100 governments on ending violence against children on Monday.

News.title: Rightmove records £6,745 fall in the average home asking price in November
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The average price tag on a home coming on the market fell by £6,745 or 1.8% month-on-month in November – which was a bigger than usual drop, according to a property website.

Across Britain, the average price of a newly listed home is £364,270, Rightmove said.

It said the average monthly drop in November over the past decade is 1.1%.

The average asking price was also 0.2% below a year ago, putting 2026 on track to end with prices lower than at the end of last year, Rightmove said.

It added that high mortgage rates continue to be a key restriction in buyers’ budgets.

open image in gallery Rightmove’s map shows changes in average asking prices across Britain (Rightmove/PA)

Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said: “Higher mortgage rates have been a feature of the market for many months now and sellers are increasingly having to adapt to buyers’ tighter budgets.

“While we’d expect new sellers to set lower asking prices at this time of year due to the seasonality of the market, the larger-than-usual November fall suggests many sellers are aware that they need to price temptingly in the high mortgage rate market.

“It’s understandable that some buyers are taking time to consider their options, and with budgets stretched, some may have even paused their plans for now.”

Rightmove said the number of homes for sale remains at a 12-year high, and with plenty of choice available, buyers can afford to be selective, increasing the pressure on sellers to stand out on both features and price.

Ms Babcock added: “Buyers have plenty of choice right now, which puts them in a stronger position to be selective, particularly where there are several similar homes competing for their attention.

“For sellers, this makes getting the asking price right from the outset particularly important.

“It’s vital that sellers work with a good local estate agent who can advise on the moving dynamics for their specific property type and location, as it certainly isn’t a one-size-fits-all market.

“Despite this year’s market challenges, most notably high mortgage rates, there is a degree of resilience coming through in the data.

“We’ve actually had a relatively steady year for buying activity, just at lower levels than last year, while new sellers are still putting their homes up for sale and getting on with their lives.”

Matt Smith, a mortgage expert at Rightmove, said: “Higher mortgage rates are having a big influence on the market, impacting what buyers can afford and the prices that sellers can achieve.”

Ben Waterhouse, director at Waterhouse Estate Agents, said: “The sales market across South Cumbria and North Lancashire remains active, but buyers are increasingly price-sensitive and selective.

“Well-presented homes that are realistically priced are still attracting strong interest, while ambitious pricing is leading to longer marketing periods and more negotiation.

“We’re also seeing a shift in buyer behaviour compared with the post-pandemic market.

“More homeowners are now starting their property search before putting their own home on the market, taking time to understand what’s available and where they want to move before committing to a sale.

“It’s a sign of a more balanced market, where buyers have more time to consider their options.”

Hollie Whittaker, founder of Block & Brick, said: “We’re seeing more flats coming onto the market this month, giving buyers greater choice and creating more competition between sellers.

“Buyers are taking their time, viewing more properties and looking beyond the asking price at the overall cost of owning a home, including service charges, leasehold arrangements and energy costs.”

Polly Ogden Duffy, managing director at John D Wood & Co said: “The market for flats remains challenging, with a considerable amount of apartments coming to market, including landlords looking to offload rental investments.

“However, for buyers with the appetite to enter the market, this presents a fantastic opportunity.

“There is plenty of choice, and buyers arguably have more scope to negotiate and secure more for their money than at any point in recent years.”

Jeremy Leaf, a north London estate agent said: “Clearly, sellers are finding it increasingly difficult to generate interest and that mirrors what we are seeing at the sharp end.

“On the other hand, buyers continue to be constrained by worries about what are seen by many as almost inevitable rises in mortgage costs and inflation, which will not leave sufficient headroom to move.”

Sports.title: ‘World class’ – James Trafford leaves England fans fearing for Pickford with stunning double save to earn Spain win

JAMES TRAFFORD showed he is ready to take the England gloves off Jordan Pickford with his heroic display against Spain.

The Leeds United goalkeeper made crucial saves to deny the world champions in the Nations League clash in Madrid.



England had taken a deserved 3-0 lead with a brilliant performance in the first 60 minutes.

Harry Kane put the Three Lions ahead from the spot before Ezri Konsa and Ben White both found the target.





Trafford, 24, had mostly been a spectator for the first 65 minutes until he had to face a penalty from Mikel Oyarzabal.

He was unable to stop the shot from the forward and then had to pick the ball out from the net again just ten minutes later after Nico Williams scored.

After that, the stopper was not beaten again despite the waves of Spanish attacks trying to find a leveller.

In the final stages, he made a brilliant double save to deny Fer Lopez and Aymeric Laporte.



Trafford was also on hand to stop shots from Lamine Yamal, Marc Cucurella and Pedri.

The stunning performance was a reward for Thomas Tuchel who made the decision to go with him ahead of Pickford.
