View image in fullscreen England's Ben White scores their third goal. Photograph: Andrew Boyers/Action Images/Reuters

Kane cleverly got his body between Cubarsí and the ball; the Spain centre-back had a problem. His challenge was necessary but clumsy; it was a clear penalty. Kane had a long wait while the video assistant referee checked for an Anderson foul on Cucurella as he followed through after his pass. It was accidental but nasty. Anderson got away with it. Kane had missed decisively in England’s 3-2 defeat against Spain at Wembley at the start of this competition. He made no mistake this time. It was his 93rd England goal.

England continued to push after half-time, especially Bellingham. He won the corner that led to Konsa heading in unmarked from a Rice outswinger and it was Bellingham who played in White, who was adventurous all night, for the third.

Quick Guide Nations League roundup: Belgium knock Italy out with victory Show Italy went into their clash in Brussels top of Group A1 after their 3-1 win against France on Thursday but came crashing back to Earth as they were comfortably beaten by Belgium. Pio Esposito gave Italy ⁠an early lead but their joy was short-lived as Belgium scored ​three times before the ​interval through Maxim De Cuyper, ​Nathan Ngoy and Jérémy Doku (pictured). Diego Moreira made it 4-1 in the 80th minute. France beat Turkey 2-1 in Bordeaux ​thanks to an own ‌goal by Emirhan ​Topcu and ​an effort by Bournemouth's Eli Junior Kroupi, meaning they won the group with 13 points, ahead of Belgium who ended on 12. Italy, on 10 points, missed out. England and Spain had already confirmed qualification to the quarter-finals before Sunday's dramatic clash between the sides in Madrid, which England won 3-2, but the remaining match in Group A3 saw Croatia beat Czechia 2-1, thanks to Lovro Majer's 87th-minute winner. In Group C1, Albania sealed top spot and promotion to League B after a 2-0 win over Belarus in Budapest. Rey Manaj and Elseid Hysaj scored goals in each half. Finland ended their campaign in the group with a 7-2 thumping of San Marino in Helsinki, headlined by a hat-trick by forward Adrian Svanbäck. San Marino are relegated to League D after failing to register a single point from their six games, ending with a goal difference of -22. In Group C2, Montenegro completed an unbeaten group campaign with a 4-1 victory in Cyprus. Genoa forward Milutin Osmajic got them off to a fast start in the fifth minute while Nikola Krstocic added a second-half double. Armenia and already-relegated Latvia played out a goalless draw in Riga. Reuters and Guardian sport Photograph: John Thys/AFP Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Nothing silly, Tuchel had to have thought. Quansah did something silly and the entire mood changed. Trafford made his first big save from the substitute Fermín López, but then it was 3-2 after Gordon was robbed in midfield. Spain went right to Lamine Yamal and his low cross for Williams was perfect.

Spain piled on the pressure. Williams went close. Lamine Yamal forced Trafford into a fine save, the goalkeeper denying Cucurella on the rebound. White made a saving tackle on Williams after a wonderful Lamine Yamal pass. Trafford saved his best until the last.

Sports.title: Mary Earps frustrates Arsenal as London City Lionesses earn battling draw
Sports.content:
Arsenal’s fifth draw from five home games in the Women’s Super League left them frustrated once again but this was a wholly different story to the previous four, as they played out an entertaining 1-1 draw with a London City Lionesses side inspired by their goalkeeper Mary Earps.

Aston Villa, Birmingham, Manchester United and Crystal Palace all came to this stadium for a point, defending resolutely and exposing Arsenal’s inability to break down low blocks, whereas London City came to play and were rewarded with a draw that maintains their six‑point advantage over Arsenal in the race for a European place, and moving within six points of the leaders Chelsea.

Earps, producing her best performance to date for the team she joined in the summer, repeatedly denied Frida Maanum and Lisa Baum and was named player of the match in a contest where both goals were scored inside the space of 99 seconds. The impressive Maanum finished off a superb team move for Arsenal to open the scoring in the 10th minute but her goal was cancelled out by a terrific finish from Isobel Goodwin whose head coach, Eder Maestre, said: “We came here to take risks. We really wanted to win.

“Our identity is playing with bravery – we were brave today. We weren’t scared about the context, the opponent, the stadium, nothing. We tried to play as we play at home.”

Arsenal had secured an impressive result in Barcelona on Thursday, drawing with the European champions, but this game against the WSL’s third-placed side felt as though it was of even greater importance, particularly if Arsenal wish to continue visiting venues such as the Camp Nou next season, and they were unable to find a way past Earps to win and close the gap in the table.

View image in fullscreen Isobel Goodwin shows her delight after equalising. Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA

Just like they had done away at Anfield last Sunday, Renée Slegers’s team made a bright start with energy, pace and the threat of Alessia Russo. Emily Fox’s shot was deflected wide, after a good move that included some excellent Maanum buildup play, before Ona Batlle’s long-range effort bounced wide. It was not long before Maanum tucked in the opening goal after an intelligent cutback from Russo.

The visitors struck back almost immediately, though, as Goodwin did superbly to turn inside Leah Williamson and then demonstrated strength and composure to hold off Baum and fire a lethal finish past Misa Rodríguez with power and precision. It was a timely moment of class from the English striker in front of the England head coach, Sarina Wiegman, who was in the stands before naming her next England squad on Tuesday morning.

Earps then twice saved from Baum from range. After the break, Earps did well again to dive low to her left to divert a Caitlin Foord strike wide, and what followed was a sustained spell of London City possession, territory and chances. Maestre’s team spent a good part of 20 minutes firmly camped in Arsenal’s half and they carved open a good chance for Kadidiatou Diani but her relatively tame, low, near-post effort was saved by Rodríguez.

Diani’s 62nd-minute replacement from the substitutes’ bench, Delphine Cascarino, drew gasps from the crowd as she unleashed a dipping strike that bounced off the top of the crossbar. It was a lucky escape for Arsenal, who had won all seven of their previous meetings with London City across all competitions but were denied by two more fine Earps stops, firstly from a Maanum close-range effort and then from Maanum’s curler, which looked destined for the top corner before Earps touched it on to the bar.

Quick Guide WSL roundup: Irons win again Show Viviane Asseyi scored twice as West Ham secured back-to-back WSL home wins after beating rock-bottom Charlton 2-0. Asseyi’s curled finish put the Irons in front just ahead of the break and she then scored a 25-yard free-kick early in the second half. The defeat saw Charlton, who remain without a point, become the first WSL team to lose all 10 of their opening matches of the season. Mathilde Harviken’s late goal gave Aston Villa a 1-0 win over derby rivals Birmingham, which gives Brian Sørensen his third win since stepping in as interim manager and leaves his side seventh. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Slegers’s 50th WSL match in charge of the north London side almost ended in defeat late on but Alexia Putellas’s rising, stoppage-time strike flew narrowly over the bar. Regarding lying sixth in the table after 10 games, Slegers said “the season isn’t over, it’s still November”, before praising her team’s resurgence in their past three matches.

“The team is in a very good place,” she said. “The preparation, the dedication, the hunger for details, doing everything they possibly can – that’s the standard. Things are clicking well. But also the [opponents], they’re teams that spend time on the ball and that are brave and want to dominate games, so the types of games have been different.”

It certainly was different but the end result was the same for an Arsenal team still unable to find that elusive home win.

Sports.title: Ronaldinho makes debut for Italian side Ravenna after 11-year hiatus in playing career
Sports.content:
Ronaldinho played 45 minutes on his return to professional football in Italy. The 46-year-old Brazil great announced in June that he had signed for the Serie C side Ravenna, 11 years after he appeared to have brought his illustrious career to a close with Fluminense.

Five months later, he was in the starting lineup as Ravenna faced their local rivals Forlì. Ronaldinho, wearing the No 10 shirt, entered the stadium to great fanfare, with the 5,000-capacity Stadio Bruno Benelli adding a temporary 1,800-capacity stand – dubbed “R10” – for the occasion. Flares and smoke bombs were let off in the stands while Andrea Bocelli’s Con Te Partiro blasted out of the stadium’s speakers.

Ronaldinho failed to add to his goal tally upon his return, showing some nice touches and playing a role in helping Giulio Donati score Ravenna’s opening goal, but unable to create a sight of goal for himself.

The 2005 Ballon d’Or winner acknowledged the Ravenna fans at the end of the first half and was replaced by Matteo Maggio when the teams returned after the break.

Ronaldinho, who has also become a shareholder in the club, hinted there could be more appearances to come, telling Sky Italia: “It went by too fast, that has always been football for me. Is this my last one? I don’t know. If the president keeps calling me, I will come back. It is always a pleasure. I told the president, if he needs me, then I will be here.

View image in fullscreen Ronaldinho is mobbed by media as he walks off at half-time. Photograph: Matteo Minnella/Reuters

“It was lovely to be here, playing, having the buildup in the dressing room. Football has always been the most wonderful thing in my life.”

Ravenna, who have not played in Serie B since 2008, are second in their regional group in Serie C and came into the weekend’s fixtures six points behind the leaders, Spezia.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It is Ronaldinho’s second spell in Italy, albeit at a much lower level, after three seasons with Milan from 2008 to 2011, where he won one Serie A title. He also played for Paris Saint-Germain and Barcelona in a trophy-laden career that included claiming the World Cup with Brazil in 2002. He scored 94 goals in 207 matches for Barcelona and 33 times in 97 games for Brazil. He has also played for Brazilian sides Grêmio, Flamengo and Atlético Mineiro, and for Querétaro in Mexico.

Sports.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
Sports.content:
“Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona.

Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.”

The highs and lows of Sir Bobby Robson’s remarkable England tenure are chronicled in a new book co-written by Butcher: Almost Immortal – When Bobby Robson’s England Gripped The Nation 1982-1990.

Your name instantly brings to mind you playing on for England with a bandaged head and bloodied shirt. With hindsight, should you have left the pitch? Sian Williams

I never contemplated leaving the pitch at all. As the captain of your country, playing in a crucial World Cup qualifier against the top team in our league, in our group, there’s no way. I said to Bobby: “If you take me off, I’ll hit you.” I don’t think I would have but I said: “No, don’t do it!” Initially, I felt the blood and it seemed like a bad one, quite severe, but when I was bandaged up I could still play and it wasn’t a problem. Heading the ball wasn’t an issue because you’re really fired up, the adrenaline’s there, so it didn’t concern me. There was no way I was going to voluntarily come off unless Bobby was of a mind to do that, but he knew my pain threshold very well and knew I would battle on. I had numerous injuries before, broke my nose in 1982, five weeks in hospital and lost a lot of blood. So he knew I had great fortitude. Things have changed dramatically now. From a medical point of view it would have been right to take me off, absolutely. But that was then and I think, as a captain, you have to lead. It’s nice that people remember me through that image, but I was just doing my job.

I once stayed at the hotel that forms part of the FA’s headquarters at St George’s Park. Above the bed, and hanging over my wife and me all night long, was a giant version of the photo of you covered in blood. It was a bit disconcerting – but what’s the strangest place you stayed in or visited while on England duty? Stu Egan

I’ve actually stayed in that room as well. Stu has told us what it was like for him and I have to say it wasn’t great for me either. I’m staring up looking at me with a bloodied head and thinking: “Oh my God, this has followed me around.” At least when you close your eyes and sleep you don’t have to see it, but I’m sorry he had to stay there.

I didn’t stay in many really strange places with England. When I was manager of Motherwell we had a Scottish Cup quarter-final and were in administration at the time. I was organising our travel myself and booked a hotel near Stranraer, online. It looked great, right by a golf course. But when we got there we realised it was a residential home for the elderly. The rooms had accessibility handles and low sinks. It wasn’t a horrible place at all, quite the opposite, it was very warm and caring. But it was strange coming down for breakfast seeing people being looked after by the nurses. We won 4-0 so it can’t have been bad for us.

View image in fullscreen Terry Butcher, bloodied head and all, was a symbol of England’s defiance in their World Cup qualifier in Sweden in 1989, which finished 0-0. Photograph: David Cannon/Getty Images

Now that time has passed and Diego has left us, has your perspective on that afternoon in Mexico City softened at all, or do you feel a professional duty to history to never let the “Hand of God” be forgotten? Victor Segovia

My feelings haven’t changed and they won’t. But I’ve learned to live with it better, I’ve learned to get through it and I’m not so annoyed by the memory. You’re just disappointed it happened. It had an influence on the game because we went one down and I think a lot of the players were shocked by what happened. Half the team saw it, half didn’t. I was one of the ones who didn’t. It had a big part to play in the fact we didn’t get switched on again and conceded the second goal. I’m more disappointed because he beat me twice. You’ve got to respect the man and respect what he did for the second goal, and what he did in that game. He was the best player I’ve played against and one that I never really got near.

Maradona’s “wondergoal” – it was really an own goal by you as you did a desperate sliding tackle, wasn’t it? David

If I’d got a touch I’d have raised my hand straight away and admitted it was the best own goal I’d ever scored. He went past Peter Shilton and I managed to get back, but I couldn’t see the ball so I was kind of feeling around him with my left foot. I couldn’t get my right foot across, but I thought I could block it. I was so surprised when he made good contact and put it in the net because I thought: “I’ve got this.” You can see me afterwards on the TV, I’m banging my shinpads, I was so angry. I was more angry about that goal than I was the “Hand of God” goal. So I’d have loved to claim that one. I know it sounds bizarre but it would have been one of my greatest achievements. Would it still have been the greatest goal scored at a World Cup?

View image in fullscreen Diego Maradona was England’s nemesis in their World Cup quarter-final in 1986 and Terry Butcher says he was the only player he ‘never really got near’. Photograph: Aflo Co. Ltd./Alamy

In the early 80s you had a brilliant side at Portman Road so I wondered if you have: “If only …” or “What if …” moments about that time. It has always felt to me that Ipswich left another big trophy or two out there. Stooze

We did. The 1980-81 season was arguably the best in our history. We lost the FA Cup semi-final, lost the league title on the last day of the season and then had to play the Uefa Cup final, which thankfully we won. It’s always at the back of your mind that you missed out on what you should have got, which was the treble. We should have done it. But I think the 66-game season was just too much for us, we didn’t have a big squad and struggled with injuries towards the end. But we came really close. Look at the teams Sir Bobby built, we were in Europe for nine seasons out of 10. There’s no particular moment I sit down and dwell on, but you know it’s there, so close but so far.

What was the one quality Bobby Robson had above all others and was he the best manager you played under? Carl Parrish

His man-management was top class. He knew how to get the best from his players, knew what buttons to press and got to know them very quickly. He could wield his strength, he was a really tough guy, but when he was friendly it was lovely. His face lit up and he made you feel really good through that man-management. He always used to say to me: “Whenever I pick you, you always do well.” When someone says that you feel really good about yourself. He knew what to say. But had an abundance of things that worked really well for him. His tactical knowledge, selection of players, the network he built up for the younger players to come through – so many things. He was the most complete manager in my eyes and I still think he’s the best. Wherever he went, home or abroad, he proved himself in a way no English manager has done.

View image in fullscreen Ipswich manager Bobby Robson (centre) is encouraged to address the crowd by players Terry Butcher (right) and (from the left) Laurie Sivell, Kevin Beattie and John Wark during the town’s civic reception for the team following their 1981 Uefa Cup final victory. Photograph: Bob Thomas Sports Photography/Getty Images

What was it like playing alongside Des Walker with England? And how close were England to winning the World Cup in 1990? Ahmed Kheyre

Des was the best centre-half I played alongside for England; he was unbelievable. He prolonged my international career because he was my pace. You never beat Des Walker. He was OK on the ball, it wasn’t his strength, but he used to give it to people that had great ability in that area so he was very astute. He was very young at the time, but dependable, talked well, shouted, pulled you about, was dominant. He was one of the reasons I made it to Italia 90. As for how close we were, I think the semi-final was the best we played all tournament. As I was walking out I felt so serene, comfortable, like I was in a dream state. It was never normally like that, but I could see our boys’ faces: steely, determined, but relaxed. It was the best I’d ever felt before a game. I even successfully backheeled the ball to a teammate. It was one of the best moments of our lives. We didn’t get to the very best one, the final, but we were so close. You’re talking inches, the shot that came off the post right between Lineker and Beardsley. Beating Argentina in the final would have been the ultimate redemption.

Is it true that during your time at Rangers, the top away scorer at Ibrox was Butcher (og)? Anonymous

I think I scored more goals past Chris Woods, my own goalkeeper, than any other Scottish striker. They were crackers: pick that one out Woodsy. He was my roommate as well, so he would say: “I don’t want any more going past me.” But they were all good ones, put it that way. They weren’t just ricochets or anything else like that. Wow, they were proper own goals. If you’re going to hit it, hit it hard.

I’m a massive fan of you as a player but think I’m even more impressed by your work with veterans following the death of your son. What would be the biggest thing we could do to support veterans? Jim

We’ve got to have a specific centre for veterans, like a St George’s Park, which would be dedicated to their health and that of their families. That would be the ultimate aim for me. We need more, and bigger, facilities to focus on veterans’ mental health and respite for those around them. It would be ideal to create a military community where you’re not in service, but the families are together. It would enable the veterans to relax, get treatment, get better, get the toolbox that provides the coping mechanisms so that if something happens they know what to do and where to go. My son didn’t have that unfortunately: he stayed in his room and that was his safe place.

I enjoy my work with Combat2Coffee, which supports veterans and their families. It’s doing really well and the togetherness is great. It’s getting exponentially bigger and we’re about to open a veterans’ hub in Ipswich. It’s a special thing, you can just walk in off the street and get that support. I’m doing this because my son would have loved it, and it’s what he needed.

Sports.title: Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain
Sports.content:
Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup.

There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution.

Those within the Scotland setup regard Robertson as the glue who holds the scene together, a decorated footballer who treats everybody the same and carries out an abundance of unseen work to make this team better. Robertson has routinely paid for squad nights from his own pocket.

The 32-year-old is as dedicated to overall environment as he is to his craft. Under Robertson’s on-field guidance, Scotland have morphed from international also-rans to serial tournament participants.

Left-backs are rarely the recipients of praise. When of the status of Robertson they do, however, receive criticism when a team struggle. He has carried the heaviest load while probably unable to celebrate the highs in an appropriate manner.

Robertson’s journey sets him apart and not only from Dalglish. By March 2014, when Robertson made his debut as a 67th-minute substitute in a friendly in Warsaw, he had been rejected by Celtic’s youth system, reset his career at Queen’s Park and turned heads in Dundee United colours. Hull would come next.

“He counts as one of my best-ever signings,” says Steve Bruce, who took Robertson to Humberside. “I still remember him holding his parents’ hands when he came down.

“He could run like the wind and had such a lovely left foot. We wanted to try and sign the best young players and thought he might get a few games due to injuries but Andy went into the side and never came out, which is testament to him. I’m absolutely delighted for him.”

Robertson and Phil Bardsley replaced Alan Hutton and Barry Bannan in Poland. “He was a young boy who played with so much freedom,” Hutton says. “He had energy and aggression to go up and down the pitch all day long, he would shell crosses into the box at 100mph. For one so young, he was also amazingly good at one v one defending. I got to 50 caps. I remember thinking there would be no chance of anybody reaching 100.”

Alex McLeish, who handed Robertson the Scotland captaincy in 2018, jokes about the possible impact on Dalglish. “Kenny will want to make a comeback,” he says. “No, he will be absolutely delighted for Andy. It tells you so much about Andy’s character that someone like Kenny Dalglish is so fond of him.

“It felt to me like a new era. We were rebuilding and Andy seemed to make the most sense as being at the forefront of that. I’m pretty sure anyone else would have made the same decision. A fantastic player with a great attitude and very well liked by all his teammates. He was a natural captain. He demands high levels without being someone to blast people. He is a hard bugger; if he talks, people shut up and listen.

“When I told him [he was captain], I still remember how his eyes lit up. He loved hearing that. He gave me such a great big smile and said how honoured he would be to captain the country.”

McLeish underplays the value of his decision. Robertson has worn the armband 80 times. McLeish could easily, for example, have handed it to Kieran Tierney, Callum McGregor or John McGinn. McLeish’s faith in Robertson and convincing of Scott McTominay to commit to Scotland were huge and lasting contributions.

Robertson’s career could easily have followed an alternative path. The Scottish game is laced with players released by major clubs who spend years lurching about in its nether regions. Blair Spittal, who played with Robertson at Queen’s Park and Dundee United, believes there may be a broader lesson here. “I’m not saying every player could do the same as Andy, but within the pyramid of Scottish football there are definitely players who just need an opportunity and someone to show their belief,” he says.

“Queen’s Park at the time was a great environment for that. We were then very lucky at Dundee United to have a manager [Jackie McNamara] who believed in young players. Andy took everything in his stride. Nothing ever fazed him.”

He has made instant impressions everywhere. John Rankin was a senior player at Dundee United as Robertson elevated his reputation. He recalls a pre-season friendly at Union Berlin, when he first clapped eyes on someone who would be a Champions League winner within six years. “Who is this?” Rankin said while watching from the stand. “On his first day at the training ground, Andy bypassed the first‑team dressing room to get changed with the youth team. He was so unassuming, no entitlement about him at all.

“He knew what he wanted to do. On the pitch it was a case of: ‘Get out my road, I’m coming through.’ Off the pitch he was such a humble guy, who knew his life was built on the hard work of his parents. He had hunger to be the best player in every single session. It was never about being flash, it was about working his way to the top.”

During a game at Motherwell, with United 3-0 up, Rankin warned teammates to remain compact. Next came a marauding Robertson, who cracked home a fourth before Rankin chastised him for not following orders. “But I scored, didn’t I?” came the retort.

Jordan Henderson and James Milner have been hugely influential in shaping how Robertson deals with others. Robertson did not want Steve Clarke to call time on his Scotland managerial career in June, but during an emotional meeting in Charlotte it was clear the latter’s mind was made up. Clarke would not have returned to Hampden Park four months later but for Robertson, who was receiving recognition for 100 caps.

It is fortunate Dalglish is not protective of his record. McGinn entered this international break with 93 caps. Ryan Christie and McTominay have an outside chance of reaching 102. Billy Gilmour is 25, but hit 50 caps in October. “It’s not about now holding on to the record for ever,” Robertson says. “That’s not really me.”

Modesty. A consistent and endearing Robertson trait. Whenever this international career for the ages ends, he will be a monumental loss.

Sports.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
Sports.content:
When you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium.

AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.”

Kitcher was speaking before kick‑off in Saturday’s League One game at home against a Blackpool side dealing with a suspected norovirus outbreak in their squad. A superb arrowed strike from Alistair Smith and some vital late saves from Nathan Bishop ended Wimbledon’s winless run of 10 matches in all competitions. The 1-0 victory moved Johnnie Jackson’s side four points clear of the relegation zone and put a positive spin on a week that started with the fallout from the withdrawal of £87m of proposed investment, leaving the club’s finances even tighter.

View image in fullscreen Alistair Smith (second right) celebrates with his Wimbledon teammates after scoring the only goal in their win over Blackpool. Photograph: Jed Leicester/Shutterstock

Wimbledon made a £2.6m loss in the 2024-25 season – a figure expected to increase by £500,000 when they publish their accounts next month – which, as Kitcher pointed out, is not as loss-making as a number of other clubs in League One. Those clubs voted in the summer to reduce spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, but now many want to go further to curb the spiralling losses at this level. “It’s an ugly way of running a sport,” said Terry Hunt, a supporter who has been attending matches with his son Billy since AFC Wimbledon were founded in 2002 after the move to Milton Keynes.

Wimbledon returned home to Plough Lane in 2020, but had to create a bond to complete the move and the club still owe £7.5m in debts. In November 2025, the DTB warned that competing in the EFL at their new stadium was “not currently sustainable” under their structure at the time.

The makeup of the club has since changed. Supporters voted last April in favour of reducing their voting rights from 75% to 50.01% – the same 50+1 model that gives fans the final say on decisions at German clubs – and Wimbledon sought a cash injection. An £87m investment proposal from Sloane Street Capital, a venture including the sole funder, Omar Mir, and the former Chelsea and England defender Ryan Bertrand, was already being voted on by fans when Mir suddenly walked away last Sunday, citing a change in his investment priorities.

Mir passed Wimbledon’s due diligence tests, but the tech businessman was not a unifying figure. A Josimar report has detailed his “various connections to some of the most influential and controversial figures in football, technology and global security”. The 44-year-old did not attend either of the information evenings at Plough Lane after the proposal was first made in October, instead sending a two-minute video message, which meant fans could not directly ask him about his intention to purchase 90% of the economic rights of a fan‑owned football club.

View image in fullscreen Dons Trust Board member Hannah Kitcher says: “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.” Photograph: Jed Leicester/Shutterstock

“We really wanted to have some kind of knight in shining armour,” said Niall Couper, a former member of the DTB and author of three books on Wimbledon. “In this case, I personally wasn’t sure how shiny that armour was.” Couper, who raised questions about Mir’s background before his withdrawal, chose not to attend the Blackpool game owing to anger from some supporters at the deal collapsing.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

But the SSC deal is not completely dead. Bertrand and his remaining SSC partners Stuart Fiertz, Oliver Ward and Hugh Rosen – who would have owned 1.25% each of Wimbledon’s economic rights in the original proposal – have renamed themselves Sloane Street Football and are talking to other potential investors.

In the meantime, the board will seek approval from fans about taking out a loan of up to £3m to “manage the club’s cash position”, but they believe they are able to manage it through to the end of this season and into the next. Which division Wimbledon end up in next season remains to be seen – Jackson’s side survived relegation by four points last April and the manager will probably have his hands tied in January.

“I think we’ll probably go down, but bouncing between League Two and League One is absolutely fine by me,” Billy Hunt said. “The main goal is security and making sure we have a football club.”

Sports.title: Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Magnusson: And your time starts … now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet …

One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago.

The problem with football is that it never sits still. What was true once isn’t necessarily true now. What is true now won’t necessarily be true in a season or two’s time. Almost nothing is absolute. What works once might not work in a different context. The key to good recruitment is identifying to what extent somebody’s past success was contingent on their environment, and how they may behave in different circumstances. And that is very difficult, which is why only four managers have won the English league title with more than one club.

The possibility of José Mourinho becoming manager of United was first raised as Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013. Mourinho has recently claimed he turned the job down; other versions of events have him raging in a Madrid hotel as he learned that David Moyes had been hired, seemingly because Sir Bobby Charlton, then a senior board member, was worried about his impact on the image of the club.

It’s impossible, of course, to say whether Mourinho would have been a success had he taken the job then. But he had the ego to ensure he would not have lived in Ferguson’s shadow and, although he had been bruised by the Real Madrid experience, English football still recognised his aura. He was still adept enough to win a third league title at Chelsea.

By the time Mourinho finally took the United job in 2016, though, events in his final few months at Stamford Bridge had undermined him. He seemed weary and fractious, the tactical doubts raised in his final year at Madrid had proliferated and there was a growing sense his methods did not quite work with elite modern players.

There was a lot of talk about him as a guaranteed winner, but there’s no such thing in football. Very few managers last more than a decade at the very top. Only the most driven personalities, the most fecund minds, can endure the process of constant evolution necessary to stay ahead of the pack for more than a few years.

It’s easy to see why a board would have looked at his list of honours and been impressed, but United were appointing a manager on the way down. Was that obvious at the time? Perhaps not, but there were warning signs, and it’s the job of those doing the job of recruitment to identify them.

View image in fullscreen Erik ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the United job. Photograph: Vince Mignott/EPA

With every appointment there are mitigations. Given the immense power Ferguson had, it would have been hard not to appoint Moyes when he had backed him. Yet if there was ever a time when he might have been the right man for United, it was surely six or seven years earlier; modern managers tend to peak in their mid-late 40s.

Louis van Gaal was 62 when he took the reins at United, enjoying a second coming after winning the Dutch title with AZ Alkmaar and an impressive 2014 World Cup campaign with the Netherlands. Perhaps the comparison isn’t fair in that he arrived as an elder statesman; nobody, other than perhaps Van Gaal, thought he would be a long-term appointment. But the idea he would bring calm after a period of turbulence was to ignore everything he had previously done. Van Gaal is many things but he is not a calming presence.

But again, the timing felt wrong. It could never have worked given he was preparing a side for the World Cup, but had he come in to replace Ferguson in 2013, as a hugely respected figure with a robust self-belief that was never going to care about breaking Fergusonian taboos, he might have been the man to see United through the awkward transition.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim were supposed to be the coming men, managers identified on the way up. Both seemed to make sense. Ten Hag’s Ajax had played astonishing football, had beaten Juventus and Real Madrid thrillingly in the Champions League, had come within Lucas Moura’s implausible hat-trick of a Champions League final. Amorim had ended Sporting’s 19-year title drought.

But it turned out they weren’t right. Ten Hag, skilfully as he managed Cristiano Ronaldo’s exit, seemed overawed by the job; Amorim’s insistence on playing 3-4-2-1 with a squad ill-equipped to play that way was one of the reasons Dan Ashworth expressed reservations, leading to his departure as sporting director.

It is possible, of course, maybe by this point even likely, that there is no right answer, that the mess United are in is insoluble, Old Trafford a meat grinder that will keep chewing up managerial reputations in perpetuity. But United’s board’s attempts to identify the rising star have been no more successful than their habit of appointing fading legends.

View image in fullscreen José Mourinho seemed weary and fractious when the former Chelsea and Real Madrid manager arrived at Old Trafford in 2016. Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty Images

Which brings us to Mauricio Pochettino. He has done remarkable things: he may not yet have won trophies in England but he effected such an extraordinary transformation at Tottenham that it seemed not unreasonable they should be part of the Super League project. He found things difficult at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, but most people do. A last-16 exit at a home World Cup with the USA was about par. The question, now he is 54, is whether the sense of drift about his career is an unfortunate and temporary state, or evidence that he is not quite what he was.

Perhaps the United job will revitalise him and he will revitalise them. But this feels like another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago; that United, once again, are answering the previous question.

Sports.title: Red Brawl New York: Fighting and six red cards mar ‘friendly’ v Club América
Sports.content:
One hallmark of Mauricio Pochettino’s time in international management has been his refusal to embrace the term “friendly”. His preferred branding is “unofficial games”.

His spin gained a bit of validity on Saturday, in the New York Red Bulls’ “friendly” against Club América, marred by a mass brawl between the sides that resulted in five red cards and a bevy of beverages thrown from the stands.

The game itself was odd for a few reasons. First, the Red Bulls have already been eliminated from MLS’s comically forgiving postseason, which means players (aside from veterans like Emil Forsberg) delayed vacations for a glorified scrimmage. Second, the match was announced on 1 October, at which point it was abundantly clear that the NWSL’s Gotham FC, a tenant of the Red Bulls’ Sports Illustrated Stadium, could host a playoff semi-final on the same weekend.

That scheduling snafu, combined with the comically poor state of the pitch, became a serious problem for the NWSL club, who settled for 5,000-seat Icahn Stadium for Sunday’s semi-final.

For the Red Bulls, the show must go on – and boy, did they find a way to entertain the fans who showed up for the low-stakes affair.

View image in fullscreen The referee issued five red cards after the fracas. Photograph: Jordan Bank/Getty Images

Not with their soccer exploits, mind you. Playing without the aforementioned veterans and US internationals Julian Hall and Adri Mehmeti, the remaining Red Bulls came ready for a scrap. At one point in the second half, América goalkeeper Rodolfo Cota required treatment for taking a boot above his knee while closing a shooting angle, putting the visitors on alert.

Roughly 40 minutes into the second half, this unofficial game abandoned any attempt to be friendly. Mijahir Jiménez dribbled toward the right corner flag, only to be taken down by a defender. He took great umbrage to the nature of the challenge, kicking off a maelstrom of shoves, punches, thrown drinks from the crowd, and men pressing their chests and foreheads together like bighorn rams in the throes of the rutting season.

The full sequence lives on thanks to a live watch-along streamed on YouTube, where former Mexico defender Miguel Layún comes to life in his gamer chair and begs his compatriots to keep the fracas alive. The fracas lasted 65 seconds, while the ensuing corner kick came a full seven minutes after Jimenez’s dribble.

The only scoreline from the night that matters: three Red Bulls sent off, three players from América, with the final five minutes being an eight-v-eight affair. The referee decided to forego any second half stoppage time, almost certainly for the best.

Sports.title: Three England stars get 10/10 rating but Thomas Tuchel told he must learn basic football lesson
Sports.content:
Three England stars get 10/10 rating but Thomas Tuchel told he must learn basic football lesson

England made Spain look like amateurs for an hour and then had to fight for their lives for an historic win in the Nations League.

The Three Lions incredibly beat the world champions 3-2 on Sunday, claiming a remarkable victory at the Riyadh Air Metropolitano.



7 Ten-man England beat world champions Spain in a stunning Nations League clash in Madrid that had it all Credit: Getty

Thomas Tuchel's men put in one of the best performances the nation has ever seen for an hour, before things completely flipped.

In the end though, after some superb backs against the wall defending and goalkeeping from James Trafford, they ended La Roja's incredible unbeaten streak.

England handed Spain their first defeat in 44 games and their first loss in a competitive game at home since March 2023 to win their Nations League group and their tenth away match in a row.



Opening the scoring, Harry Kane became the first England player for 78 years to score in seven consecutive away matches.

The Ballon d'Or winner netted a penalty just before half time before things got even better for Tuchel's men after the break.



At the start of the second half, Ezri Konsa found himself free in the box from a corner to score, with Ben White netting quickly after.

At 3-0, England were cruising to victory - that was until a poor mistake from Jarell Quansah gave the ball to Lamine Yamal.



Yamal was dragged down by Elliot Anderson in the box and the Manchester City man was sent off as a penalty was awarded, with Mikel Oyarzabal dispatching from the spot.

That set up a tense final half an hour, with Nico Williams tapping home another goal with 15 minutes to go...

But the Three Lions stepped up and defended with their lives, leaving Spain with a special three points, in an international classic.

7 White received a 10/10 rating for his performance on his first competive start for England on Sunday Credit: Getty



7 The Three Lions won their Nations League group with the historic three points picked up in Madrid

Here is how talkSPORT's Adrian Durham rated the England players and manager in their history-making 2026 finale...

Perfect 10/10 for three England stars

After that performance, White's England redemption may well be complete, at least according to Durham.

“Stop the booing now, just stop it, he was incredible," he said.

White put on a defensive masterclass and also grabbed a goal as part of England's rampant hour against Spain.



The Arsenal defender had not been called up for the Three Lions since 2022 until earlier this year, but he's back in the fold.

And now he's shown everyone why he should be forgiven for his 2022 World Cup controversy.

7 Trafford made two unbelievable saves in stoppage time to prevent Spain from grabbing a last-gasp equaliser Credit: AFP

Another with a 10/10 rating is Trafford, with Durham saying: "Tuchel may still say Pickford is his No.1, but Trafford’s saves tonight...”



"Incredible saves, I mean, saves you literally could not believe, and a number of them."

The Leeds goalkeeper incredibly denied Gavi and Aymeric Laporte in the final moments of the game, saving England (literally).

Meanwhile, Lewis Hall, who starred at left back up against Yamal in Madrid, was also handed a perfect report for his showing.

"Lewis Hall has been sensational, he’s been world class tonight," Durham said during the match.



Anderson drops a rare poor performance

On what was a special night for England, Anderson was one man who came out of the game with a poor rating.

7 Anderson was given a 2/10 after his red card completely flipped the game on its head in Madrid - thankfully for him, England held on Credit: AFP

The Man City man made six fouls throughout the action and brought down Yamal in the box in the game-changing moment.

Durham said: "He could’ve been sent off first half and was sent off second half and it changed everything.



"He mixed brilliant with stupid in a way I’ve rarely seen at this level."

Tuchel needs to learn Bellingham lesson

Tuchel may have led England to an incredible victory, but one thing is sticking in Durham's mind about the manager...

He said: "Thomas Tuchel needs to learn this basic football lesson - NEVER EVER TAKE JUDE BELLINGHAM OFF."

The Three Lions boss substituted Bellingham with the score at 3-2, and the Real Madrid superstar was fuming at the decision.



7 Taking Bellingham off was a big mistake from Tuchel, who needs to learn not to do that going forward, according to Durham Credit: Getty

He wasn't happy to have been withdrawn with the game on the line, but thankfully, his teammates managed to hold on.

Bellingham was given a 9/10 for his showing, where he provided a perfect assist for White's goal that made it 3-0.

The 23-year-old's general influence on the game was stunning, with him showing yet again just how much of a leader he is.



As for Tuchel, Durham only gave him a 6/10, but he almost joined the group with a perfect rating until the hour mark.

"I gave him a 10 for the first hour, ill-discipline at half time (when the England and Spain players clashed in the tunnel) led to what happened second half.

"The manager needs to get a grip on that ill-discipline."

Sports.title: Ten-man England achieve 34-year first as they beat Spain in stunning performance for the ages
Sports.content:
Ten-man England achieve 34-year first as they beat Spain in stunning performance for the ages

England have beaten the team ranked No.1 in the world on foreign soil for the first time ever.

The Three Lions battled to victory over Spain in an enthralling contest in Madrid to clinch top spot in their Nations League group.



3 England beat Spain despite playing the final 25 minutes with 10 men Credit: Getty

It marked a tenth consecutive away victory for England for the first time ever.

Harry Kane's penalty broke the deadlock as he scored in a seventh successive away appearance for his country.

Further goals from Ezri Konsa and Ben White helped seal a 3-2 away win for Thomas Tuchel's side.



A second half red card for Elliot Anderson had threatened to ignite a Spanish comeback with Mikel Oyarzabal scored the resulting penalty.

The Manchester City midfielder was sent off for bringing down Lamine Yamal as he raced through on goal.



Substitute Nico Williams pulled another goal back for the home side with 15 minutes remaining.

However, the visitors were able to hold on to cap an exceptional away performance.



Their resilient display was aided by a string of saves from goalkeeper James Trafford.

The Leeds United stopper had been brought into the starting line-up in place of Jordan Pickford by Tuchel.

Trafford saved his most important intervention for stoppage time as he produced a stupendous double save to keep Spain at bay.

Historic England win

In doing so, England achieved an historic 34-year first by beating the world champions at the Metropolitano Stadium.



3 Kane's record-equalling goal set England on the way to victory Credit: Getty

Prior to the win, they had lost every match outside of England against the No.1 ranked team in the world.

Since the introduction of the FIFA rankings in 1992, the Three Lions had suffered six successive defeats.

Meanwhile, Spain had not lost a home match since March 2024, with their last competitive home defeat coming a year earlier.



Their World Cup triumph in July saw Luis de la Fuente's side return to the top of the rankings having slipped to second in April.

Spain had occupied top spot for seven months during their previous stint in the position.

As for England, who have never placed higher than third, they have been ranked fourth since July 2024.

3 Trafford's heroics helped England hold on for a famous victory Credit: AFP



The victory also saw the Three Lions leapfrog their opponents into top spot in their Nations League group.

It means they will be seeded for the quarter-final draw, where they will be matched up against a side who finished second elsewhere.

Spain, who hadn't lost in 43 competitive matches prior to the game, had only needed a point to hold on to first place thanks to their win at Wembley Stadium in September.

talkSPORT reaction

Reacting to England's third goal on Kick Off, talkSPORT's Jim Proudfoot exclaimed: "This has been a performance for the ages."



Meanwhile, former Three Lions striker Dean Ashton added: "World Cup semi-final forgotten," following White's goal.

The travelling England fans even belted out chants of 'Are you Scotland in disguise?' as they raced into a commanding lead.

Their mood appeared to have changed as Spain mounted a fight back, though.

Following Williams' goal, Ashton admitted: "We’ve gone a bit, that’s for sure. It’s going to take a huge effort to win this game."



Once the final whistle blew, though, Proudfoot hailed the result as: "One of the most famous wins in England’s history. A game none of us will ever forget."

Sports.title: Harry Kane equals 78-year record from England icon
Sports.content:
Harry Kane has become the first England player for 78 years to score in seven consecutive away matches.

The Three Lions captain opened the scoring from the penalty spot as England secured a famous win at Spain on Sunday night.

3 Kane has scored in seven consecutive away matches for England Credit: Getty

His 93rd international goal extended his record of scoring in every fixture during the current Nations League campaign.

Meanwhile, Kane has also matched a scoring feat which had been unmatched since 1948.

Dating back to June 2025, he has scored in each of England's last seven away fixtures.

The last trip to a non-neutral venue without Kane on the scoresheet came against Greece in November 2024.

Record-equalling goal

He is the first Three Lions player to do so since legendary Tom Finney, who did so between September 1946 and May 1948.

Kane and Finney are the only two players in history to score in seven successive away appearances for England.

The former will have to wait until March to extend his run to eight, though, with the trip to Spain their last of 2026.

His effort broke the deadlock in the final minute of the first half at the Metropolitano Stadium.

Ezri Konsa added a second for the visitors with a bullet header from a corner just eight minutes after the restart.

The defender's Arsenal teammate Ben White made it three for England four minutes later.

3 Kane is the first England player since Finney in 1948 to achieve the feat Credit: Getty

A red card for Elliot Anderson and goals by Mikel Oryazabal and Nico Williams led to a grandstand finish but England bravely held out to win 3-2.

The victory sees Thomas Tuchel's side finish top their Nations League group at the expense of their opponents.

Both sides had already qualified for the quarter-finals ahead of their final league phase outing.

The four group winners will be drawn against the four runners-up for a two-legged tie during the March international break.

A semi-final berth in June will then await the winners of those contests.

Kane on target

As for Kane, he has now extended his all-time scoring record for England to 93 goals in 127 caps.

3 Kane has scored in each of England's six Nations League matches Credit: Getty

The 33-year-old also redeemed his penalty miss against Spain at Wembley Stadium back in September.

It was only his fifth penalty miss for the Three Lions and his first since their quarter-final defeat to France at the 2022 World Cup.

He had already scored in their opener against Spain, kickstarting a run of scoring in all six Nations League fixtures.

Those matches have produced eight goals for Kane, who grabbed a brace in wins over both Croatia and Czechia.

The Bayern Munich striker subsequently leads the Nations League scoring charts as he aims to win the Golden Boot in the competition for the first time.

Sports.title: Arsenal star makes debut for new international team despite 13 senior caps for home country
Sports.content:
Arsenal star makes debut for new international team despite 13 senior caps for home country

Kepa Arrizabalaga debuted for a new international team on Saturday despite being left out of the latest Spain squad.

The Arsenal goalkeeper has not featured for the World Cup winners since earning his 13th cap in 2023.



3 Kepa made his international debut for a second international team on Saturday night Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

However, he was amongst those included by the Basque Country for their friendly clash with Venezuela in Bilbao.

Kepa subsequently kept a clean sheet as he played the opening 45 minutes for the hosts in a 1-0 victory at the San Mames.

It marked the Basque Country's first international fixture for a year and only their third since the start of 2024.



Why could Kepa play for the Basque Country?

As a non-FIFA or UEFA affiliated national team, they can only play friendly matches.

Meanwhile, players who represent the senior side are not prevented from representing another FIFA-recognised team.



Similarly, senior caps for another national side do not rule out players from featuring for the Basque Country.

As a result, Kepa was able to earn his first cap despite playing for Spain on 13 occasions since his debut aged 23 in 2017.



The Basque Country does hold ambitions of one day being recognised by FIFA and UEFA.

However, the region would have to gain independence in order to join either confederation.

The Basque Football Federation have previously applied to Spain's National Sports Council to be recognised as an official national side.

3 Mikel Jauregizar's goal secured a 1-0 win against Venezuela for the Basque Country Credit: Shutterstock Editorial



They currently continue to operate as a non-FIFA member, though.

Kepa was one of two English-based players included in the squad by manager Jagoba Arrasate.

Bolton Wanderers wing-back Gaizka Larrazabal was also named in the 22-man selection for the match against Venezuela.

The Basque Country would go on to win 1-0 thanks to a goal from Athletic Bilbao's Mikel Jauregizar.

Kepa's international career

Kepa qualified for the side having been born in Ondarroa in the Biscay province of the Basque Country.



The region spreads across north eastern Spain and the south west of France.

3 Kepa kept a clean sheet on his debut for the Basque Country Credit: Shutterstock Editorial

Having been born in Ondarroa, Kepa went on to join Athletic Bilbao's academy before progressing into the first-team.

He also represented Spain at Under-18, Under-19 and Under-21 level before earning his first senior cap.



His international career also includes winning the Nations League in 2023 as well as an Under-19 Euros triumph as a teenager.

At club level, the 32-year-old has made just one first-team appearance for Arsenal this season.

Sports.title: Non-league club’s first match since death of player abandoned after gruesome injury
Sports.content:
Non-league club’s first match since death of player abandoned after gruesome injury

Hendon's first match since the death of player Ezekiel Williams was abandoned in the opening ten minutes due to a horror injury.

The non-league side, who play in the eighth tier of English football, were taking on Bedfont Sports on Saturday when the incident occurred.



2 Hendon defender Ethan Creary suffered a serious injury against Bedfont Sports in his side's first match since the death of teammate Williams Credit: X @HendonFC

With the score at 0-0 and the game just getting started, Hendon's Ethan Creary suffered a double collarbone break, possible shoulder ligament damage and a concussion.

The club posted on social media that there had been a pause in play since the seventh minute before going on to confirm that the teams had been taken off the pitch almost 20 minutes later.

A stretcher was called onto the pitch for Creary after he picked up what Hendon described as a 'horrible injury' at the time.



And eventually, after over half an hour of the match being halted, it was confirmed that the game had been abandoned.

Hendon wrote on X on Saturday: "Match abandoned. A huge thank you to Bedfont Sports for their class, compassion, and understanding during such a difficult situation. And to the match officials who have been incredibly supportive."



Hendon player suffers gruesome injury

Following the match, Hendon then posted a fresh update on the condition of Creary, who was taken to hospital.

They said: "We are pleased to be able to report that Ethan Creary is conscious, talking, and feeling better than earlier.



"Early signs are that he's suffered a double break to the collarbone, possible shoulder ligament damage and concussion.

"We are hopeful he will be released home tonight ahead of surgery in the next few days and then a lengthy rehabilitation.

"The club will, of course, support Ethan in the coming days, weeks, and months ahead."

Creary also sent a message from his hospital bed to the Hendon players, staff and fans in another social media post on Sunday.



“Yes boys, thank you for all the messages, sorry for not getting back to you all individually, I thought it would be easier to put a message in the group for now," he wrote.

"I have a double break to the collar bone, will find out sometime this week whether it requires surgery.

"I have to be in the ward for 24 hours to assess any potential bleed in the brain, it’s just protocol and I woke up feeling okay.

"The reason I wanted to come here boys is because something special will happen here. Nothing changes in my eyes, with God & Ezekiel watching over us, no one can stand in our way.



"Hoping to come back to playoff positions at the absolute minimum, but my personal aim was always the title. See you lot soon."

2 Hendon's Williams tragically died in hopsital due to head injuries after being allegedly attacked, with three men arrested Credit: X @HendonFC

First match since Williams' tragic death

Creary's injury came in Hendon's first match since the tragic death of Williams, who passed away aged 26 after allegedly being attacked.

Williams, who had joined the club in September, is said to have been attacked in Milton Keynes in the early hours of November 1.



A murder investigation was launched after he died the following day in hospital due to a head injury.

Two men, 28-year-old Sameull Hussein, of no fixed abode, and 21-year-old Arman Uddin, of Luton, were arrested for murder on November 6.

A third man, aged 30, also from Luton, was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and was released on bail while the investigation continues.

Hendon and Bedfont Sports held a minutes' silence for Williams before their game that was eventually abandoned.

Sports.title: Former Manchester United star left shocked by £150,000 Jude Bellingham offer
Sports.content:
Former Manchester United star Ben Foster has entered the realm of trading card collecting and one moment in the hobby left him in awe.

The ex-England goalkeeper has built a successful media empire, starting just before his retirement and continuing it as he, supposedly, sticks his feet up.



1 Foster has transitioned from playing to broadcasting about sports with great success

What is Ben Foster doing now?

His YouTube channel and his podcast have got him hitting new heights, along with the odd appearance on talkSPORT too.

And now he's also entered the booming hobby of football trading card collection, already snagging a Rio Ngumoha one of one.

Panini and Topps have completely changed the landscape of the industry with the latter now having flagship stores in London and Paris.



How valuable are sports trading cards?

Meanwhile, the amounts paid for cards is going through the roof with one Lewis Hamilton card around the £1million barrier.

As you might expect, Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo have seen their cards hit the seven-figure mark.



With their era ending, the next generation of superstars could also see their cards reach extraordinary sums.

Real Madrid star Jude Bellingham is one of those and Foster couldn't believe a story he heard about one of his cards.



What happened at the London Card Show?

"The London Card Show was incredible. Honestly," Foster said on the Fozcast.

"The amount of cards that people have in these collections and they have just got them behind a Perspex screen. You're talking collections worth £250,000.

"I watched a guy do a deal for a Rio Ngumoha one of one booklet for £14,000.

"Just watching them negotiating the deal. Just these two guys...

"One guy hit it on a Whatnot break, the other guy went 'I love that card, it's a one of one. It's beautiful. It's got an unbelievable Liverpool patch - £14,000'.



"I'm like 'wow'."

Co-host Tubes added: "Listen to this, Liam. He was there the other week. He's got that Jude Bellingham card.

"A guy walks up, he's like - '£150,000 for that card'. Liam went no."

"Wow," said a shocked Foster.

"That was his opening offer to buy that one card," Tubes continued.

"[Liam] went no because he's so passionate about Jude Bellingham and Birmingham, and his cards."

Why is the Jude Bellingham card worth more than £150,000?

The card in question is a 2023/24 Topps Stadium Club Chrome UCL, Marks of Excellence black foil one of one.

It's completely unique thanks to the inscription above the autograph 'Brum to the Bernabeu'.



It's now owned by a collector who also owns a number of other Bellingham cards as well as being a Birmingham City fan.

The card was even pictured at St Andrew's where they will no doubt hope Bellingham returns to when he's finished conquering in Madrid.

Sports.title: EFL boss threatens to quit after blaming ‘poor players’ for club’s eighth league defeat in ten
Sports.content:
EFL boss threatens to quit after blaming ‘poor players’ for club’s eighth league defeat in ten

Steve Evans has sparked uncertainty over his Bristol Rovers future by threatening to leave should he feel unwelcome.

The Scot took aim at his players after their 2-0 home defeat against Chesterfield in League Two on Saturday afternoon.

2 Evans made it clear that he is not afraid to walk away from Rovers after their latest League Two defeat Credit: Getty

Rovers have lost eight of their last ten league matches and are only four points above the bottom two in England's fourth tier.

Evans made two substitutions before the interval as they delivered a poor first half, with a third coming due to a Ben Purrington injury.

Having been top of League Two in September, the Gas' recent form has seen them drop towards a potential battle against relegation.

And when head coach Evans spoke to BBC Radio Bristol after defeat to Chesterfield, he made it clear that he isn't worried about quitting.

He also gave an assessment of his squad, insisting that their drop in standards is not solely down to him and his staff.

Evans hits out at Rovers players

"My message has always been the same - if I'm not wanted, I'll leave. I'm not like the others that hang on for paydays. Let's not mince my words," Evans said.

"I sat on the bench for ten seconds to have a conversation with Paul Raynor (assistant), somebody shouts when I came out, 'He's come out from hiding!'

"I answer them, I don't hide, I'm out the trenches. I don't hide, I'm not like the others who hide behind the ownership, I don't do that.

"I'm not doing my job, neither is Paul, neither is Byron, neither is Tomo (Lee Tomlin, coach).

"We're not doing our jobs, but we're being let down by inconsistent players. Poor players, in my opinion."

2 Evans took responsibility for their poor run, but also called out the inconsistency from his players Credit: Getty

Formerly of now Premier League side Leeds United, Evans joined Rovers in December on a deal that ran until the end of the 2025/26 season.

He secured their League Two safety and was rewarded with a two-year contract at the Memorial Stadium.

They finished 14th at the end of their first season back in tier four following relegation from League One.

After losing to York City on the opening weekend, they went top and into contention for promotion with successive wins against Newport County, Crawley Town, Colchester United and Rotherham United.

However, a 1-0 victory over Exeter City on September 26 is their most recent such result in the league.

Elsewhere, they are through to the FA Cup second round and will face Rotherham away on the weekend of December 5.

Sports.title: National League side sack manager a week after FA Cup exit to EFL team
Sports.content:
Eastleigh have sacked manager Matt Gray after less than five months in charge.

The National League side confirmed their decision following Saturday's home defeat to AFC Fylde.



3 Eastleigh have sacked Gray after Saturday's defeat to AFC Fylde Credit: Getty

Whilst the loss was only their second at the Silverlake Stadium this term, it left the Spitfires with just one win in their last seven league matches.

Their only win during that period, which stretches back to September, was a 4-2 victory over Boston United on October 24.

Gray now departs with Eastleigh sat 18th in the table, three points above the relegation zone.



Eastleigh statement

In a statement announcing his exit, Eastleigh said: "Eastleigh Football Club can today confirm that we have parted company with first-team manager Matt Gray with immediate effect.

"The club would like to thank Matt for his efforts during his tenure and wish him all the best for the future.



"Further updates regarding the management situation will follow in due course."

Gray becomes the third manager sacked in the National League this season.



He follows Gateshead's Lee Cattermole and former Scunthorpe United boss Andy Butler in being dismissed.

The former was let go with Gateshead sat bottom of the table at the start of last month. Gateshead are still at the foot of the division with four points from 16 games.

Scunthorpe then followed suit by sacking Butler following a 4-1 defeat to Tamworth on October 27 which left them inside the relegation zone. Scunthorpe are currently second from bottom in the table.

3 Eastleigh sit three points above the relegation zone in 18th Credit: Getty



Who is Matt Gray?

Meanwhile, it is the second time Gray has left Eastleigh during his managerial career.

The 45-year-old previously spent four years in charge of the club between 2007 and 2011 before returning this summer.

During his 15 years away from Eastleigh, Gray had spells as manager of both Sutton United and Eastbourne Borough.

The Hampshire outfit are now on the search for a new boss ahead of their next fixture.



They return to action with a trip to fellow strugglers Tamworth on Saturday.

Gray's exit also follows Eastleigh's elimination from the FA Cup earlier this month.

3 Gray returned to Eastleigh for a second spell as manager in the summer Credit: Getty

His side were beaten at home in the first round by Shrewsbury Town on November 7.



The tie had appeared destined for extra time before the visitors scored an 87th minute winner to clinch a 2-1 victory.

Sports.title: 'Managers now are b****y boring! NEIL WARNOCK on the lack of characters in football, his friendship with Pep Guardiola, why he is open to managing again post-Christmas - and how he almost became a chiropodist!
Sports.content:
Spending time in the company of Neil Warnock is always an education, be it witnessing one of his legendary foul-mouthed touchline rants or perched at one of his stage shows at grand venues like London Palladium. On this occasion, Daily Mail Sport is perched in an east London bar watching on as one of English football's national treasures is posing for some modelling. Yes, you read that right, Mr Warnock is here to launch his own pair of socks with a tipple of Famous Grouse whisky in hand. The complements on Warnock's 77-year-old feet are soon over, though, and we can get on to talking about a life in football that started six decades ago as a winger for Chesterfield and has traversed 10 clubs as a player, 17 as a manager and more than 2,000 games in the dugout. So where to start? Maybe his reflections on nearly five decades in management – and how the whole conversation about feet is not too out of place… 'You don't realise how long it has been really, I started off just a team of ragamuffins as I call them,' he says in his iconic Yorkshire accent. 'They used to train on the green where I had digs in Hartlepool and asked me to coach them. 'I remember we scored from a set-piece we worked on, I was running up and down the touchline high-fiving everyone. I got the bug. I knew I could never get to the top as a player, I was quick but I was brainless. Daily Mail Sport caught up with Neil Warnock to discuss his six decades in football After representing 10 different clubs as a player, Warnock became one of the most compelling managers in the game 'I could've been a chiropodist if not in football. That could be on a quiz, couldn't it? I had bad feet at Scunthorpe, I used to get massive blisters so the physio there started getting me to do some of the players' feet. 'I enjoyed doing ingrown toenails and things like that! So I thought why not? Then I had a practice in Sheffield. I had to make a decision when we won the league at Scarborough whether to go full-time or pack it in. I thought, "Oh, go on then, let's give it a little go". 'It's not worked out badly, really, has it? 'People come up to me every day and say, "You're a legend, you". And I say, "Oh, thank you very much". Then they tell me what club they support, I have had so many haven't I? Last week I went out for a minute and had four selfies. They all appreciate what I did for their club. 'There aren't as many characters in the game now, you wouldn't get upset with managers now like in my day because now they are that b****y boring! Some of them barely speak. 'They won't get the rapport we had. I managed at a good time. The way I managed, I needed that humour. I needed the lads to enjoy it. I signed a lot of players that many managers wouldn't touch with a barge pole, are you with me? They ended up getting me promotions.' The aforementioned humour brings us on to a private conversation he had with the great Pep Guardiola, one of the millions of anecdotes up Warnock's sleeve but one that he has not told until now. 'I went to a training session and he asked me to say a few words,' explains Warnock. 'I said, "Well lads I bet you're glad I'm not your manager because we'd be kicking balls from there to there, chasing it, heading it, practicing our tackles"... everyone laughed. Warnock views Pep Guardiola as the best manager of his lifetime, while the Spaniard praised the veteran's humour after once addressing his Man City squad at a training session Warnock has led teams to promotions on eight occasions over the course of his career 'After the session we had a coffee and Pep said to me, "Neil, that was amazing, you know when you talked to the players? I understood why you had so many promotions". 'He started counting and said, "What we have is all these staff… computers, details, nutritionist, all these staff, but you know what we don't have? Humour". He noticed why my lads had done well in my teams, just in that meeting. It was good, that. He is amazing. 'Pep is the best manager of my lifetime. They say he had all the best players but it is not easy managing them. Pep did things with players and now there are non-league teams trying to play like Manchester City!' Warnock is now doing stage tours - Guardiola attended one last season - and had a tear in his eye when he stepped out at London Palladium given he used to watch shows there with his mother, who was in a wheelchair, on the TV as a child. So what is Warnock up to these days? His current role is advisor at Torquay United but last management job was at Aberdeen two years ago… so is he out of the rat race for good this time? 'No, not really, no,' he says. 'I only work from February to April! So the phone will be on after Christmas. You never know, do ya? There will be someone thinking "why don't we get that Warnock in?". 'I've retired 40 times! Every time I have said it, I have meant it. But it's that dressing room camaraderie. There's something about football, when I look at some of the managers now… they just don't excite me. 'I remember Ruben Amorim (breaks down laughing). He's got his computer out on the bench! I remember watching and thinking, "I'm sorry, son, you need more than a computer to help you tonight!". Warnock is currently doing stage tours, with Guardiola among the attendees last season Warnock's current role is advisor at Torquay United and briefly served as interim manager last season, with the 77-year-old admitting he had not completely ruled out a return to the dugout 'And likewise, I see them making notes on the bench, oh my god. I think "what are you doing, your shopping list for Tescos?". 'I do enjoy walking and I enjoy photography, believe it or not. I go up the river with my phone, there's so many lovely things to see. 'I've got an electric bike and I sometimes do about 25 miles. I was thinking of doing a cycle of all my clubs but that would take me five years! They go at about 30mph down the hills, you've got to be careful, you wouldn't want to come off them.' He is also enjoying fishing, being with the family and playing golf with his son, a PGA rising star William - though Warnock Sr insists he often embarrasses himself playing off 'the ladies' tee'. The thing that makes Warnock most proud is the four promotions at Wembley but also the togetherness he fostered in his many teams. He tells us: 'What I like about the teams I had, they all have reunions. You look at the tele now, someone will score a goal and kiss the badge… they won't have a reunion. 'When I go to these reunions, I see all my lads and how I blended that dressing room together and I look at the comradeship they still have now, they are the same as they were just a lot older. 'This year, my Scarborough team are having a 40-year celebration and the lads have invited me. I said there's no way I'm going out with that lot after the do because they can drink, let me tell you!' * The Famous Grouse has teamed up with Happy Socks to launch an exclusive limited-edition collection, available at Tesco stores across the UK. Shoppers can pick up a free pair of colourful, collectable socks with selected 70cl bottles of The Famous Grouse whisky, priced from £18.50. Available in-store only, while stocks last.
