World.title: Disu assures Abia residents of improved security
World.content:
By Steve Oko

UMUAHIA — The Inspector-General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Disu, has assured residents of Abia State of improved security, pledging that the Nigeria Police Force would intensify efforts to protect lives and property across the state.

Disu gave the assurance during a courtesy visit to Governor Alex Otti at Government House, Umuahia, where he commended the governor for his sustained support to the police.

The IGP, who said he had received positive reports from the Commissioner of Police and the Assistant Inspector-General of Police on the state government’s assistance to the Force, promised that the police would reciprocate the gesture through improved service delivery.

“I want to thank you for all you have been doing for my officers. My Commissioner of Police has told me all you have been doing for us. The AIG too reiterated it. Thank you so much for it,” Disu said.

He assured the governor that the police would remain committed to tackling security challenges and ensuring the safety of residents.

“I will give you my word that we will continue to do our best to ensure proper policing so that people of the state will be able to sleep with their two eyes closed,” he said.

Disu explained that his visit to Abia was primarily to attend the traditional marriage ceremony of his orderly, Victor Nnah Sunday, at Amangwu, Abaki-Ndoki, in Ukwa East Local Government Area.

He, however, said he considered it necessary to pay homage to Otti, as the state’s Chief Security Officer, before proceeding to the wedding venue.

Responding, Otti commended the police leadership for its professionalism and prompt response to the state government’s requests for assistance in addressing security challenges.

“Thank you for what you do for the country. Thank you for the professionalism of the Force and for making everyone realise that the safety and security of the people is paramount.

“We have had instances where we called upon you and you responded swiftly,” the governor said.

Otti also praised the promotion of the immediate past Commissioner of Police in Abia to the rank of Assistant Inspector-General of Police, describing his service in the state as professional and tactful.

He said the former police commissioner demonstrated commitment in handling security matters, adding that although the state would have preferred to retain him, his elevation was a welcome development.

“He demonstrated professionalism and tact in the discharge of his duties. If not that it is a promotion, we would have resisted it, but we believe it is good for him to move on,” Otti said.

The governor expressed optimism that the officer would sustain his relationship with Abia despite his new position.

Otti also congratulated the IGP’s orderly on his traditional marriage, recalling that he had met him during an earlier encounter with the police chief.

The governor further commended Disu for what he described as his demonstration of national inclusiveness through the choice of aides and associates from different ethnic and geographical backgrounds.

He specifically noted that some of the IGP’s close aides hailed from different parts of the country, including Ohafia in Abia State.

Otti urged Nigerians to rise above ethnic and geographical sentiments, stressing that national unity would be strengthened when citizens saw themselves first as members of one country.

The IGP was accompanied on the visit by his wife, AIG Afolabi and some Commissioners of Police.

Members of the governor’s delegation included the Chief of Staff, Pastor Caleb Ajagba; Commissioner for Information, Prince Okey Kanu; Commissioner for Arts, Culture and Creative Economy, Dr Matthew Ekwuribe; and other top government officials.

World.title: 2027: Atiku promises to end insecurity if elected
World.content:
By Nabilu Balarabe

The Presidential candidate of African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar has promised to tackle insurgency and other forms of insecurity, if voted in the 2027 Presidential election.

Atiku made the promise in Potiskum on Sunday during the party’s campaign rally.

He also promised to provide an enabling environment for youths to develop careers in all areas of their interest.

“Whatever you want to do, my administration will support you. But we will not allow all acts of violence,” he said.

Abubakar said he would revive the economy by providing affordable fuel, electricity and cutting taxes.

He, however, said all these could only be achieved if voters came out en-mass to vote for him in the forthcoming election.

Abubakar advised the electorate to vote wisely for candidates that would better their lot and reject corrupt and selfish politicians.

“Vote the ADC for your future and the future of your children. We are ready to serve you in every way we can,” Atiku said.

In his remarks, the ADC National Secretary, Mr Rauf Aregbesola, thanked the people of Yobe for their warm reception to the party’s candidates.

He urged the electorate to vote for change and ensure that due process was followed in counting and collation of votes cast.

World.title: CHATHAM HOUSE: WHAT I SAW VS SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNT
World.content:
The social media amplified Amupitan’s outing at Chatham House in London, reckons CHETA NWANZE

This is one of those moments for the kind of self-reflection that, I’ll admit openly, Nigerians don’t do very well as a people. The question is, what do you do when reality collides with your preconceptions?

This is about what I saw at Chatham House in London three days ago, vis-à-vis the narrative that has come to dominate the online space. I’ll stick with the facts of what I saw and heard first, and then give my opinion afterwards. I’m writing this in the full knowledge that some would accuse me of having corn in my pocket. A Nigerian expression, for those who may not know, that indicates the accuser believes I have sold out to the Tinubu movement.

The first point I need to make is that at no point during the day-long occasion did the INEC chairman wear APC paraphernalia. By day-long, I mean the private discussion where various academics, researchers, and civil society actors spoke and made presentations, and then the public event where he and I were on a panel with two others. He was professional all through, came across as sincere in his intentions, and while publicly I told him that his main job is to conduct an election that everyone would agree with, even if they weren’t happy with the outcome, privately I asked him if he would be able to resist the political pressure from the ruling party when it comes, and it will come. His response satisfied me in the sense that he didn’t give a definite answer, but he wasn’t evasive either. He said something along the lines of his integrity matters to him, and he knows he has a lot of work to do. I equate that kind of response to a new groom who is asked if he would ever cheat on his wife. For me, an immediate and emphatic negative answer is the response of someone who hasn’t given the matter any thought and would fall at the first real hurdle. I’m not holding brief for Prof Amupitan here; I’m just saying that he struck me as a person who thinks. That gives room for the benefit of the doubt, and I must also say that I’m fully aware that his predecessor was at the same venue four years ago, made promises, and fell when the time came.

Second is the APC UK chair, Mr Tunde Doherty. I have never spoken to Mr Doherty before, but I have been in the same space with him four times – the first time I noticed him was four years ago when Peter Obi came to Chatham House for his event. Doherty was present. The second time was during President Tinubu’s state visit to the UK. I was involved in something at Southwark Crown Court, which required me to pass through Westminster Tube Station on my way to the court. On the day of the state visit, on my way back, I saw Mr Doherty at Westminster Tube Station in his full APC/Tinubu regalia, marshalling crowds of “volunteers” to go and do the hailing thing for the President’s entourage. The third time I was in the same space as the man was during the infamous Daniel Bwala interview. He was on the panel; I was in the crowd. After the interview, the other panellists, who happen to be my friends, invited me upstairs to meet Mehdi Hassan. Doherty was there, hobnobbing with pretty much everyone else. From the APC side of the aisle, Juliana Olayinka spoke with me. The next time I saw Mr Doherty was, of course, on Thursday at Chatham House, and here it is critical for me to state that contrary to the stories making the rounds, he did not arrive at Chatham House with the INEC delegation of three people, nor did he leave with them. He did what a professional networker would do – after the public event, he walked up to them, introduced himself and did a small chitchat.

This is where something needs to be said about work rate, turning up, and, as some would have it, hustle culture. Whatever you want to say about the APC UK chairman, Tunde Doherty, he is always present, advancing his interests. Many of his detractors are happy to stay online heckling, and that heckling is essentially what the ‘protest’ against the INEC chair amounted to, which I will come to. The needle won’t be moved by staying on the sidelines throwing stones. I won’t hold it against the Nigeria Democratic Congress or the African Democratic Congress as bodies because they are relatively new arrivals on the political party scene in Nigeria, so I don’t think they have strong enough branches in the UK to have someone who is always at events. However, the Obidient movement and the Atikulated movement have been around for a bit. Why have they not identified a committed person to attend all events and ensure that their interests, visual interests at least, are represented?

Third, the ‘protest’. Protest? It was between six and ten individuals who surrounded the INEC chair’s car. It did not interrupt anything; it was over before one could say balablu, and the day went on as if nothing happened. So I was very surprised later in the day when I saw stories making the rounds about the INEC chair being “disgraced in the UK”, and the next day, when I turned on Arise News, I saw a report about the man’s “convoy” being stopped. One car does not a convoy make. In any event, and this is important, I think the photograph that captured the ‘protest’ in its true glory was in Daily Trust.

This brings me to my opinion: I have just witnessed the power that social media has to reinforce people’s biases. We have an election coming, and because of our unfortunate history, so many Nigerians are, quite correctly, already wired to distrust the electoral umpire. I hope Prof Amupitan has an understanding of that reality, which is what informed my challenge to him at the end of my opening remarks. It is not just about conducting an election; the election must be seen by all sides (well, except those who have their minds completely made up regardless) as credible. That is a bar that he must clear.

A lot must be said about people’s yearning to believe stuff that reinforces their perceptions. I saw a number of clips on Twitter where people claimed that Mr Doherty was the INEC chair; someone would come and correct them, but the person making the claim would double down. This atmosphere of mistrust is amplified by the social media algorithm simply because it is profitable. To be fair, it’s not happening only to Nigeria’s democracy; it’s a genuinely global problem among democracies, which makes a strong case for the Chinese approach of tight control. But tight control only works when the government has repeatedly shown that it has the population’s interests at heart, and that can hardly be said about the Nigerian government in a historical sense.

Then I must express a lot of sympathy for Prof Amupitan. Something changes when you have had a chance to meet a figure in person; suddenly he becomes human, and you see his motivations, fears, and challenges through the man’s eyes, not through a television screen. The man is facing a challenging election, and he thinks he understands how he can be undermined by the political class he is meant to referee. I fear that he is unprepared for how desperate these guys can be.

Finally, I will come back to the theme of what I presented at the event. The violence is ticking up, and the political class, especially people from the ruling party with access to the levers of power, are getting more and more desperate. It does not matter how well-intentioned Prof Amupitan and his fellow INEC staff are; what matters is the outcome of what they give us in January and February. Given the suffering Nigerians have endured over the last four years, if the elections are seen as less than kosher, we are in for serious trouble.

Nwanze is CEO at SBM Intelligence

World.title: FROM REFORM PAIN TO GAIN
World.content:
BISI ADEGBUYI argues why subsidising farming and local government autonomy matter

In March 2026, I published an article titled, From Reform Pain to National GAIN, examining the relationship between Nigeria’s economic reforms, their immediate costs and the prospects for sustainable prosperity. My central proposition was that economic correction must lead to stabilisation, stabilisation must encourage productive investment, and investment must ultimately translate into improvements in the lives of ordinary Nigerians.

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s recent announcement in Jigawa State of a proposed shift towards subsidising farming rather than fuel provides an opportunity to revisit that proposition.

The proposed agricultural interventions, including interest-free loans, mechanisation and irrigation, raise a fundamental question: how can Nigeria translate macroeconomic stabilisation into tangible microeconomic benefits for ordinary and vulnerable Nigerians at the last mile?

Nigeria’s economic reforms have sought to address fiscal imbalances, fuel-subsidy distortions and foreign-exchange challenges. While some macroeconomic indicators have improved, inflation, food prices and household purchasing power remain pressing concerns.

Macroeconomic stabilisation is not an end in itself. A stronger fiscal position does not automatically put affordable food on the table. Greater investor confidence does not immediately improve the income of a smallholder farmer or informal trader.

The next stage must connect economic reforms to productive opportunities, affordable services and household welfare.

Macroeconomic stability creates the conditions for progress. Microeconomic benefits are how ordinary Nigerians experience that progress.

Agriculture provides a practical opportunity to establish that connection.

Redirecting public support towards agricultural production can improve productivity through affordable financing, mechanisation, irrigation and better inputs.

But agricultural subsidies are not inherently effective. Without credible implementation arrangements, they can be diverted, captured by intermediaries or distributed without measurable improvements in production.

A farmer registry alone cannot establish that farming is taking place. A fertiliser allocation does not prove delivery. An irrigation project does not necessarily mean water reaches the intended farms.

Government must establish who receives support, where agricultural activities take place, whether promised services are delivered and what results follow. The objective must be productive agricultural investment, not merely another expenditure programme.

Nigeria’s agricultural economy includes numerous smallholders, customary cultivators, tenant farmers and seasonal producers operating outside comprehensive formal records.

Many cultivate inherited family land, community holdings or rented plots without registered Certificates of Occupancy. Their farms may lack conventional addresses, yet their activities sustain rural livelihoods and contribute to food production.

A subsidy programme relying exclusively on formal land documentation risks excluding genuine producers.

The absence of registered title should not automatically disqualify an otherwise eligible cultivator from agricultural assistance. Equally, evidence of cultivation must not be confused with proof of ownership.

Technology can help locate farms, document productive activities and support verification through local-language descriptions, basic mobile phones and assisted registration.

The appropriate progression is visibility, verification, inclusion and, where appropriate, progressive formalisation.

Why Local Government Autonomy Matters: The imperative of local government autonomy becomes particularly evident when agricultural policy is examined through Nigeria’s land administration framework.

Under Section 1 of the Land Use Act, land within each state is generally vested in the Governor, subject to the Act. However, Section 2 assigns control and management of non-urban land to local governments, subject to statutory provisions, while Section 6 empowers them to grant customary rights of occupancy for agricultural and other purposes within prescribed limits.

Governors retain important statutory powers, but local governments possess distinct responsibilities directly relevant to rural agriculture.

The Supreme Court’s July 2024 judgment on local government financial autonomy therefore has implications extending beyond public finance.

Local governments cannot meaningfully perform grassroots development functions without adequate resources, administrative capacity and operational independence.

Yet financial autonomy must be accompanied by democratic accountability, transparent expenditure and safeguards against patronage.

Local government autonomy must mean more than control of funds. It must translate into measurable improvements in grassroots economic opportunities and public services.

Agricultural subsidy implementation offers an immediate opportunity to demonstrate this principle.

Land alone does not guarantee agricultural productivity. Water is indispensable.

Nigeria’s 12 River Basin Development Authorities provide an institutional foundation for irrigation, water-resource development and related agricultural infrastructure.

Their responsibilities can complement those of Governors and local governments through dry-season farming support, irrigation development and water-service delivery.

Because river basins frequently cross state boundaries, cooperation among federal water institutions, state governments and local councils is essential.

The performance of irrigation investment should be measured not simply by construction expenditure but by whether water reaches farms and improves productive activity.

International experience offers useful lessons.

Brazil’s support for family agriculture connects agricultural finance with production and market access. India’s PM-KISAN programme illustrates digital beneficiary administration and direct payments, although landholding-based eligibility also raises concerns about the exclusion of genuine cultivators without formal ownership records.

Indonesia’s subsidised fertiliser arrangements demonstrate the importance of linking beneficiary information to actual input distribution.

Nigeria should adapt these lessons to its informal agricultural economy, customary land arrangements and institutional realities rather than copy foreign systems uncritically.

Before Identity, there is location.

Every agricultural intervention has a geographic destination. Seeds are planted somewhere. Fertiliser is applied somewhere. Tractors operate somewhere. Irrigation facilities serve identifiable locations.

Yet many Nigerian farms are described through streams, footpaths, neighbouring settlements and familiar landmarks rather than conventional street addresses.

Technology can translate these descriptions into usable geographic references and support subsequent verification.

Importantly, the technological foundations required for such an approach are no longer merely theoretical. Home-grown Nigerian innovations have already demonstrated the capacity to interpret informal descriptions of places, establish precise geographic references and support evidence-based verification. The challenge is increasingly one of institutional readiness, responsible integration and practical deployment rather than the absence of indigenous technological ingenuity.

But identifying a farmer, locating a farm, establishing cultivation and determining ownership are separate questions.

A credible agricultural programme must distinguish them and verify actual delivery rather than equate expenditure with success.

From Reform Pain to National GAIN:

The debate about Nigeria’s economic reforms must increasingly focus on the relationship between national economic indicators and household welfare.

The proposed shift towards agricultural support offers an opportunity to connect macroeconomic improvements with productivity, rural employment and grassroots inclusion.

But successful implementation requires more than federal financing. It requires Governors exercising their lawful responsibilities, autonomous and accountable local governments performing their statutory functions, River Basin Development Authorities supporting irrigation, and technology strengthening verification and transparency.

In my earlier writings, I argued that economic reforms require continuity and productive investment if their intended benefits are to materialise. The agricultural initiative provides an opportunity to test that proposition through implementation and measurable outcomes.

Reform pain cannot be its own justification. The dividends must become visible, inclusive and measurable.

Before government subsidises a farm, it should be able to locate it. Before declaring assistance delivered, it should verify the delivery. Before claiming success, it should demonstrate the results.

That is how Nigeria can move from reform pain to national GAIN—and take the benefits of economic change to the last mile.

Adegbuyi is a lawyer, technology entrepreneur, former Postmaster General of Nigeria and a 2018 World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS) Prize Laureate

World.title: NIGERIA’S UNFINISHED SANITATION BUSINESS
World.content:
World Toilet Day (WTD) is here again. Every November, for the last five years, I return to the same issues: poor sanitation, open defecation, the health implications of inadequate toilet facilities and the responsibility of governments, businesses and individuals to address the problem.

This year, frankly, I wondered what to say differently. I even thought of writing something about the World Men’s Day instead – plenty to talk about there. Yet, I find myself drawn to WTD. I suspect we are making some progress, although measuring how much remains difficult.

For example, I noticed that a shopping complex in Ikeja, known for its rather unpleasant toilet facilities, has entered into a partnership with a restaurant around the beginning of Olowo Street to improve access to decent toilets. A shop owner offered me a ticket to use at the eatery.

More companies are renovating their facilities, while corporate interventions are helping to improve water and sanitation infrastructure in schools. Nestlé Nigeria, for instance, continues to support initiatives to provide water and improve sanitation in schools and host communities. Reckitt, through its toilet care brand, Harpic, is on this table.

These developments may appear small, but they suggest that sanitation is gradually receiving attention beyond government campaigns and annual declarations.

As the world marks World Toilet Day on November 19, 2026, under the United Nations theme, ‘Safe Toilets. Equal Futures’, the question is whether these individual improvements are translating into meaningful national progress.

Globally, approximately 3.4 billion people still lack safely managed sanitation services, according to the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme. Although 1.2 billion people gained access between 2015 and 2024, the world remains significantly behind the Sustainable Development Goal target of universal access by 2030.

Nigeria’s situation is particularly concerning. The 2024 Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey, released in 2025, found that only 49 per cent of the household population had access to at least basic sanitation services. Approximately 20 per cent (one in five) still practised open defecation, while others depended on limited or unimproved facilities.

These figures represent millions of Nigerians whose health, dignity and opportunities are compromised by inadequate sanitation. The 2026 theme makes an important connection between sanitation and gender equality.

A toilet is more than a facility for disposing of human waste. It is a place where people should be able to attend to their most basic needs safely, privately and with dignity.

For women and girls, the absence of functional toilets creates additional difficulties. Consider a teenage girl attending a school without separate toilets, running water or facilities for managing menstrual hygiene. She may choose to stay away from school during her menstrual period, losing valuable learning time. Women working in markets, factories and commercial centres face similar challenges.

A toilet without a working lock, adequate lighting, water or appropriate accessibility provisions is hardly a safe facility.

It is clear that Nigeria’s sanitation challenge cannot be left to government alone. Shopping complexes, markets, restaurants, hotels, transport terminals, filling stations and office buildings should recognise that providing clean, accessible toilets is part of responsible business practice. The Ikeja example above is a good start.

Now, Nigeria is not short of sanitation policies and campaigns. The Clean Nigeria: Use the Toilet campaign, the national WASH action plans, and the ambition to eliminate open defecation by 2025 demonstrate that government recognises the problem.

But policy commitments have not translated into universal access. The government must now move beyond awareness campaigns to measurable interventions.

First, national and state governments need regular sanitation assessments and publicly accessible scorecards. These should show household toilet access, school facilities, public toilet availability and open defecation rates.

Second, resources must go to communities with the greatest deficits, particularly rural areas and underserved settlements. A state with just nine per cent basic sanitation coverage requires a different intervention from one exceeding 80 per cent.

Third, public toilets must become an essential component of urban planning. Markets, motor parks, schools, healthcare facilities and commercial centres should have functional, accessible and properly maintained facilities.

Finally, sanitation financing and enforcement must improve. Governments should establish dedicated budget lines, encourage private-sector investment and provide targeted support for low-income households. Building regulations and environmental sanitation standards must also be enforced.

To me, the most important lesson from another World Toilet Day is that sanitation cannot remain an annual publicity exercise. I may be running out of fresh ways to write about toilets, but the problem has certainly not run out of reasons to demand attention.

The real concern is that isolated improvements are not systemic progress. Nigeria needs to connect these efforts to a coherent sanitation strategy backed by funding, reliable data, accountability and enforcement.



Ultimately, the success of World Toilet Day should not be measured by the number of speeches delivered, campaigns launched, or promises made on November 19. It should be measured by how many more Nigerians can walk into a toilet, use it safely and leave with their dignity intact. This is what Safe Toilets. Equal Futures should mean. This is progress worth measuring.

Elvis Eromosele is a corporate communications expert, elviseroms@gmail.com

World.title: Rotary International to Flag Off Life-changing Humanitarian Initiative
World.content:
Rotary International District 9111 is set to take another bold step towards transforming lives as the Mega Medical Mission 2026 officially gets underway with a flag-off ceremony to be officiated by the Rotary International President, Rotarian Hakeem Yinka Babalola.

According to District 9111 Governor, Rotarian Bukola Bakare “ the landmark ceremony, scheduled for Sunday, November 15, 2026, at 3pm at Redeemer’s Health Village, Mowe, Ogun State, will bring together beneficiaries, Rotary Club Presidents, Rotarians, donors and other supporters whose generosity has helped make the humanitarian initiative possible.”

Bakare stated, “the Mega Medical Mission underscores Rotary’s enduring commitment to improving access to healthcare, bringing hope to vulnerable communities, and ensuring that financial limitations do not prevent people from receiving essential medical attention.”

Speaking ahead of the ceremony, the Chairman of the 2026 Mega Medical Mission Committee, Professor Femi Oloyede stated that “Rotary Mega Medical Mission 2026 is a free health and surgical outreach organized by Rotary International Districts 9111 and 9112 across communities in Lagos and Ogun States.’

Oloyede disclosed that “screening and medical examination of beneficiaries took place between August 18–20, 2026, across designated centers in Lagos and Ogun States: Ikeja, Alimosho, Festac, Sango-Ota, Abeokuta, Gbagada, and Ikorodu.

He added that “main surgical Intervention and procedure holds at Redeemer’s Health Village, Mowe, and covers free medical treatment and specialist care for gynaecological and major medical cases, dental and eye care services, and surgical operations.”

He urged all philanthropists, Rotary Club Presidents in District 9111 and individual Rotarians who contributed financially to the initiative to be part of the historic occasion.

In his words, “your donations have been instrumental to the mission and described their presence at the flag-off as a meaningful demonstration of continued commitment, partnership, and collective responsibility towards humanitarian service.”

World.title: DIGGING DEEP FOR HUMAN CAPITAL
World.content:
Uba Sani is honoured with CIHCDN award, writes ISMAIL MUHAMMED

The true wealth of a society is not measured exclusively by the size of its budget, the number of roads constructed or the volume of physical infrastructure delivered. Its greatest asset lies in the knowledge, skills, health, productivity and opportunities available to its people. Governments that understand this fundamental truth do not merely build structures; they build human capacity, empower communities and prepare successive generations to create wealth and sustain development.

This philosophy appears to be at the heart of Governor Uba Sani’s approach to governance in Kaduna State. His emergence as the recipient of the Distinguished Human Capital Development Champion Award from the Chartered Institute of Human Capital Development of Nigeria (CIHCDN) is therefore significant beyond the prestige of the recognition. It brings attention to a development agenda that places education, vocational skills, healthcare, agriculture, financial inclusion and youth empowerment at the centre of public policy.

Presented at the Institute’s National Conference at Merit House, Maitama, Abuja, the award recognises the governor’s investments in expanding opportunities and improving the living conditions of Kaduna residents. The Institute specifically acknowledged his initiatives in education, healthcare, skills development, rural transformation, economic inclusion, youth empowerment and capacity building.

In a country where the debate about governance often revolves around political contests, infrastructure projects and financial allocations, the recognition provides an opportunity to refocus attention on an equally important question: what is the government doing to improve the capacity of ordinary citizens to participate meaningfully in economic and social development?

Perhaps one of the most striking elements of the governor’s human capital agenda is the investment in vocational training and practical skills development. Through the establishment of three Vocational Training and Skills Development Centres in Rigachikun, Soba and Samaru Kataf, the administration is seeking to create a structured pathway through which young people can acquire industry-relevant skills and become economically productive.

According to the Commissioner for Information and Culture, Malam Ahmed Maiyaki, the centres are designed to equip approximately 32,000 young people annually with practical skills across 14 trades.

This is an ambitious intervention, particularly at a time when youth unemployment, underemployment and the mismatch between educational qualifications and labour-market requirements remain major national concerns.

A university degree is valuable, but not every productive career must follow the conventional academic route. Modern economies require technicians, artisans, construction professionals, digital specialists, entrepreneurs and other skilled workers capable of translating knowledge into economic value.

The Kaduna initiative reflects an understanding that young people need more than encouragement to seek employment. They need the technical competence, practical exposure and entrepreneurial capacity to create opportunities for themselves and others.

The ambition, as Maiyaki explained, is to transform young people from job seekers into skilled professionals, entrepreneurs and employers of labour.

That is an important shift in development thinking. It moves beyond the assumption that the government alone must provide jobs and recognises the role of skills, innovation and enterprise in expanding economic opportunities.

The administration’s investments in formal education provide another major pillar of its human capital development agenda.

Maiyaki disclosed that the government has constructed 736 new classrooms, renovated more than 1,200 classrooms, recruited 10,000 teachers and trained over 33,000 teachers to improve access to quality education across the state. These interventions address two essential dimensions of education: the availability of learning facilities and the quality of instruction.

A classroom without a competent teacher cannot deliver the desired learning outcomes. Similarly, qualified teachers operating in overcrowded or poorly equipped facilities face significant limitations. Investment in both infrastructure and teacher development is therefore essential to building an effective education system.

The recruitment and training of thousands of teachers demonstrate the importance attached to strengthening the human resources that sustain public education. Beyond the numbers, the ultimate objective must be improved literacy, stronger learning outcomes and better preparation of children for the demands of a changing world.

The reduction of tuition fees in state-owned tertiary institutions by up to 50 per cent is another significant aspect of this approach. For many families, the cost of higher education can become an insurmountable barrier, forcing capable young people to abandon their academic ambitions or place additional financial pressure on their households.

By reducing tuition fees and expanding scholarship and bursary interventions, the administration is seeking to make higher education more accessible.

This is particularly important because education should serve as a pathway to social mobility, not a privilege reserved for families with substantial financial resources. One of the most compelling features of the administration’s approach is its recognition that human capital development extends beyond schools and vocational institutions.

Agriculture, for instance, remains a major source of livelihood for many households in Kaduna State. Supporting smallholder farmers is therefore not merely an agricultural intervention; it is an investment in rural incomes, food security and community development.

Maiyaki disclosed that the government distributed 1,400 trucks of free fertiliser to 420,000 smallholder farmers. The scale of this intervention highlights the importance of agriculture in the state’s development priorities. By supporting farmers with essential inputs, the administration is seeking to strengthen productive capacity, improve rural livelihoods and contribute to food production.

A farmer who can cultivate more efficiently, improve yields and earn a better income is better positioned to educate children, access healthcare and invest in household welfare. The benefits of agricultural empowerment therefore extend across several dimensions of human development.

The revitalisation of 255 Primary Healthcare Centres, alongside improved welfare for healthcare professionals and initiatives to expand access to medical services, particularly in underserved rural communities, represents another investment in the wellbeing and productivity of citizens.

Healthcare is not simply a social service. It is a critical component of economic development. A healthy population is better able to learn, work, innovate and contribute to national productivity.

For rural communities, accessible primary healthcare can make a significant difference by bringing essential services closer to households that might otherwise face difficulties accessing medical attention. By connecting education, skills development, agriculture and healthcare, the administration is advancing a broader understanding of what it means to invest in people.

Another important dimension of Uba Sani’s development philosophy is the emphasis on inclusion. Maiyaki stressed that the administration’s interventions are designed to reach communities irrespective of political, religious or ethnic affiliations.

In a diverse state such as Kaduna, this principle carries considerable significance. Development should not be distributed according to political loyalty, religious identity or ethnic considerations. Every community deserves a fair opportunity to benefit from public investment.

Inclusive governance strengthens social cohesion because citizens are more likely to trust public institutions when they believe government programmes are accessible to them without discrimination.

It also helps ensure that development does not remain concentrated in major urban centres while rural communities are left behind.

The recognition by CIHCDN is particularly relevant in this regard because sustainable human capital development must be broad-based. It cannot be achieved if certain groups are excluded from education, healthcare, employment opportunities or access to productive resources.

Speaking after receiving the award on the governor’s behalf, Maiyaki described the recognition as a testament to Uba Sani’s belief that the greatest investment any government can make is in its people, particularly young people, women and vulnerable citizens.

He also emphasised that the award should serve as encouragement to do more, rather than a reason for complacency. That is perhaps the most important message arising from the recognition.

Awards provide valuable acknowledgement, but the real test of human capital development lies in measurable improvements in people’s lives. The vocational centres must translate training into employment and enterprise. Investments in classrooms and teacher development must improve learning outcomes. Reduced tuition must enable more young people to complete their education. Agricultural support must contribute to stronger productivity and rural incomes. Revitalised healthcare facilities must provide accessible and dependable services.

The administration must also sustain these interventions, monitor their outcomes and ensure that public resources produce lasting value. For Kaduna State, the stakes are considerable. Its young population represents an enormous reservoir of potential. Properly educated, skilled, healthy and economically empowered, this population can become the driving force of industrial growth, entrepreneurship, innovation and social transformation.

Ultimately, Uba Sani’s recognition as a Distinguished Human Capital Development Champion speaks to a development philosophy that places people at the centre of governance. It reinforces the idea that the most enduring legacy of leadership is not simply what the government builds during its tenure, but the capacity it creates in citizens to build a better future for themselves and society.

Roads, bridges, schools and hospitals are important. But the people who use, manage, improve and derive value from those facilities are even more important. That is the larger significance of the governor’s human capital agenda: investing in the abilities of today’s citizens while preparing the next generation to lead Kaduna State into a more productive, inclusive and prosperous future.

Muhammed writes from Lagos

World.title: THE GROWING FATALITIES ON OUR HIGHWAYS
World.content:
All stakeholders could do more to stem the carnage

Yesterday, several countries marked the 2026 World Day of Remembrance for Road Traffic Victims with the theme, “A Light That Unites Us”, accompanied by the global slogan “Remember. Support. Act.” Ahead of the day, the Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) disclosed that 3,445 persons died in road traffic crashes across Nigeria between January and September 2026. According to the Abia State FRSC Sector Commander, Ngozi Ezeoma, no fewer than 7,156 road traffic crashes were recorded nationwide within the nine-month period, leaving 22,292 persons injured. “These numbers are more than just statistics as they represent human lives, families in grief and communities in distress,” she said.

Since Nigeria remains in the league of countries with the highest per capita rate of car fatalities in the world, any real search for solutions to this sad situation should start with a proper understanding of its likely causes. Thankfully, the World Health Organisation (WHO) has already identified reasons for most of these road accidents. They include over-speeding, driving under the power of alcohol and other intoxicating substances, non-use of protective gadgets like seatbelts, distractions caused by passengers, decrepit or substandard road amenities, unsafe vehicles, inadequate post-collision response, and poor enforcement of traffic laws.

Interestingly, the profile of the offenders is as diverse as the triggers of road mishaps suggested by WHO. Some public transport drivers, their private and corporate counterparts, uniformed personnel, chauffeurs of dignitaries and convoys are united in unsettling an otherwise tranquil motoring environment. The exuberance of the last group of transgressors is traceable to the ubiquity of Very Important Personalities (VIPs). The United Nations evidently had Nigeria in mind when it declared in 2008 that road safety was a “public health crisis, on the scale of AIDS, malaria and TB.”

The irony is that many of these crashes were either preventable or could have been drastically reduced through inexpensive remedial interventions. For instance, it is common knowledge that there are too many rickety vehicles on our roads while several taxis and minibuses often used for transportation are old. Some of them were manufactured in the 1980s and 1990s and have logged hundreds of thousands of kilometres. Besides, many of the vehicles that ply our roads are often overloaded with passengers and driven by people with little or no regard for speed limits.

To worsen matters, many commercial vehicles are ill-maintained, some adorned with worn-out tyres. The drivers of a good number of these vehicles, including trailers and tankers, were often either drunk, or half asleep behind the wheels, many out of exhaustion. The long stretch of dilapidated roads across the nation, besides causing unacceptable loss of man-hours and unbearable discomfort to road users, partly accounts for the high body count of road crashes. What compounds the situation is that when accidents occur, the victims are hardly given prompt attention. This is because the crop of road safety personnel patrolling the highways is inadequate. Emergency clinics are few and far between, just as ambulances on the highways are grossly inadequate.

Going forward, the FRSC needs to be equipped to do more in the business of saving lives, and in enlightening drivers and all road users on safety tips. They should ensure that the recently introduced speed limiting devices are installed in all commercial vehicles while those drivers who flout routine laws must be visited with stiff penalty. We urge a more creative and sustainable funding strategy for our road infrastructure as way of containing the highway carnage.

World.title: MTN Defends Data Billing, Says Apps Driving Rapid Consumption
World.content:
Blessing Ibunge in Port Harcourt

The Mobile Telecommunications Network (MTN) Nigeria has defended its data billing practices, insisting that it does not “steal” customers’ data, but acknowledged growing concerns among subscribers over unexplained data depletion.

The telecom giant made the clarification in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, during its “Data on Trial” initiative, a courtroom-style engagement designed to allow customers to question MTN officials over how their data is consumed.

The event, held at the weekend, featured customers and content creators as the prosecution, while MTN executives constituted the defence team.

MTN’s Chief Customer Relations and Experience Officer, Ugonwa Nwoye, said the initiative was a response to persistent complaints from customers who wanted greater visibility into their data consumption.

According to her, “customers have been telling us that they want to know what uses their data,” adding that the company had embarked on sensitisation campaigns for about two years before deciding to introduce face-to-face engagements. What we want is a better understanding for our customers about how their data is used, how they can track the use of their data on their phone or on platforms that we have built for them.”

MTN Nigeria’s General Manager, Network Performance and Quality Assurance, Mike Ndukwe, attributed increasing data consumption largely to the migration from older network technologies to 4G and 5G, alongside the rapid growth of smartphones, social media and high-definition video content.

He disclosed that Nigeria consumed about 13.2 million terabytes of data in 2025, while consumption in the first half of the current year had already reached 8.52 million terabytes, representing about 43 per cent year-on-year growth compared with the corresponding period.

World.title: Keyamo Insists NDC Erred in Singing Old National Anthem During Townhall Meeting in Lagos
World.content:
Chinedu Eze

The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, has repudiated those who try to justify the singing of old national anthem by the National Democratic Congress (NDC) by saying that All Progressives Congress (APC) also sing ‘On Our Mandate’, insisting that Senator Seriake Dickson led party was wrong, after all.

On Thursday, November 12, NDC held townhall meeting at the Classic Event Centre, Oregun Ikeja, Lagos, where old national anthem was sung instead of the new; although party members claimed that the new national anthem was sang later.

However, Keyamo, in his verified X (Twitter) account insisted that NDC was wrong and rejected the attempt to justify their action by the NDC party members, saying that APC also sing ‘On Our Mandate’.

The Minister explained, “Let me educate some mischievous persons who try to equate singing the on your mandate song, which is used to serenade President Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu, with singing an outlawed anthem in place of a legally approved National Anthem.

“At no time have supporters of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu sung on your mandate in place of the National Anthem. At every occasion, the National Anthem is always sung as a mark of recognition of one of our most important national symbols, and then the President is serenaded by his supporters with on your mandate.”

He said that nobody stops Peter Obi from adopting a song, even the old anthem, as his own song. But it must be sung either before or after the legally recognised National Anthem is given its due recognition.

“Again, as part of presidential protocol, whenever the President walks into an event or gets up to speak, the Police Band usually plays any instrumental to herald his presence or speech. They simply choose anyone they fancy. Check all videos of Presidents Obasanjo, Yar’Adua, Jonathan or Buhari entering the National Assembly or getting up to speak. It must be preceded by an instrumental from the Police Band. In this case, the Police Band sometimes plays the on your mandate instrumental to herald the President’s speech. This comes after the national anthem has been played,” he said.

Keyamo also noted that many states in Nigeria today have their own anthem, but it is always sung after the National Anthem has been rendered.

“Singing an outlawed anthem in place of a legally approved national anthem by the NDC is surely an expression of a desire to have a separate country, and that is an ingredient of a secessionist group,” Keyamo insisted.

World.title: Miss SA’s creative genius: Where is Werner Wessels now?
World.content:
Where is Werner Wessels now? Images via IG

South Africans are flooding Werner Wessels’s comment section with desperate calls for him to return to the Miss SA organisation as creative director.

The pageant guru made headlines in January 2025 after announcing he was stepping down from his long-running position.

During his 14-year tenure, Werner was credited with two Miss Universe wins, a Miss World and Miss Supranational victory, and several runner-up placements.



WHERE IS FORMER MISS SA CREATIVE DIRECTOR WERNER WESSELS NOW?

Over the weekend, a new Miss SA was crowned, 27-year-old media graduate and entrepreneur Tiyani Makamu, in a finale many claimed was not only underwhelming but substandard as a national pageant.

Pageant fans quickly flooded the comment section under the social media posts of Werner Wessels with pleas for him to return to Miss SA as creative director.

Werner resigned from the organisation in January 2025, just months before CEO Stephanie Weil stepped down. The organisation was acquired by the Motspe family, who have placed the emphasis on more investment and entrepreneurial skills and less on traditional pageant talent.

Fast forward to the present, and Werner is still doing what he loves in the pageant industry.

However, he has swapped Miss SA for an international pageant – Miss Supranational Organisation- as a brand development consultant.

He’s also worked on several pageant judging panels and offers his skills through services such as workshops and masterclasses, pageant consulting and training, photoshoot styling and creative direction, and much more. 

A CHILDHOOD DREAM

In his resignation statement, Werner Wessels revealed that his childhood dream was to work for the Miss SA organisation.

Since joining the Miss SA family in 2011, Werner has trained and led the following women to victory:

Rolene Strauss – crowned Miss World in 2014

Demi-Leigh Nel-Peters – crowned Miss Universe in 2017

Tamaryn Green- placed first runner-up in Miss Universe in 2018

Zozibini Tunzi – crowned Miss Universe in 2019

Lalela Mswane – crowned Miss Supranational in 2022 and placed second runner-up at Miss Universe, also in 2022

He shared: “This journey has been a dream come true, a journey filled with purpose, passion, and pride. I’m immensely proud of the work we have done and the impact I’ve made. I will forever be grateful to the Miss South Africa Organisation for entrusting me with the responsibility that comes with this role I created”.

Werner thanked Miss SA contestants, including past winners, who worked alongside him. He also vowed to continue to empower South African women.

He continued: “I have always said I want my career to be a love letter to women. A celebration of their courage, brilliance, and limitless potential. It is a tribute to South African women who, despite challenges, rise above and continue to inspire.

World.title: Zoalize speaks out over Miss SA shocker
World.content:
Zoalize Janse van Rensburg did not make the Miss SA Top 5. Images via IG

Zoalize Janse van Rensburg has spoken out for the first time after her premature exit from the Miss SA pageant over the weekend.

The 20-year-old beauty queen – a firm fan favourite – failed to make the Top 5.

Tiyani Makamu was crowned the new queen, alongside runner-ups, Cwenga Koyana Kotu-Rammopo and Lesego Khumo Nyathela.



ZOALIZE SPEAKS OUT AFTER MISS SHOCKER

On social media, many South African pageant fans have expressed their shock at Zoalize Janse van Rensburg’s disappointing exit from Miss SA.

The 20-year-old law student and published children’s book author was tipped to win the crown, ultimately taken by 27-year-old media graduate and entrepreneur Tiyani Makamu.

In a subsequent Instagram post, Zoalize congratulated Tiyani and thanked her followers for their support.

She shared: “Proud of what we did here, guys…Onto the next chapter”.

Zoalize did not respond to comments claiming that she was “robbed” of the crown.

EXPERIENCED BEAUTY QUEEN

Before her premature exit, Zoalize van Rensburg had been tipped as a favourite to win the Miss South Africa crown as she was a familiar face in the pageant world.

In 2023, she placed as first princess at the Miss World South Africa finale, and a year later re-entered and won the crown.

Last year, she represented South Africa at Miss World in India. Although she failed to make the Top 40, she won the Best Designer Dress award for Africa.

This year, Zoalize – a law student and published children’s book author – entered Miss South Africa for the first time.

At just 20 years old, she had a strong fan base and an even stronger advocacy campaign – Her Never Too Young to Advocate initiative focuses on youth empowerment, education and giving young people a voice.

She has also used her platform to speak at the 2024 United Nations International Social Justice Conference.

Zoalize has teased the “next chapter”.

World.title: Not just a crown: Miss SA misses out on luxury car and penthouse
World.content:
Miss SA winners will reportedly no longer recieve a luxury apartment or car as part of the prize package. Images via IG

It’s not just a crown that Miss SA 2026 Tiyani Makamu has forgone under the pageant’s new ownership. The new queen has also missed out on a posh penthouse and luxury car too, which were previously included in the prize package.

MISS SA NO LONGER INCLUDES CAR AND APARTMENT AS OFFICIAL PRIZES

Many South Africans have expressed their disappointment that Tiyani Makamu was not given the pageant-worthy crowning moment she deserved after receiving an underwhelming headpiece.

But that’s not all she’s missing out on. Under the new ownership of the Motsepe family, the new Miss SA’s prize package no longer includes the use of a luxury penthouse and car for the duration of her reign.



Up until this year, winners were granted the use of three-bedroom apartments in luxury estates, as well as various luxury Mercedes-Benz models.

According to Miss SA chairperson, Dr Precious Moloi-Motsepe, who took over ownership late last year, the pageant’s new model featured fewer luxury lifestyle benefits and more investment in leadership, entrepreneurship and measurable community impact.

“Our ambition is not simply to crown a woman, but to support a generation of women leaders who will help shape South Africa’s future”, Moloi-Motsepe told the public.



The Miss SA winner will also no longer compete in international pageants such as Miss World, Miss Universe, and Miss Supranational, and will focus more on domestic endeavours.

Miss SA used to have sponsors for Skin Care, Make-Up, Dental cover, clothing from YDE and Truworths I think, shoes, Mercedes car, an apartment, Jewellery from Pandora etc keep your crown!! #MissSA2026 — Yolanda_N2Lee (@symo_summer) November 14, 2026

WHAT HAS SHE WON?

Apart from the title of Miss SA, the new queen receives a R1 million cash prize and R500 000 in dedicated funding for her social-impact projects.



The first princess, Cwenga Koyana Kotu-Rammopo, receives a R250 000 cash award and a dedicated R150 000 Impact Fund, whilst the second princess, Lesego Khumo Nyathela, gets a R150 000 cash award and a dedicated R100 000 Impact Fund.

The top three contestants will also receive executive development opportunities, mentorship, wellness support, access to regional and international leadership networks, and the chance to lead initiatives in education, entrepreneurship, health, and youth development.

World.title: Palesa to Mowana: Miss SA crowns over the past decade [photos]
World.content:
Miss SA crowns over the past decade. Images via Miss SA

The Miss SA pageant has been trending on social media after it crowned its new queen, Tiyani Makama, with a headpiece resembling a party favour from a fast-food restaurant.

Unlike years before, the organisation – now run by the Motsepe family – failed to showcase the significant piece of jewellery, which is considered a symbol of national identity, heritage, and the responsibility that comes with representing the country.

WHAT HAPPENED TO MISS SA AND MOWANA?

Over the weekend, the Miss SA organisation trended online after chairperson, Dr Precious Moloi-Motsepe, gifted Tiyai Makema a makeshift crown and a cape.



The organisation later claimed that the headpiece was a “temporary ceremonial crown”, and invited designers to collaborate with it to create an official piece of jewellery.

#MissSA #MissSouthAfrica2026 this years crown 👑 is a joke though 😭, the Burger King Crown pic.twitter.com/78GgjzSXLO — Lady_L_ (@Lee_Raa_Tuu) November 15, 2026

Did you guys see the back of the crown for Miss South Africa 2026? Omg! Embarrassing 💔 pic.twitter.com/DF0W1KKKQr — Lihle (@Cebe_Lihle23) November 15, 2026

Later, Nungu Diamonds set the record straight, stating that Miss SA had failed to renew its sponsorship agreement to continue using its Mowana crown.

Nevertheless, it had offered the use of the crown to the pageant, in good faith, as negotiations continued.

However, Miss SA organisers decided against using the crown and were likely left scrambling for a replacement.



CROWNS OVER THE PAST DECADE…

Take a look at some of the crowns worn by Miss SA winners over the years…

Palesa : 2014 – 2015

Created by Jack Friedman Jewellers and Malcolm Kluk, the crown featured titanium designs of indigenous South African plants.

The crown was worn by Rolene Strauss and Liesl Laurie.

Enhle: 2016 – 2018

Have you heard? The #MissSA2016 crown has been named "Enhle". pic.twitter.com/0kXtkPzXbn — Miss South Africa (@Official_MissSA) February 28, 2016

American Swiss, in collaboration with Johan Louw, created a sterling silver crown featuring 2,500 cubic zirconia stones.

It was inspired by the Ndebele culture and was designed to resemble shooting stars.

It was worn by Zozibini Tunzi, Shudufhadzo Musida, Lalela Mswane and Ndavi Nokeri.

They say that a girl can't love anything more than diamonds, but we love our @AmericanSwiss created Buhle crown just a little bit more. pic.twitter.com/g8VPPfCePK — Miss South Africa (@Official_MissSA) November 11, 2019

Nungu Diamonds created the last crown – a silver frame featuring hundreds of diamonds, gemstones and cubic zirconia.

It was inspired by the baobab tree, indigenous to Limpopo and was worn by Natasha Joubert, Mia Le Roux and Qhawekazi Mazaleni.

World.title: A home you can buy for nothing goes on sale this week
World.content:
Home goes to auction with no reserve. Image for illustration purpose only. Image: Pexel

Of all the homes in South Africa going to auction this week, only one doesn’t have a reserve price.

This home in a middle-income suburb has no asking price.

Buyers could get the bargain of a lifetime: a home below R1 000.



But there are conditions.

A home you could buy for free

This week, a home in Welkom makes its way to a sheriff’s auction. The home doesn’t have a price.

Instead, bidders decide how much they’re willing to pay.

The sheriff has to accept the highest bid, regardless of the amount.

Of course, when the final hammer falls, the bidder will be responsible for paying the sheriff’s commission and settling the balance.

The auction will take place at the Welkom Sheriff’s Office: 366 Stateway, Doorn, Welkom, Free State, on Wednesday 26 November at 11:00.



The home going under the hammer is a 3-bedroom, 1-bathroom property with a garage on Van Wyk Louw Street in Jan Cilliers Park.

It’s a suburb where homes start at R650 000, and the average sale price is R1.1 million.

But this property is sold as-is, and buyers cannot inspect it before bidding.

The downside of buying at auction

Auction properties are routinely damaged by former occupants, and when the property isn’t vacant, buyers will have to spend money evicting the residents.

The buyer is also responsible for paying any municipal debt.

The home going to auction this week has R332 763 in municipal debt.

What is a no-reserve auction and what will you pay?

Before a bank can take a property to auction, it approaches the court.

In court, a judge sets a reserve price.

The reserve price is the lowest bid needed for a transfer of ownership.

To take possession of the home, a buyer must bid more than that price; otherwise, the bank becomes the owner.

But a no-reserve auction means there’s no minimum.

In theory, a bidder could bid R1 000.

If no one places a higher bid, they become the owner.

Because property owners can still owe the bank money after their home sells at auction, courts often place a reserve price, even if it’s R50 000.

World.title: Springbok and wife make miracle baby announcement
World.content:
Springbok Willie le Roux and his wife Holly Clare are expecting their first child. Images via IG

Springbok Willie Le Roux and his wife, Holly Clare, have announced their pregnancy, just months after sharing their struggle with infertility with the public.

The rugby player and the professional nutritionist – who wed two years ago – have been together since 2019.

WILLIE LE ROUX AND WIFE HOLLY CLARE ARE EXPECTING!

In their Instagram post, Willie Le Roux and wife Holly Clare went public with news of their first pregnancy.



“Some dreams take a little longer”, Holly shared.

The couple announced the news with a tennis-themed celebration with friends and family – including fellow Springbok Handre Pollard- at the Nieuwe Sion Estate near Franschhoek

The “Le Roux Open” featured a fun day of games and drinks between pals.



In February, Holly Clare shared her infertility struggle.

The Springbok WAG revealed she had suffered from “silent endometriosis” and had undergone an “exploratory” operation.

Holly Clare shared that the recovery was long and painful. However, she was using her platform to encourage women in similar situations to explore their options.



She shared at the time: “You don’t get given any promises in infertility, but the days you feel hopeful, you grab them. Children are the biggest blessing, and I am hopeful we will have our own one day”.

SPRINGBOK BABIES ON THE WAY

Willie le Roux is one of several Springboks whose wives are pregnant.

Others include Kwagga Smth – also set to become a first-time dad – and Jasper Wiese.



Other players like Makazole Mapimpi, RG Snyman and Vincent Tshituka have also recently welcomed their bundles of joy.

World.title: Pitso Mosimane on Lyle Foster’s quality
World.content:
Bafana Bafana coach Pitso Mosimane enjoyed the moment Foster chose to pass the ball to Relebohile Mofokeng instead of going for goal himself.

Mofokeng made no mistake with the opportunity, putting South Africa 2-1 ahead in the 76th minute at the Orlando Amstel Arena.

Foster had come on as a substitute in the second half and was making his first appearance under Mosimane.



PITSO MOSIMANE EXPLAINS FOSTER’S ASSIST

The Houston Dynamo striker had missed the coach’s opening three matches following his club move and returned to the squad after a difficult 2026 FIFA World Cup.

He had already come close to scoring after receiving a delivery from fellow substitute Puso Dithejane, but his effort went narrowly wide.

The next opportunity was different. Instead of trying to finish the move himself, Foster picked out Mofokeng. The striker then ran towards the technical area, where Mosimane embraced him.

Speaking to FARPost, Mosimane explained that the celebration was mainly about Foster’s decision to put the team first.

The coach felt the striker could have tried to score himself, but was pleased that he chose to give Mofokeng the opportunity.

“He showed me that he’s not here for himself. Normally, he would not pass that ball back… So he shows that he wants to play for the team and he shows that he’s not selfish. And that’s the embrace. I appreciate that.



Mosimane also praised Mofokeng’s finish, describing it as a quality goal.

He explained that while he would have been happy to see Foster score, the decision to create an opportunity for a teammate made the moment even better.

“Well-taken goal, world-class finish. I celebrated with Rele a lot. But more to Lyle, to say, ‘You really show that you want to play for the country,’ Mosimane added.

FOSTER SENDS A MESSAGE TO HIS TEAMMATES

Mosimane believes players show their attitude through what they do on the pitch.

For him, Foster’s decision was an example of how a striker can contribute to the team even when he has an opportunity to score himself.

“And that’s the only message you can send. You send the message on the pitch by your behaviour. The behaviour tells everything. If he scores without passing it, it’s good also. But it’s also sweeter when we score when he passes, because normally strikers don’t pass.”

Foster’s first appearance under Mosimane therefore gave the coach something positive to take from an otherwise disappointing evening.

Bafana had taken the lead through an own goal before Kenya fought back to level matters.

Mofokeng then restored South Africa’s advantage with his 76th-minute goal, but the hosts could not hold on.

Ryan Ogam scored a late equaliser to make it 2-2 and ensure Kenya left Soweto with a point.

The two teams will meet again in Nairobi on Tuesday, where Foster could get another opportunity to make an impression under the Bafana coach.

World.title: Explainer : Why your child may end up in a different school
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Gauteng Education is racing against time to place pupils in schools for the 2027 Academic Year.

While some households will receive a notification of a successful placement at a selected school, others will have to adjust to a whole new school.

Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile revealed that more than 77,000 applicants are yet to be placed, with Grade 8 pupils making up the largest share.

According to Maile, the department has identified more than 139,000 available spaces, but acknowledges that these are not necessarily in the schools or communities where demand is highest.

READ | Over 77,000 pupils in Gauteng remain unplaced

To date, 278 schools have reached capacity, including 174 primary schools and 104 secondary schools.

Pressure, according to Maile, remains concentrated in key urban centres, with the highest volumes recorded in districts located within the metropolitan municipalities of Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni.

This revelation by the provincial government may leave many parents, some still clinging to their phones for a notification, with one question: When and where will my child be placed?

Maile indicated that unplaced applicants who cannot be accommodated at these 278 schools are being transferred to the next closest school with available space.

“Gauteng does not experience uniform pressure across its schooling system. Some schools have available capacity, while others receive substantially more applications than they can reasonably accommodate. “Consequently, the challenge is not simply to count available spaces. It is to align those spaces with learner demand, geographical accessibility, school infrastructure and the practical circumstances of families,” Maile explained.

Maile said areas of high demand must be understood within the country's broader spatial and geo-social realities.

READ | Gauteng's 2027 school placement scramble

Not only does Gauteng have the highest population, but it also experiences a significant in-migration, with many turning to the province for employment or to improve their livelihoods.

These implications, according to the MEC, are evident in the province's schooling system.

“With an annual population growth of 1.6%, which outpaces the national average of 1.2 %, the province’s growth results in greater demand for schools, classrooms, educators, transport and associated infrastructure, "Maile added.

Maile said these pressure areas remain the primary focus for placement interventions, capacity optimisation and transfer management to maximise available spaces and reduce the number of unplaced applicants.

He said as of 13 November 2026, the Department commenced issuing transfer offers.

These offers are intended to help address outstanding placements, particularly where schools originally selected by applicants have reached capacity.

World.title: Gauteng's 2027 school placement scramble
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Parents and guardians of Grade 1 and Grade 8 pupils who have not been placed at their desired school due to capacity will be issued transfer offers to alternative schools.

They will then have seven days to accept or decline the offer.

This is according to Gauteng Education MEC Lebogang Maile, who gave an update on placement for the 2027 academic year, scholar transport as well as school funding.

Maile said the issuing of transfer offers began on 13 November and forms part of the admission process.

To date, more than 77,000 applicants are yet to be placed, with Grade 8 pupils making up the largest share.

READ | Over 77,000 pupils in Gauteng remain unplaced

The department says it has identified more than 139,000 available spaces, but acknowledges that these are not necessarily in the schools or communities where demand is highest.

“We understand that receiving an offer from a school other than a preferred institution may not be preferable. However, it is important to recognise that the Department must balance individual preferences with the available capacity of schools and the obligation to provide access to education across the province,” he said.

Parents and guardians who want to challenge placement outcomes will also be given an opportunity to raise objections and appeals through an established process.

An objection may be lodged within the prescribed seven-day period, with the Department required to consider and determine it within the applicable 14-day period.

World.title: The new Miss SA and the missing Mowana crown: Nungu Diamonds explains
World.content:
JOHANNESURG - Tiyani Makamu is South Africa's new beauty Queen.

But the 27-year-old's crowning on Saturday night was not without controversy, as social media attention turned to the crown on her head.

While many hailed the moment, others questioned why she did not wear the iconic Mowana crown by Nungu Diamonds.

Nungu Diamonds, which took note of the commentary, broke their silence on Sunday in a statement, explaining the crown and their relationship with the Miss South Africa Organisation.

READ | Miss SA 2025 | Qhawekazi Mazaleni crowned new queen

The fine jewellery company set the record straight, saying Nungu Diamonds did not design, craft, or supply the 2026 Miss South Africa crown.

This follows the non-renewal of a sponsorship agreement with the Miss South Africa Organisation for the 2026 pageant.

“Negotiations were conducted in good faith and continued into the final days before the finale; the parties were ultimately unable to reach a mutually beneficial agreement,” the statement read.

The company says its representatives had initially granted Miss South Africa permission to use the Mowana Crown at the finale on the understanding that sponsorship discussions would resume after the event.

However, it seems Miss SA opted otherwise

“The decision not to use the Mowana Crown rested solely with the Miss South Africa Organisation. We respect that decision,” Nungu Diamonds said.

The partnership between the Miss South Africa Organisation and Nungu Diamonds spans more than three years, starting in 2023.

Natasha Joubert became the first Miss South Africa to wear the Nungu Diamonds Mowana crown in 2023.

Miss South Africa 2024 Nia Le Roux and Miss South Africa 2025 Qhawe Mazaleni then wore it.

The crown, dubbed Mowana, is inspired by the baobab tree of Limpopo and stands as a symbol of strength, resilience and transformation

World.content:
Former Kenya Air Force officer and security analyst Mwenda Mbijiwe disappeared in June 2021. [File, Standard]

World.title: Thwake Dam project reaches 94pc completion
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Thwake Multipurpose Dam, which is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment.[File,Standard]

Thwake Dam is 94.2 per cent complete, with the government targeting April 2027 for water impoundment as residents seek a review of alleged construction-related damage claims.

Principal Secretary for Water and Sanitation Julius Korir told the National Assembly Departmental Committee on Blue Economy, Water and Irrigation that construction had reached 94.2 per cent.

The dam is being built at the confluence of the Athi and Thwake rivers along the Makueni-Kitui border. It is designed to provide water for domestic use, irrigation and electricity generation.

Martin Kimeu, a resident of Wote, said the project would improve access to water for farming in the region.

“Ukambani is fertile. Water has been the biggest impediment to the realization of our agricultural potential. Thwake Dam water is the clear solution to this,” he said.

Kimeu also defended the compensation process, saying he had followed the project since its inception and believed the exercise had been conducted properly.

Jacob Mwanzia, a resident of Madangi Village, said households in his area had been assessed and compensated. He argued that outstanding complaints should be addressed without delaying the project.

Mariam Mwikali, another resident, said assessments had been conducted on affected properties and residents given an opportunity to raise concerns.

However, some households have complained that construction-related blasting damaged their homes. Residents have reported cracks in walls, windows and foundations as well as dust, noise and ground vibrations.

In August 2026, residents from villages in Mavindini Ward, organised under the Thwake Dam Blasting-Affected Community Committee, sought an independent review by the African Development Bank (AfDB).

The residents alleged that some properties had been left out of assessments and compensation. They also sought access to assessment reports, photographs, measurements, valuation records and estimates for repairs or reconstruction.

A project official said the dam's safety department invited competitive bids for an independent assessment of properties potentially affected by blasting. Agile Consulting was selected to conduct the exercise.

The official said the consultant assessed 330 households within a two-kilometre radius of the construction site and submitted its report to the project implementation team. A large proportion of those assessed were satisfied with the exercise, the official added, without giving a breakdown.

Ben Mwongela, a director at Agile Consulting, said the assessment reviewed blasting records, vibration data and compliance with regulatory standards.

The exercise also involved documenting households, classifying structural defects and preparing bills of quantities and cost estimates for repairs or reconstruction, he said.

The AfDB conducted a field mission to the project between September 21 and 25, with its report published on October 21, 2026.

The bank's team, led by project task manager Nancy Ogal, met residents whose homes had been affected by blasting and identified outstanding health, safety, environmental and social issues, including homeowner grievances.

The bank called for timely compensation and continued monitoring of the project's environmental and social performance.

During a stakeholder engagement visit to Mavindini in October, Korir said the government had secured additional funding after the project experienced cash-flow constraints.

“When we ran short of cash, we engaged with our development partners, and they allocated additional funding, and this money will now go towards total completion of the project,” he said.

In June 2026, the AfDB approved additional financing of €68.39 million to support completion of the first phase, alongside funding from the Kenyan government.

The bank said the financing would support engineering refinements and safety works, including strengthening foundations, raising the dam and constructing two additional saddle dams.

The project has four phases. The first involves construction of the dam, while the subsequent phases cover hydropower generation, water supply and sanitation infrastructure, and irrigation.

The dam is approximately 80.5 metres high and has a planned storage capacity of 688 million cubic metres.

Once the water supply component is operational, the project is expected to provide 150,000 cubic metres of treated water daily to an estimated 1.3 million people in Makueni and Kitui counties and Konza Technopolis in Machakos County.

The irrigation scheme is designed to cover 40,000 hectares, equivalent to about 100,000 acres of agricultural land.

The project is also designed to generate 20 megawatts of hydropower.

The water supply, irrigation and hydropower components require infrastructure beyond the dam structure, including treatment and distribution networks and power generation facilities.

World.title: Love under watch: How technology is fuelling intimate partner abuse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Your enemy is closer than you think. For many Kenyan women, the person who demands a phone password, reads private messages and tracks their movements through a screen is not a faceless troll. He is the man they live with, or the one they used to.

That is the uncomfortable picture painted by the recently released 2025–2626 Kenya Mini Demographic and Health Survey (KMDHS), which measured technology-facilitated gender-based violence, abuse committed, assisted, aggravated or amplified through digital tools.

The most common form of abuse is online control, reported by 19 per cent of women, followed by hacking at 5 per cent and online sexual harassment or cyber sexual abuse at 3 per cent. Most of it happens on platforms women use every day.

“Sixty-seven per cent of women who experienced digital gender violence say it happened on social media, with Facebook cited by 59 per cent. Messaging apps follow at 47 per cent, with WhatsApp at 26 per cent. Among girls aged 15–19, 77 per cent reported abuse on social media.”
