World.title: Africa: How Africa Can Mobilize More Climate Finance
World.content:
Catherine Kaufman, the Green Climate Fundâs regional director for Africa, takes part in a panel discussion at COP31 in Antalya, TuÌrkiye, on November 11, 2026.

interview

The Green Climate Fund’s Africa director tells bird story agency at COP31 in Antalya that stronger local financial institutions, African investment and greater ownership of critical minerals would help the continent capture a bigger share of the green economy’s rewards.

Africa needs to look to its own banks, financial markets and institutions to fund its green economy, according to Catherine Koffman, the Green Climate Fund’s regional director for Africa.

The Green Climate Fund approved a record US$3.3 billion in new funding worldwide in 2026, bringing its global portfolio to US$22.3 billion. Koffman puts Africa’s cumulative share of that portfolio at US$8.3 billion, or about 37%. She says much of the Fund’s financing for Africa has historically been channelled through international institutions, leaving local financial institutions with a smaller role in managing those investments.

“We also need to work on investments on the continent by the continent, as opposed to seeking constantly partners from outside the continent,” she told bird story agency at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Koffman, who oversees the fund’s work across 54 African countries, said the GCF is increasingly helping African institutions develop the capacity to access and manage climate finance directly.

She also questioned whether Africa’s growing interest in processing its critical minerals would deliver lasting economic gains without greater ownership of the resources themselves.

She argued that African countries need to work together to protect their economic interests rather than pursue individual arrangements that weaken their bargaining power.

In this exclusive interview, Koffman discusses Africa’s share of global climate funding, the barriers facing African investors and what the continent needs to do to finance more of its own development.

The GCF has approved $3.3 billion in financing this year. How much of that is going to Africa, and how does the continent compare with other regions?

Generally, Africa enjoys about 40% of the whole book of the four regions. So it’s just under half.

The tally at year-end was about 37% of the total $3.3 billion. For the total $22.3 billion that we have funded in the last 10 years, Africa’s portion is $8.3 billion.

Which African countries are struggling most to secure climate investment, and what is holding them back?

Our ambition is always to look for countries that are underserved, that are not getting the funding. When we look at Africa, we also map which ones still need money from us, and we try to go to those ones.

West African countries tend to struggle a little bit more with access to finance. Actually, it’s not access, but rather implementation once they receive access.

I think that’s a language issue compared to Anglophone Africa, eastern and southern Africa.

Where do you see the greatest opportunities to attract more investment into Africa’s green economy?

How we invest in Africa is based on what the regional strategies are.

We look at the African Union, we look at the African Continental Free Trade Agreement Secretariat and, for instance, the greening of trade corridors. So there are a number of interventions on the continent that we follow because those already have regional mandates and regional agency. And then, of course, we are very much focused on regional and national priorities. That’s what drives us.

What attracts private sector investment, or other investors besides public finance, tends to be where revenues are a little easier to generate, like in the renewable energy space, the mitigation space.

However, for Africa, the focus is very much on adaptation. That is where GCF plays a significant role because funding is scarce. It’s harder to fund adaptation because there aren’t usually ready cash flows.

Notwithstanding this, $3.1 billion of our $8.3 billion African portfolio is private sector money.

African leaders often say the continent needs more climate finance. What should African countries themselves be doing differently to attract investment?

To catalyse more funding, we first of all need to make ourselves more investable.

But we also need to work on investments on the continent by the continent, as opposed to seeking constantly partners from outside the continent.

GCF is very much focused on strengthening local institutions to access finance. We provide different packages of grant funding to allow institutions to get equipped to manage climate finance.

For me, the one answer is to stop being externally focused and focus on strengthening our own institutions.

Most of our funding in the past has gone through international institutions. Eighty percent of our funding has gone to international institutions into the continent.

What we are doing more and more is helping the ones that are based in the region.

Beyond access to international funding, what would make African countries more attractive to investors?

Stronger institutions, which means, from a public sector perspective, stronger governance, stronger fiduciary management and enterprise risk management.

Stronger institutions, stronger financial systems, so you can attract more capital and diversity of capital into the market.

If you’ve got strong financial markets, you have more liquidity. You can bring in green bonds. You can bring in guarantee structures. You can have better ways of dealing with local currency risk or foreign exchange risk.

We must also have people investing in early-stage project preparation capital, early-stage high-risk capital that will convert projects from ideas into actual investable pipelines.

GCF is great in that sense because we also match other financial institutions with blended instruments.

We can provide what multilateral development banks provide in terms of loans and guarantees. We can also provide equity capital, including really junior capital, which many development finance institutions cannot provide.

Africa has vast reserves of minerals needed for the global energy transition. How can the continent use those resources to secure a greater share of the wealth they generate?

As GCF, we provide assistance to countries through readiness funding. Readiness is a grant that allows you to start thinking about what your policy should look like for climate finance.

It could help countries in the critical minerals space.

What should our policies look like? How should we make sure that we determine a future which creates livelihoods, jobs and prosperity for us?

GCF can unlock that through readiness funding.

African countries often speak of negotiating together, yet many continue to strike individual deals over their resources. Is that weakening the continent’s bargaining power?

Close 

Koffman, speaking in a personal capacity: As an African, I think it’s extremely important that we work together as a continent to determine policies that benefit all of us equally, and not divide-and-conquer policies.

It’s also important that we look beyond beneficiation. We think if we get beneficiation, that’s great. No, no, no. You must have ownership of your own resources.

Beneficiation is a byproduct of ownership. Otherwise, you’re always working for somebody else.

With the current geopolitical tensions and pressure on international climate funding, do you expect Africa’s share of investment to grow?

The geopolitics are difficult. They are challenging, as you are aware, but for me that is just an opportunity.

The geopolitics really woke Africa up to some extent.

How do we become more self-sufficient? How do we contribute more towards our own climate finance future?

Last night, at the GCF event, one of the developing countries that we fund actually made a contribution itself. It made a pledge for its own climate finance.

That was the Solomon Islands.

It wasn’t much, around $400,000. Our contributors normally contribute hundreds of millions or billions.

But there is a signal that developing countries are making at the moment. They are saying that we are responsible for our climate ambition and our climate future.

We want to be equal partners, not just recipients, but equal partners in the investment of our future.

World.title: Africa: Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games - After The Historic Achievement, The Challenge of a Lasting Legacy for Africa
World.content:
The first Youth Olympic Games held on the African continent, the Dakar 2026 YOG, concluded on November 13th with a record praised by leaders of the Olympic movement. Beyond the organizational success and popular enthusiasm, Senegal and its partners now face a major challenge: transforming this historic first into an engine of sporting, economic, and social development. Youth training, job creation, infrastructure development, and the emergence of new talent are the main priorities for the post-Games period.

Senegal is preparing to close a historic chapter in world sport. For two weeks, from October 31 to November 13, 2026, Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly hosted the first Youth Olympic Games (YOG) organized in Africa, placing the continent at the center of attention of the international Olympic movement.

With approximately 2,700 young athletes representing 204 National Olympic Committees, 25 competitive sports, ten engagement sports and 153 medal-winning events, this fourth edition of the Summer Youth Olympic Games was an exceptional showcase for Senegal and, beyond, for the entire African continent.

But behind the sporting performances, the ceremonies and the popular mobilization, a question now arises: how to make Dakar 2026 more than just a successful event and ensure its lasting impact on the development of Africa?

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

This question was a major theme of the joint press conference of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and the Organising Committee of the Youth Olympic Games (COJOJ), held on November 12 in Diamniadio.

IOC President Kirsty Coventry hailed the event as a "100% organizational success," stating that expectations had been exceeded. She particularly encouraged the continent to build on this experience.

"My wish is that Africa and the continent become fully aware of their potential. It is now up to us to make it a reality," she said.

A message that sums up the challenge of the post-Dakar 2026 era: to transform the international recognition acquired during the Games into concrete prospects for new African generations.

An Olympic first that changes the way we see Africa

By hosting an Olympic event of this magnitude, Senegal has taken a symbolic step in the history of African sport. Long absent from the map of host countries for Olympic competitions, the continent has demonstrated its ability to mobilize infrastructure, skills, and human resources around a major international event.

For the IOC's executive director of the Olympic Games, Christophe Dubi, one of the most striking elements of this edition will remain the welcome given to foreign delegations and the enthusiasm of the Senegalese people.

From Dakar to Saly, via Diamniadio, the mobilization of the public helped to give these Games a popular dimension, beyond just the competition venues.

This success also sends a signal to other African countries that aspire to host major international sporting events.

However, this does not mean that all organizational and financial obstacles have been removed. The Senegalese experience will need to be analyzed to identify financing, governance, and infrastructure management models that could be replicated elsewhere on the continent.

The stakes thus go beyond mere symbolic recognition: it is about making Dakar 2026 a reference for the organization of future sporting events in Africa.

New talents and disciplines to develop

From a sporting perspective, the Youth Olympic Games provided an international platform for a new generation of African athletes, while also allowing the Senegalese public to discover disciplines that are still underdeveloped in the country.

The chairman of the IOC Coordination Commission for Dakar 2026, Humphrey Kayange, particularly emphasized the interest generated by the sporting activities organized on the Corniche of Dakar.

These discovery spaces have allowed many young people to try out different sports and consider new opportunities for involvement.

But this enthusiasm will need to be maintained.

For Humphrey Kayange, national sports federations now have an essential role to play in order to extend this momentum, structure emerging disciplines and facilitate their access for young people.

The issue of talent identification and support is another major challenge. Kirsty Coventry pointed out that approximately 15% of participants in the Youth Olympic Games go on to compete in the Olympic Games.

This proportion highlights the role that the Youth Olympic Games can play in preparing future generations of elite athletes.

For Africa, where many young athletes still face difficulties accessing equipment, qualified coaches and funding, the continuity of training programs will be crucial.

The true sporting success of Dakar 2026 will therefore not be measured solely by the number of medals won, but also by the ability of African countries to support the talents revealed during the Games.

Training and employment: the economic legacy takes shape

Beyond sport, one of the most promising achievements of Dakar 2026 concerns the development of professional skills.

The Dakar 2026 Learning Academy, set up to prepare young professionals for jobs related to the organization of major events, has trained more than 300 participants, from 21 African nationalities, according to information provided by the IOC.

This program is a concrete example of how an international sporting competition can contribute to strengthening human capital.

Event management, operational coordination, communication, logistics and sports organization represent all areas in which the skills acquired could be valued after the Games.

The challenge now is to transform these training programs into sustainable career opportunities.

The president of the COJOJ, Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye, notably mentioned discussions with the World Bank regarding employment prospects and integration of young people.

Presented in Washington before the Games, the Learning Academy reportedly attracted the interest of the international financial institution, particularly for its potential in terms of training and employability.

In this context, closer ties have been envisaged with the World Bank's regional SIRA program, dedicated to skills development and access to employment.

These discussions, however, have yet to be finalized. No definitive funding has been announced at this stage.

For Senegal, the sustainability of this type of program could contribute to developing a pool of African professionals capable of intervening in the organization of sporting, cultural and institutional events on an international scale.

Infrastructure to be valued beyond the Games

Another central question of the Olympic legacy: the future of the sports facilities mobilized or modernized for Dakar 2026.

Organizing the Youth Olympic Games required investments in infrastructure and reception facilities, particularly in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly.

While this equipment has met the requirements of the competition, its future use will represent a real test for public authorities and sports federations.

International experience shows that the legacy of major sporting events largely depends on the ability of host countries to ensure the maintenance, financing and accessibility of facilities after the competitions.

For Senegal, several perspectives could be explored: development of training centers, organization of regional competitions, hosting of international internships and opening of infrastructure to schools and sports associations.

The development of these facilities could also contribute to the development of a local sports economy, by promoting training activities, event services, sports tourism and related jobs.

These potential benefits will, however, need to be accompanied by appropriate management mechanisms and a long-term financing strategy.

Sport as a response to the social challenges facing youth

Beyond infrastructure and performance, Senegalese officials also want to inscribe the legacy of the YOG in a social perspective.

Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye thus mentioned a project to create sports academies in several coastal localities, including Saint-Louis, Kayar and Rufisque.

This initiative aims to offer young people new opportunities for training, guidance and integration through sport.

It takes on a particular dimension in areas facing youth unemployment, economic insecurity and perilous departures by sea.

The ambition would be to make sport a tool for support and opening up towards professional prospects, possibly involving public actors, federations and development partners.

The project remains at a design stage and will need to specify its financing arrangements, its operating model and the target audiences.

Its success will also depend on its ability to combine sports practice with education, vocational training and access to employment.

Because while sport can play an important role in social inclusion, it cannot, on its own, address the structural difficulties faced by African youth.

A legacy to be built on a continental scale

The organization of the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games finally raises the question of African sports cooperation.

Close 

By bringing together athletes, coaches, officials and professionals from different countries, the Games have created opportunities for exchange and collaboration that can continue after the competition.

This dynamic could promote the sharing of expertise between federations, the implementation of regional training programs and the development of partnerships around emerging sports disciplines.

The participation of young professionals of several African nationalities in the Learning Academy already illustrates this continental dimension.

But to produce lasting effects, these initiatives will need to be part of coordinated sports policies, supported by long-term institutional funding and commitments.

Africa has significant demographic and sporting potential. However, its development requires regular investments in local infrastructure, coach training, athlete support, and the professionalization of sports-related jobs.

Dakar 2026 could thus serve as a starting point for a broader reflection on the place of sport in African development strategies.

After the celebration, the test of the results

As the first Youth Olympic Games held in Africa come to a close, Senegal can boast of international recognition and popular mobilization that have marked this edition.

But the Olympic legacy is not decreed at the end of a closing ceremony. It is built over time, through public policies, sustained investments and programs capable of producing measurable results.

How many young people trained by the Learning Academy will find employment? How will the sports facilities be used? Will the disciplines discovered during the Games find a place in national federations? Will the sports academy projects actually come to fruition?

These are all questions that the coming years will need to answer.

Dakar 2026 will have demonstrated that Africa can host a major international Olympic event. The next challenge will be to prove that such an event can also contribute sustainably to the economic, social, and sporting transformation of the continent.

Only under this condition will the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games be able to transcend its status as a historic first and become a true legacy for future generations.

This article was originally published in French

World.title: South Africa: Africa's Waste Pickers Demand Recognition in Climate Action
World.content:
As COP31 puts zero waste on the climate agenda, waste pickers across Africa say the continent's circular-economy transition cannot succeed without the people who already recover and recycle much of what it throws away.

Waste is the third-largest source of human-caused methane emissions, accounting for nearly 20% of the global total, yet the sector remains underfunded and inadequately monitored.

The UN Environment Programme estimated that municipal solid waste reached 2.1 billion tonnes in 2023 and will be at 3.8 billion tonnes by 2050. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), improved waste management, through a circular economy and better treatment technologies, has the potential to make a substantial contribution to reductions in national GHG emissions.



Under its Global Climate Action Agenda, COP31 is championing the Zero Waste initiative, which seeks to unlock the climate potential of waste management through scalable circular economy solutions. The initiative is focused on preventing food waste, moving towards circular economy solutions that turn waste into resources, and encouraging countries to include waste-related methane reductions in their updated Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs). The aim is to prevent emissions at source and make waste management an integral part of national climate strategies.

The need is greatest in low-income countries, where 97% of waste is openly dumped or burned. Uncontrolled dumpsites and open burning threaten communities, contaminate water and release climate pollutants, and without knowing where these sites are, how much waste they receive and what they emit, effective intervention is extremely difficult. As COP31 pushes countries to include waste methane in their climate plans, some African investors say the continent has a chance to turn waste into an economic resource.

Waste pickers say they must be part of that shift.

Across Africa, waste pickers and reclaimers collect, sort and recover recyclable materials that would otherwise end up in landfills, rivers or the environment. Many still work with limited formal recognition, social protection, and decent working conditions. Their inclusion is therefore emerging as a key question in discussions about Africa's zero-waste future. A transition to more sustainable waste management systems, advocates argue, must build on the knowledge and contribution of existing waste workers rather than exclude them.

For the International Alliance of Waste Pickers (IAWP), the success of such initiatives will depend in part on whether the people already driving recycling and resource recovery are recognised as essential partners in their implementation.

In an interview, Eva Mokoena of South Africa's African Reclaimers Organisation (ARO) discusses the role of waste pickers in climate action, the opportunities presented by the Zero Waste Districts initiative, and the changes needed to secure their place in Africa's transition to a circular economy.

Waste is often seen as an environmental and sanitation problem, but it is increasingly recognised as a major climate challenge. Why does tackling waste matter for the fight against climate change, and what role can zero waste play in reducing emissions?

Waste is a climate issue because what we throw away does not disappear. Organic waste buried in landfills and dumpsites rots without oxygen and releases methane, a gas that traps far more heat than carbon dioxide in the short term. Open burning of waste adds black carbon and toxic smoke to the air our communities breathe. Every item that is landfilled or burnt also means new materials must be extracted, manufactured, and transported to replace it.

Zero waste addresses all of these at once. When materials are separated at source, recovered, reused and recycled, and when organic waste is composted or turned into biogas, methane from landfills falls and the demand for virgin materials drops. This is one of the fastest and most affordable ways to reduce emissions.

The key to making it work is already on the ground. Waste pickers and reclaimers are the people removing waste from landfills, rivers, and streams every day. With proper recognition, equipment, and collaboration from governments, municipalities, and residents, they can multiply the climate impact they already deliver.

Waste is often overlooked in climate talks, yet food waste and landfills are major sources of greenhouse-gas emissions, especially methane. What practical policies and local actions would most effectively reduce food waste and keep organic waste out of landfills?

The most effective policies are the ones that recognise and include waste pickers and reclaimers. They are the frontline educators of their communities: they already teach residents to separate and recycle what they buy and eat. Governments and policymakers should write waste pickers into waste and climate legislation, so that this work is formally recognised, supported and paid for.

In practice, this means separation at source, in households, markets and businesses before it reaches the landfill, with waste pickers leading door-to-door awareness and collection.

In logistics, waste picker organisations need access to land, storage facilities and transport, so that organic material can be collected, stored and processed close to where it is generated. Local processing of food waste should be turned into compost, manure and biogas through community-run facilities, creating useful products and income instead of methane.

Investment in people is also important. Incubating reclaimer cooperatives, with full access to logistics and infrastructure, is what turns good policy into results.

If we continue to ignore the people on the ground, we will keep struggling. If we invest in them, organic waste can become a resource for our communities.

How can African governments make waste reduction and the circular economy a more central part of their national climate policies?

Governments can start by recognising who already runs Africa's circular economy. Waste pickers and reclaimers are unrecognised heroes: many spend their own time and resources recovering materials and cleaning public spaces without pay or protection. Bringing them into national climate policy means three things.

First, recognition in law. National climate plans, including Nationally Determined Contributions, and waste management legislation should name waste pickers as essential service providers and set out their rights, their role and how they will be paid.

Second, a seat at the table. Waste picker organisations should take part in designing, implementing and monitoring these policies. When waste pickers help shape the rules, the rules work on the ground, and waste pickers gain the recognition and confidence to expand their work.

Third, real support. Recognition has to come with resources: equipment, infrastructure, social protection and fair payment for the services waste pickers provide to cities and to the climate.

Looking at initiatives such as Zero Waste Districts and the 1x100 campaign, how can these programmes translate into tangible benefits for African communities, from cleaner cities and reduced landfill waste to decent jobs and better livelihoods for waste pickers?

These programmes deliver real benefits when everybody works together: governments, municipalities, residents, the private sector and waste picker organisations. Waste pickers are already on the ground, in every neighbourhood and in every landfill. What makes the difference is giving them space, resources and a central role.

Education is the most important key. With educational tools, training and empowerment, waste pickers can lead awareness campaigns, help households separate their waste, and recover a much wider range of materials at once. The result is cleaner streets, less waste reaching landfills and rivers, and recycling that actually works.

For waste pickers, the benefit must be decent work: formal contracts, fair payment for collection and recovery services, safe working conditions and social protection. When district programmes are built around existing waste picker cooperatives, the jobs and income they create stay in the community.

Two African nations that have joined the Zero Waste Districts programme are Ghana and Kenya. What are the biggest waste management challenges these countries are hoping to address, and what makes the district-level approach different from previous efforts?

What makes the district-level approach different is that it starts from the community and from the organisations that already exist, rather than from large, centralised projects designed far away from the people who manage waste every day. Our affiliates in both countries describe it in these terms.

In Ghana, the Green Waste Pickers Cooperative Society Limited and the Kpone Landfill Waste Pickers Association are supporting community-led circular initiatives that build on existing cooperatives. These cooperatives drive the process of diverting waste at source, adopt measures to pre-process materials, and lead environmental campaigns in their communities.

In Kenya, the Nakuru County Waste Pickers Association is advancing zero waste through waste reduction, reuse, recycling and waste picking, alongside community-led initiatives, progressive policies and the promotion of a circular economy.

In both cases, the district becomes the unit where waste pickers, residents and local authorities can work side by side, and where results can be seen and measured.

Many African cities are still grappling with poor waste collection, overflowing landfills, and very limited recycling. What kind of investment and what kind of partnerships are required to build effective waste management and recycling systems across the continent?

Close 

The investment that works is investment in the people already doing the job. Instead of expensive systems that bypass or displace waste pickers, African cities should incubate reclaimer and waste picker cooperatives and give them full access to what they need.

In infrastructure, sorting centres, storage space and land can help make the work safer. In logistics, vehicles and equipment to collect and move materials efficiently are needed. Processing capacity with facilities to recycle materials and to turn food waste into compost, manure and biogas is necessary. Fair contracts are also a key issue to provide payments from municipalities for the collection and recovery services waste pickers provide.

The partnerships that work are inclusive ones. Municipalities, national governments, producers, funders and residents should partner directly with waste picker organisations, as equals and from the design stage. If we keep ignoring the people on the ground, cities will keep struggling with the same problems. If we invest in them, Africa can build recycling systems that are effective, fair and locally owned.

Given that COP31 is placing such a strong emphasis on zero waste, what specific commitments should African countries be demanding in order to ensure that waste reduction actually becomes a measurable element of climate action rather than just another one of the international promises?

African countries should demand commitments that reach the ground, not only the negotiating rooms. In particular, direct funding for equipment and machinery that allows waste pickers and reclaimers to recover and recycle more materials, including food waste.

Educational tools must also be designed with waste pickers and be easy to use for both reclaimers and residents, so that separation at source becomes everyday practice in every household.

Formal recognition of waste pickers in national climate plans and waste policies, with a guaranteed role in their implementation and measurable targets for diverting organic and recyclable waste from landfills, monitored with the participation of waste picker organisations, are commitments that promote long-term climate solutions.

Waste pickers are good at what we do, and we make sure that everyone we work with understands our livelihoods on the streets and in the landfills, and the important role we play. Climate commitments on waste will only become real when they are built with us.

World.title: Nigeria: Index Ebola Case - Swiss Diplomat's Wife Recovers, Discharged From Hospital
World.content:
Nigeriaâs Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) issued a public health advisory following the countryâs confirmed Ebola case.

Abuja — Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) has said that the Nigeria's Ebola index case- Swiss diplomat's wife has recovered and discharged from hospital in Switzerland.

The disease intervention centre had confirmed the infection on October 20, 2026 after the patient's blood samples tested positive at the Abuja Reference Laboratory.

After receiving preliminary treatment at an undisclosed private hospital in Abuja, she and her husband were subsequently medically evacuated to Switzerland with an air ambulance on October 26, 2026.

Addressing journalists in his office in Abuja on Friday, NCDC Director General, Dr. Jide Idris, said the Swiss authorities had announced the recovery and discharge of the woman after testing negative.

He said index case tested negative after receiving treatment in an isolation facility in Switzerland.

World.title: South Africa: Joburg Turns Up the Heat As Residents Wait for Relief
World.content:
Outdoor workers should take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

Cooler weather and thunderstorms are expected over the weekend, offering some relief from the heat.

Johannesburg residents face another scorching day on Friday, with emergency services urging people to drink water, take breaks and stay out of the midday sun.

The City of Johannesburg's Emergency Management Services says extremely hot conditions are expected to continue across much of the city. Outdoor workers have been urged to take regular breaks and residents should avoid direct sunlight between 11am and 3pm.

The South African Weather Service's heatwave advisory issued earlier this week included southern Gauteng, with persistently high temperatures expected until Friday, 13 November.



But some relief could arrive over the weekend.

Weather service senior forecaster Tokelo Chiloane said cooler conditions, accompanied by thunderstorms and thundershowers, are expected over the weekend.

Until then, residents have been urged to protect themselves from the heat.

"Residents are urged to stay hydrated, drink lots of water, avoid direct sunlight especially between 11h00 and 15h00 in the afternoon," Johannesburg emergency services spokesperson Robert Mulaudzi said earlier this week.

For street traders, gardeners, construction workers and others spending hours outside, regular breaks in a cool or shaded place are especially important.

The World Health Organization says older people, babies, outdoor workers and people with existing medical conditions face greater risks during hot weather. Residents should also check on relatives and neighbours who live alone.

Keeping cool does not have to mean switching on an air conditioner. The organisation recommends loose, light clothing, cool showers and wetting the skin with a damp cloth. Drink water regularly and avoid alcohol.

Never leave children, dependent adults or pets alone in a parked vehicle, even while running a quick errand.

Parents have also been warned to watch children seeking somewhere to cool off.

Mulaudzi urged families to keep young children away from dams and river streams to prevent drownings.

Heat illness needs prompt attention. Dizziness, weakness, intense thirst and headaches are signs to move into a cool place and drink water.

Confusion, seizures or a loss of consciousness require urgent medical help. Move the person into shade or a cool room and use cold, wet cloths to help cool them while waiting for assistance.

Close 

For life-threatening emergencies in Johannesburg, call 011 375 5911. The city says this number connects residents to emergency assistance, including ambulance and fire services.

World.title: Africa: Africa Made It: Turning Africa's Cotton Wealth into Jobs, Industry and Economic Power
World.content:
Africa Made It campaign was launched in Lagos, Nigeria, aiming to drive Africa's industrial sovereignty under the theme, "Power, Protect and Purchase."

Africa produces cotton, inspires global fashion and boasts a vibrant creative industry. Yet much of the economic value generated from these resources is captured beyond the continent. Launched during CANEX WKND 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria, the Africa Made It campaign seeks to change that narrative by promoting local manufacturing, strengthening Africa’s textile value chain and encouraging consumers to support African-made products.

Africa’s fashion and textile industries hold considerable potential to drive industrialisation, create employment and strengthen the continent’s economic independence. However, despite its abundant natural resources and creative talent, Africa continues to capture only a limited share of the value generated by its cotton and fashion industries.

The Africa Made It campaign, launched during the Creative Africa Nexus (CANEX) WKND 2026 in Lagos, aims to address this imbalance by encouraging African countries to move beyond exporting raw cotton and invest in a fully integrated fibre-to-fashion value chain.

Built around three pillars “Power, Protect and Purchase” the campaign seeks to mobilise governments, investors, manufacturers, fashion brands and consumers to strengthen local production and retain more economic value within Africa.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The initiative highlights the potential of the sector to contribute an estimated US$34 billion annually to Africa’s GDP through increased domestic textile and garment production.

In an interview with AllAfrica’s Nontobeko Mlambo, Abimbola Ogundairo, Senior Consultant at Africa Practice, discusses the campaign’s ambitions, the challenges facing Africa’s textile industry and the lessons other African countries can draw from Benin’s emerging manufacturing sector.

What inspired the Africa Made It campaign, and why is it important for the continent?

Africa Made It is a movement designed to showcase the investment potential of African-made brands, starting with the fashion industry.

Its significance lies in a challenge we have faced for decades: Africa contributes enormous value to the global economy but captures very little of the wealth generated from its resources.

Take cotton, for example. Thirty-seven of Africa’s 54 countries produce cotton, yet the continent captures less than 2% of the global cotton economy. And cotton is only one example. The same challenge exists in other sectors, including cocoa and gold.

Africa Made It aims to bring these conversations together and address the missing links in our value chains, particularly the lack of local processing and manufacturing capacity. We want to engage policymakers, development institutions, investors, businesses and other stakeholders across the value chain to explore how we can connect these different elements.

The objective is to ensure that more of the value Africa produces remains on the continent rather than being exported for others to benefit from.

How does the campaign align with CANEX’s broader ambition to develop Africa’s cultural and creative industries?

Platforms such as CANEX are incredibly important because the creative industries have long been overlooked as sources of economic value and cultural identity. Across Africa, young people are achieving remarkable things in fashion, music, art and other creative sectors, often despite limited institutional support.

Africa already exports enormous cultural influence and creative talent. Our fashion, music and artistic expressions have a global presence. The question is whether we have the mechanisms in place to capture the economic value associated with that influence.

CANEX provides an opportunity to bring the right stakeholders together. It allows creatives to showcase their achievements while engaging directly with policymakers, investors and institutions capable of providing the infrastructure, financing and policies they need.

What makes these platforms particularly valuable is their ability to move the conversation beyond isolated initiatives towards coordinated, sustainable solutions. We need to institutionalise the support systems that allow creative businesses to grow and ensure that the economic benefits generated by African creativity remain within the continent.

What are the campaign’s main objectives, and what changes does it hope to bring to Africa’s fashion and textile industries?

The campaign aims to unlock the enormous economic potential of Africa’s cotton-to-fashion value chain.

Research estimates that an investment of approximately US$1.8 billion across the continent could help create up to two million permanent jobs and generate US$33 billion in annual household income. For African countries seeking to accelerate industrialisation, increase revenue and create employment, this represents a significant opportunity.

Benin provides an interesting example. Through the development of the Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone, the country has begun transforming its cotton industry.

According to the figures we have seen, Benin has moved from exporting approximately 90% of its raw cotton towards processing around 30% locally. The country is also reportedly exporting about 10 million garments annually and aims to create 300,000 permanent jobs by 2030.

These developments demonstrate what can be achieved when investment, infrastructure and industrial policy are aligned. This is why our campaign is built around three pillars: Power, Protect and Purchase.

Power means providing African manufacturers and businesses with the energy, financing and infrastructure they need to operate and expand.

Protect focuses on creating fair trade policies and addressing illicit imports and other practices that undermine the competitiveness of local industries.

Purchase is about encouraging governments, businesses and consumers to buy African-made products.

We must move away from the assumption that foreign products are inherently better. Buying African is not only an expression of cultural identity and pride. It is also an economic decision that supports local businesses, creates employment and strengthens our economies. Ultimately, we want to build a movement that brings all stakeholders together to close the gaps in Africa’s manufacturing value chain.

Why is it important for African consumers to recognise, support and take pride in locally made fashion?

As a Nigerian, I grew up in a society where people take enormous pride in wearing traditional clothing and expressing their cultural identity. For many Nigerians, wearing local styles is already part of everyday life. However, there is an important economic dimension to this conversation.

We may proudly wear African prints and traditional fabrics without realising that some of these materials are manufactured outside the continent. Ankara, for example, is widely associated with African fashion and identity, yet much of the fabric is produced elsewhere.

This raises an important question: when we celebrate our cultural identity through fashion, are we also supporting the local industries and workers who should benefit from it?

Cultural pride should translate into economic empowerment. We need to ensure that the clothes we wear and the products we celebrate contribute to employment, manufacturing and wealth creation within our own countries.

Africa has contributed immense cultural and economic value to the world for generations. We should also be able to capture the financial benefits of that contribution. We do not want to become a continent that proudly wears its cultural identity without benefiting economically from it. We can do both: celebrate who we are and build industries that create prosperity for our people. That is the thinking behind Power, Protect and Purchase.

What specific activities, partnerships or initiatives are needed to turn the campaign’s ambitions into tangible results?

Everyone has a role to play in building a sustainable African fashion and textile industry. The value chain begins with cotton farmers, who need access to agricultural inputs, technical skills and resources to improve the quality and productivity of their crops. It extends to processing facilities, storage, transportation, manufacturing infrastructure and the policies required to attract investment.

Governments have a responsibility to create enabling environments, while investors must recognise the opportunities available across the industry. Fashion businesses also have an important role. They should consider whether they are sourcing materials locally, working with African manufacturers and supporting artisans within their communities. The media and other storytellers can help raise awareness of the industry's potential and highlight successful initiatives. Development institutions and international investors also have opportunities to contribute.

Regional integration is particularly important.

The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) provides a framework for strengthening trade and industrial cooperation across African countries. For example, cotton could be grown in Nigeria, processed in Benin and transformed into finished garments elsewhere in the region. Different countries could contribute at various stages of production, allowing more of the economic value to circulate within Africa.

We should also recognise that fashion extends beyond clothing. Technology is creating new opportunities, including the use of artificial intelligence to improve garment design, sizing and the consumer experience.

The industry encompasses accessories, innovation, logistics and many other activities. Our challenge is to connect these different elements and ensure that businesses have access to the resources they need to grow.

You have highlighted Benin as a success story. What lessons can other African countries learn from its experience?

Close 

One of the most important lessons from Benin is the value of creating an environment that encourages private investment. The Glo-Djigbé Industrial Zone demonstrates how cooperation between the public and private sectors can support industrial development. The government has played a role in facilitating investment and establishing conditions that encourage manufacturing. Such partnerships are important because building a textile industry requires substantial investment in infrastructure, energy, transport and production facilities.

Benin’s experience also shows the importance of moving beyond the export of raw materials towards local processing and the production of finished goods. The country is now reportedly exporting approximately 10 million garments annually. Other African countries can learn from this approach by developing policies that attract investors, encourage industrial partnerships and support local manufacturers. Ultimately, the lesson is that industrial transformation requires coordination, long-term commitment and a willingness to invest in domestic value creation.

How will you measure the success of the Africa Made It campaign?

The campaign is designed to raise awareness, encourage dialogue and connect stakeholders across Africa’s cotton-to-fashion value chain. In the short term, success will mean generating greater recognition of the opportunities available in the sector.

We want to see more conversations involving policymakers, investors, development institutions, manufacturers and fashion businesses. We also want these discussions to lead to practical collaboration. That means identifying where investment is needed, which policies require reform and how institutions can work together to support local businesses.

African entrepreneurs should not have to succeed despite structural obstacles. They should be able to thrive because the right infrastructure, policies and institutional support are in place. In the longer term, success will be measured by tangible economic outcomes. We want to see investment mobilised, manufacturing capacity expanded and sustainable employment created.

The estimated US$1.8 billion in investment and the potential US$33 billion in annual household income illustrate the scale of the opportunity.

If African countries, investors and businesses work together, we can build stronger industrial value chains and ensure that more of the wealth generated by Africa’s resources and creativity benefits African people. That is the transformation Africa Made It hopes to achieve.

World.title: Ethiopia: Mekelle Residents Call for Sustained Federal Govt Efforts to Advance Reforms in Tigray
World.content:
Addis Ababa — Residents of Mekelle have urged the Federal Government to sustain and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development efforts in Tigray region.

The inhabitants further emphasized the need for consolidating progress toward lasting peace, stability and prosperity in the region.

The call was made during a consultative forum of Mekelle residents, presided over by Chief of Staff of the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF), Field Marshal Birhanu Jula.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Speaking at the gathering, Field Marshal Birhanu said the defunct TPLF faction had aligned itself with the so-called "Tsimdo" group, an alliance orchestrated by Ethiopia's historical adversaries to wage war against the country.

He said his engagement with residents was aimed at fostering dialogue, strengthening cooperation and encouraging collective efforts to ensure lasting peace and stability in Tigray region.

During the discussions, residents underscored their strong desire to see an end to conflict, identifying peace, security and sustainable development as their foremost priorities.

They called for the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure, expanded employment opportunities for young people and the restoration of security to enable communities to resume normal life without fear.

"Our foremost priorities are the reconstruction of critical infrastructure, the creation of meaningful employment opportunities for our youth, and the restoration of security so that citizens can go about their daily lives in peace," participants said.

Residents also welcomed the resumption of salary payments for civil servants and ongoing infrastructure rehabilitation efforts, describing them as important steps toward restoring normalcy and accelerating the region's recovery.

Concluding the forum, participants called on the Federal Government to maintain its commitment to Tigray, sustain ongoing interventions and accelerate reform, reconstruction and development initiatives to secure lasting peace and improve the livelihoods of communities across the region.

World.title: Africa: How African Women's Rugby Teams Broke The Glass Ceiling At Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics
World.content:
An emotional moment for Team Kenya as they received their gold medals at Dakar 2026 Youth Olympics.

Kenya's all-women coaching staff turned a squad full of wingers into a team that could come from behind to win Olympic gold. As Madagascar's players balanced school and training to earn a historic bronze, both teams showed what it took to reach the rugby sevens podium.

Before heading to the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, every player on Kenya's girls' rugby sevens team wrote down what she wanted to achieve. They all had the same goal.

"Before heading to Dakar, every player had written down their goal and it was to win gold," Kenya coach Knight Otuoma said in Dakar.

"In our first game, despite being a former player, I tensed, but they were so relaxed and this made everything easy."



The Rising Lionesses delivered on that ambition with a 17–12 extra-time win over Australia, one of the tournament favourites. They became the first African team to win rugby sevens gold at either the Olympic Games or the Youth Olympic Games. It was Kenya's first medal in Dakar, the country's first Olympic gold in a team sport and the first time a Kenyan rugby team had won gold at a major global championship.

The final was a nerve-wracking affair for Otuoma and her players. Darci Mackay opened the scoring for Australia before Kenya captain Zain Hido crossed the line to make it 5–5 at half-time. Grace Buchanan scored after the break, and Billie Backus converted to put Australia 12–5 ahead.

"When we were down in that final, I reminded everyone where most of us came from and the difficulties we have faced in our lives," said captain Hido. "We did not need any motivation from the coach because we knew this could be a potentially life-changing moment."

With time up, Josphine Kerubo crossed for Kenya and Diana Wanjiku added the conversion to level the score at 12–12 and force sudden death. Two minutes into extra time, Mitchelle Chemtai scored in the corner to seal a dramatic 17–12 victory.

"It is still hard to believe," said Chemtai, who only took up rugby three years ago, when she joined high school. "This win made my parents emotional because they have seen my struggles. They never doubted me and I believe now, there is a chance to land further scholarships and contracts that could change our lives."

Kenya opened their campaign with a 12–5 win over China, then beat hosts Senegal 19–0 to reach the semi-finals with a pool match to spare. They lost their final pool match 17–5 to Australia, then beat Madagascar 15–5 in the semi-finals to earn another shot at the Australians.

Getting the Rising Lionesses ready for Dakar meant finding out what each player could do beyond the position she usually played.

"Ninety per cent of those girls came in as wingers and as a coach, I had to identify other attributes and strength to see which other positions they could fit. We trained them until everything went well," Otuoma said.

She said understanding her players' backgrounds and working with an all-women coaching staff were just as important. The squad was made up of students aged 16 and 17. Many came from families with limited means and relied on rugby scholarships to stay in school.

Kenya went into camp in the second week of September. With nearly two months together before the Games, Otuoma wanted the players to feel comfortable asking for what they needed.

"As a female coach and having an all-female technical coaching team, they could share personal stuff like if they needed soap, sanitary pads, or if they wanted to eat something different, things they would ordinarily not share if it was a male coach," she said.

Those conversations helped the team grow closer. Otuoma went a step further, handing out sticky notes every day so the players could raise anything they felt uncomfortable discussing in person.

"Most of the girls could not open up to me directly but they were comfortable writing down their issues. So every morning, I would read and address them," said the former Kenya international.

Chemtai, whose try won Kenya gold, said the trust she and her teammates built with the coaching staff gave them confidence.

"It was so easy sharing our issues with the coach… she made us feel very important. That gave us confidence and we did not want to let her down," said the 16-year-old.

Otuoma also discovered what some of her quietest players could do on the pitch.

"We have two shy girls who rarely talk but when they stepped onto the pitch, they were the fastest and the most fearless when tackling," she said.

One of them was Elizabeth Naliaka. The 17-year-old came from Dakar, eager to finish school, play rugby professionally, and earn a place in Kenya's senior team.

"I hope to make the senior team soon and help them qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics," she said.

In Kenya, the men's rugby teams get most of the funding and the biggest contracts while women lag behind but the triumphant Youth Olympics team feel they have earned the right for a change in fortunes.

"We want to be treated equally, if not better, because we are the first Kenyan team to win an Olympic gold medal," affirmed Diana Wanjiku.

"If they invest in us fully, we will deliver more. Most of us are finishing high school soon and we do not want to get lost after that. There must be a structured pathway so that we make that transition to the senior team and help them qualify for the LA 2028 Olympics and World Cup."

Close 

Madagascar had a milestone of its own to celebrate. The team's only defeat in Dakar came against Kenya in the semi-finals. They went on to beat Czechia 26–10 to win bronze, Madagascar's first medal at either the Olympic Games or the Youth Olympic Games.

For Madagascar captain Tracy Ftiavananomenjanahary, 17, the bronze medal rewarded the time she and her teammates had put into rugby while keeping up with school.

"It is incredible," said the 17-year-old. "This medal is for the country. We put in a lot of effort as we had to balance rugby training and our studies."

"None of us came to Dakar thinking that we could win a medal. We grew in strength with every win and now back home, our families are happy," stated Princia Ranaivoson.

At Nanjing 2014 and Buenos Aires 2018, the two previous editions to feature rugby sevens, Tunisia were Africa's only representatives in the girls' competition and finished sixth both times.

At the first Youth Olympic Games held on African soil, Kenya and Madagascar took two of the three places on the girls' rugby sevens podium. Their results offered a glimpse of how the balance of power in the sport could shift as this generation moves into senior rugby.

World.title: Blinken warns US ground invasion of Iran would be 'absolute disaster' as Tehran escalates attacks
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned Saturday that airstrikes alone may not eliminate Iran's weapons capabilities, but said a U.S. ground invasion would be an "absolute disaster."

Speaking at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi, Blinken, who served under President Biden, pointed to Iran's massive territory, population of roughly 90 million and ability to produce weapons deep inside the country as obstacles to any military campaign aimed at dismantling its arsenal.

"The weapons that it continues to produce are back far enough, the range is great enough that you can't just take everything out," Blinken said. "You'd probably have to have a land invasion of some kind to do that, which would be an absolute disaster."

TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING

Blinken's warning came ahead of Iran claiming Sunday to have launched six drones at a U.S. military installation in Bahrain, while reports surfaced that neighboring Iraq faced concerns that its territory could be drawn into a potential American ground operation.

Bahrain said its air defenses blocked several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, the first such interceptions since September.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted a U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base with six drones in retaliation for what it described as "hostile US actions," according to Iranian state media, Reuters reported.

Bahraini officials said the drones were intercepted before reaching their targets.

IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS

The latest escalation came amid further fighting in Yemen, where the Houthis made advances against Saudi-backed forces, raising additional concerns about the conflict spreading across the region.

Blinken warned that Iran retains the ability to widen the confrontation despite the United States' overwhelming conventional military superiority.

While Washington can "escalate vertically" by intensifying its bombing campaign, Blinken said, Tehran can "escalate horizontally" by targeting American military installations, regional allies and critical infrastructure, either directly or through allied armed groups.

"Even though we're much more powerful, that asymmetry in their ability to escalate horizontally as opposed to vertically is not to our advantage," Blinken said.

The former top diplomat also emphasized the geographic challenges facing U.S. forces.

"That coastline along the Strait of Hormuz goes on forever," Blinken said.

Iran is roughly four times the size of California, with a coastline and weapons production facilities that could complicate efforts to eliminate its military capabilities through air power alone.

TRUMP'S MOAB THREAT COULD PUT IRAN'S DEEPEST BUNKERS IN AMERICA'S CROSSHAIRS

Concerns about a potential ground operation have also intensified in neighboring Iraq, where officials have resisted proposals to sharply restrict trade and movement across the Iranian border.

Iran International reported that Tehran has become concerned that Iraqi territory could be used as a staging ground for a potential U.S. operation into southern Iran.

The Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada reported Nov. 9 that Iraq's prime minister privately briefed Shiite political leaders on an alleged American military plan involving a ground offensive, the outlet said.

In an interview with France 24 published Friday, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein had also warned that the region's unstable security environment could not continue indefinitely.

The current state of "no war and no peace" is unsustainable, Hussein said, warning that the confrontation "either goes towards peace or it goes towards war."

AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

Hussein also said Baghdad has a responsibility to pursue diplomatic mediation because Iraq has already been drawn into the conflict.

He pointed to recent outreach to Tehran, including discussions with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

The Iraqi foreign minister also rejected a reported U.S. demand that Baghdad close all but two of its land border crossings with Iran, describing the proposed restrictions as "not possible" and "a kind of sanction against the Iraqi people."

The border dispute comes as U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) expands efforts to disrupt Iranian weapons shipments and illicit trade through Task Force Iron Gate.

CENTCOM announced the task force would coordinate with other U.S. agencies to prevent Iran from transporting advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue across its land borders and the Caspian Sea.

World.title: NTSB details warning whistles and emergency orders before tanker collision capsized New Orleans riverboat
World.content:

A tanker suffered a steering problem about two minutes before slamming into a docked New Orleans riverboat Friday, federal investigators said Sunday, detailing warning whistles, calls for help and emergency orders before the collision.

The Atlantic Asphalt was heading upriver near the Crescent City Connection Bridge at about 12:26 p.m. when its rudder remained turned to the right, sending the ship toward the Mississippi River’s east bank, National Transportation Safety Board senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum said.

The tanker struck American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage at about 12:28 p.m. The riverboat capsized in about 22 minutes, according to preliminary information presented by the NTSB.

NEW ORLEANS BOAT CRASH CALLED ‘MIRACLE ON THE MISSISSIPPI’ AS EVERYONE IS ACCOUNTED FOR, OFFICIALS SAY

Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of data from the tanker’s voyage data recorder, including bridge audio, rudder angle, engine RPM, course and speed.

The recordings captured sounds consistent with the ship’s whistle, warnings and requests for assistance over its marine radio, commands to deploy anchors and emergency shiphandling orders, Barnum said.

11-NIGHT CARIBBEAN CRUISE ABRUPTLY CANCELED AFTER COAST GUARD DETAINS SHIP

Officials described the steering problem as a "steering casualty," but cautioned that the term does not establish what went wrong.

"It could be many different things. That is something that we are investigating very closely," Barnum said.

AT LEAST 6 PEOPLE INJURED AFTER BOSTON DUCK BOAT OVERTURNS NEAR ENTRANCE TO POPULAR TOURIST ATTRACTION

NTSB board member John DeLeeuw said investigators have data on the tanker’s speed but are still analyzing it before releasing it publicly. Video showed anchors were down, but investigators are still determining which ones were deployed and how far, he said.

The findings follow a frantic rescue effort that officials said left everyone aboard the American Heritage alive. Roughly 100 people were pulled from the Mississippi River, while responders evacuated more than 80 before the vessel overturned, Port of New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said Saturday.

TWO DEAD, INCLUDING INFANT, AFTER BOAT CAPSIZES IN NEW YORK HARBOR; 12 RESCUED

"This is a miracle. It is a literal miracle on the Mississippi," Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry said Friday.

Eight people remained hospitalized Saturday, including two in serious condition. The other six were stable, officials said.

FBI INVESTIGATES SUSPECTED HOMICIDE ABOARD MSC SEASCAPE CRUISE SHIP AFTER SUDDEN RETURN TO TEXAS

The NTSB said Sunday that 140 passengers and 50 crew members were aboard the riverboat, a total of 190.

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno also said the American Heritage’s captain was injured but stayed aboard until passengers and crew were accounted for, becoming the last person to leave.

MOM LOSES GRIP ON DAUGHTER AS PASSENGER FERRY CAPSIZES WITH 20 PEOPLE STILL MISSING

"Every moment of the critical time [Friday], he did not want to leave his ship," Moreno said Saturday.

Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Saturday that crews were preparing to remove 16,000 gallons of fuel before salvage operations, warning that removing the capsized vessel could take weeks. DeLeeuw said Sunday that divers had been in the water, with salvage work overseen by the Coast Guard and salvage companies.

UNLICENSED NYC BOAT OPERATOR ALLEGEDLY IGNORED SAFETY WARNINGS BEFORE MOTHER, BABY DIED IN CAPSIZING: FEDS

Interviews with American Heritage crew members were underway Sunday. Interviews with the Atlantic Asphalt’s crew were scheduled to begin Monday and continue through the week, Barnum said.

World.title: Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings are reunited and it feels so good after win over Green Bay Packers
World.content:
We found out a lot about Kirk Cousins and the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday because it is hard to add a new quarterback on a Tuesday, have him in full practices only two days during the week, and by week's end win a game in the same venue where he tore his Achilles three years ago.

All that happened Sunday when the Minnesota Vikings beat the Green Bay Packers.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

But of all the things we learned from this game, maybe the most important is that Cousins and the Vikings maybe should not have broken up a couple of years ago.

Perhaps they shouldn't have gone looking for greener pastures, shouldn't have believed for better outcomes, should not have quit on each other and the pretty good thing they had.

VIKINGS ACQUIRE KIRK COUSINS FROM RAIDERS WHO TURN TO FERNANDO MENDOZA AS THEIR STARTING QB

The Vikings and Cousins are together again. They're reunited and after winning in Lambeau Field, and they both feel so good.

"It's been a blast to do ball with him again," coach Kevin O'Connell said afterward.

"Football's an emotional game, and my football journey goes way back, and, you know, there's been highs and lows," Cousins told reporters after the victory. "And there's more of the story to write up ahead, but the last three years since being here have been a tough three years.

"And, there's a lot of gratitude right now for being in this group again."

The story of the misguided direction perhaps began in 2023 when Cousins tore his Achilles at Lambeau Field. Unable to overcome the injury by delivering a good season in 2026, the Vikings and Cousins went their different directions in March of 2024.

Cousins went to the Atlanta Falcons as a high-priced free agent, believing he could ultimately finish his career there. But that changed weeks after signing him, the Falcons drafted Michael Penix Jr. in the first round of the draft and anointed the rookie their starter before that very season was over.

Cousins sat much of 2025, and then went to the Raiders last offseason knowing he was keeping the starter's seat warm for Fernando Mendoza. Little did he know that seat would be pulled out from under him last week.

MINNESOTA VIKINGS' SOFT BENCHING OF KYLER MURRAY LEADS TO CARSON WENTZ TAKING OVER AS NEW STARTING QB

The Vikings? They didn't move on from Cousins to live happily ever after.

When Cousins left in 2024, the Vikings thought replacing him wasn't an issue. They had found Sam Darnold in 2024, they were getting ready to draft J.J. McCarthy in the first round, and there was a certain arrogance within the organization that they could find someone, anyone, and turn him into a treasure.

VIKINGS QUARTERBACK BATTLE MEETS EXPECTED END AS KYLER MURRAY BEATS OUT JJ MCCARTHY FOR STARTING JOB

But then Darnold left. And McCarthy didn't work out. And Carson Wentz didn't work out, and Kyler Murray didn't work out earlier this season.

And after those missteps, the Vikings decided last week that Cousins was their best option once again – just as he'd been from 2018 to 2023.

And Cousin showed he's all of that in this one game.

Cousins was already an upgrade by the time the Vikings held a 20-0 lead in the third quarter and scored twice more when the Packers tried to rally.

And, yes, we know ... That is not exactly Super Bowl caliber quarterback play we saw from Cousins, because he did throw an interception and he still has to clean up some stuff.

But having Cousins at quarterback clearly raised the Vikings' hopes. Justin Jefferson played with energy again. The offense could run the ball better because the Packers had to respect the passing game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

And the defense that is among the best in the NFL sacked Jordan Love eight times – the most by any team in a game this season – because the unit was in the mostly unfamiliar spot of playing with a lead.

"I thought for one of the first times this year, we played complimentary football," O'Connell said.

Cousins was careful when it was over to remind everyone that the story of his return and this Vikings' season is not fully written. But we have a good start to the tale:

It begins with the fact this combination maybe would have been better off staying together.

Former President Joe Biden described Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as difficult in private and insufficiently grateful in a forthcoming memoir reviewed Friday by The Wall Street Journal, adding his assessment to a relationship President Donald Trump has also publicly criticized.

Zelenskyy "could be moody and stubborn in our private conversations, and not as grateful as I would have expected," Biden said in "Promise Me, America," according to the newspaper.

Zelenskyy previously addressed questions about his gratitude during a February 2025 interview with Fox News' Bret Baier on "Special Report," following his Oval Office clash with Trump and Vice President JD Vance. When Baier asked whether he owed Trump an apology, Zelenskyy emphasized his appreciation for American support.

"I'm thankful to President Trump and to Congress, bipartisan support, and I was always very thankful from all our people," Zelenskyy said.

TRUMP CALLS FOR UKRAINE TO REPLACE ZELENSKYY AFTER CLASH OVER RUSSIA DIESEL DEAL: 'GET A NEW PRESIDENT'

In a November interview with Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst, Zelenskyy defended Ukraine’s strikes on Russian oil refineries despite objections from the Trump administration.

Biden’s memoir also addresses his handling of the presidential transition and his concerns about the incoming Trump administration’s approach to negotiations with Moscow.

According to the account, Trump’s team sought a letter authorizing direct negotiations with Russian President Vladimir Putin before Trump returned to office. Biden said he declined because of what he believed such talks could mean for Ukraine.

KUSHNER ENTERS UKRAINE PEACE TALKS AS TRUMP EYES SECURING SAFEGUARDS AGAINST ANOTHER RUSSIAN INVASION

He was "unwilling to give them carte blanche for what I expected would be a kind of surrender, at Ukraine's expense," Biden said.

The former president also offered a personal assessment of Putin’s behavior during their encounters, describing an effort to project disinterest.

Putin "liked to slouch during a meeting, feigning indifference, like a teenager," Biden said.

Biden’s criticism of Zelenskyy appears alongside a favorable assessment of the Ukrainian leader’s previous career. His acting background "turned out to be very good training," Biden said.

ZELENSKYY CAN LEVERAGE MOSCOW TIES FROM COMEDY DAYS TO MAKE PEACE DEAL, SAYS FORMER KEY AIDE

During Biden’s presidency, Ukraine’s requests included stronger air defenses, expanded weapons production and assistance disrupting Russian military logistics, according to a December 2023 account from Zelenskyy’s office. Before that White House meeting, Zelenskyy expressed appreciation for international assistance.

"I’d like to thank America and our partners for their support," Zelenskyy said.

Biden subsequently announced additional assistance in September 2024, including $2.4 billion through the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, another Patriot air defense battery and expanded training for Ukrainian F-16 pilots. His statement framed the measures as part of helping Ukraine defeat Russia’s invasion.

"The United States will provide Ukraine with the support it needs to win this war," Biden said.
