World.title: Trump plans to take Qatari jet to Asia, but it’s unclear whether it’s been ‘maxed out’
World.content:
President Donald Trump is expected to take the Qatari-gifted Air Force One to Asia on Monday as questions linger about upgrades the White House said were needed after a security threat from Iran forced the president to fly home from Turkey on a secret military plane in July, according to two U.S. officials.

For months, Trump has said the jet from the Qataris would be “going away” to get “maxed out” so it could “go into any territory.” In September, he said those changes to the plane would “take about 60 days.” The president flew on the new Air Force One to Ireland that month without any issues. He then used the plane regularly during a midterm travel blitz in October, which meant it was not out of commission for an extended period.

Instead, the plane has received some improvements and periodic maintenance, but it is unclear whether it has been fully “maxed out,” per the officials. A longer upgrade period is expected in the future, according to one of the officials, but those upgrades will not take a full 60 days.

In recent months, the plane has received some “cosmetic” enhancements to the interior, the other U.S. official said, but that did not cover the larger work that the White House said would take place eventually.

“We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force Once,” a senior administration official told NBC News in a statement. “We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture. It is the greatest Presidential plane ever built.”

In July, Trump said the plane “has a lot of capability.”

“But as I understand it, in about a month ​or so, they’re gonna send it to have it be maxed out,” he said. “It’ll take about a month.” Trump did not detail the nature of the work, and the White House has not explained why the original assessment of 30 days later doubled to 60 days.

At the time, then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement that the new Air Force One was “perfectly safe” for domestic and overseas travel but noted in July that the plane would “receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete.”

World.title: Here’s the biggest news you missed this weekend
World.content:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country following a router issue that derailed air traffic control communications.

Instead, the secretary blamed his predecessors for “30 years of a lack of investment,” telling NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that previous presidential administrations did not do enough to modernize the nation’s air traffic control system.

“It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or in decades, and I’m proud of the work we’re doing, the attention we’re bringing to this issue,” Duffy said.

Federal Aviation Administration contractor L3Harris was working on replacing a copper line with a fiber line at a remote site when the work led a router to overwhelm the national FAA telecommunications network, Duffy said Saturday.

On “Meet the Press,” the transportation secretary reiterated a call he’s made all weekend for more funding from Congress to modernize the nationwide air traffic control system, which has long been outdated and faced problems.

Duffy expects airports and airlines to resume normal operations by the end of the day or early Monday morning.

Sen.-elect Scott Colom says investing in the South can help Democrats

Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., emphasized on NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats need to invest more in Southern states like Mississippi, where he flipped a seat blue for the first time in decades.

“What we need to do now as a Democratic Party is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment to occur,” he said.

Colom’s projected win brings Democrats to a 55-seat majority in the Senate, with Alaska’s Senate race yet to be called. His victory over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, marked a seismic political shift in a state that last elected a Democrat to the Senate 44 years ago and has not had a Black senator since the Reconstruction period.

Mike Pence says GOP voters ‘didn’t turn left’ but were ‘turned off’ in midterms

Former Vice President Mike Pence said on “Meet the Press” he disagrees with Vice President JD Vance’s assessment of Republican midterm losses, saying that the problem Americans have with the Iran war is that the U.S. “stopped short.”

“We sunk their navy, we had complete air superiority, took down 15,000 military sites in Iran. And then, we paused and began to embrace the politics of appeasement,” Pence said.

Why Democrat Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race

Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola speaks during an election night watch party in Anchorage. Justin Sullivan / Getty

As Alaska continues to count and report votes weeks after Election Day, it is increasingly unlikely that Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan will hang on to his job.

His Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola, is on track to win the still-unresolved Senate race under either possible scenario — with an outright majority, or if the race goes to ranked choice ballots, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis of outstanding and tabulated votes.

It’s possible that the final result won’t arrive until Nov. 18. Wednesday is Alaska’s deadline for election officials to receive final mail absentee ballots, one reason why this close race has lingered for so long.

Politics in brief

Widening the lead : Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won the Alaska governor’s race , NBC News projects, flipping the office from Republican control and extending Democrats’ gains at the state level in this year’s elections.

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has won , NBC News projects, flipping the office from Republican control and extending Democrats’ gains at the state level in this year’s elections. Par for the course: The Trump administration cannot close East Potomac Park to the public for now, a federal judge in Washington ruled Saturday, dealing a blow to the president’s effort to renovate the park’s golf course.

Megaspeed says Alice Huang left in 2025 as company conducts probe over Nvidia fallout

Jensen Huang and Alice Huang at a restaurant in Taipei in 2025. TVBS via AP

Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed International said that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang sparked U.S. national security concerns, left the company last year.

Megaspeed, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers.

Could a viral teen comedy be Netflix’s answer to YouTube?

Hyde Healy, Julia Dicesare, Grace Reiter, Ryan Micho, Tommy Armstrong and Aidan Micho in "Minimum Wage." Netflix

Inside a make-believe pizza shop overlooking Onondaga Lake, a team of digital creators, filmmakers and young actors spent months cooking up a show that they hope will serve Netflix something it craves: a fresh audience.

“Minimum Wage,” a mockumentary that follows teens who work at a pizza shop, has garnered more than 30 million views across YouTube, TikTok and Instagram since launching in May 2024.

The media company’s decision to acquire the show for its platform reflects a broader shift in Hollywood’s battle for younger viewers, as streamers increasingly turn to internet creators and their built-in fan bases to drive subscriptions and engagement.

Women with autoimmune diseases often misdiagnosed for 4 years or more

Women with autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to be misdiagnosed or get delayed treatment compared with men. BSIP / Universal Images Group via Getty

Women with autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to be misdiagnosed or get delayed treatment compared with men, with their symptoms often dismissed as “psychological.”

An online survey by British researchers found that it took women with an autoimmune disorder about four years to get a diagnosis, while it took men around three months to less than a year.

“Women in particular felt not listened to or not heard or not believed by their medical professionals,” said Sydnae Taylor, a co-author of the study published recently in eClinicalMedicine.

Autoimmune conditions can affect anyone but are more common in women than in men, according to the federal Office on Women’s Health.

World.title: Women with autoimmune diseases often misdiagnosed for 4 years or more
World.content:
Women with autoimmune diseases such as lupus or rheumatoid arthritis are more likely to be misdiagnosed or get delayed treatment compared with men, with their symptoms often dismissed as “psychological.”

An online survey by British researchers found that it took women with an autoimmune disorder about four years to get a diagnosis, while it took men around three months to less than a year.

It adds to previous research showing disparities in diagnosis between men and women with autoimmune disorders.

“Women in particular felt not listened to or not heard or not believed by their medical professionals,” said Sydnae Taylor, a doctoral researcher at the University of Oxford in the U.K. and co-author of the study published recently in eClinicalMedicine.

Autoimmune diseases — including Type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, inflammatory bowel disease and psoriasis — occur when the immune system mistakenly attacks the body. More than 23 million people in the U.S. have an autoimmune disease, and most of them are women.

Autoimmune thyroid disease, which includes Hashimoto’s, was the most common type reported by women in the survey. It typically causes fatigue, unexplained weight gain and sensitivity to cold, among other symptoms.

Autoimmune conditions can affect anyone but are more common in women than in men, according to the federal Office on Women’s Health. For example, around 90% of people with lupus are women, according to the Lupus Foundation of America.

It’s not clear why women are more at risk. Research from the Mayo Clinic has suggested differences in the microbiome, sex hormones and that women’s bodies produce higher levels of antibodies that are associated with autoimmune disorders. A 2024 Stanford Medicine study found clues in a molecule connected to the X chromosome.

Because many of the disorders share similar symptoms in the early stages — fatigue, dizziness, low-grade fever, as well as stress, anxiety and depression — they can be difficult to diagnose.

Women and men have similar symptoms, but with women specifically, “they develop over time, so it’s often hard to recognize right at the beginning,” said Dr. Saira Z. Sheikh, the director of the UNC Rheumatology Lupus Clinic in Chapel Hill, North Carolina. Symptoms can appear during childhood and last throughout adulthood.

The survey was conducted through social media, patient support groups and community groups of underserved populations such as religious groups and the homeless population. It was translated into five languages as a way to reach diverse communities.

Participants shared data about symptom onset, how many clinicians were consulted and misdiagnosis. The data was then compared between men and women. Out of the 6,607 participants, 91.2% were women and the majority of them were from the United Kingdom.

Misdiagnosis is more likely when symptoms are “invisible,” meaning they aren’t detected in a blood test or involve pain, fatigue and neurological symptoms such as tingling, Taylor said.

In these situations, accurate diagnoses rely on doctors listening and believing the patient.

“We shouldn’t assume that women’s symptoms are psychological simply because the initial investigations are inconclusive,” Sheikh said.

World.title: The biggest move of the NFL trade deadline paid immediate dividends
World.content:
Making his first start for the Minnesota Vikings since 2023, quarterback Kirk Cousins picked up where he left off — almost literally.

Cousins led the Vikings to a 30-10 victory over the Green Bay Packers on Sunday, ending Minnesota’s two-game losing streak and improving the team’s record to 7-2.

Cousins’s most recent start for the Vikings prior to Sunday also came at Green Bay. It was in 2023, and he tore his Achilles during that game, and Minnesota moved on from him the following offseason.

The Vikings have been looking for an answer at quarterback since, and they eventually came back around to Cousins at this year’s trade deadline. Cousins got the start Sunday only five days after he was acquired from the Las Vegas Raiders, and he made some big throws as he led Minnesota to its highest scoring output since Week 1.

“I didn’t even know what my code was to get into the building on Wednesday,” Cousins said postgame. “It took a village. I’m just grateful for all the people that stepped up to help.”

Cousins finished the game completing 21 of 31 passes for 207 yards, with two touchdowns and one interception. While his stats weren’t spectacular, he made a meaningful impact on money downs, as the Vikings finished the game converting eight of 16 on third down. (Entering Sunday, Minnesota was ranked 30th in third-down conversion percentage at 33.3%.)

Minnesota’s first touchdown came on a third and 23, as Cousins made a beautiful, drop-in-the-bucket throw to Myles Price, who bounced off defenders en route to the end zone. Cousins described it as a “big-time” play by Price.

Cousins made another great throw on a third-and-long later in the game, connecting with Tai Felton on a wheel route on a third and 15 in the second quarter. The pass set up a one-yard touchdown run on the next play.

Later, after the Packers had cut the Vikings’ 20-0 lead to 20-10, Cousins picked up another massive first, checking into a screen pass on third and 12 and finding Justin Jefferson for a first down.

“It was fun, it felt like old times watching Justin do what he just did on that play,” Cousins said. “It was like, ‘I remember that guy. He’s pretty special.’”

Five plays later, Cousins threw his second touchdown of the game and effectively iced any chances of a Green Bay comeback.

“[He] just brought a certain amount of poise, leadership, execution,” head coach Kevin O’Connell said postgame. “Ran the show incredibly clean. Can’t say enough about him, I know everybody in the organization felt it this week.”

Jefferson, one of the game’s top receivers, was perhaps the biggest individual beneficiary of his old quarterback’s return. Jefferson’s nine receptions and 13 targets were both season highs.

Though Cousins didn’t exactly light the box score on fire, his presence Sunday made Minnesota’s championship formula incredibly clear: Play lights out defense, and do just enough on offense with above-average quarterback play.

With Cousins helping push the Vikings out to an early lead, Minnesota’s defense pinned its ears back and got after Jordan Love. The Vikings finished the game with eight sacks, and limited the Packers to only 56 yards rushing.

Love, one of the game’s great deep-ball throwers, finished the game with 220 yards, his fewest since Week 4. His 46.6 QBR was also his third-worst mark of the season.

“For one of the first times this year, I thought we played complementary football,” O’Connell said.

The win was an important one for Minnesota. The Vikings are now two games clear of Green Bay in loss column in the loaded NFC North, and now also own the tiebreaker between the two teams. Minnesota kept pace with the Detroit Lions and Chicago Bears, both of whom are also 7-2.

The Vikings’ offense didn’t necessarily look perfect Sunday. But their quarterback making big throws and providing a steady hand while the defensedefense continued to dominate showed exactly why Minnesota decided to bring Cousins back.

World.title: Russell Brand says ‘I am not guilty’ in statement from prison read by his wife
World.content:
Russell Brand declared “I am not guilty” in a new statement read by his wife on his YouTube channel Sunday, days after a London court sentenced him to prison on rape and sexual assault charges.

The 51-year-old comedian and former actor was sentenced Nov. 9 to 10 1/2 years in prison after a London court found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He pleaded not guilty to all counts and denied all of the allegations.

In a new YouTube video, Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read the statement on his behalf.

“So, Russell has asked me to read something to you today: ‘Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening,’” she said.

“I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. ... I’m in the biggest sex offenders prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated,” she continued, reading his statement.

“And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone. I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us,” the statement said.

Brand closed by asking the public to support his wife and family. “I feel your prayers,” the statement said.

Brand’s YouTube channel features Christian-themed content, including a “Sunday Service” series he hosts with his wife. At the start of the video, Laura Brand said she would continue the series. Sunday’s episode included prerecorded video of the couple discussing faith and morality.

“Even though it’s painful, and obviously will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my my companion, my person, with me, but I want to continue,” she said.

Justice Joel Bennathan called Brand a “sexual predator” before delivering his sentence. At sentencing, Brand’s victims shared in-person and written statements about the trauma and its effects on their daily lives.

Brand was convicted of raping a female fan at his home in 2009 after she met him at one of his shows. He was also found guilty of sexually assaulting three other women: one whose breasts he grabbed at a party in 2004; one who said he kissed and groped her at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005; and one who said he pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an  in 2009.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The sentence marked a stunning fall from grace for Brand, who rose to fame as a broadcaster and stand-up comedian and went on to a Hollywood career, starring in films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek.”

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at https://www.rainn.org/get-help.

World.title: We want to hear your experience with changes to student loan repayment plans
World.content:
President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” has transformed the sprawling federal student loan system — and student borrowers are feeling the effects of the most consequential changes.

This year, the approximately 7.5 million student borrowers under the Biden-era Saving on a Valuable Education, or SAVE, plan had to select a new one. So far, about 2 million borrowers have done so, after the Education Department warned that the SAVE plan was “illegal” and would be discontinued. The remaining borrowers who did not select a new plan were set to start receiving notices this month informing them that they missed a final deadline and were automatically moved to a new plan.

The Trump administration has said ending the SAVE plan would help streamline repayment programs while ensuring borrowers are paying off what they owe to the federal government. But student advocacy groups fear lower-income borrowers who had benefited from smaller monthly payments — or even qualified to make no payments at all based on their income — will end up with significantly higher bills under the other available plans.

We want to hear from you, whether you’re in this situation or are facing another challenge related to the recent student loan changes. Please share your experience by filling out the form below.

World.title: 60 Minutes Transcript: John Malkovich on his career
World.content:
John Malkovich is so distinctive he's almost his own genre. His unique persona is conspicuous in every character he's played, even though this soft-spoken 72-year-old grandfather has nothing in common with his gallery of villains: the murderous Cyrus the Virus in "Con Air;" the duplicitous seducer Valmont in "Dangerous Liaisons;" and the aspiring assassin he played with such creepy precision in "In the Line of Fire." For over five decades now, Malkovich's performances have been as nuanced as they are mysterious; even he doesn't know how he does it.

We spoke with him at the legendary and newly restored Cherry Lane Theatre in Greenwich Village, the first place he performed in New York City in 1982. He was 28 and had just come from Chicago and the famed Steppenwolf Theater Company to star in Sam Shepard's ferocious two-act play, "True West," with his friend, Gary Sinise.

John Malkovich: Sometimes on Saturday night, just to wind Gary up on one level and amuse him on the other, I would get a six-pack and I would ch-- the fridge was right over there and I would chug 'em, one at a time, one, two, three, four, five, six, right, just like that, right down the hatch.

Ariel Levy: I mean, you must have been as trashed as the set.

John Malkovich: I think I was pretty trashed. And we had a lot of fun doing it.

John Malkovich 60 Minutes

Malkovich played Lee, a charismatic lowlife bully, in Sam Shepard's dark comedy about sibling rivalry. His blistering performance became the talk of the town. Everyone who was anyone in New York came to check him out at the Cherry Lane.

John Malkovich: You know, every night there would be Antonioni or Mick Jagger or David Bowie or Jackie O. It was wild.

Ariel Levy: Did you see them when you were up on stage. You would say, "Oh, my God--"

John Malkovich: They're right there. You're doing whatever. You look out and it's Jackie O. Not much you can say to that.

His triumph on stage was a catalyst for Malkovich's entree into movies, first as an American photojournalist covering wartime Cambodia in the killing fields, and then starring alongside Sally Field in "Places in the Heart."

That performance in 1984, as a blind World War I veteran who became the family's unlikely protector, earned Malkovich his first Oscar nomination.

Ariel Levy: Early on in your career, you were sort of the opposite of method. You just would be in it instantaneously without, you know, a lot of what other people would call preparation. Film must have been fine for you?

John Malkovich: It is fine.

Ariel Levy: You could just go right in morsel by morsel.

John Malkovich: Yeah, Yeah. I'm not someone who sits and suffers that. I have to be in some particular way. I have to be not thinking, when the play starts, but doing.

He returned to the stage in "Death of a Salesman," sharing the playbill with Dustin Hoffman on Broadway in 1984.

John Malkovich: When you do a play, it's the whole play. You don't do just some little bit of it and go, "Do you like it?" It's the whole thing. It's ahead of you. Then it's with you. Then it's behind you every night. And it has momentum. There's no momentum in movies.

Malkovich says that acting in a movie is like "being in someone else's dream." You're shooting scenes out of sequence. You rarely have any say in the final product. It's one reason he's returned to the theater over and over again throughout his 50-year career, acting in and directing dozens of plays all over the world, notably starring in the original 1987 production of Lanford Wilson's "Burn This."

Ariel Levy and John Malkovich 60 Minutes

Ariel Levy: After seeing your performance in that play the director, Stephen Frears comes backstage to talk to you.

John Malkovich: Uh-huh. Yeah. He asked me why I was never good, actually, in movies. He may have said, "Cinema."

Ariel Levy: Surely, there was an upside, too? "You're great in plays…"

John Malkovich: That upside didn't occur. But I got the point that has not much to do with me, but a lot to do with how movies are made. And we discussed, for the purposes of "Dangerous Liaisons," how that could apply to how we were going to set about making it.

Malkovich's lothario, Vicomte de Valmont, was introduced to audiences in 1988 in the iconic adaptation of the 18th-century novel. He says it was one of just a handful of truly great scripts he's read in his career.

Ariel Levy: What appealed to you about doing "Liaisons"?

John Malkovich: Great characters, and a fantastic adaptation by Christopher Hampton, whose writing I did and still respect, a great deal. So there was kind of, for me, nothing. There was no downside, really.

He chalks up other movies to interesting ideas with great parts, like the aspiring assassin he portrayed in Wolfgang Petersen's "In the Line of Fire," where Malkovich's performance earned him his second Oscar nomination.

He played a different kind of killer in "Con Air," a film that brought Malkovich to the masses.

Ariel Levy: What was your first impression of the "Con Air" script?

John Malkovich: 500 million was my first impression, honestly. I knew it was Jerry Bruckheimer. I knew Nick Cage was in it. I looked at the title page of the names of the people who were named after Victorian-era poets. And I just thought, "Okay. That's, like, 500 convicts on an airplane, $500 million…

Ariel Levy: You do the math

John Malkovich: Yeah, do the math

"Con Air" grossed more than $200 million at the box office. Though Malkovich is seen as an intellectual — and is in fact a man who has designed fashion, produced pinot noir in France, and travels the world collaborating with classical musicians — he' not a snob.

He's made well over 100 movies, and he claims to enjoy acting in blockbusters as much as arthouse films.

John Malkovich: Each bring their own gifts. They really do. It doesn't matter to me if it's Proust, or Faulkner, or "Con Air."

John Malkovich 60 Minutes

Malkovich's democratic approach to material and clear-eye view of life proved instrumental when he lost his entire savings to Bernie Madoff's ponzi scheme in 2008.

John Malkovich: I found out… I had directed a play in Mexico City and then, I got home from that. And I saw this photograph of Bernie Madoff in handcuffs and I thought, "Oh. Well, that-- that could prove interesting." And I went in and said to my wife, "You know, I'm just gonna go around the corner, buy a pack of cigarettes. I said we have a little problem, Bernie Madoff just got arrested."

Ariel Levy: I take it you didn't smoke, when you told her that.

John Malkovich: I had stopped. Yeah for a while, you know, that was pretty much everything I'd ever made.

Even more remarkable than Malkovich's loss was his expedited recovery.

John Malkovich: And, you know, you look to blame. You're gonna do this and that. And then, you realize that, "Look. Why don't you shut up? Whatever you lost, most people who were ever born will never have a tenth of that, no matter what they do, no matter what they do. Get on with your life. And that's it."

John Malkovich grew up in the Midwest. His mother's family owned the daily newspaper in Benton, Illinois, and his father was a conservationist. For Malkovich, the idea of becoming a movie star—or doing anything to draw attention to himself—was inconceivable. One of five children, Malkovich says his parents never found him particularly impressive.

John Malkovich: It's just not a family you-- you could never have been praised for anything. If you built a rocket in the yard that took you to space and back, people would kinda say, "We wondered where you were." But it wouldn't go much beyond that.

That fanatical modesty was one of the reasons Malkovich initially resisted making the unforgettable comedy "Being John Malkovich" with director Spike Jonze, a surreal journey through an imaginary portal in the actor's brain.

John Malkovich: I loved Spike. I thought it was hilarious.

Ariel Levy: It was an amazing movie. There's nothing like that.

John Malkovich: I can't think of anything that was more originally voiced and expressed. It was really a cinematic universe, as they use the term for Marvel. That actually was one.

Ariel Levy: How much John Malkovich was in "Being John Malkovich?"

John Malkovich: None.

Ariel Levy: None?

John Malkovich: I'll let Spike Jonze say it best. I did-- so we were rehearsing, one day, I don't remember what it was, and Spike said to me, "That's okay, but John Malkovich wouldn't do it that way." And I just thought that was a fantastic note.

Before making the movie in 1998, Malkovich tried to convince screenwriter Charlie Kaufman to use a different actor. He thought "Being Tom Cruise" might work well but Kaufman refused. There is no other actor with a more distinctive persona than Malkovich. And then there's that unmistakable way of speaking parodied by Bill Hader on "Saturday Night Live."

A Malkovich favorite is the Coen brothers' "Burn After Reading," in which he played the prickly, recently fired CIA officer, Osborne Cox.

Now he's back in the CIA in Martin McDonagh's latest film, "Wild Horse Nine," a black comedy set on Chile's Easter Island, shortly before the engineered coup d'etat in 1973. Malkovich plays Chris, a spy haunted by the ghosts of assassinations and unsavory operations past. We spoke with him after the movie screened at the London Film Festival.

Ariel Levy: How did you make someone who'd done so much bad stuff so irresistible?

John Malkovich: I think first of all I'd say, somehow I think there has been a loss of making characters that an audience simply cares about, whether they're salvageable or redeemable people who've done terrible things, or just terrible people.

Ariel Levy: Martin McDonagh's movies are about such dark subject matter, but the dialogue is hilarious, bordering on absurd.

John Malkovich: When you have great writing, you can go from something remarkably sad in a millisecond to something very funny and-- and all that's forgotten.

Ariel Levy: There's a line in the film where, I think it's your character, says, "Do you think there are any Nazis in heaven?" The answer is, "Maybe, if one, like, laid down on a grenade to save his mother." And to me that was the crux of the movie, is what damns us, what redeems us.

John Malkovich: I think it's absolutely correct. I think Chris has great worries where he will stand in the-- in that decision, what will be his destination. He's very Catholic. And so he believes in that.

"Wild Horse Nine" has already won accolades at film festivals in Venice, Toronto and London and there's talk of Oscars. If Malkovich wins, it would be his first.

Ariel Levy: Do you even know what you do?

John Malkovich: No.

John Malkovich: I have an awareness, but I can't tell you where it comes from because I never think about it. -

Ariel Levy: Like, you wouldn't be able to teach the John Malkovich method?

John Malkovich: No. There is no such thing, I think and I certainly wouldn't recommend studying it.

Ariel Levy: You're just being John Malkovich?

John Malkovich: Yeah.

Produced by Michael Karzis and Katie Kerbstat. Broadcast associates, Jessica Schwalb and Lola Jahant. Edited by Mike Levine.

World.title: Parents whose sons died from kratom use warn about the substance
World.content:
Kratom, a substance that acts on opioid receptors, can be as easy to obtain as a bag of chips.

Kratom is derived from a tree native to Southeast Asia, where for generations people have chewed the leaves or boiled them to make a stimulating tea with opioid effects.

The sales of kratom in the U.S. have fueled a billion-dollar industry, with products containing the plant available online and in tens of thousands of stores across the country, including gas stations.

The kratom industry hails the substance as a mild stimulant that can also aid in recovery from opioid addiction. The kratom industry has supporters in the highest ranks of government and is legally sold in most states. But health experts warn that kratom use can lead to addiction and death. Dr. Andrew Kolodny, the medical director for the Opioid Policy Research Collaborative at Brandeis University, said that it has effects very similar to those of oxycodone, heroin and even fentanyl. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has detected kratom in more than 5,000 overdose deaths from 2020-2024.

Helping shape perception of kratom as a benign health supplement is the consumer advocacy and lobby group the American Kratom Association. The group describes natural kratom as "a safe food used by many as an herbal supplement" taken for "health and wellbeing or for an energy boost."

Four families told "60 Minutes" that their sons, all recently deceased, started using kratom for those kinds of benefits. Susan Eppard's son Matthew told her it was like coffee, because he read it was related to the coffee family. Patti Wheeler's son Wyatt said it was helping him ease away from alcohol.

These parents say itheir sons, all recently deceased, used kratom. 60 Minutes

"He was looking for something for energy. A friend of his told him it was safer than Red Bull," said Wendy Chamberlain about her son Joe.

The deaths of Matthew and Joe were attributed solely to mitragynine, the main opioid in kratom. Daniel Bregger and Wyatt Wheeler's causes of death included mitragynine along with prescription or over-the-counter medications.

Susan Eppard said her son collapsed suddenly while playing cards with friends. She recalled the day her son died.

"They tried resuscitating him for a long time. [By the] time I got there, they wouldn't let me in at first, so I'd just sit out on the ground outside screaming for God to keep my baby here," Susan Eppard said. "And they finally let me go in there and see him. I knelt down to him and gave him a kiss on his forehead. And he was just cold and dark and gray."

Justin Brower, a toxicologist at NMS Labs, a forensic testing facility 40 minutes outside Philadelphia, said he has analyzed thousands of deaths involving kratom. "Dozens and dozens" have been attributed "just to kratom, no other drugs at all," he said. Fatalities linked to kratom have "increased probably about tenfold" since 2014, he said.

"It's pretty incredible how it's taken hold of the United States and how many people are using it now, compared to, you know, a decade-plus ago," Brower said.

The Food and Drug Administration warns "consumers not to use kratom because of the risk of serious adverse events, including liver toxicity, seizures, and substance use disorder." With concern growing over kratom-derived products, including the concentrated kratom-related synthetic substance 7-OH, the federal government announced in July that it would restrict 7-OH and three related substances found in kratom products. But then last month, the Department of Health and Human Services changed its recommendation. Among the new recommendations: increasing the amount of 7-OH allowed in products by 20-fold.

Some health officials, including former FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary and former senior HHS advisor Calley Means, were stunned by the decision. "60 Minutes" found public filings from the last decade that show a constant stream of cash -- much from the American Kratom Association — earmarked for lobbying the FDA, HHS, the White House, and members of Congress. Millions of dollars committed to keeping kratom legal.

Even more money has come in the form of political contributions and investments. Kolodny compared it to the lobbying actions of Purdue Pharma, the manufacturer of OxyContin.

"Some of the same scientists who Purdue Pharma hired to make sure that regulators wouldn't take action against OxyContin are now working for the Kratom Association and delivering the same message, downplaying the risks, exaggerating the numbers of people who are potentially benefiting," Kolodny said.

HHS declined an interview request with "60 Minutes," but said in a statement that "Neither political contributions nor outside pressure influenced" the decision to increase the amount of 7-OH allowed in products. The American Kratom Association gave a statement to "60 Minutes" and emphasized the distinction between natural kratom and "dangerous chemically manipulated products."

Eppard said she can't believe that kratom, in any form, is still for sale. She said she often goes into convenience stores to ask employees if they realize what they are selling. Often, they don't, she said. So she tells them about her son.

"We all just miss him terrible," she told "60 Minutes."

World.title: 60 Minutes Transcript: Kratom faces scrutiny over health concerns
World.content:
Over the next two weeks, we bring you a special report on the status of the American opioid crisis that's claimed nearly a million casualties and is far from over. We start with kratom. You've probably seen the signs advertising kratom, a substance that can be no harder to obtain than a bag of chips. It's become a billion-dollar industry, the products available online and in tens of thousands of stores around the country. The kratom industry hails the substance as a mild stimulant, even an aid in recovery from opioid addiction, and has supporters in the highest ranks of government. Increasingly, though there's outrage that kratom, an opioid that can lead to addiction and death, still in most states remains legal.

A trained opera singer living in Michigan, Melanie Clark struggled with post-partum depression and fatigue. In 2022, scrolling Instagram, she saw ads for Feel Free Classic Tonic, a plant-based energy drink, enticing her with catchphrases like "Feel Free to be SuperMom."

Jon Wertheim: How are you hoping it would make you feel?

Melanie Clark: Focused, energized. You know, I really just was hoping it would give me a little boost.

Jon Wertheim: Did it meet your expectations initially?

Melanie Clark: It more than met my expectations.

Jon Wertheim: How did it make you feel?

Melanie Clark: Just almost like, like I had super powers.

Melanie Clark 60 Minutes

An active ingredient in Feel Free: kratom: derived from a tree native to Southeast Asia, where for generations people have chewed kratom leaves or boiled them to make a stimulating tea with opioid effects.

Jon Wertheim: And you were getting this product where?

Melanie Clark: You know, gas stations near my house. There was a little corner market really close to my house that sold them.

Jon Wertheim: When did you realize this was a problem?

Melanie Clark: I probably only took one bottle my first week and then, you know, a couple the next. And then soon, I felt like I needed them to just even kind of get going for the day. So that was probably only three weeks in, that I felt really addicted.

Feel Free, priced around $10 a bottle, is one of hundreds of kratom products on the market. There are bags of leaf powder, capsules, gummies, extracts, available at smoke shops, convenience stores and corner delis.

Dr. Andrew Kolodny: The effects produced by kratom are very similar to the effects produced by oxycodone, heroin, even fentanyl.

Dr. Andrew Kolodny is the medical director for the Opioid Policy Research Collaborative at Brandeis University. He has treated hundreds of patients addicted to opioids. He's also worked for states as an expert witness, testifying that pharmaceutical companies, in part, caused the opioid crisis.

Jon Wertheim: How did kratom come across your radar?

Dr. Andrew Kolodny: I remember hearing from people concerned about kratom and I was just blown away by how pretty much everyone I was seeing who had developed opioid addiction in the past few years, they developed their opioid addiction taking kratom.

Why is kratom an opioid? Its main compound, mitragynine, activates opioid receptors in the brain. Some of that mitragynine gets converted by the body into what's called 7-OH, which activates those same receptors even more intensely, eliciting an opioid high.

Helping shape perception of kratom as a benign health supplement: the American Kratom Association, a consumer advocacy and lobby group.

American Kratom Association video: "Natural kratom is a safe food used by many as an herbal supplement and is used by millions for their health and wellbeing or for an energy boost."

Those promised benefits?

Susan Eppard: We all just miss him terrible.

These parents say it's why their sons, all recently deceased, started using kratom in the first place.

These parents say itheir sons, all recently deceased, used kratom. 60 Minutes

Susan Eppard: He said it was just like coffee, because he read that it was from the coffee family.

Wendy Chamberlain: He was looking for something for energy. A friend of his told him it was safer than Red Bull.

Patti Wheeler: And he said, "Oh, mom, it's just an herbal supplement. It's helping me ease away from alcohol."

David Bregger: He was looking for a natural way to deal with his anxiety, is what we believe the issue was, yeah.

"Cause of death" for David Bregger's son, Daniel, and Patti Wheeler's son, Wyatt, lists mitragynine, alongside prescription and over-the-counter medications.

The deaths of Wendy Chamberlain's son, Joe, and Susan Eppard's son, Matthew, were attributed solely to mitragynine, the main opioid in kratom. At 22, Matthew was playing cards with friends when he suddenly collapsed.

Susan Eppard: They tried resuscitating him for a long time. Time I got there, they wouldn't let me in at first, so I'd just sit out on the ground outside screaming for God to keep my baby here. And they finally let me go in there and see him. I knelt down to him and gave him a kiss on his forehead. And he was just cold and dark and gray.

Mac Haddow is the public voice of the American Kratom Association.

Mac Haddow at Congressional Brief June 2026: "They are wrong. They perpetuate this myth about kratom, they say that kratom is dangerous."

Convicted of felony ethics violations committed in the 1980s while working as chief of staff for HHS, the Department of Health and Human Services, Haddow claims, repeatedly, that there is no proof that kratom can be deadly.

Mac Haddow at Congressional Brief June 2026: "There is no known dose of mitragynine or kratom that would cause a death."

Jon Wertheim: We've spoken to people. They say you can't die from kratom.

Justin Brower: Yeah, that's not true at all.

Justin Brower is a toxicologist at NMS Labs, a forensic testing facility outside Philadelphia. He's analyzed thousands of death cases involving kratom.

Justin Brower: I know there's a lot of advocates out there for kratom. And kratom has helped a lot of people, you know, to alleviate withdrawal symptoms, to help with chronic pain and depression.

Jon Wertheim: You sound unmistakable. There can be deaths.

Justin Brower: There can be. Correct, and I've seen dozens and dozens of deaths attributed just to kratom, no other drugs at all.

Justin Brower 60 Minutes

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has, since 2020, identified more than 5,000 overdose deaths involving kratom.

Jon Wertheim: What has been the arc of fatalities?

Justin Brower: It's probably increased probably about tenfold…

Jon Wertheim: Tenfold?

Justin Brower: …from 2014 through 2025 into 2026. It's pretty incredible how many people are using it now compared to, you know, a decade-plus ago.

The rare chance of death associated with kratom has been acknowledged by the Food and Drug Administration, which warns about the "risk of serious adverse events, including liver toxicity, seizures, and substance use disorder."

In 2014 the FDA issued an import alert to stop the flow of kratom. But millions of pounds, mostly from Indonesia, continue to make it here every month, labeled as substances like cosmetics and incense. But there is a loophole: once here in the country, kratom can be sold in most states. Options for consumers have evolved. Products containing synthetic 7-OH have hit the market. Remember 7-OH, that opioid in kratom, triggering the more intense high? Manufacturers concentrate it, in tablets and liquid shots, products more potent than morphine – earning them the nickname, "gas station heroin."

Alex Krotulski: Typically, you have these cardboard packets that have individual pills in them.

Jon Wertheim: We have mango and wild cherry.

Toxicologist Alex Krotulski, director at the Center for Forensic Science Research and Education, tracks the emergence of new drugs in the U.S. and he's not surprised by the user migration from leaf-based kratom products to synthetic 7-OH.

Alex Krotulski: They're trying to chase this high that they have. But as their tolerance increases, they can't get there. So, they shift to more potent drugs. I think that understanding does align well when you think about the shift from mitragynine to something ten times more potent, 7-hydroxy, or 7-OH.

Alex Krotulski and Jon Wertheim 60 Minutes

Melanie Clark has lived that trajectory. After weaning herself off of Feel Free, the leaf-based kratom drink, she relapsed and last year started using synthetic 7-OH tablets made by another company, which landed her in the hospital.

Melanie Clark: So this is from the end of my 7-OH use. It's hard to believe that this is me.

In withdrawal, she had panic attacks and became suicidal to the point her husband called the police.

Melanie Clark: As soon as I heard that the cops were coming, I took off, like sprinted across our yard, hopped a fence.

Jon Wertheim: Just for people that may not understand addiction, they say, "Here's this nice woman from the Midwest with three kids who studied opera in college and now she's in a field running from the cops."

Melanie Clark: It's hard for me to believe, too. But that's-- that's what addiction will do to you.

With concern growing over 7-OH and other kratom-derived products, the federal government in July announced an intent to restrict, or schedule, 7-OH and three related substances, referred to as "dangerous opioids" by Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Health and Human Services secretary. But then, unexpectedly, last month, HHS changed its recommendation, increasing the amount of 7-OH allowed in products by 20-fold — a decision that stunned some health officials.

Calley Means on Joe Rogan Podcast: It's causing deaths. It's causing devastation. It is an opioid.

Earlier this year on Joe Rogan's podcast, Calley Means—until recently, a senior advisor at HHS—asserted that the loosened standards were the result of entanglements with the kratom lobby.

Calley Means on Joe Rogan Podcast: "The amount of lobbying on this was unrelenting… huge pushing, huge, huge pushing meetings, pushing from the West Wing to relax the standards."

60 Minutes found public filings from the last decade showing a constant stream of cash—much from the American Kratom Association—earmarked to lobbying the FDA, HHS, the White House, and members of Congress. Millions committed to keeping kratom legal.

Further compounding matters: political contributions. Botanic Tonics, maker of Feel Free — and its founder, J.W. Ross, a convicted felon — donated nearly $1.2 million to RFK Jr.'s political campaigns and the PAC, Make America Healthy Again. What's more, Markwayne Mullin, secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, has disclosed an investment in Botanic Tonics, of up to $1 million. 60 Minutes reached out to Botanic Tonics, without response. Mullin confirmed the Botanic Tonics investment but denied lobbying.

Calley Means, as well as Dr. Marty Makary, former head of the FDA, both told 60 Minutes they recently resigned from their posts in part because of recent changes to kratom policy shaped, as they say, by business interests, rather than public health.

HHS declined our interview request but said in a statement that "Neither political contributions nor outside pressure influenced our recommendation. Our responsibility is to protect Americans, and that is exactly what we did." The AKA, in a lengthy statement to 60 Minutes, stressed the distinction between natural kratom and, quote, "dangerous chemically manipulated products."

Dr. Andrew Kolodny says he recognizes the kratom industry's playbook.

Jon Wertheim: You have drawn considerable parallels between Big Pharma lobbying and Kratom lobbying. What specific overlap are you seeing?

Dr. Andrew Kolodny: Some of the same scientists who Purdue Pharma hired to make sure that regulators wouldn't take action against oxycontin are now working for the Kratom Association and delivering the same message, downplaying the risks, exaggerating the numbers of people who are potentially benefiting.

We asked Dr. Kolodny whether these products might aid the recovery of the nearly 10 million Americans struggling with opioid use disorder. He was unequivocal.

Dr. Andrew Kolodny: Don't use kratom. When it comes to kratom for opioid use disorder, we don't have the evidence. And what is available suggests that the risks of kratom outweigh the potential benefits.

Susan Eppard, one of the parents we met, can't fathom that kratom is still for sale. She goes into convenience stores, as she did last summer in New York City, asking folks if they realize what they are selling. Often, she says, they don't.

Susan Eppard: I just wanted to show you this is my son who died from kratom. Something very similar to that product. And this is his death certificate.

Still today, hundreds of kratom products remain on the shelves, including Feel Free, the drink Melanie Clark says brought about her addiction.

Jon Wertheim: How are you doing now?

Melanie Clark: So much better.

Jon Wertheim: What would you tell people after all you've been through about Feel Free?

Melanie Clark: That it's a drug. It's a dangerous drug. You should not be able to buy bottled euphoria from the gas station. It will slowly steal your soul.

Produced by Denise Schrier Cetta and Elizabeth Germino. Broadcast associate, Mimi Lamarre. News associate, Eric Frank. Edited by Warren Lustig.

World.title: U.S. families demand answers on Iran war deaths
World.content:
Joey Amor's wife, Master Sgt. Nicole Amor, was one of the first six Americans to die in the war with Iran. Their flag-draped caskets were met at Dover Air Force Base by the president and top military leaders in March.

"She was proud. She was constant. She was unwavering. She was dedicated," Joey Amor said of his wife.

The six Americans were killed in the first 24 hours of fighting when an Iranian drone hit an Army command post in Kuwait. It was Iran's deadliest strike against the U.S. military and shattered any perception that American troops were beyond the reach of an enemy, skilled in a new type of warfare.

"There are soldiers that are signing up now that are going to go," Joey Amor told 60 Minutes. "And they have to trust that what happened to my wife isn't gonna happen to them."

Nicole Amor served in the Army Reserve's 103rd Sustainment Command, a unit for which her husband now says he doesn't "have anything nice to say."

"I love those soldiers. And my wife loved those soldiers," Joey Amor said. "But the command of the 103rd has handled this so poorly. And if I'm being frank, it's on them. They killed my wife. They killed these soldiers. And it's not political. There are individuals in that command that made choices."

Joey Amor 60 Minutes

Those choices by command have been the focus of an eight-month-long investigation into the first American deaths of the war. The day after the attack, on March 2, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth insisted the troops there were well-protected.

"Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately we call it a 'squirter,' that makes its way through," Hegseth said at the time. "And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified. But these are powerful weapons."

The U.S. military had built up a significant presence in the Middle East. But in the weeks leading up to the Iran war, the Pentagon moved 90% of its ground forces out of Kuwait and away from Iran, fearing retaliatory strikes. But some 70 members of the 103rd, which handles logistics, were sent closer to the threat, to the small Army outpost known as Port Shuaiba — about 65 miles from Iran.

"The protection that was there was to stop car bombs and threats like that," Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, the 103rd's deputy chief of operations and a combat veteran, told "60 Minutes." "There was nothing there designed to protect from an aerial attack."

Ramsbottom said the threat of a drone attack was well-known. It was raised to the unit commander, Brig. Gen. Clint Barnes, and Ramsbottom said he warned Maj. Gen. John Hinson, the two-star general overseeing logistics for the U.S. Central Command.

"I brought it up twice in various meetings, basically saying, 'Hey, I don't see how we're protected here,'" Ramsbottom told 60 Minutes. "He said, 'We don't have to worry about protection.'"

Ramsbottom said that's the reason he's speaking up about the incident.

"I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself, all the way down to my level," he said. "Yes, we did not plan this well. And this needs to be a lesson that we learn."

60 Minutes spoke with six soldiers who said they had seen U.S. intelligence before the war started that put Port Shuaiba on an Iranian list of targets.

Ramsbottom said they asked for a counter-drone defense system, and military brass said they'd try to get it sent out to them.

"It never arrived at Shuaiba. And we don't know if it was ever even ordered or requested," he said.

Major Stephen Ramsbottom 60 Minutes

This past week, Ramsbottom filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress, demanding an investigation into why there was no "dedicated protection against one-way attack drones." He also claims the site "had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance."

The week before her death, Joey Amor said his wife told him she was worried about her unit's safety.

"It's the only time in 15 years that I've ever heard her like that," Joey Amor said. "She knew something was coming. They all knew something was coming."

At 9 a.m., the morning after the initial strikes on Iran, the soldiers at Port Shuaiba received the all-clear and went back to their workspace. Some 30 minutes later, the Iranian drone hit.

Nicole Amor was still breathing when soldiers loaded her into an SUV and drove her to a local Kuwaiti hospital, according to several soldiers who survived the attack.

"They were googling hospitals to try to take some of the soldiers to," Joey Amor said. "That's absurd."

Does he think she had a chance to survive if there was a proper plan in place? "I think my wife had a shot, yeah," he said.

Delivering the news of troops' deaths

When American troops are killed in action, it falls on fellow soldiers to deliver the news.

Joey Amor tried to shield their 10-year-old daughter and 18-year-old son from the two soldiers walking up their driveway.

"My daughter didn't understand," he said. "And my son said, 'I know.'"

Among the last to be notified was Tina Marzan, whose husband, Chief Warrant Officer Robert Marzan, was among those killed. She said they had to use DNA to identify her husband.

"I think the drone hit them directly. And I don't know who knew that they were still in the building, in this metal shed that they were in," Tina Marzan said. "And I know they found his hat next to him and that's why they knew."

Tina Marzan, whose husband served for 36 years, got a visit from troops the night after her husband was killed.

"And immediately when you see them standing outside, you know," she said. "I just didn't want it to be real."

Michelle Tietjens, whose husband, Sgt. 1st Class Noah Tietjens, was also killed in the Kuwait strike, had to break the news to her 13-year-old son.

"I gathered a few items that my son would want," she said. "One of 'em was his dad's sweatshirt that he left at home. An Army little teddy bear, and I went back to where my son was, and I had to tell him daddy wasn't coming home."

Investigation to be released to families this week

The Gold Star families told 60 Minutes they have received military honors and outreach from the Trump administration, but don't feel like they've gotten the full story about what happened and why.

Tina Marzan and Michelle Tietjens 60 Minutes

Tina Marzan summed up what she's heard from the Pentagon in the eight months since her husband died in one word: "Nothing." Michelle Tietjens was briefed by Army officials yesterday. She said they did not acknowledge any mistakes.

The Pentagon declined to answer whether the 103rd was denied adequate force protection. 60 Minutes also reached out to the two generals who allegedly ignored warnings about drone attacks. Hinson and Barnes did not respond to our request for comment.

The Army finished its investigation into the attack in June. This week, the families are finally being briefed on the results.

"You trust your leadership to put you in the best possible position," Joey Amor said. "And my wife's death, I already know, was preventable. I will not accept, 'That's the cost of war.'"
