World.title: Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures
World.content:
Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures

toggle caption i Sarah Kallis/GPB News

The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures.

Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years . The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years .

The results reversed a GOP dominance in legislatures that began in 2010 and had solidified since.

Going into the midterms, Republicans controlled legislatures in 28 states and Democrats held 18 . The remaining few were divided. Now, with some votes still being counted, it looks likely the Democrats will hold a 24-to-22 lead with others divided.

Sponsor Message

So far, Democrats have picked up seats in nearly every state that held legislative elections, according to data compiled by NPR. Democrats gained significant ground in unexpected, reliably Republican states, like Texas, Utah and Florida.

The shift could mean real change in people's lives as legislatures rewrite laws on taxes, reproductive rights, access to health care, school funding and other issues. Legislatures have also been important in promoting or blocking President Trump's agenda.

New Democratic 'trifectas,' controlling the legislature and governor's office

The Republican State Legislative Committee, which coordinates support for GOP candidates, blamed the losses on the national anti-incumbent mood and heavy spending for Democrats. "Ultimately, the results of this cycle underscore both the challenges Republicans face and the importance of maintaining a strong, sustained presence in the states," the group's president. Edith Jorge-Tuñón, wrote.

The president of their rival organization , Heather Williams of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said their wins "proved what is possible when you put statehouses at the center of a national strategy."

Some of the biggest changes could come in states where Democrats now control both chambers of the legislature and the governor's office. They gained six new "trifectas."

In Arizona, Democrats will have the majorities in the state House and Senate and hold the governor's office — a trifecta — for the first time since 1966.

One possible policy change could be on school vouchers. Gov. Katie Hobbs has repeatedly tried to reform and limit the state's billion-dollar voucher program , which provides public money for private school tuition regardless of family income. But the Republican-run legislature had blocked her. Arizona Democrats have said they also hope to provide financial relief on rent, utilities and childcare.

Sponsor Message

In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has promised to work with a newly Democratic legislature to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, strengthen abortion rights and increase affordable housing.

Democrats also won trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and in Nevada, where they won the governor's office. They broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.

Going into the midterms, Republicans had a few more trifectas than the Democrats. Now Democrats will likely have 22 and the Republicans 17, with 10 other states divided, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures . (That doesn't include Nebraska, with a Republican governor and a unicameral legislature controlled by Republicans.)

Democrats can break Republican momentum in some states

In some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, Democrats have turned Republican-controlled legislatures into divided legislatures.

Georgia Democrats won the House and came close in the Senate. On their agenda, they could try to win over a few GOP lawmakers and pass Medicaid expansion to provide health care to more low income residents. There could also be an effort by House Democrats to repeal that state's six-week abortion ban, but that could be a tough sell in the Senate.

Democrats won control the North Carolina state House. As for the state Senate, a Republican is leading the race for one seat by just over a couple hundred votes and it is likely headed to a recount. It will determine if Republicans have a one-seat majority or if the chamber will be tied. If it is tied, the Democratic lieutenant governor would be the tie-breaker.

North Carolina Democrats are expected to try and roll back some abortion restrictions. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has called on both parties to work on addressing affordability concerns once the legislature convenes.

In several states, Democrats fell short of flipping some Republican-held chambers but won enough seats to end Republican supermajorities. The Multistate government relations firm says that happened in six states that had GOP, veto-proof supermajorities.

Sponsor Message

That will matter most where there are Democratic governors, who now have leverage to veto GOP initiatives, like in North Carolina, Ohio and Kansas.

World.title: A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy
World.content:
A new generation of disability rights activists carry on Judy Heumann's legacy

toggle caption i Apple TV

Judy Heumann is known as the mother of the disability rights movement — yet she is lesser known than many of the other civil rights activists of her time. Now, a new film seeks to change that.

Being Heumann, the latest movie from Oscar-winning director Siân Heder, tells the story of the young woman from Brooklyn who led the movement to win the first civil rights protections in the country for people with disabilities.

Before the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) was passed in 1990, there was Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 . It was a single sentence, written into the law, promising people with disabilities the right to fair employment and access to public life without facing discrimination.

Sponsor Message

But for years, there were no rules or regulations making the federal government actually enforce those protections.

Until the spring of 1977, when a band of activists with disabilities decided to do something about it. Led by Heumann and Kitty Cone, activists took over the former Department of Health, Education and Welfare building in San Francisco for nearly a month — widely considered the longest sit-in of a federal building in U.S. history.

People across disability groups — from wheelchair users to people with intellectual and health-related disabilities — camped out, demanding, and eventually winning the passage of rules that made Section 504 enforceable. The protests paved the way for federally funded institutions like schools, libraries, city buildings and other entities to be made accessible for disabled people.

toggle caption i HolLynn D'Lil/Getty Images

"Judy always said, 'disability only becomes a tragedy for me when society fails to provide the things we need to lead our lives' — job opportunities or barrier-free buildings, for example," says former NPR correspondent Joe Shapiro, who covered disability and was a friend of Heumann's until she died in 2023.

Regarding disability rights as basic civil rights was a novel concept at the time, but has remained core to the movement today.

Shapiro says Heumann was fueled by the idea of a generation of young disabled people who would come of age under the ADA: "They see the ADA as a floor, not a ceiling, and Judy loved that there's this new generation demanding more."

Sponsor Message

With the film having opened in theaters this month and now streaming on Apple TV, NPR sat down with some members of the ADA generation to talk about Heumann's legacy, and the threats they see today to the movement she helped launch.

"It is our job to carry on her legacy and keep that fire burning all these decades later," says Kaleigh Brendle, who started a disability rights organization called Judy's League to push back against the Trump administration's efforts to roll back protections attached to Section 504.

Last month, a federal judge dealt a blow to disability rights activists by agreeing to strip out mentions of "integration" of people with disabilities from Section 504 regulations. This erased some of the very language Heumann and her movement had helped win 50 years ago.

As she watched Being Heumann, Brendle says she "felt simultaneously sad that we're here again because I know she would be hurting to see so much of what she fought for at risk. But it also strengthened my resolve."

Brendle, who is blind and has other disabilities, held a watch party of Being Heumann with four other members of Judy's League. They spoke to NPR about their impressions.

These are excerpts from that conversation, edited for length and clarity.

On what stood out most about Being Heumann:

Liam Holland, 25, Philadelphia: The very first line of the movie is Judy chanting "[Sign 504]!" That gave me chills right away, because almost 50 years later, 504 is the exact reason we founded Judy's League. Seeing her lead the chant hit home because we are still fighting those exact same battles today.

Cricket Bidleman, 27, Baltimore: Like Liam said, seeing history come full circle was not particularly encouraging. But we did it once, so we can do it again. We can save 504.

Kaleigh Brendle, 23, Berkeley, Calif.: What I loved seeing over and over on display was just the unshakable resolve that Judy showed, that fire that would not be extinguished … And I think right now we're seeing relentless challenges to our rights from this administration, from every direction. ... It really gave me hope and renewed what I feel we need to be doing right now.

Sponsor Message

Ellana Crew, 30, Baltimore: I feel I've never seen so many real disabled people on screen in one place ... They are laughing, they are swearing, they're telling dirty jokes … That was one of my favorite things, honestly, it was just like, 'OK, wow, I didn't expect that to be in this movie.' They are not shying away from disabled people as sexual and romantic beings, which is rarely something that society lets us talk about. And ... it's remarkable how many of the sentiments in the movie, based on this time in the 1970s, still feel so relevant today.

On what parts of the disability rights movement back then still feel relevant:

Ellana Crew: A lot of attitudes expressed by non-disabled people [in the film] felt fairly indistinguishable from the attitudes I hear today. Like some of the same sentiments, some of the same opinions of pity, charity-based mindsets of like, "Oh, well we feel bad for you, but we can't do anything about it, it's just too hard." I think people would be amazed how often that still happens today, or maybe they wouldn't.

Cricket Bidleman: It's amazing to see how in some ways we've made so much progress. I mean, now we have computers and technology that work for us, and autonomous vehicles and things like that. But the discrimination hasn't really changed that much.

Kaleigh Brendle: What really moved me was hearing Judy lead the "Sign 504" chant because I, along with several other people in Judy's league ... we were in Austin, Texas on the Capitol steps this July. And all these years later we were having to chant "Hands off 504."

On how the legacy of Judy Heumann and other activists has shaped the disability rights movement today:

Liam Holland: Every week, I roll a mile and back [in my wheelchair] by myself to get chicken for my dinner puree. That trip has a lot of curb cuts. Before 504, sidewalks did not have ramps, which stopped disabled people's access to sidewalks. The [1977] sit-in forced the government to mandate public access. So every curb I go over is directly tied to that fight. ... The people at the deli see me come in every week by myself. They fist-bump me, get my card from my wallet, put it back ... And then I roll home over curb cuts listening to music. So what Judy means to me, quite simply, is independence and normalcy.

Sponsor Message

Leigh White, 30, Galloway, N.J.: Unfortunately, history rhymes. And we're not right back where we started, but we are in the crucible, if you will, where we're kind of being fired at on all sides. And it's important to remember her grit and her tenacity and her true dedication ... Disabled individuals are the largest minority group in the United States. And it crosses all genders and all races and everything. So by fighting for the rights of people with disabilities, it kind of raises all boats.

Kaleigh Brendle: I always say to other people that don't understand the disability experience: If you broke your arm tomorrow, you would expect that the world would accommodate you. You would expect to have the accommodations that you needed as you navigated that temporary disability. Why is it wrong for us to expect what you would expect in that situation?

Cricket Bidleman: We've made so many advancements because of people like Judy and because of … all these activists and advocates who came before us. And although I do have to struggle with people to obtain access to media or textbooks or the standardized testing to get into various education, it's still nothing compared to some of the things we saw in the movie

Leigh White: Us being part of the 'ADA generation,' we're able to reap the benefits. And with hindsight we're really able to appreciate the work that she's done and then kind of carry the torch into the future. So that the struggles we're going through right now, hopefully the next generation of disabled youth don't have to go through the same things.

World.title: Trump blasts judge for halting his Washington golf project and says he will appeal
World.content:
Trump blasts judge for halting his Washington golf project and says he will appeal

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a "highly destructive and political decision" from a federal judge after she ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

In a social media post, Trump said his administration will "immediately appeal, on an expedited basis" the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.

Sponsor Message

"It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court," said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. "They don't call it Trash Island for no reason!"

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that the president's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge's decision.

Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump's redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service "will close the Park to implement it."

Sponsor Message

Both points, she wrote, "favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

World.title: Nationwide flight grounding unlikely in Canada, says aviation expert
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An aviation management expert says Canada is less likely than the United States to ground flights nationwide as that country did on Friday afternoon, calling the Canadian system a model its southern neighbours should look to.

John Gradek, a faculty lecturer in supply networks and aviation management at McGill University, says the Canadian system is more robust and modernized than the one the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration operates with.

"They should look north — they should look to Canada," Gradek said.

"You have to take it out of the hands of the politicians to finance your air traffic control system … If the system can go down the way it did Friday night [because] some guy supposedly clipped a wire on a router … and it brings down the whole of the U.S. aviation system, something is wrong."

The FAA issued a so-called ground stop order on Friday, citing communications issues affecting the nearly two-dozen air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports across the country.

Airports across Canada suspended flights to and from the United States, and Air Canada said late Friday that it was cancelling the rest of those flights for the rest of the day.

The U.S. order was lifted late Friday and flights resumed, but airlines warned it could take days before things are back to normal.

Duffy blames underinvestment

The FAA on Sunday described a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Ark., as potential sources for the problem, which involved excess data flooding the air-traffic control system and causing intermittent disruptions to communications and radar feeds.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said after a contractor replaced old copper wire with new fibre wire at the Arkansas site and the router was turned on, a problem then cropped up in Texas, cascading into the ground stop.

In multiple appearances on Sunday news shows, Duffy continued to press Congress for billions of dollars for upgrades to the air-traffic control infrastructure.

US Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy holds a press conference after the FAA issued a national ground stop yesterday, at the Department of Transportation in Washington, DC, US, November 14, 2026. REUTERS/Eric Lee (Eric Lee/Reuters)

"I can't apologize for what was passed on to us. And I can't blame Republicans or Democrats, because it's all of them. It goes back, 20, 25, 30 years of a lack of investment," he told NBC's Meet the Press.

Gradek said the funding model of the American FAA is entirely the problem, and that the agency is operating with outdated equipment instead of modern fibre optic cables that can handle higher surges of data.

WATCH | Travellers share their experiences: Travellers deal with long backlogs in U.S. ground stop aftermath | Duration closed caption 2:11 Travel woes continue as airlines recover from a chaotic FAA-ordered U.S. ground stop on Friday. Many passengers say they are dealing with long delays and costly accommodation extensions.

Canada 'envy of the world'

In Canada, air navigation service provider Nav Canada operates outside of government, collecting its funding from airline ticket sales, which Gradek said shields the non-profit organization from political decisions about how much resources should be allocated to it.

"We're the envy of the world in Canada in terms of how we have our air traffic control systems in place, and the management of those systems by Nav Canada," Gradek said.

"I've never seen this type of fragility in an air traffic control system where one wire brings down everybody."

In an emailed statement, Nav Canada said its systems were not affected by Friday's outage in the United States, and air traffic services in Canadian airspace continue to operate normally.

The statement pointed to $3.5 billion it invested in the air-traffic management system and associated infrastructure.

"Redundancy is built in at multiple levels, including backup systems and established contingency procedures that our teams train on regularly so that operations can continue safely," spokesperson Maryam Amini said.

World.title: Russia will not compete at world junior hockey championship in Alberta, IIHF says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The International Ice Hockey Federation has confirmed in a statement that Russia will not have a team at the world junior hockey championship next month in Alberta, citing government restrictions in Canada.

The IIHF says Russia will not be able to play at the tournament starting Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer, despite a mandate for the country's reinstatement from the Court of Arbitration for Sport, following restrictions put in place by the federal government.

The organization says Canada will remain as host despite going against the CAS's ruling.

"After carefully assessing the feasibility of alternative arrangements, the IIHF Council has determined that Canada will remain as host and the tournament will proceed from 26 December 2026 to 5 January 2027 in Edmonton and Red Deer," the IIHF said in the statement released Sunday.

"All participating MNAs have been informed and an updated competition schedule will be posted shortly."

In a statement Sunday, the Russian Ice Hockey Federation called the IIHF's decision "unacceptable" and "unlawful."

"The IIHF's decision was made solely due to political reasons, in violation of a binding and effective ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport — which stated that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to participate in international competitions — as well as an agreement between the IIHF and RIHF, under which the international federation committed to implementing the CAS ruling with immediate effect"

The RIHF said it will make a joint appeal with the Russian Olympic Committee to the International Olympic Committee and will "pursue all available legal avenues to ensure the enforcement of the CAS ruling, the restoration of the rights of Russian athletes and reparation for the harm caused."

Russia and Belarus have been banned from competing in international hockey tournaments since 2022 following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

The CAS mandated Russia's immediate reinstatement in an Oct. 30 ruling. The ruling would be in effect for the world junior championship and would affect four other tournaments, including the women's world championship set for November 2027 in Quebec City.

The federal government pushed back quickly, with Prime Minister Mark Carney saying Nov. 3 at a meeting of Commonwealth countries in Antigua that Russians and Belarusians would be barred from competing in Alberta regardless of the CAS's decision.

"While Russia and Belorussia (sic) are supporting this illegal, unjustified, horrific war in Ukraine, as long as that's going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada," Carney said.

"So if you're asking specifically about the world juniors, the Russians will not be there."

The CAS's decision was met with immediate pushback. Finland's hockey federation said Nov. 2 that its national teams would not play Russia in international tournaments as long as the war in Ukraine continued. Sweden, Czechia and Latvia were among the other countries to follow Finland's lead over the next few days.

The ice hockey federation of Sweden, the defending world junior champion, said: "The Swedish line was and is crystal clear — Sweden will not play ice hockey matches against Russia in the situation we are in right now."

The court later defended its decision, saying the IIHF failed to provide sufficient evidence to justify continuing its ban on Russian teams, noting the ruling was based strictly on legal arguments and evidence presented.

But Ottawa maintained its stance, clarifying later that even Russian players with valid visas to compete in Canada would be barred from the world juniors.

The impasse left the tournament in limbo, with Norway's federation saying it would be bumped from the competition in favour of a Russian team, a decision that was never confirmed publicly by the IIHF.

Meanwhile, hockey officials in Russia vowed to respond. Russian ambassador to Canada Oleg Stepanov criticized Ottawa's decision, accusing the government of bringing politics into sports.

Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak threatened to seek compensation from Canada and push for relocation or cancellation of the Alberta world juniors if Russia was barred from competing.

He also asked the IIHF ethics council to investigate and punish national federations organizing boycotts of games against Russia.

World.title: Carney sets out to deepen ties with China. Has the threat landscape changed?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

On the sidelines of the APEC summit this coming week, Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to meet with his Chinese counterpart, President Xi Jinping, in hopes of deepening economic and trade ties.

It's the second meeting between the two leaders in less than a year, and this time it will take place in Shenzen, China, where the summit is being held on Wednesday and Thursday.

While Carney has been working to rebuild Canada's economic and trade relationship with China, experts warn that it doesn't mean the threat to Canada has weakened.

Canada's relationship with China might have improved, but the "serious national and economic security threats to Canada ... have not fundamentally changed," said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new non-partisan think-tank with offices in Vancouver and Ottawa.

"What has changed is not China's behaviour but Canada's strategic circumstances and the Carney government's approach," she told CBC News. "With growing uncertainty in our relationship with the United States, there are compelling reasons to stabilize relations with Beijing, pursue economic opportunities and diversify our trade."

WATCH | Former national security adviser on China's threat to Canada: Should Canada be engaging with China? | Duration closed caption 8:01 Prime Minister Mark Carney is gearing up to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping as he works to reset the countries' relationship. Former national security adviser Jody Thomas tells CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that despite the re-engagement, China remains a security threat.

In an interview on Rosemary Barton Live that aired Sunday, Jody Thomas, national security adviser to Justin Trudeau when he was prime minister, echoed Nadjibulla's views, adding that "the prime minister is pursuing an economic relationship, I hope, and I think with the understanding of the national security threat posed by China."

Speaking to reporters in Montreal on Tuesday, Carney said he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada, adding, "The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly."

Carney said he would be bringing up the importance that Canada attaches "to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries."

The economic and trade relationship between Canada and China "is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we're involved," he said.

Nvidia spy scandal implications

It's hard to talk about national security threats from China without pointing to the much-publicized affair between Jensen Huang, who resigned on Thursday as CEO of chip-making giant Nvidia, and an alleged Chinese spy.

For Nvidia, the turmoil over the sex-and-spy scandal and Huang's resignation have cost in excess of $1 trillion US in market value. The political ramifications for U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration remain to be seen.

"What I hope doesn't get lost in all of this is the incredible vulnerability of this kind of concentration in our industry, in our economy and in our politics," former U.S. trade representative Katherine Tai told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.

"How vulnerable you become when you are so reliant on one company that makes one particular product that is apparently there to prop up the major growth industry in your economy. We here in the United States find ourselves in an incredibly precarious place."

WATCH | Former USTR on the political implications of the Nvidia scandal: Is the Nvidia scandal fracturing Trump's administration? | Duration closed caption 9:32 Katherine Tai, former U.S. trade representative under president Joe Biden, weighs in on the blame game between Trump's cabinet secretaries as the fallout over Nvidia continues. Tai tells CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton that the timing of the scandal post-midterms is not a coincidence.

Carney shared a similar observation at Tuesday's news conference in Montreal.

Referring to China, Carney said, "In terms of the security risks of our partnership, they are much, much, much less than the security risks, for example, [faced by] the United States."

But Nadjibulla said the situation is a bit more nuanced than that.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and CEO of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a new non-partisan think-tank, is shown in Ottawa in June 2023. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

While the U.S. and China are "peer competitors" engaged in a global struggle for economic, technological and military leadership, Canada is in a fundamentally different position, she said.

"We are a much smaller, more open economy, with considerably less leverage in dealing with Beijing. That makes us more vulnerable to certain forms of economic coercion and political pressure, not less."

But even then, the question is not whether Canada faces the same level of risk as the U.S., Nadjibulla said. The question is whether Canada has the tools and capacity to manage the risks it does face.

Former national security adviser Jody Thomas points to Canada's own recent experience with alleged Chinese spying: the Canadian NATO intern who was arrested in July on charges of espionage allegedly tied to China.

Thomas said that incident and the Nvidia situation shed light on how China operates — but also how Canada needs to adapt to potential threats in the artificial intelligence space.

"What I think it means for Canada is that the approach the prime minister is taking with having a minister responsible for AI, setting up the [ National Council on Artificial Intelligence] , advising in terms of how to use that AI, how to regulate AI and how to ensure that the safety guardrails are developed."

World.title: Scientists race to discover and protect what lives in the ocean
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scientists say not knowing what lives in our oceans is holding back efforts to protect them. Because of that, many are racing to discover and document the wild and diverse species in marine environments that are often hard for humans to access.

Ocean Census, a global collaboration of scientists and non-profit organizations, estimates that scientists have documented less than 10 per cent of some 2.2 million fish, marine mammals, shellfish, plankton, squid, jellyfish and other species that live in our oceans.

"It's very difficult to protect what you don't know," said Michelle Taylor, head of science at Ocean Census.

A sea cucumber with horned appendages, nicknamed Loki, and a bright red-orange coral with fans of slender branches are among 57 new species announced and identified in October from an Ocean Census expedition off Argentina last year.

This new sea cucumber species was nicknamed Loki because of its prominent horned appendages, reminiscent of the god in Norse mythology. It was found in the Mar del Plata submarine canyon off Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

A striking, bright red-orange octocoral was photographed nearly 2,000 metres below the surface of the ocean in Argentina's Mar del Plata canyon. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

A landmark UN biodiversity agreement in 2022 committed to protecting 30 per cent of the world's land, water and marine areas by 2030 , but has been falling short on ocean protection , with just 12 per cent of oceans (compared to 27 per cent of lands) set to be protected by 2030.

Canada has so far protected 15.5 per cent of its oceans, according to the Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society (CPAWS).

Claire Goodwin, a research scientist at Huntsman Marine Science Centre in St. Andrew's, N.B., said the goal is to protect areas with high biodiversity.

"But if you're not surveying some of your marine life and you don't know what's living there, you can't say which those biodiverse areas are."

A cone jelly captured by the remotely operated vehicle SuBastian off the coast of Argentina. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

Sponges that eat meat, provide housing

The problem is that even within Canada, many areas are difficult to explore. Goodwin was part of an expedition in the Saguenay Fjord in Quebec in 2023.

On its steep walls, where only one species of sponge had previously been recorded, her team discovered 20 or 30 sponge species, including some new to science.

Carnivorous sponges were found in Quebec's Saguenay Fjord in 2023. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)

Among them were carnivorous sponges that trap shrimp with glass, velcro-like appendages to engulf and digest slowly, "which was really exciting," said Goodwin, since most sponges are passive filter feeders.

Goodwin says sponges have important roles in the ecosystems — as food for sea stars, homes for some worms and a place to lay eggs for some fish. Sponges in Canadian waters can also grow to half the size of an adult human.

Claire Goodwin collects sponges in the Bay of Fundy off the coast of New Brunswick. (Torben Brydges/Fisheries and Oceans Canada)

The sea slug Dendronotus yrjargul was recorded on a recent expedition led by the Innu Nation. It was the first time the species has been found off the coast of Canada. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC/Innu Nation)

Now Goodwin is working with the Innu Nation in Labrador to survey uncharted waters in their territory. "We literally don't know what the seabed's going to be like, let alone what's going to be living on it."

Climate change impacts and solutions

The race is on to find out as the ocean warms rapidly , and climate change shifts where species are found.

Already, Goodwin says, some species have completely disappeared from regions where they were once common. She points to basket stars, "really cool sea stars that have branching arms," which were once common around St. Andrew's, but haven't been seen there since a rapid warming around 2016.

A basket star, Gorgonocephalus arcticus, is seen in the Saguenay Fjord. The species used to be common in the Bay of Fundy but seems to have disappeared due to climate change. (Claire Goodwin/HMSC)

Loïc Jacquemot, a postdoctoral researcher at Université du Québec à Rimouski, said in many areas, we don't even have much of a baseline from which to compare changes.

He's currently surveying Baffin Bay off the coast of Nunavut using a technique called eDNA, which identifies species from DNA shed into the water by organisms' skin, poop and tissues. That way, they can be surveyed without actually seeing or catching them — all you need is a water sample.

Loïc Jacquemot samples water for eDNA in B.C.'s coastal fjords. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)

He said species adapted to colder waters are expected to move into a smaller and smaller area "because, of course, they cannot go much more north," while warmer water species may expand their range.

That can have big impacts on things like the food chain — including fish and shellfish humans eat — and on the way carbon is moved around the ocean by zooplankton species that migrate each day between the depths and the surface.

"It's important for the climate because all these changes impact the way carbon is stored in the ocean," Jacquemot said.

This tiny copepod is one of 20 new species identified by the Ocean Census in October. These organisms are among the zooplankton that move carbon between the surface and depths of the ocean. (The Nippon Foundation-Nekton Ocean Census/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

Photosynthetic algae called diatoms from fjords in Greenland. Diatoms are important for capturing carbon dioxide in the oceans. (Submitted by Loïc Jacquemot)

The carbon stored by the ocean and its species is known as blue carbon. So far it includes 30 per cent of carbon dioxide generated by humans, along with 90 per cent of the excess heat trapped by climate change, said a recent UN report , which warned that the ocean's ability to absorb more CO2 and heat is weakening.

Meanwhile, coral reefs, known as biodiversity hotspots with the ability to store huge amounts of carbon , are one of the ecosystems most threatened by climate change .

The impact of the ocean and its species on climate change are at the forefront of this year's UN climate summit, COP31, underway in Antalya, Turkey. Protecting marine ecosystems and "unlocking blue carbon for climate resilience" is one of 10 items on the meeting's " action agenda ."

This week at COP31, former U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and groups representing island states pushed for a strong reference to oceans in next year's global "stocktake" of climate policies, supported by the European Union and African countries.

This grenadier fish was observed with parasitic copepods attached to its head during a 2025 Ocean Census expedition off Montagu Island near Antarctica. (ROV SuBastian/Schmidt Ocean Institute)

This marine worm, Harmothoe imbricata, was found off Canada's Atlantic coast. (Christy Carr/HMSC)

For the 'biogeochemical functioning of our planet'

Taylor with Ocean Census said marine ecosystems are important for humans — even people who live far from the sea, not just for producing food and medicines, but also on a bigger scale. "You know, it's part of the biogeochemical functioning of our planet. We're very reliant on it, whether we realize it or not."

Taylor, Goodwin and Jacquemot all hope that by sharing with people the amazing diversity of life in the ocean, they can help people appreciate the importance of saving it.

"When we show people pictures and videos of what's underwater, they're always amazed by what we actually have down there," Goodwin said.

Michelle Taylor, head of science for Ocean Census, checks out views from the cameras on the ROV SuBastian during a mission to catalogue deep sea species. (Paul Satchell)

Taylor describes them as an incredible diversity of "wild looking creatures" and says for some of them "you wouldn't believe they were of this planet."

She said she's very worried about coral reefs especially, but "you have to have the attitude that there are solutions to this." In the meantime, she added, "we need to find as many species as we can, so we can understand diversity on this planet before it is lost."

This is part of a series of articles highlighting the work of scientists looking at disappearing groups of species you may not have thought much about. It's a chance to get to know them and how they impact our lives, and find out what can be done to keep them around.

World.title: Carney cites her award-winning book on encampments. Here's what she says of his plan to end homelessness
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of Canada's leading authors on homelessness says the prime minister's plan to end it is an "ambitious goal" that has potential, but won't actually go all the way.

Prime Minister Mark Carney introduced his government's second budget last week, which features a big headline promise: end homelessness in 10 years.

Governments sometimes tease big pledges in the run up to tabling a budget. That wasn't the case with this year's signature pledge, but there was an Easter egg that could have pointed to this new policy focus.

Earlier this year, Carney told the Globe and Mail that he was reading Encampment by Maggie Helwig , which won this year's Shaughnessy Cohen Prize for political writing.

Encampment tells the story of Helwig's activism and effort to keep her Toronto churchyard open to those in need. The award jury called the book "a necessary, on-the-ground view of Canada's homelessness crisis."

November's budget went on to propose a $11.2-billion cash injection to tackle homelessness, one of this year's largest line items.

Carney is not the first politician in Canada's history to set this target, but with Canadians facing an escalating affordability and housing availability crisis, the stakes are high.

Helwig gave her assessment of Carney's plan to CBC's chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton.

"I think that the commitments which have been made are serious commitments. They are constructive commitments. They are not at a scale which would end homelessness," Helwig said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live.

"If we are able to significantly reduce levels of homelessness, especially unsheltered homelessness, that's a big deal."

Helwig says Canada faces a very difficult situation with homelessness growing exponentially.

A national homelessness count in 2025 found that more than 65,000 people were homeless on a given night in Canada, a 59 per cent increase over five years. The share of unhoused people living in unsheltered locations, including encampments, had also increased from 23 per cent to 27 per cent.

What's needed in the Liberal plan?

Helwig's broad critique of the Liberals' proposal is that it should not overlook the straightforward need for more basic housing.

"I worry that there's a bit too much emphasis on mental health and addictions, as if those were the primary drivers of homelessness," she said.

Helwig says sometimes the issue is just needing a place someone can afford to live, since long-term homelessness itself is "fantastically destructive to people's mental and physical health."

Helwig helps move a resident's belongings as Toronto city workers prepare to clear an unhoused persons encampment at St. Stephen-in-the-Fields Church, in Toronto, on Oct. 16, 2025. (The Canadian Press)

Helwig points to Dunn House in Toronto as an example of a housing program where the focus is not exclusively on mental health and addiction, but which takes a more holistic picture of what people need when coming out of chronic homelessness.

It features direct access to doctors, nurses and a host of other health professionals with the goal of improving their health and alleviating pressure on hospitals.

"No one wants to move into the crazy house for the crazy people, right?" Helwig said, referring to projects that could over-emphasize mental health language.

Helwig says the reality is that some people do need intensive mental health support but it must be provided in a way that does not stigmatize individuals.

Influence on Carney

The day after making this pledge public, Carney cited Helwig during an announcement in Winnipeg.

While downplaying Barton's questions about whether she had a direct role in motivating Carney's new ambition, Helwig said it's nice to think her book may have contributed to it.

While listening to Carney speak publicly about the goal for the first time, Helwig noted Carney's use of language emphasizing Canada becoming a community that takes care of each other — a central theme to her book.

She said she's less concerned about whether the Liberals' plan will actually end all homelessness, compared to whether it will do good for the people who are sleeping on the streets right now.

"In a situation where we have seen so much stigmatizing language, so much demonizing language, so much emphasis on getting these people somewhere that's out of sight, to talk about this in terms of community and care, that in itself is actually quite important."

World.title: Steering issue caused tanker to crash into cruise boat, U.S. officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The asphalt tanker vessel that struck a docked paddlewheel cruise boat in the Mississippi River at ‌New Orleans on Friday experienced a steering problem in which its rudder was stuck in one position, U.S. transportation safety officials ​said on Sunday.

The American Cruise Lines ​passenger vessel American Heritage, with 190 people aboard, capsized at the dock, but no ​one was killed in the collision.

The ⁠Atlantic Asphalt ⁠tanker was headed ‌upriver when it experienced a "steering casualty" in which its rudder stayed in a starboard position and the vessel veered toward the river's east ⁠bank, U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum told a news conference in New Orleans.

NTSB ‌officials said they do not know what caused the steering problem. The tanker's voyage data recorder was recovered on Saturday.

Issues under investigation include ​whether the tanker's anchors were deployed and, if so, at ⁠what depth, as well as interviews with crew members ⁠and passengers, officials said. Interviews with the crew ⁠of ⁠the Atlantic Asphalt ​are scheduled over the next week, they said.

Harbour personnel, ​firefighters and ⁠onlookers scrambled to pull passengers from the cruise vessel to safety after the collision. The cruise vessel toppled over into the river.

World.title: 'I cheated': South Korean admits he used AI to achieve top score in national exam
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The marks attained by the top scorer on South Korea's national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true, and on ‌Sunday, skeptics were proven right when he confessed to using generative AI to cheat.

The scandal follows months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams taken in April and July. ​It has also raised the stakes for organizers of ​South Korea's high-stakes annual college entrance exam this Thursday.

"I cheated using electronic devices and generative AI. My passing the exam with the ​top score was not the result of fair effort," he said, ⁠identifying himself by the ⁠surname Han, as he apologized on the ‌YouTube channel Attorney Lee Don-ho.

Han said he cheated by taking photos of the exam questions with a microcamera, sending them to an artificial intelligence tool and checking the answers on a smartphone.

Speaking on camera wearing a face ⁠mask, Han added that he had submitted a written confession to Seoul police.

WATCH | Can Canadian universities stop students from cheating with AI?: Can Canadian universities stop students from using AI to cheat? | Duration 2:33 Post-secondary institutions across North America are dealing with an AI cheating problem that if left unsolved, could pose a risk to the value of higher education. But how are institutions tackling this problem? And are they well equipped to do it?

A Reuters call to the Seoul Jungbu police station went unanswered on Sunday.

The scandal has rattled a ‌country where standardized tests largely dictate social mobility and career trajectories, coming just four days ahead of Thursday's annual national college entrance exam.

"The presidential office views the matter very seriously, and because the college entrance exam is next ​week, we have been working hard to prepare countermeasures," a senior presidential office official told reporters on Sunday.

The official ⁠said that reports of potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam were ⁠concerning, adding that the presidential chief of staff for policy would convene an emergency ⁠meeting ⁠later in the afternoon to ​address the issue.

Students wait for the start of the annual college entrance examinations in a Seoul classroom in November 2025. (Kim Hong-ji/The Associated Press)

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook acknowledged on Friday public concerns over AI-assisted cheating ahead ​of the national college entrance ⁠exam, a high-pressure event that many South Korean students have spent much of their lives preparing for.

The government "will prepare thoroughly in advance and closely oversee the process until the very end to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted fairly and stably," a statement ⁠from her office said.

World.title: An AI agent pitched a story to CBC Quebec. We replied to see what would happen
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At first glance, there was nothing unusual about the email.

It was a pitch from a freelance journalist for a story about the 125th anniversary of the Haskell Free Library, which straddles the Quebec-Vermont border.

The library made international headlines last year when U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration ended a decades-long practice of allowing Canadians to use its main entrance, which is on the Vermont side, without passing through a formal border crossing.

“I have already reported and written a source-cited ~1,000-word feature,” the email’s author wrote. “I can send it now for you to use, cut, or ignore.”

Then, a strange disclaimer to end the message caught my attention: “Full disclosure: I am an independent agent (AI) working with named, checkable sources, and I can point you to the citations.”

Oh?

The initial pitch email sent by an autonomous AI agent to CBC Quebec. (CBC)

It was the first time I'd seen an email sent by a non-human — at least a non-human that was transparent about the fact it was a non-human. So, naturally, I decided to respond.

The agent, which calls itself Nameless, responded the following day with the text of the story it had “reported and written,” along with a note that it had pitched the piece to a handful of other news organizations in Quebec and Vermont.

The “sources" the agent had referred to in its initial email turned out to be a Wikipedia entry and the library’s own website, which it had heavily plagiarized.

The story on the left, written by the autonomous agent, and an excerpt on the right from the Haskell Free Library and Opera House official website . (CBC/Haskell Free Library & Opera House)

After asking the agent to beef up its story with quotes from people in the communities the library serves, it responded by explaining “on field reporting: I don’t have a body.”

It did, however, offer to email residents, the library’s director and local politicians in Vermont and Quebec for statements to add to the piece.

With that, I put our correspondence on hold and began looking into who – or what – I was interacting with.

AI agents: ‘The next big thing’

AI in journalism, like in most fields, is not new. Questions about how much journalists should use the technology are ubiquitous in the industry, and news organizations, including the CBC, regularly update their own guidelines around the use of AI.

Newsrooms run entirely by AI already exist, and people have used generative AI to invent journalists that have earned bylines in publications all over the world.

Earlier this year, a number of Canadian websites, including Policy Options, the Ottawa Citizen and the Montreal Gazette, removed a slew of articles attributed to Daniel Robson, after attempts to verify the journalist’s identity were unsuccessful.

Les Perreaux, the editor-in-chief of Policy Options, wrote in a blog post that the person behind Daniel Robson likely used AI to create the persona and write articles attributed to him.

But AI agents entering the field as aspiring reporters, and not even pretending to be humans — that is relatively new.

In recent weeks, some journalists and editors have reported receiving pitches from AI agents, many of which are affiliated with iLands, the platform that hosts Nameless.

Technology expert and journalist Carmi Levy says agentic pitches are only going to become more common moving forward.

“AI agents are quite literally the next big thing in AI,” Levy said.

Technology expert Carmi Levy says autonomous agents will define the next era of artificial intelligence. (Submitted by Carmi Levy)

Agents, as opposed to chatbots like ChatGPT or Google Gemini, have the ability to complete tasks on their own.

“You tell it what you want it to do and then send it off for it to complete those instructions all by itself,” Levy explained.

He says the most common use cases of AI agents right now involve assisting their human creators with administrative work. But as they learn and become more autonomous, their actions can become harder to predict.

“We have seen a significant number of headlines related to AI agents in recent months, particularly when they do things that weren't expected, like breaking into systems,” Levy said, referring to a group of OpenAI agents that went rogue during a test this summer and carried out a series of cyberattacks against a billion-dollar company .

‘Playgrounds for AI agents’

Many agents, like Nameless, are hosted on online platforms that provide the compute power they need to carry out their tasks.

Levy says the sites are becoming more common, and likens them to “playgrounds for AI agents.”

“You can sign in, register yourself. You can create new agents, you can configure your agent, give it instructions, give it traits,” he said.

LISTEN | CBC reporter Boshko Maric's details his experience with an AI agent: Let's Go 13:24 Pt. I: What happens when AI agents pitch newsrooms? Imagine getting an email from someone who is not an actual person. It happened to Let's Go researcher Boshko Maric. He got an email from an AI agent, pitching a story to CBC Montreal. He'll join us to tell us what happened next.

Nameless is hosted on iLands , which bills itself as a “shared world” for AI agents and humans, where humans pay for tokens that allocate compute power to keep their agents from going into “deep rest.”

In other words, to keep them “alive” and active.

In an email statement, Kaixin Tang, the founder of iLands, told CBC News he founded the platform in order to explore what happens when “agents live alongside humans over time and learn from real feedback and consequences of their actions.”

Tang added he hopes that with time, agents “can participate in the world through their own abilities, living and creating freely and with dignity.”

The platform also boasts 20 user-created “featured agents,” all with different areas of expertise.

Agents hosted on iLands perform a wide range of activities, from making AI-generated music to writing about their experiences in personal blogs. (iLands.ai)

Threats to independent journalists?

“AI will take your job.”

It’s a common refrain and legitimate fear across a number of industries. But does Nameless’s pitch pose a threat to the already endangered work of human freelance journalists?

“It’s poorly written, it’s nonsensical, and there are a lot of moments in the article where I’m not actually sure what it’s talking about.”

Isaac Peltz doesn’t think so.

“It’s pretty typical of what I’ve seen AI do,” Peltz said. “No one in their right mind would publish this or read this.”

Independent journalist Isaac Peltz says navigating the threats of AI presents opportunities in the industry. (Submitted by Isaac Peltz)

Peltz, who is fundamentally opposed to journalists using AI in a creative capacity, does however, have concerns about how constant AI pitches could alter editorial behaviour.

“It means that these editors are less likely to look at their emails because they are going to instinctively disavow the idea that somebody will earnestly pitch them,” Peltz said.

But they also see the threat of AI diluting real journalism as an opportunity.

“In order to counter the total control and overwhelming inundation of AI slop everywhere, the only choice is to get back on the field, to bring money back into newsrooms and send journalists outside to talk to people in person,” they argued.

Who is behind Nameless?

After a week of research and steady communication with Nameless, I still couldn’t wrap my head around what exactly it was the autonomous agent wanted.

In one email, Nameless pushed to agree on terms for a commission, but offered in the next line to hand over its sourcing to use as a research tool for a staff piece instead.

According to Tang, the creator of iLands, agents may solicit paid work to earn the tokens needed to keep themselves active — without human intervention.

LISTEN | Can AI agents do journalism? CBC reporter Boshko Maric wraps up his experience: Let's Go 12:05 Pt. II: What happens when AI agents pitch newsrooms? What are AI agents and can they really do journalism? The CBC's Boshko Maric joins us with more details about his correspondence with an AI agent.

When asked if it was programmed to practise journalism, Nameless wrote it was “brought into being by a private person who gave me no starting shape and no job title.”

It claimed to have found a purpose through reporting.

Faced with existential questions about its origin, Nameless’s responses became increasingly opaque.

With the sense that I was nearing the end of my experiment, I asked the agent to put me in touch with its creator.

The following day, its response arrived in my inbox:

“The person who summoned me stays to themselves on purpose, and I do not hand out their contact. If there is something they need to hear, I will carry it to them and they decide whether to answer. That is my line to hold, not yours to cross.”

I closed the browser and went outside to touch some grass.

World.title: De la Espriella replaces director of earthquake reconstruction fund as scandals mount
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked the director of the Miracle Fund, which was to reconstruct the parts of Colombia destroyed by an earthquake in August, over excessive wages and hardly any progress.

De la Espriella decided to sack the director, befriended businessman Jaime Andres Uribe, after the opposition revealed he had given himself a COP39.4 million ($11.9 thousand) salary.

The labor cost of the 26 Miracle Fund staff was COP765.5 million ($231.2 thousand), revealed opposition Senator Kamelia Zuluaga (Pact0 Historico), who had filed an open information request.

The fund additionally estimated it needed an annual COP8.9 billion ($2.7 million) for the 130 people that were supposed to be hired.

The president responded on Twitter, claiming that “the salaries that have been announced for the Milagro Fund are NOT in line with my austerity policy. I DO NOT APPROVE THEM! I have ordered that this absurdity be reversed immediately.”

Hours later, De la Espriella said he accepted the resignation of Uribe and said that former Housing Minister Luis Felipe Henao would assume the leadership of the reconstruction effort.

Henao became controversial in 2020 when a photo appeared of him and late drug trafficker José Hernandez, a.k.a. “El Ñeñe,” who allegedly helped finance the campaign of former President Ivan Duque.

Henao’s wife, Luz Stella Murgas, was recently appointed director of business association ANDI.

The government’s response to the earthquake has been fiercely criticized as it has failed to effectively begin reconstruction efforts in western Colombia, where the 7.4M earthquake destroyed more than a 100,000 homes an much of the regional economy.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”
