World.title: The death of the night out? How Mexico City’s youth are socializing
World.content:
What if the problem isn’t that young people have stopped going out, but that we’ve been getting the night out wrong all along?

For decades, the formula seemed pretty straightforward: Friday night meant getting dressed up, meeting friends, drinking too much, dancing until the early hours and spending Saturday recovering. Going out was practically a weekend obligation.

But for a growing number of young people, getting wasted is losing its appeal. And the traditional clubbing experience is no longer the default way to socialize.

Instead, think dinner with friends, a long walk, a fitness class, a coffee that turns into a three-hour conversation, or a night at someone’s apartment. Alcohol hasn’t disappeared, and neither has the desire to have fun. But the priorities seem to be shifting.

So, is the night out dying? Or are we simply learning to have a good time differently? In Mexico City, where nightlife has long been part of the city’s appeal, I wanted to find out.

Is Gen Z drinking less?

There is evidence that young people are drinking less in several countries, although the trend isn’t universal. According to the European School Survey Project on Alcohol and Other Drugs, the proportion of European students who reported drinking alcohol in the previous month fell from 55% in 1995 to 43% in 2024. The figures concern school students across participating European countries, not all young adults worldwide.

Mexico offers another interesting example. The country’s 2025 National Survey on Drug, Alcohol and Tobacco Consumption (ENCODAT) found that the percentage of adolescents aged 12 to 17 who had consumed alcohol in the previous month fell from 16.1% in 2016 to 7.5% in 2025. That’s a substantial decline among teenagers, although it doesn’t tell us exactly how much Mexico City’s 20-somethings are drinking.

So, what’s behind the change?

Health consciousness is an obvious place to start. Fitness has become part of everyday life for many young adults, from Pilates and running clubs to strength training and early morning workouts. When your Saturday plans involve a long run rather than nursing a hangover, Friday night suddenly looks different.

There’s also a growing awareness of alcohol’s health risks. We know more about its relationship with sleep, physical performance and long-term health, including cancer. And when social media is full of people sharing their workouts, wellness routines and carefully curated lives, waking up feeling terrible can seem like a particularly bad trade-off.

But there’s a contradiction: The same social media that encourages us to go to bed early also makes us feel as though we should be doing something worth posting about. The perfect workout, the perfect job, the perfect group of friends and the perfect weekend have become another set of expectations to keep up with.

I still tell my friends to send me pictures when they travel. Increasingly, though, they would tell me they can’t wait to see my stories when it’s my turn to go somewhere. Sometimes it feels as if an experience isn’t quite complete until you’ve posted about it.

Could the pandemic have played a part, too? Young people who spent months isolated during formative years may have developed different social habits. But it would be too easy to blame COVID for an entire generation’s changing relationship with nightlife. Technology, money, work, wellness culture and shifting social norms may all be part of the picture.

And there’s another question worth asking: If drinking less is becoming more acceptable, does that mean we’re becoming less social, or simply less dependent on alcohol to socialize?

Everything in moderation

I’ve been doing Dry January for four years. Back in 2022, only one of my friends had even heard of it. She was the one who introduced me to the idea.

At the time, not drinking seemed strange unless you were taking antibiotics. How could you possibly go out and not drink? Every January, I’d find myself explaining why I was doing it and why taking a break from alcohol appealed to me. Most people weren’t particularly interested. They only wanted me to have a glass in my hand.

This year was different. By the end of January, I realized I didn’t really feel like drinking. I didn’t miss it at all, and when the month ended, I didn’t see a reason to start again.

I’d already been going out less, drinking fewer cocktails and mostly having wine when I went to restaurants. My first alcoholic drink of the year eventually came in May, at a friend’s wedding. I had a few cocktails, enjoyed myself and moved on.

What surprised me most wasn’t how easy it was to say no to alcohol. It was how much I enjoyed the mornings afterwards. Waking up after a fun evening with no hangover, enough energy to exercise, go for a walk or visit a museum felt like getting an extra day back.

Mexico City has also made it easier to experiment. There are bars and restaurants where alcohol-free drinks feel like a genuine part of the menu rather than an afterthought. A good mocktail can be just as enjoyable as a cocktail, without the alcohol.

Still, I don’t think everyone needs to give up drinking. If I go to Italy with my best friends, I’ll be more than happy to have a Spritz. At Christmas, I’ll gladly share a bottle of wine with my family.

For me, the shift has been about choice rather than restriction. I don’t want to drink just because everyone else is drinking, or because I’ve convinced myself that a night out requires alcohol. And I don’t think there’s anything wrong with someone who feels differently.

Perhaps that’s the real change: Not that drinking has become unacceptable, but that not drinking is becoming less of a big deal.

What do young people actually want from a night out?

To understand what’s happening in Mexico City, I asked young people about their habits, what they do instead of going out, and what would make them want to go out more often.

In my survey, 55% said they go out less frequently than they did three years ago. Respondents also described drinking less when they do go out. Their explanations were revealing.

Several said their friends simply weren’t interested in going clubbing as often. Instead, they preferred daytime plans, relaxed dinners or meeting at someone’s home. These gatherings felt more intimate and made it easier to catch up, have proper conversations and spend time together without feeling rushed.

Sports and wellness came up, too. For young adults juggling work, studies and other responsibilities, a weekend workout or an early start the next morning can take priority over a late night.

What stood out in my conversations was that the issue wasn’t always a lack of desire to socialize. It was a lack of enthusiasm for the available ways of doing it.

In my survey, respondents talked about wanting clubs closer to home, shorter queues and friends who were more willing to go out. Some described asking their friends to make plans and feeling as though they were begging.

That last detail stayed with me. Imagine wanting to go dancing, getting a group together and feeling as though you’re asking everyone for a favor.

But we should be careful not to confuse a preference for smaller gatherings with a rejection of nightlife altogether. People can want fewer nights out without wanting nightlife to disappear. They may simply be more selective about when they go, who they go with and what makes the evening worthwhile.

In fact, 65% of respondents in my survey said they still went to bars, clubs or parties at least once a week. That complicates the idea of a dying night out. Going out less often doesn’t necessarily mean giving it up.

Are bars noticing the shift?

If young people are changing their habits, what does that mean for the places where they spend their evenings?

I spoke to young people about what they drink and to bar and club owners in La Roma about what they have noticed since the pandemic.

In my survey, respondents described drinking less hard liquor and fewer cocktails, such as gin and tonics or rum and Coke. Beer and wine remained popular, while some said they alternated alcoholic drinks with water or delayed their first drink until later in the evening.

Others admitted that they didn’t particularly enjoy the taste of alcohol. For them, drinking was more about loosening up, feeling more sociable and having fun with friends.

Alcohol-free options therefore have an obvious appeal. But mocktails aren’t a complete replacement for the drinking experience: Some respondents said they found it boring to spend an entire evening drinking sodas or alcohol-free cocktails, particularly when everyone else was drinking.

The message isn’t necessarily that young people want bars without alcohol. They want more choice, a good atmosphere and a reason to stay.

The owner of a bar in La Roma that also serves food offered another perspective on the experience of running a venue where people can eat, drink and socialize. His observations, alongside those of a local club owner, suggest that the relationship between nightlife and the pandemic deserves a closer look.

The club owner described a shift after COVID, with fewer young people going out, while holidays and days off could still bring busy nights, including crowds of international visitors.

These are individual observations, not proof of a citywide decline. But they raise an interesting question for Mexico City’s nightlife industry: If people still want to meet friends, what kind of venues and experiences will persuade them to leave home?

The answer might not be another club with louder music and more expensive cocktails. It could be a place where the music is good but conversation is still possible, where food is as important as the drinks, or where people can spend an entire evening without feeling pressured to keep ordering alcohol.

What does the perfect night out look like now?

For many of the young people I spoke to, the ideal evening sounded surprisingly simple: dinner and drinks with friends, either at a restaurant or at someone’s home. Good food, music they actually like, an intimate atmosphere and, crucially, music that isn’t so loud they have to shout to hear one another.

They still enjoy dancing, meeting new people and discovering new places. But they also want to talk, catch up and feel comfortable.

Perhaps the problem with the traditional night out is that it sometimes asks us to choose between the things we want from socializing. We want music, but we also want conversation. We want to meet new people, but we also want to feel safe. We want spontaneity, but we don’t necessarily want to spend hours queuing or traveling across the city.

And Mexico City has no shortage of alternatives.

The night isn’t dead; it’s simply being redefined.

What if the best place to read were also the last place you’d expect to find a book?

From Tokyo to Amsterdam, book raves have been bringing reading into clubs and cultural venues, turning it into a collective experience. The idea is simple: a book, some music and the pleasure of being together, without the pressure to talk. Less noise, more pages. Silence, too, can bring people together.

Mexico City has its own version of this quieter pleasure. The city’s audioramas, including those in Parque México and Chapultepec, offer spaces where people can sit among the trees and listen to music. I discovered them recently and was fascinated by the idea of spending an afternoon there reading or even learning Italian, as I did on my last visit. Just watch out for the person beside you who might have decided to take a nap and start snoring…

Then there are running clubs, which have turned exercise into a social activity in its own right. From themed runs and coffee meet-ups to longer races that bring strangers together, the possibilities go well beyond a night at the club.

These activities aren’t necessarily replacements for nightlife. They’re reminders that socializing doesn’t have to revolve around alcohol, a late bedtime or a particular kind of venue.

Think about your own life for a moment. When you meet your friends, does it always involve drinking? Could it be a museum, a fitness class, a walk through Chapultepec, dinner somewhere new or a Sunday morning spent running and getting coffee afterwards?

None of these plans is inherently better than going dancing until sunrise. And there’s no reason we can’t enjoy both.

Maybe the death of the night out is really the death of the idea that there’s only one way to have a good time.

Young people still want connection, excitement, music, romance and stories to tell the next morning. They just seem increasingly willing to decide for themselves what those things look like.

So, no, I don’t think the night out is dead.

But perhaps the best night out is no longer the one you barely remember. It’s the one that leaves you with a good story, people you feel closer to and a Saturday morning you’re actually excited about.

And you? What’s your perfect night out?

Marta Delgado is a Spanish writer and marketing professional from Galicia, Spain, currently based in Mexico City. She writes about culture, lifestyle, and what it means to build a life abroad, drawing from her own time living in different countries.

World.title: Mexican Drug Lord Félix Gallardo Dies at 80
World.content:
Mexican National Guard vehicles at the entrance of Guadalajara International Airport, 4 March 2022; the National Guard is one of the forces named in the operation. Photo: ProtoplasmaKid, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Key Facts —Who. Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, 80, founder of Mexico’s Guadalajara drug cartel, convicted in two cases. —When. He died on Sunday 15 November 2026 in Guadalajara, Mexico. As of 15 November 2026, 5:00 p.m. ET (22:00 GMT)

Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, the convicted founder of Mexico’s Guadalajara drug cartel, died on Sunday 15 November 2026 at the age of 80. The man nicknamed “El Jefe de Jefes” (Boss of Bosses) died in Guadalajara, the capital of Jalisco state, according to the state’s security secretariat.

Americans care because he was convicted of the kidnapping and murder of Enrique “Kiki” Camarena, an agent of the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). Many also know his story from the Netflix series “Narcos: Mexico”, in which the actor Diego Luna plays him.

What We Know

The Jalisco state security secretariat (Secretaría de Seguridad de Jalisco, SSJ) said he lost his life on 15 November at medical facilities in Guadalajara. It said he had been kept under observation with a “guarded prognosis” beforehand.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The SSJ is the Jalisco state body responsible for public security. Jalisco is the western Mexican state whose capital is Guadalajara.

Medical staff put the time of death at about 14:00 local time. The cause was multiple organ failure, known in Spanish as “falla orgánica múltiple”.

Milenio, a Mexican newspaper, reported the news at 15:15 Mexico City time. Aristegui Noticias, a Mexican news site, followed at 15:34.

Milenio reported that he was moved on Friday 13 November from Puente Grande, a prison in Jalisco state, to a private hospital in the Lomas del Country neighbourhood. The newspaper said he reportedly had low blood-oxygen levels.

He was held at Puente Grande when he died. In 2022 a judge granted him the possibility of serving the rest of his sentence under house arrest.

Aristegui Noticias reported that he stayed in prison because the federal prosecutor’s office (FGR) challenged that ruling. The FGR is Mexico’s national prosecution service.

Church and fountain square in Ocotlán, in Jalisco state, the state where Félix Gallardo was held. File photo, not from the day. photo, undated. A church and fountain on a town square in Ocotlán, Jalisco, the town at the other end of the Tototlán road. Photo: Bambirucho, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on DEA (Mexico) Email address Follow

Why the Camarena Case Still Matters

Félix Gallardo received two sentences totalling 77 years. One was 40 years for drug crimes, arms possession and bribery.

The other was 37 years for the kidnapping and murder of DEA agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena. El Financiero, a Mexican business newspaper, also names the pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar in connection with the case.

He was arrested in April 1989. El Financiero gives the date as 8 April 1989 in Guadalajara.

Camarena was a US agent, so the case concerns Americans as well as Mexicans. Félix Gallardo was convicted of that crime, and his death does not change the verdict.

El Financiero reported on 15 November 2026 that “Narcos: Mexico” portrays him, with Diego Luna in the role. Luna has said of Félix Gallardo and people tied to him: “no quiero ningún contacto con ellos” (I want no contact with them).

“Narcos: Mexico” is a Netflix crime drama about the rise of Mexican drug trafficking. El Financiero published its Luna story on the day of the death.

What Is Not Known

We found no statement from a family member or lawyer, and funeral plans are not known. We also found no statement from US authorities, including the DEA, by 5:00 p.m. ET (22:00 GMT).

It is unclear whether the private hospital named by Milenio is the same place where he died. The SSJ referred only to “medical facilities” in Guadalajara.

What It Means for US Readers

Readers should note that the hospital details come from a single newspaper, Milenio. The 14:00 time of death comes from medical staff and we have not confirmed it independently.

Those most directly connected are the DEA, whose agent Camarena was killed, and Americans who know the case through “Narcos: Mexico”. The confirmed facts show no effect on markets, travel or policy.

Reports so far describe a death in hospital after a transfer from prison. We do not go beyond what the SSJ and the named outlets have confirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo?

He founded the Guadalajara cartel and was known as “El Jefe de Jefes” (Boss of Bosses). He was convicted in two cases, with sentences totalling 77 years.

When and how did he die?

He died on Sunday 15 November 2026, aged 80, at about 14:00 local time. The Jalisco state security secretariat confirmed his death, and the reported cause was multiple organ failure.

Why was he in prison?

He received 40 years for drug crimes, arms possession and bribery. He received another 37 years for the kidnapping and murder of US DEA agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena.

Was he still in prison when he died?

He was held at Puente Grande, but Milenio reported he was moved to a private hospital on Friday 13 November. A judge allowed house arrest in 2022, yet prosecutors challenged the ruling and he stayed in prison.

Sources: Jalisco state security secretariat (SSJ) statement; Milenio; Aristegui Noticias; El Financiero.

Troops: Estimates range from about 2,000 to 2,500 Salvadoran soldiers, most outside the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force.

Gang offer: Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, asked the UN on Nov. 1 (ET) for dialogue.

Published Sunday, Nov. 15, 2026, 4:30 p.m. ET (Eastern Time, also the clock in Port-au-Prince) · Source: UN, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, IFES, Salvadoran and Haitian officials

Haiti’s prime minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, is due in El Salvador on Nov. 16 and 17 (ET) to discuss the future of Salvadoran troops in his country, as the Haiti crisis enters a new phase. Salvadoran Vice President Félix Ulloa said the troop question would be raised on the sidelines of an international democracy conference.

It is not confirmed whether Fils-Aimé will meet President Nayib Bukele. For US readers, the outcome matters because Washington backs the wider security effort and has a stake in how it ends.

Why Salvadoran Troops Are in Haiti

Bukele sent troops after four Salvadoran aviation technicians disappeared in an ambush on Oct. 18. Estimates of the force run from about 2,000 to about 2,500 soldiers, depending on the count.

Most of them operate outside the Gang Suppression Force (GSF), the UN-backed multinational unit that helps Haitian police. Neither government has published the agreement setting out the Salvadoran troops’ rules of engagement, duration or legal basis.

Our earlier reports covered the retaking of a stadium from gangs and the gang chief’s call for a UN probe of drone strikes.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Haiti Email address Follow

The Gang Leader Asks for Talks

Wilson Joseph leads the 400 Mawozo gang, which operates around Port-au-Prince, and uses the Creole alias Lanmò Sanjou. On Nov. 1 (ET) he wrote to the UN Secretary-General asking for a UN delegation for “dialogue and mediation”.

UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said receiving the letter “does not constitute endorsement of its contents”. The US State Department has offered a reward of up to US$1 million for information on Joseph since 2022.

The Raid and the Reactions

Haitian police, backed by Salvadoran troops, raided a site in Croix-des-Bouquets, near Port-au-Prince, on Sunday, Nov. 8 (ET), reportedly killing 20 people. Bukele announced the operation on X on Tuesday, Nov. 10 (ET), saying the house of Lanmò Sanjou and the 400 Mawozo headquarters had been destroyed.

Ana Piquer, the Americas director of Amnesty International, called on both governments to make public the agreement governing the deployment. US diplomats sent a formal note on Nov. 5 (ET) about the risks to troops and civilians.

There are also reports that Salvadoran gunfire hit the US embassy in Port-au-Prince. Salvadoran authorities dispute that.

Drones, Deaths and the Election Calendar

Human Rights Watch, a New York-based rights group, counted at least 1,243 deaths in 141 drone operations from March 2025 to January 2026. At least 60 of the dead were not gang members, 17 of them children.

The IFES ElectionGuide database, run by a US-based election-support group, lists a first election round on July 18, 2027 and a tentative second round on Oct. 4, 2027. A Dec. 13, 2026 date was postponed.

What It Means for US Readers

The US is watching a Salvadoran offensive it did not lead, and it has formally raised safety concerns. Any deal between Haiti and El Salvador will shape a security effort that Washington supports.

The US reward on Joseph also makes his appeal to the UN awkward for American policy. Talks with a gang leader wanted by US authorities would be a sensitive step.

What Is Not Known

We found no new, verified development dated Nov. 14 or 15 (ET), no poll by a named institute and no prediction-market odds on Haiti. The fate of the four Salvadoran technicians is unresolved.

The toll of 20 dead in the Croix-des-Bouquets raid is reported only, and we found no official Haitian figure. We also could not confirm Haiti’s electoral calendar with the electoral council or the agenda of the prime minister’s trip.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Salvadoran troops in Haiti?

El Salvador sent troops after four of its aviation technicians disappeared in an ambush in Haiti on Oct. 18. Estimates of the force range from about 2,000 to 2,500 soldiers.

What has the 400 Mawozo gang asked for?

Its leader, Wilson Joseph, asked the UN Secretary-General on Nov. 1 (ET) to send a delegation for dialogue and mediation. The UN said receiving the letter does not amount to endorsement of its contents.

When is Haiti’s next election?

The IFES ElectionGuide database, run by a US-based election-support group, lists a first round on July 18, 2027 and a tentative second round on Oct. 4, 2027. We could not confirm the dates with Haiti’s electoral council.

World.title: Antalya Climate Talks Hit Halfway Mark
World.content:
Dan Jorgensen, EU Commissioner for Energy and Housing, attended the COP31 Presidency’s Energy Ministerial Meeting in Antalya on 10 November 2026. Photo: Necati Savas/EU.

Climate talks in Antalya reached their halfway mark on Saturday, and thousands marched outside as ministers arrived for the hard part. The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, the 31st annual UN climate conference, is due to close on Friday, 20 November.

March: Police estimated more than 7,000 people marched in Antalya on Saturday, 14 November.

Police estimated more than 7,000 people marched in Antalya on Saturday, 14 November. Talks: The negotiations reached their midpoint with limited progress, and ministers are arriving to settle the political issues.

The negotiations reached their midpoint with limited progress, and ministers are arriving to settle the political issues. Closing: The talks are due to close Friday, 20 November; a first draft of the final decision text is expected early in the week of 16 November.

The talks are due to close Friday, 20 November; a first draft of the final decision text is expected early in the week of 16 November. Prediction markets: none found for this summit on Polymarket or Kalshi.

Marchers Fill Antalya’s Streets

Police estimated that more than 7,000 people marched through Antalya on Saturday, 14 November. Environmental groups, trade unions and rights organisations organised the march, which passed without any major incident.

Marchers were searched before joining and moved under close police supervision. Some carried rainbow flags, after activists raised safety concerns over Türkiye’s crackdown on the LGBT community in September.

Halime Saman of the People’s Climate Summit platform said: “We are suffering the consequences of climate injustice, yet our voices are never heard at the COP.”

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on COP31 Climate Summit Email address Follow

Negotiators Reach the Halfway Mark

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate minister and president of the negotiations, described “really good and positive conversations” but said some issues need more time. Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the UN climate change secretariat (UNFCCC), said “There’s no climate quick fix.”

A stocktaking plenary, a full session to review progress, presided over by Türkiye and Australia, was scheduled for Saturday night, local time. Countries’ first red lines, the points they will not concede, were expected to emerge there.

The presidency circulated an informal paper titled “Reflections on Proposed Cover Decision,” a menu of ideas for a short final decision text. It does not reflect consensus.

Finance and Fossil Fuels Remain Open

A draft text includes an option for tripling adaptation finance, money to help countries cope with climate impacts, to at least US$120 billion a year by 2035. Another option would start a review of the COP30 finance target set at last year’s summit.

An informal note on the Mitigation Work Programme, the track on cutting emissions, is heavily bracketed, meaning wording is still disputed. EU options would extend it to 2030, 2031 or 2040.

Türkiye and Australia are urging countries to join a voluntary pledge to raise electricity’s share of final energy use to 35% by 2035, from 23% now. Sources give both 14 and 15 as the number of countries that have backed it.

What Comes Next

A first draft of the final decision text is expected early in the week of 16 November. Negotiators aim to reach a deal by Friday, 20 November.

What It Means for US Readers

Antalya is eight hours ahead of US Eastern time, so a midday Antalya session falls around 4 a.m. ET. Official session times were not available to us, so no ET schedule can be given.

Any finance or fossil-fuel language agreed in Antalya will shape the rules companies with global operations work under. Our COP31 hub will carry updates as the draft texts appear.

What Is Not Known

The outcome of the Saturday-night stocktaking plenary has not been reported in the sources available to us. It is unclear which red lines countries laid down.

It is not confirmed whether the Antalya Declaration, a text the Turkish presidency announced it was preparing, will be adopted.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people marched in Antalya on 14 November?

Police estimated more than 7,000 people. Organisers’ own figure was higher.

When is COP31 due to end?

The official closing date is Friday, 20 November. Negotiators aim to reach a deal by then.

World.title: Alaska Count Will Settle Last Midterm Seat
World.content:
Archive photo. The US Senate chamber in Washington. Photo: Library of Congress.

The 2026 US midterm elections are settled except for one Senate seat. Alaska, where voters rank candidates in order of preference, runs its final count on 18 November.

Last open seat: Alaska is the only uncalled US Senate race; Democrats hold 55 seats and Republicans 44.

Alaska is the only uncalled US Senate race; Democrats hold 55 seats and Republicans 44. Alaska lead: With about 97% of the expected vote counted, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 50% to 46% in first-choice votes.

With about 97% of the expected vote counted, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by roughly 50% to 46% in first-choice votes. Next date: The ranked-choice count is scheduled for Wednesday, 18 November 2026.

The ranked-choice count is scheduled for Wednesday, 18 November 2026. Prediction markets: Polymarket priced a Peltola win by 3 to 6 points at 98%, with US$77,215 traded (15 November).

Alaska Is the Last Seat Left

Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for Wednesday, 18 November 2026, and it is the last major step in the midterm Senate map. In ranked-choice voting, voters rank candidates, and the last-placed candidate’s votes are redistributed to the voters’ next choices.

Mary Peltola, a Democrat, led Dan Sullivan, the Republican senator, by about 49.9% to 46.0% in first-choice votes with 97.4% of the expected vote counted. Her lead was 2,517 votes on 9 November and has since grown to several points.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Alaska Email address Follow

Democrats Already Hold Senate Control

Democrats hold 55 Senate seats and Republicans 44, so Alaska cannot change which party controls the chamber. It can only change the size of the majority.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

In the House of Representatives, Democrats hold 256 seats and Republicans 170, with nine races uncalled. A party needs 218 for a majority, so Democrats are already past that line.

These are unofficial counts from the latest tally we checked on 15 November, and states have not yet certified results. The new Congress convenes in January 2027.

Mississippi Was the Late Flip

Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi, and the race was called on Wednesday, 11 November, after absentee and affidavit (provisional) ballots were counted. Hyde-Smith conceded that evening.

Colom’s win left Alaska as the only Senate race still without a winner.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction market, the Alaska Senate final-round margin market priced a Peltola win by 3 to 6 points at 98% on 15 November, with US$77,215 traded. These are real-money bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

The result will fix the size of the Democratic Senate majority that confirms judges and shapes spending bills from January. A 55-seat majority is more comfortable than a bare 51.

Ipsos, a polling firm, found President Donald Trump’s approval at 32% in a poll fielded 6 to 9 November, with prices the main drag. Immigration was his best issue at 38%.

What Is Not Known

The time of the 18 November tabulation was not available to us. The final margin after redistribution is not known, and the Division of Elections has not yet certified any result.

Final House totals are also open, with nine races uncalled at the last count we checked.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will Alaska’s Senate race be decided?

Alaska’s ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for Wednesday, 18 November 2026. Official certification follows later.

Who leads in the Alaska Senate race?

Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan by about 49.9% to 46.0% in first-choice votes, with 97.4% of the expected vote counted.

Who controls the US Senate?

Democrats, with 55 seats to 44 for Republicans. Alaska is the only race still uncalled.

World.title: Colombian Rights Group Counts 26 Massacres
World.content:
File photo. The Casa de Nariño, Colombia's presidential palace, Bogotá, 2015. Photo: Juanjo70000, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Indepaz, a Bogotá human-rights research institute, counted 26 massacres with 87 victims in Colombia since President Abelardo de la Espriella took office on 7 August, it said in a report published on Sunday 15 November 2026. The institute tracks violence across the country.

Five of the 87 victims were minors, Indepaz said in the same report on 15 November. The institute also counted 45 social leaders, meaning community and rights activists, killed over the same period, according to the report.

Valle del Cauca, a department in the south-west, had the most massacres and the most victims in Indepaz’s count. Indepaz says its categories count different things and must not be added together.

Key Facts 26 massacres and 87 victims in 100 days, five of them minors.

Valle del Cauca, a department (Colombian state), had the most: six massacres, 18 victims.

Also killed: 45 social leaders (rights activists) and eight ex-fighters of the FARC, a former guerrilla army.

As of 15 November 2026, 18:00 GMT

What We Know

Indepaz’s Observatory of Human Rights and Conflicts, its research unit, counted the 26 massacres between 7 August and 15 November 2026, it said in its report “100 DÍAS: el costo humano de la violencia” on 15 November. Among Colombia’s departments (states), Valle del Cauca had six, Antioquia and Tolima three each, and Huila two.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

By number of victims, Indepaz reported on 15 November that Valle del Cauca had 18, Tolima 12, Huila 10 and Antioquia nine. The institute cited Suaza, a town in Huila, as a case with seven victims in the same report.

Indepaz defines a massacre as the intentional, simultaneous killing of three or more people in a state of defencelessness by the same perpetrator, in common circumstances of mode, time and place. The institute said on 15 November that this definition lets events be compared but does not replace a criminal investigation.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Beyond massacres, Indepaz reported on 15 November that 45 social leaders and human-rights defenders were killed in the period, 36 men and nine women. That is about one every 2.2 days, the institute calculated in the same report.

Cauca had 11 of those killings, Antioquia eight and Putumayo four, and in 44 of the 45 cases the record names no suspect, Indepaz said on 15 November. The figure is not a judicial conclusion on motive, and our earlier report on social-leader killings covers the longer trend.

Indepaz also counted eight former fighters of the FARC, the old guerrilla army that signed a peace agreement with the state in 2016, killed in the period, all men, it said on 15 November. Two died in Nariño and two in Cauca, with one each in Valle del Cauca, Cesar, Norte de Santander and Putumayo, the same report said.

For August and September only, Indepaz reported on 15 November that 6,667 people were displaced in 17 events, 13 of them mass displacements. Cauca accounted for 3,474 people (52.1%), Chocó 1,609, Antioquia 739 and Bolívar 424, according to the report, which says 63.7% fled fighting between armed groups.

Indepaz listed figures it attributes to Colombia’s Defence Ministry, saying on 15 November that 43 uniformed personnel were killed and 219 wounded. It also cited 339 terrorism cases reported by the ministry, with a cut-off of 5 November, and lists at least six cases of alleged extrajudicial executions reported to it, which are denunciations and not court findings.

Chapel of La Ermita in Roldanillo, Valle del Cauca, the department with the most massacres in Indepaz’s count. File photo, July 2012: Jarp1218 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0).

Why It Matters

Valle del Cauca alone accounts for 18 of the 87 massacre victims, and Cauca for 52.1% of the people displaced in August and September, according to Indepaz’s report of 15 November. Travellers and expats planning trips to those departments should read their own government’s current travel advice.

In plain English Indepaz is an independent research institute, not a government body, and it keeps its own count of killings. A department is a Colombian state, and a social leader is a community or rights activist.

What Is Not Known

Indepaz’s counting method is its own, so official government figures may differ. The institute said on 15 November that it is not rigorous to attribute all 26 events to one organisation or one dynamic, because causes need case-by-case analysis of armed disputes, criminal structures, retaliation and local context, and that its categories must not be added together.

The 100-day tally is a snapshot of Indepaz’s own records, not a verdict on any policy. Our Colombia coverage will track later figures.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many massacres did Indepaz count?

Indepaz counted 26 massacres with 87 victims, five of them minors, between 7 August and 15 November 2026, it said in its report of 15 November. The institute is a Bogotá human-rights research body.

What counts as a massacre?

Indepaz defines it as the intentional, simultaneous killing of three or more defenceless people by the same perpetrator in common circumstances. It said on 15 November that the definition aids comparison but does not replace criminal investigation.

Which areas were hit hardest?

Valle del Cauca had six massacres and 18 victims, Antioquia and Tolima three massacres each, and Huila two, according to Indepaz’s 15 November report. By victims, Tolima had 12 and Huila 10.

Is this an official government count?

No, Indepaz is a research institute that counts cases by its own method. It says the 26 events should not be attributed to one organisation.

World.title: Venezuela Vote Timetable Tied to Law
World.content:
Venezuela · Politics

A Venezuelan opposition negotiator says the election timetable will follow the Constitution and the laws.

Juan Miguel Matheus, a member of the opposition delegation at the US-backed dialogue table in Caracas, said on Sunday 15 November 2026 that the election timetable follows what the Constitution and the laws establish, according to Monitoreamos, 15 November 2026. He spoke in an interview with Margarita Oropeza, a Venezuelan television journalist.

Monitoreamos is a Venezuelan news site. Washington facilitates the talks, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said elections should ideally be held in 2027, as Anadolu Agency, a Turkish news agency, 6 November 2026, reported.

For US readers the open question is when Venezuelans will vote, and no date has been fixed.

Key Facts —What. Matheus says the election timetable follows the Constitution and the laws. —Date. No election date has been fixed at the Caracas talks. —Who. The United States facilitates the talks, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio hopes for elections in 2027. —Open. Pending topics include Venezuela’s Supreme Court, the Parties Law on party rules and free speech. —Prediction markets. Polymarket, a prediction platform, gives 9.5% for a vote scheduled by 31 December 2026 (15 November, 1:13 p.m. ET).

What Matheus Said

In the interview carried by Monitoreamos on 15 November 2026, Matheus said: “The timetable will be set according to what the Constitution establishes and what the laws establish.” He said this in an interview that Monitoreamos reported (our translation from Spanish).

He also said: “More than talking about dates, we have to talk about certainty and deep conditions” (Monitoreamos, 15 November 2026; our translation).

Matheus said the change must go deep, to inaugurate “a democratic system that can last over time”, according to Monitoreamos on 15 November 2026. He did not name a date.

He said a political agreement could come with the backing of the United States as facilitator (Monitoreamos, 15 November 2026). The interviewer recalled Rubio’s remark about 2027, but Matheus did not confirm that year.

File photo. The Hospital Clínico Universitario on the Central University of Venezuela campus, Caracas, 2023. Photo: Warairarepano&Guaicaipuro, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Venezuela 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 3 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Where the Talks Stand

The table was installed on Thursday 6 August 2026 at La Carlota, a military air base in Caracas, backed by the United States, El Peruano, Peru’s official state daily, reported on 6 August 2026. The government delegation is led by Jorge Rodríguez, president of the National Assembly, and the opposition group by former deputy Dinorah Figuera.

Matheus sits in the opposition group. María Corina Machado and Edmundo González Urrutia do not take part, El Peruano reported on 6 August 2026.

Before the talks, El Tiempo, a Colombian daily, reported on 4 August 2026 that the agenda was to include the electoral timetable and the naming of a new National Electoral Council (CNE). It was also to cover the mechanism to enable candidates and the return of party registration cards to political organisations.

Rubio said at the White House on Thursday 5 November 2026 that elections in Venezuela would “ideally” take place next year, Anadolu Agency reported on 6 November 2026. He did not guarantee it.

Matheus said on 15 November 2026 that the negotiation runs in cycles, and that the fourth cycle takes up earlier work and opens new topics, including transformation of the electoral system (Monitoreamos). The pending topics he named are the justice system, the appointment of new Supreme Court magistrates, reform of the Parties Law (the rules for political parties) and freedom of expression.

For earlier coverage, see our report on the fourth round of talks. More is in our Venezuela news section.

In plain English: The opposition delegation is formed by members of the 2015 National Assembly, the last Venezuelan legislature won by the opposition. The talks are a negotiating table in Caracas between government and opposition delegations, with the United States as facilitator.

What Is Not Known

No election date has been fixed. Rubio’s “ideally 2027” is a stated hope, not a date.

Matheus did not confirm 2027 in the interview reported by Monitoreamos on 15 November 2026. The government side is led by Jorge Rodríguez and the opposition side by Dinorah Figuera, according to El Peruano on 6 August 2026.

Readers should watch whether the next cycle of talks produces a confirmed date.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, an online prediction market, lists the question “Venezuela presidential election scheduled by…?”, with US$679,909 traded across the whole event, although the open date markets trade far less, as of 1:13 p.m. ET on 15 November 2026 (18:13 UTC). The prices below show the chance traders give to a vote being scheduled by each date, and the later dates trade thinly, with the 30 June 2027 price resting on very little volume.

By 31 December 2026: 9.5%

By 31 March 2027: 28.5%

By 30 June 2027: 49.0%

These prices are bets, not polls. They price the scheduling of a vote, not who wins and not when ballots are cast, and the resolution rules are Polymarket’s.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will Venezuela hold its next presidential election?

No date has been fixed. Rubio said on 5 November 2026 that elections should ideally be held in 2027, and Matheus did not confirm that year on 15 November 2026.

Who is Juan Miguel Matheus?

He is a member of the opposition delegation at the US-backed dialogue table in Caracas. He gave an interview to journalist Margarita Oropeza on 15 November 2026, carried by Monitoreamos.

What is on the agenda of the talks?

El Tiempo reported on 4 August 2026 that the agenda was to include the electoral timetable, a new National Electoral Council, a mechanism to enable candidates and the return of party registration cards. Matheus named further pending topics on 15 November 2026.

Sources: Monitoreamos, 15 November 2026; El Peruano, 6 August 2026; El Tiempo, 4 August 2026; Anadolu Agency, 6 November 2026; Polymarket, 15 November 2026, 1:13 p.m. ET.

World.title: Gasoline Could Drop in December as Cooking Gas Jumps
World.content:
Filling your tank in Costa Rica should get cheaper in December but cooking with gas will cost more. The Costa Rican Oil Refinery (Recope) has asked regulators to cut the price of regular gasoline by ₡103 a liter, while the standard 11.3-kilogram (25-pound) cylinder of cooking gas would rise by ₡912, according to preliminary figures Recope presented on Friday to the Public Services Regulatory Authority (Aresep).

Under the proposal, regular gasoline would fall from ₡807 to ₡704 a liter, a drop of about 13%. Super would fall ₡28, from ₡805 to ₡777, and diesel would ease by ₡9, from ₡807 to ₡798. The 25-pound gas cylinder, the best-selling size in the country, would climb from ₡7,721 to ₡8,633, an increase of about 12%. None of the new prices is final. Aresep must review Recope’s figures and approve them before they take effect.

For anyone driving, the cut on regular is by far the largest of the three. At the proposed price, a liter of regular would cost about $1.58, or roughly $5.97 per US gallon, at the current exchange rate. On a 45-liter (11.9-gallon) tank, the change would save about ₡4,635, or roughly $10, each time you fill up. It would also undo an unusual situation that began in October, when regular became more expensive than premium. In December, regular would again cost ₡73 less per liter than super.

Recope attributed the lower gasoline and diesel prices to falling international oil prices, easing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and greater availability of crude on world markets, according to Teletica. The gas increase has a different cause. Recope said cooking gas it bought on international markets at higher prices during October kept later price declines from showing up in this adjustment, Monumental reported.

The cylinder increase will be felt in a lot of kitchens. About half of Costa Rican households use liquefied petroleum gas, mostly for cooking, according to Aresep. At the proposed price, a 25-pound cylinder would cost about $19.35, up from about $17.31. If you are due to swap a tank, buying before the new price takes effect would save you the difference, and it is worth taking 30 seconds to check that the cylinder is safe before you carry it home.

The December adjustment follows a stretch of rising energy costs. Fuel and transport fares drove consumer prices higher for a second straight month in October, when diesel alone rose more than 17%, and Costa Rica has paid $701 million more for imported fuel this year. Aresep has not said when the new prices would take effect. Adjustments normally apply from the day after the regulator’s resolution is published in the official gazette, La Gaceta.

World.title: El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo Opens ATP Finals With a Win
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo and Croatian partner Mate Pavić began their ATP Finals campaign with a 7–6 (7), 6–4 victory over France’s Theo Arribagé and Albano Olivetti on Sunday. The fourth-seeded pair recovered from a 2–0 deficit in the second set to win their opening match in the Todd Woodbridge Group at Turin’s Inalpi Arena. The match lasted one hour and 27 minutes.

Arévalo and Pavić had to work through a tense first set before taking control. They missed five chances to win the set, including four in the tiebreaker, but eventually claimed it 9–7. The French pair responded by breaking early in the second set. Arévalo and Pavić fought back, winning six of the next eight games to finish the match in straight sets.

The final numbers showed how close it was. Arévalo and Pavić won just five more points than their opponents but converted two of their four break-point chances. The win gives the Salvadoran-Croatian team a strong start in a tournament where one loss does not mean elimination. The eight doubles teams are divided into two groups of four, and each pair plays the other three teams in its group.

The top two teams from each group advance to the semifinals. Also in their group are defending champions Harri Heliövaara of Finland and Henry Patten of Britain, and Brazil’s Orlando Luz and Rafael Matos. Heliövaara and Patten won their opening match Sunday, beating the Brazilians 6–3, 5–7, 10–4.

Arévalo and Pavić are seeking their first ATP Finals title together. They reached the final in 2024 and return to Turin as one of the more experienced teams in the field. This is Arévalo’s fifth appearance at the year-end event and Pavić’s ninth. Their opponents on Sunday were making their ATP Finals debut after winning six doubles titles during the season.

Arévalo and Pavić still have two group matches to play. The semifinals are scheduled for Nov. 21, with the doubles final on Nov. 22.

World.title: Costa Rica Free Zones Barely Grew and Jobs Disappeared
World.content:
Production in Costa Rica’s free zones, the export parks that host most of the country’s multinational employers, grew just 0.6% year-on-year in September, according to the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR). That is 13.6 percentage points slower than in September 2025, when the sector was riding a surge in medical-device exports.

Employment in the regime is also slipping. The Central Bank’s three-month moving average put free-zone jobs at 195,410 in August 2026, down from 197,101 a year earlier, a loss of 1,691 positions.

The Central Bank now projects free-zone output will expand about 3% in 2026, compared with a preliminary 12.7% in 2025. The rest of the economy, known as the definitive regime, grew 3.3% in September and accounted for 96% of national growth, according to the bank’s monthly economic activity index (IMAE).

The slowdown has revived a long-running dispute over the strong colón. The weighted average dollar price on the Monex exchange market fell from 503.02 colones on Nov. 6, 2025, to 449.58 colones on the same date this year, a drop of 10.6%. Exporters and multinationals earn in dollars but pay salaries and local costs in colones, so each dollar they bring in now covers less of their payroll. The dollar hit a record low of 446 colones this week.

According to minutes of the Central Bank board’s Oct. 23 session, Henry Vargas, the bank’s division manager for data and statistical analysis, told directors that the 2025 export spike had to normalize and that international uncertainty is the main drag on the sector. He cited a U.S. Commerce Department study of possible new tariffs. Vargas said the exchange rate did not rank among the leading factors that companies named in a regional business survey the bank conducted with other central banks in October and November 2025, in which about 70% of firms said international uncertainty affected them deeply, though he acknowledged that business chambers do raise it.

Board member Jorge Guardia questioned why the exchange rate did not appear among the factors, noting that outside reports frequently point to it, according to the minutes. Central Bank President Róger Madrigal said job reductions in the sector are tied mainly to decisions by parent companies rather than directly to the exchange rate, while allowing that profit margins may have narrowed even where output has not.

Vargas also told the board that the closures of operations by Intel and Qorvo had been fully completed by September. The bank has attributed part of the year-on-year slowdown to that base effect, along with the exceptional medical-implement exports of 2025. September did bring the first month-to-month acceleration in free-zone output after 12 consecutive months of deceleration.

Business groups dispute the bank’s reading and the free-zone association Azofras has said the colón’s appreciation pressures operations and could weigh on company decisions to stay, expand or keep staff. Sergio Capón, president of the Costa Rican Chamber of Industries, has said it is unreasonable to separate multinationals’ decisions from the exchange-rate trend.

The debate comes after free zones lost jobs for the first time in seven years, and as several companies have scaled back hiring plans, including a call center that cut its Costa Rica job pledge over competition from Asia. Analysts have also warned that office vacancy could climb as multinationals cut jobs.

The Central Bank has bought more than $1.2 billion on the exchange market this year to slow the colón’s rise, and Madrigal has said the market has an excess supply of dollars.vFree zones employ close to 200,000 people and are one of Costa Rica’s largest sources of dollars, so a sustained slowdown would reach well beyond the export parks themselves. Whether the sector’s first monthly uptick in a year marks a turning point or a pause will become clearer as the Central Bank releases its October and November figures.

World.title: Should You Buy Travel Insurance for Costa Rica After the US Ground Stop?
World.content:
The nationwide ground stop that froze US air travel on Friday lasted a little more than four hours, but it left a question that will outlast the backlog. If a failure inside the air traffic control system can strand thousands of people bound for Costa Rica, should you buy travel insurance for your trip?

The quick answer to this is that insurance would not change what you get back for your flight, but it could cover almost everything else. Ten flights were canceled at Juan Santamaría International Airport on Friday and 23 were affected in all, according to airport operator Aeris, as the US ground stop spilled over into Costa Rica.

In the United States, airlines canceled more than 5,000 flights on Saturday as planes and crews worked their way back into position, according to the flight-tracking service FlightAware. For visitors, that meant missed first nights at hotels, lost tours and unplanned nights at a gateway airport or in San José.

Airfare is the one part of your trip you do not need insurance for. Under US Department of Transportation rules, if your flight is canceled and you choose not to travel, you are owed a full refund, even on a nonrefundable ticket, and that holds no matter what caused the cancellation. Airlines also waived change fees after the ground stop.

What airlines do not owe you is the cost of being stranded. Their promises of meals and hotels cover only disruptions they cause, and federal rules treat air traffic control failures as outside their control. After an outage like Friday’s, you pay for your own hotel, meals and ground transport unless the airline chooses to help.

That gap is where a comprehensive policy comes in. This kind of plan insures the full prepaid cost of your airfare, hotels and tours and bundles several benefits together. Trip delay coverage pays for a hotel room, meals and transport when you are stuck, usually after a wait of 3 to 12 hours and up to a daily limit. Trip interruption coverage reimburses prepaid nights and tours you lose when you arrive late. Missed connection coverage helps with the cost of catching up, which matters if you are booked on a domestic flight to the coast or a boat transfer to a remote lodge.

The wording matters more than the brand. The strongest policies cover a delay by a common carrier for any reason. Others list specific causes, so check that air traffic control failures or government action are on that list. Coverage that comes with a credit card tends to be narrower. During last year’s US government shutdown, American Express said its card benefits, including trip delay and trip cancellation coverage, would not pay for cancellations or delays caused by the FAA’s emergency order.

There are other limits. Insurance pays only what you cannot recover from the airline, hotel or tour operator. Canceling your entire trip over a one-day delay is rarely covered. Cancel for any reason upgrades cost more, usually return only part of your trip cost, often up to 75% or 80%, and generally require you to cancel at least two days before departure. You also have to buy a policy before trouble starts, because once a disruption is in the news, new policies will not cover it.

Comprehensive policies are commonly priced at about 4% to 10% of the insured trip cost, depending mostly on your age and coverage limits. For a couple spending $6,000 (about ₡2.68 million) on a Costa Rica vacation, that works out to roughly $240 to $600 (about ₡107,000 to ₡268,000). The same policy usually includes medical and evacuation coverage, which many US health plans, including original Medicare, generally do not provide outside the United States.

Whether that is money well spent depends on how you book. If your hotels are refundable and you have a spare day at each end, you have little to lose beyond a night or two. If you have a prepaid week at a jungle lodge, a sportfishing charter and a tight connection home, you have far more at stake. With the high season only weeks away and no way to rule out a repeat, it is worth doing that math before you book.

If you decide to buy, you can compare quotes from multiple travel insurers side by side and filter by the coverage that matters most for your trip, such as trip delay and missed connections.

World.title: The Perfect Family Beach Day at Playa Carrillo, Costa Rica
World.content:
This is between me and you. Don’t tell anybody else. We don’t want too many people overcrowding the places I’m about to tell you about. Here’s how to spend a perfectly wonderful day at the beach in Guanacaste with your family. My little family and I have done this a bunch of times, so we’ve now got it down to a science. We’re going to spend the day at Playa Carrillo.

This works best if you’re staying along the coast in the general Tamarindo/Playas del Coco area in which case it can be a there and back again day trip. Here we go. First, you and your significant other have to plan on leaving at a decently early hour in the morning. For us it’s something like 9am. This will allow you plenty of time for driving, lunching, beaching, and returning. Of course, you’ll never hit this lofty goal. Anyone with kids knows that a series of things will inevitably happen that will push back your departure time, but that’s life.

Once everybody’s finally in the car with seatbelts in place the drive begins. The drive is actually part of the fun of this day trip. The most common route takes you through the historic city of Nicoya. When I say through it, I mean wiggling your way through the city’s narrow, sometimes one-way streets, past all of the little stories, people selling things on the sidewalks, and a mix of contemporary and historic-looking buildings. If you feel like it, you can pull over at the park with the neat old church and buy the kids some ice cream. Even if you don’t stop, driving through the buzz of human activity has a nice vibe.

The nice drive portion of the day continues after you make it out of Nicoya. As soon as the city ends you drive through a series of adorable little towns separated by hilly green cow pastures dotted with palm trees. For reasons that are unclear to me, the houses on this stretch of road are particularly well maintained, brightly painted with well-manicured gardens. ‘What a nice place to live’ comes to mind as you drive.

Right about now everybody in the car is starting to get antsy and that’s ok because I know exactly where you need to stop. Since you missed that departure time by about an hour, it’s time for lunch anyway. As you approach the coast, you need to wind your way steeply uphill before cresting the mountain and riding downhill to the coast. As you reach the highest point of this mountain (almost definitely driving 5 miles per hour behind an enormous truck that you can’t pass), there’s a restaurant called La Roca.

I have no affiliation with La Roca. This info is all coming from the love in my heart. My family has been going there for years. Originally, it was pretty rustic, but sometime over the last few years they completely remodeled it and now it’s modern and very nice. Either way, the magic of the restaurant was, and still is, the view. It sits atop the mountain with a stunning view of the countryside below. You can even see a waterfall in the distance.

There’s a clearly marked trailhead right next to the restaurant and you can hike to the waterfall that you can see from the balcony. We always say we’ll do the hike next time and never do. Waterfall hike or not, order anything on the menu, it’s all delicious. Enjoy the view, recharge your batteries, and then pack everybody back into the car and start driving downhill to the beach.

As you arrive at the coast, you’ll hit the small beach town of Samara, which is a fun place to explore, but you’ll have to save that for another day because you’re heading to Carrillo. After Samara you only have about ten minutes left in the car. After you cross a one-way bridge over a small river, you’ll want to pull over at the little store for snacks and drinks because it’s the last one before the beach.

Fully stocked with goodies from the store, you’ll drive five more minutes until you hit Playa Carrillo. You’ll know you’ve made it when you’re driving next to an enormous beach with calm waves, the entirety of which is lined with several rows of palm trees. You can pull over at any spot you please. Throughout the entire palm tree section of the beach there are benches, tables, and grills. The vibe is laidback and local, with lots of families enjoying the shade and waves.

After several hours of fun in the sun, it’s time to pack everybody and everything back into the car and start the drive home. If your family is anything like mine, the return trip is a lot quieter than initial drive as your kids will be slouched over sleeping like a pile of puppies. So, there you have it, the perfect family beach trip. Remember, this is between me and you. I don’t want the tables at La Roca and the shady spots at the beach to be full of other people.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica

World.title: Costa Rica Flights to the US Back on Track as Trump Blames Biden for Ground Stop
World.content:
If you’re flying between Costa Rica and the United States today, your flight should run close to schedule. The nationwide US ground stop that froze departures on Friday afternoon ended after about four hours, and airports in Costa Rica reported operations returning to normal on Saturday.

Check your flight in your airline’s app before you leave for the airport anyway. Aeris, which runs Juan Santamaría International Airport outside San José, has asked passengers to confirm their flight status directly with their airline, since itineraries can still change. Friday’s disruption hit both of the country’s main airports. At Juan Santamaría, Aeris said 12 departures and 11 arrivals were affected, and six departures and four arrivals were canceled. The rest were moved to overnight and early Saturday slots.

In Liberia, Guanacaste Airport representative Renata González said seven flights were canceled and that operations returned to normal over the course of Saturday. The outage was not an attack. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said it began during maintenance work to replace old copper wiring with fiber-optic cable, which disrupted communication with planes and radar feeds. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no evidence of hostile action.

Duffy said more than 9,000 US flights were canceled and nearly 25,000 were delayed. It was the longest nationwide ground stop in the United States in 25 years. On Sunday, President Donald Trump made his first public comments on the ground stop and blamed his predecessor. In posts on Truth Social, he called the Biden administration “an FAA disaster” and said “everything they touched turned bad.”

Trump said his administration has a plan for the flight control systems and urged Congress to approve the money quickly, saying much of the current air traffic control system is 50 years old. Efforts to modernize the FAA’s systems have spanned several administrations of both parties.

If your flight was canceled Friday and you have not rebooked, start with your airline’s website or app rather than the airport counter. If you decided not to travel at all, US rules entitle you to a refund for a canceled flight, even when the cause was out of the airline’s control. Whether a policy would have covered you is a separate question, covered in our guide to travel insurance after the ground stop.

Many US airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same jet straight back, so delays at a US hub can still ripple into a departure here, as Friday’s cancellations showed. Air traffic between the two countries has largely recovered, but the episode has renewed debate in Washington over how quickly, and at what cost, the US air traffic control system should be replaced.

World.title: Costa Rica Banks Pay as Little as 436 Colones per Dollar – Here’s How to Get More
World.content:
If you are changing dollars into colones, where you do it matters more than ever. With the dollar at a record low, Costa Rica’s banks closed Friday buying dollars for between ₡436 and ₡440 each, according to Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) data compiled by El Observador. On $1,000, the gap between the best and worst of those rates is ₡4,000, or about $9.

The dollar closed Friday at a weighted average of ₡446.10 on Monex, the foreign exchange market run by the BCCR, a new record low and the lowest level since Monex began operating in 2006. It was the eighth straight session of declines and broke the previous record of ₡446.80, set on Sept. 17. The dollar has lost 10.3% of its value against the Costa Rican currency so far this year, according to El Observador.

Bank counter rates, as reported to the BCCR on Friday, varied by up to ₡4 per dollar. Banco Cathay offered the most, buying dollars at ₡440 and selling them at ₡452.50. Banco Nacional and BAC bought at ₡439 and sold at ₡453. Banco de Costa Rica (BCR) and Banco Popular bought at ₡438 and sold at ₡452. BCT paid the least, buying at ₡436 and selling at ₡454. The BCCR’s official reference rate in effect for the weekend is ₡442.56 for buying and ₡448.34 for selling.

Every bank pays less than the market rate when you sell it dollars. At BCT’s ₡436, changing $1,000 brings in ₡10,100 less than the Monex average, about $23. For a retiree converting a $2,000 monthly pension, choosing the best counter rate over the worst is worth about ₡8,000 a month. Changing money twice costs even more. At Banco Nacional’s rates, converting dollars to colones and back again loses ₡14 on every dollar, or roughly $31 on $1,000.

The BCCR publishes the buying and selling rate of every bank and exchange house each business day on its website, so you can compare before you go. Rates posted on Friday afternoon generally carry through the weekend, but they will move again when Monex reopens on Monday. If you already bank in Costa Rica, ask whether your bank applies a different rate to conversions made through online banking than at the teller window.

If you are paying with a foreign card, choose colones when a card terminal or ATM offers to charge you in dollars instead. That on-the-spot conversion, known as dynamic currency conversion, usually uses a less favorable rate than your card network applies. Shops, restaurants and tour operators that accept cash dollars set their own exchange rate, so it is worth checking it against the bank rate before you pay.

The Central Bank has been buying heavily without stopping the slide. On Friday it bought $41.8 million, or 84.8% of the $49.3 million traded on Monex, including $32.3 million in purchases meant to stabilize the market, according to El Observador. Its stabilization purchases total $1.39 billion so far in 2026, with no stabilization sales recorded. Specialists have said the dollar’s decline tends to deepen toward the end of the year, particularly in November, as companies pay year-end aguinaldo bonuses and taxes in colones.

For residents whose income arrives in dollars, including retirees, remote workers and landlords who charge rent in dollars, the slide has meant a steady loss of purchasing power. By early November, each $1,000 bought 46,810 fewer colones than in January, and the weak dollar has also hit businesses that earn in foreign currency, from exporters to Costa Rica’s medical tourism industry. With no sign yet that the slide is ending, the few colones you gain by shopping around for a rate are among the only savings within your control.

World.title: Costa Rica Moves to Demolish Narco Airstrips Without a Conviction
World.content:
Costa Rican authorities could destroy clandestine airstrips used by criminal groups without waiting for a final court ruling, under a bill that cleared a key legislative committee this week with unanimous support.

The Security and Narcotrafficking Committee approved the bill on Thursday. It is titled the Law to Sanction and Disable Clandestine and Unauthorized Airstrips and Allow the Confiscation of Assets Linked to Illicit Activities. The bill now goes to the full Legislative Assembly for a first-round vote and is not yet law.

President Laura Fernández submitted the measure in June as one of six bills in her administration’s package against organized crime. It is the fourth of the six to clear the committee. Under the bill, the Civil Aviation Directorate (DGAC) would declare an airstrip, airfield or helipad clandestine or illegal through a reasoned administrative resolution. Owners, tenants and administrators would first get a 10-business-day hearing to present evidence.

Once that resolution is final, the Public Security Ministry’s Air Surveillance Service could disable, demolish or destroy the site, with help from other agencies and municipalities. The rules would cover facilities used for drug trafficking, money laundering, human trafficking and organized crime.

Prosecutors could also ask a criminal judge to freeze the property in the National Registry, which would block its sale, donation, transfer or mortgage while the measure is in force. Machinery, vehicles and aircraft used to build or operate the strips could be seized and later permanently forfeited. The Costa Rican Drug Institute (ICD) would administer them.

The bill raises the prison sentence for building, enabling, facilitating or allowing a clandestine airstrip from the current three to eight years to five to 10 years. Owners, tenants or administrators who rebuild, rehabilitate or reuse a strip that authorities have already closed or destroyed would face 10 to 15 years.

Fines for operating aircraft at unauthorized facilities would double, from 20 to 40 base salaries. Deputy Kattia Calvo of the governing Pueblo Soberano party said changes were added to guarantee due process, including a way for property owners to present evidence of their innocence. Social Christian Unity Party deputy Abril Gordienko backed the bill, noting that clandestine strips can also enable crimes beyond drug trafficking.

Frente Amplio caucus leader José María Villalta said it was the first bill the committee had discussed that could truly hit organized crime, because it targets the assets criminal groups use to operate. He also raised procedural concerns. He warned that a separate bill on tourist airparks could create conflicting rules on air surveillance.

Costa Rica already allows the Air Surveillance Service to identify, declare illegal and disable clandestine strips under Law 9902, in force since 2020. According to the new bill’s statement of purpose, that law has no specific tools to act on the assets used to build or maintain the strips.

How many strips exist is unclear because they are built to go unnoticed. Fernández has said there are close to 200. The Public Security Ministry’s last official figure, from 2020, put the number of identified unauthorized strips at more than 140, and at least 20 were reported destroyed between the law’s entry into force and the end of 2024.

Some legal analysts have questioned whether the property freeze adds much to existing organized crime and registry security laws. They have also warned that a landowner may not know a strip is operating on their land. The bill now awaits a first-round vote in the full Assembly.

World.title: Holness urges labourites to push back against ‘lies and misinformation’
World.content:
Prime Minister Andrew Holness addresses Jamaica Labour Party supporters at a mass rally on Sunday, August 10, 2025. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Prime Minister and Jamaica Labour Party (JLP) Leader Dr Andrew Holness has implored party workers and supporters to push back aggressively at what he said are lies being spread about the Government, in particular as it relates to the distribution of hurricane relief.

Holness made the rallying cry Sunday, as he addressed the 83rd annual conference of the governing JLP at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James. This year’s scaled-back conference was a delegates-only affair.

The prime minister said there was a thought process around how information surrounding the distribution of hurricane relief should be disseminated.

“Should we publish a list reserving the private information of the beneficiaries or we could create a little database and if you want to go on the list and you want to look at what anybody get, then you have to put in your ID and a notification is sent to the person that got the benefit that you scrutinising them,” Holness said.

The reaction of the crowd suggested they were not in favour of such an approach but the prime minister said, “We’re at this point because we cannot allow the lies that they have told about our distribution to stand”. He said the Government was not afraid of criticism, declaring that he was first to be critical of himself when things were not happening fast enough.

“I’m the first to come out and say I’m not satisfied, I’m the first to say people haven’t gotten [aid],” said Holness.

The Government has for sometime been forced to push back at what it has deemed to be lies and misinformation in the public space, in particular on social media, about how hurricane relief has been distributed, and the pace at which it is distributed.

The Administration has been locked in a war of words with veteran entertainer Beenie Man since late last month following a controversial interview the dancehall artiste gave on a British broadcaster. During the interview on ITV News, Beenie Man questioned how millions of dollars in donations intended for Hurricane Melissa victims was distributed.

“This is nothing new that the Government get the money, the Government distribute the money the wrong way. The people who supposed to get the money haven’t been getting any,” Beenie Man claimed.

That was met with vigorous pushback from senior members of the Government including the prime minister. But, with no side backing down, and with several other entertainers throwing their support behind him, Beenie Man has since penned and released a song titled Weh di money deh. He has also reacted with colorful language to a senior Government minister who suggested that he was a washed-up entertainer seeking relevance.

Last Thursday the Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Delroy Chuck admitted the Government had failed to adequately communicate to the Jamaican people how hurricane relief has been allocated.

On Sunday the prime minister warned that where substantial effort has been made, where changes are being made, “and we continue to portray this general view that there are no systems and there is no distribution taking place, then people look on at us will say ‘why should we give Jamaica?’”

“There is a level of thinking in the country that labourites must stand up against, don’t be afraid, challenge the lies, don’t be afraid to speak the truth, let your voices be heard,” Holness encouraged.

“We are not afraid of criticism and we will make our own criticism as well, that is a democracy,” he added.

He said: “They have been used to making lies and falsehood and we sit down and tek it and say a so it go but we cannot do that [anymore]”.

World.title: Road woes deepen
World.content:
Traffic, including a tour bus, is seen manoeuvring the Shettlewood to Mackfield main road in the vicinity of Chester Castle, Hanover, last Friday. Photo: Garfield Robinson

Tourism stakeholders in Treasure Beach have expressed concern over the deteriorating main road linking the south coast community to Montego Bay through eastern Hanover and southern St James, warning that its deplorable state is already triggering booking cancellations and threatening business ahead of the crucial winter tourist season.

Meanwhile, residents and business operators along the Anchovy-Shettlewood and Mackfield main roads, which traverse southern St James and eastern Hanover, are cautiously welcoming repair work that began last week, but are questioning how long the improvements will last.
