World.title: The Disappearing Homeland – A Crowdfunding Campaign
World.content:
November the 15th, 2026 – Podravina-based geographer Vedran Šikić and film director Vedran Štefan have joined forces to tell the story of 37 villages with fewer than 50 residents in the documentary film Disappearing Homeland.

After two years of filming, more than 25 interviews with local residents, and over 20 hours of recorded footage, the film is entering the final stage of production. A crowdfunding campaign has been launched on the Bona Fides Invest platform to complete the film, with a fundraising target of €15,000.

The village of Srdinac, not far from Koprivnica. Beside an old, abandoned house, of which only crumbling walls and an old gate remain, a shepherd tends to a flock of sheep. It is a scene that can still be found in Podravina’s villages, but one that many people would no longer even stop to notice. For Vedran Šikić, a geography professor from Koprivnica, this particular scene was one of the first things that inspired him to take a closer look at the villages of Podravina.

As he cycled through the villages of Podravina, Šikić gradually began to discover just how little we know about places that are, in fact, right on our doorstep. His friends, for example, had often never even heard of certain villages located just a few kilometres from Koprivnica. They knew even less about how many people still lived there, how they lived, and what was happening to places that had once been much more vibrant.

This realisation gave rise to the Disappearing Homeland project, followed by the documentary film of the same name, which seeks to capture life in small Podravina settlements before their residents, homes, and memories become nothing more than entries in historical records. After two years of work, filming has been completed, and the filmmakers are now facing the demanding final stage of production, which requires additional funding.

37 villages, less than 1,000 residents

The selection criteria were straightforward: all villages with fewer than 50 residents according to the 2021 population census, located within a 20-kilometre radius, measured as the crow flies, of Koprivnica. Since official census figures do not always fully reflect the actual situation in the smallest settlements, Šikić also verified the data directly in the field by speaking with local residents.

In the end, he included 37 villages. The smallest is Mali Botinovac, which today has just six residents.

The scale of demographic change becomes particularly evident when comparing past and present figures. Around thirty years ago, all 37 villages together had more than 2,500 residents. Today, that number has fallen to fewer than 1,000.

Most villages are now predominantly inhabited by older people, and their age structure is particularly unfavourable. Nevertheless, there are exceptions showing that the future of rural settlements is not equally uncertain everywhere. In Vojvodinec, for example, more than 30% of the population is under the age of 19, considerably above the Croatian average of less than 20%.

“Some villages have a future, but unfortunately, there aren’t many of them,” Šikić points out.

The reasons why young people leave are complex. A lack of infrastructure, poor transport connections, and inadequate internet access are just some of the problems. In certain villages, the internet connection is, as he puts it, “catastrophic”. The vast majority of working-age residents are still engaged in agriculture, but even this activity can no longer ensure the demographic renewal of villages on its own.

the asphalt ends at the village sign

The first phase of the project consisted of cycling trips through the villages. These journeys allowed Šikić to meet people, earn their trust, and document scenes that would later become part of the film’s story.

One such moment took place in Kostadinovac. “The asphalt road reaches the village sign, and then there’s nothing. It’s tragically comical. And it’s still the same today,” he recalls.

Yet alongside the shortcomings in infrastructure, it was the people who left a lasting impression on him. In Pobrđani Vojakovački, during one of his most demanding cycling routes, the local hosts immediately offered him homemade food to help him regain his strength. Later, those same people treated the film crew on several occasions during filming.

A particularly touching encounter took place with an elderly woman in Velika Branjska. Speaking about her neighbours from nearby Mala Branjska, and visibly moved while discussing the project, she pointed out with tears in her eyes that she is an Orthodox Christian and that the best people in the world are her neighbours from Zagorje.

Her testimony also reveals a lesser-known dimension of Podravina’s villages, connected with the history of migration and the shared lives of people from different backgrounds and religious traditions. Part of the local population consists of descendants of settlers from Hrvatsko Zagorje who, both before and after the Second World War, driven by poverty and overcrowding in their homeland, moved to Podravina in search of work as domestic servants and day labourers. In some settlements, Catholic and Orthodox families lived side by side for decades, building communities in which mutual respect, good neighbourly relations, and everyday solidarity mattered more than their differences.

It is precisely these encounters that give the project its particular value. Disappearing Homeland is not simply about documenting empty houses and demographic statistics, but also about recording human relationships, shared history, and ways of life that have shaped this region.

Gaining the trust of interviewees was not difficult. Šikić had met most of them during his cycling trips, and the residents were pleased that someone was showing an interest in their small villages. Nobody refused to speak in front of the camera, resulting in more than 25 interviews.

two vedrans, and the story that became a film

A documentary film was not the original idea. Šikić initially considered publishing a monograph, but over time he concluded that a film would be a more effective way of bringing the story to a wider audience.

His collaboration with film director Vedran Štefan of the production company TETRABOT Ltd. began following one of Šikić’s presentations about the project. Together, they concluded that making a documentary was a natural next step in the research.

Over the two years of filming, the villages changed somewhat. In some, the population declined; in others, new residents arrived, while certain settlements gained paved roads, playgrounds, or water supply infrastructure. Nevertheless, these remain small improvements compared with the long-term demographic trends.

The film material comprises more than 20 hours of footage, interviews, and scenes from everyday life. It is from this material that the final story of the 37 villages, their residents, their past, and their possible future will take shape.

agro-tourism: untapped potential waiting for better days…

The economic dimension of the project is particularly interesting. Disappearing Homeland is not only about demographic decline, but also about the untapped opportunities offered by rural areas.

The Podravina region has relatively fertile soil, arable land, forests, and a diverse landscape. On one side are the Drava River lowlands and the river itself, while on the other are the hills of Bilogora and the foothills of Kalnik.

Most of the land surrounding the villages included in the project is still cultivated, although some areas remain unused. Farmers interviewed by the film crew pointed to difficulties in consolidating agricultural holdings, which makes it harder to expand production.

Several villages are home to a number of family farms engaged in dairy farming. However, they face problems related to labour shortages and an ageing population. Increasingly, young people are reluctant to pursue this type of work.

The tourism perspective is also interesting. Despite the natural beauty of the area and its proximity to Koprivnica, there are only three holiday homes across all 37 villages, all located in a single settlement, Segovina.

“Perfect for holiday homes,” says Šikić, describing a landscape that, with adequate infrastructure and entrepreneurial initiative, could attract significantly more visitors.

However, potential alone is not enough. Without good transport connections, communal infrastructure, reliable internet access, and favourable conditions for business development, it is difficult to expect new residents and investments to arrive.

Šikić believes that the future of some villages may not resemble the way they were lived in fifty years ago, but that rural areas can take on a new role. He envisions a kind of “Village 2.0” model, in which older residents connected with agriculture would live alongside younger families or individuals seeking peace, nature, and a better quality of life, while working in a town just 15 to 30 minutes away by car.

crowdfunding as a way to complete the film

The filming has so far received financial support from the City of Koprivnica, the Municipalities of Rasinja, Novigrad Podravski, and Legrad, as well as the company Hartmann.

The City of Koprivnica provided funding through its annual public call for cultural projects, while the other partners supported the project through donations. In this way, slightly less than €15,000 was raised. However, completing the film to full professional standards requires between €60,000 and €70,000. The production company has therefore also invested some of its own funds to ensure the highest possible quality of filming.

After the project failed to secure funding through the public call of the Croatian Audiovisual Centre, the filmmakers had to find an alternative way to obtain the resources needed to complete production. They decided to turn to crowdfunding, a form of collective financing in which a large number of individuals and organisations contribute smaller individual amounts towards achieving a shared goal.

The campaign is being conducted on the Bona Fides Invest crowdfunding platform, with the aim of raising an additional €15,000.

The funds raised will be used to engage the film professionals whose expertise is essential to completing the documentary. Most importantly, a film editor will need to review and process more than 20 hours of footage and shape it into the final cinematic narrative. A composer will prepare the music in collaboration with KUD Rudarice, while a sound designer will process the recorded audio and create the final sound mix.

The production also requires the creation of graphics and animations of historical maps featured in the film, final colour grading, and preparation of the documentary for screening in cinemas, on television, and on online platforms.

supporters become guardians of their homeland

The crowdfunding campaign is open to everyone who wishes to support the project, regardless of whether they live in Podravina, have family roots in one of the villages featured in the film, or are simply interested in preserving Croatia’s rural heritage.

Contributions start at €10, and supporters are assigned to different categories depending on the amount they contribute. These include Donors, Friends of the Village, Friends of the Homeland, Guardians of the Village, Guardians of the Homeland, and Guardians of Heritage. Those making larger contributions can also become sponsors of an individual village or the entire homeland.

The names of supporters will appear in the film’s end credits in accordance with their selected contribution category. Particularly interesting is the opportunity to sponsor a specific village, symbolically connecting a financial contribution with a place the supporter wishes to help preserve from oblivion.

Contributions can be made by credit or debit card, KEKS Pay, Aircash, cryptocurrency, or through a general payment slip, online banking, or mobile banking.

According to the figures published during the campaign, the public response has been encouraging. The project’s Facebook page has attracted approximately 4,700 followers and more than 2.3 million views. Support has come from the authors’ friends and acquaintances, active followers of the page, as well as residents of the villages featured in the film.

Šikić openly admits that one particular aspect of the campaign is especially difficult for him.

“We are sorry that people from the very areas we are filming have to finance this documentary. We wanted to make this film for them and their region, without them having to financially support the project.”

He had hoped that the necessary funding could be secured through larger sponsorships and donations, for example from major companies in the region for which many residents of these villages had worked for many years. Nevertheless, the very fact that local people are supporting the project shows how much they care about having their stories documented and preserved.

a record for future generations

The plan is to complete the film in the spring of 2027, followed by festival distribution and efforts to secure screenings on television and online platforms. No concrete acquisition agreements have been made so far, as the filmmakers have focused most of their energy on fundraising and completing production.

They are particularly excited about the possibility of organising free outdoor screenings in several of the villages featured in the film during the summer of 2027. They hope to secure support from local tourist boards and other partners who could assist with the technical and logistical arrangements. A photography exhibition has also been scheduled for the spring of 2027, while a monograph is being considered as a possible continuation of the project.

Nevertheless, the film’s greatest value may not lie in its initial screenings, but in what will remain long after them. Šikić makes no secret of the fact that some villages may no longer be capable of demographic recovery. Those with fewer than 20 residents, and especially those with fewer than ten, could disappear completely over the coming decades.



This is precisely why the film also has an important archival dimension. Its creators want to produce a high-quality documentary that will remain valuable 50 or even 100 years from now, when some of these villages may no longer exist.

“One of the purposes of the film is to record these places forever, while they are still here,” Šikić emphasises.

Although he often encountered pessimistic reflections from older residents who remember the time when the villages were full of life, the film’s conclusion nevertheless carries a message of hope. He believes that rural areas possess values that contemporary society fails to recognise sufficiently.

“As a society, we have too little respect for nature, agriculture, and the people who put food on our tables,” he warns.

He hopes the film will encourage viewers, as well as decision-makers, to become better acquainted with the region, explore its historical, recreational, and tourism opportunities, and recognise its uniqueness and the value of preserving it. A village does not have to remain forever as it was fifty years ago, but it should not disappear simply because we have failed to recognise its value and the opportunities it still holds.

At the end of the conversation, Šikić shares the words of an elderly local resident, which perhaps best summarise the entire story:

“Once, the village fed the town, and today the town feeds the village. Think about whether this is realistic and sustainable in the long term for the village itself and for agriculture.”

how you can support the disappearing homeland

The crowdfunding campaign to complete the documentary is being conducted on the Bona Fides Invest platform. The goal is to raise €15,000, with contributions starting at €10. Depending on the amount contributed, supporters will be included in the corresponding acknowledgement category in the film’s end credits, with the additional opportunity to sponsor an individual village. Every contribution helps preserve the stories of 37 Podravina villages, their residents, and their way of life for future generations.

Visit the crowdfunding campaign here.

World.title: Advent Zagreb 2026: Festive Cheer, Cultural Highlights, and a Packed Calendar
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – It’s that time of year again! Advent Zagreb 2026 is just around the corner, promising a programme packed with festive cheer and a very full calendar.

The most wonderful time of the year is knocking at the door. Advent in Zagreb, which is considered one of the best in Europe, starts on the 28th of November and lasts until the 7th of January.

The multi-award-winning Advent Zagreb once again brings a rich cultural, entertainment and food programme, which, along with New Year’s events, will take place from the 28th of November 2026 to the 7th of January 2027. Organised by the City of Zagreb, the Zagreb Tourist Board (TZGZ) and numerous institutional and private partners, the programme will officially kick off with the traditional lighting of the first Advent candle on Ban Jelačić Square, after which the other locations will open.

zagreb’s progression as a festive city delight

Boska i Kreso/TZGZ

Director of TZGZ, Martina Bienenfeld, stated that “Advent Zagreb has grown into one of the most recognisable Advent events in Europe, and this year’s edition brings new cultural content and more strongly connects city locations into a unique holiday experience. We pay special attention to culture and programmes for children and families. Among this year’s novelties intended for the youngest, I’d highlight LumiLicious on Mažuranac, which starts on the 6th of December, the feast of St Nicholas. Novelties are also The Magic Within on Marulić Square and the festive decoration of the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts, whose ceremonial openings are planned for the 18th of December. Together with the new arrangement of the space in front of the Croatian National Theatre, these contents will connect the locations of the Green Horseshoe into a unique Advent promenade. In this way we enrich the Advent offer and open new possibilities for exploring the city, while at the same time putting Zagreb’s historical spaces, architecture and cultural heritage in the foreground.

The international recognisability of Advent Zagreb is also confirmed by this year’s awards and recommendations from world media. We are particularly pleased that Zagreb has been declared the best European destination for a Christmas city break in the selection of the European Best Destinations organisation, while the prestigious Time Out ranked it first on its list of the best European destinations for a winter city break in 2026, highlighting its attractiveness for family travel. Such recognitions have significant promotional value because they strengthen Zagreb’s international visibility, encourage interest in coming and contribute to its positioning on key source markets. In this context we continue with intensive promotional activities on 17 international markets, including targeted campaigns at stations of the London Underground and the Milan metro, as well as long-standing cooperation with Croatia Airlines and HŽ Passenger Transport.

Julien Duval/TZGZ

I believe that Advent Zagreb will once again achieve good tourist results this year and further strengthen Zagreb’s position as an attractive year-round destination. At the same time, we do not measure its success exclusively by tourist indicators, but also by the quality of the experience it provides to visitors and our fellow citizens. Precisely in this balance between tourist attractiveness and value for the local community we see the foundation of its long-term development and sustainability.”

The entire programme, detailed schedules of all events and current information can be found here, and we’ll also bring you descriptions of each below.

what’s on this festive season for europe’s best advent?

Julien Duval/TZGZ

What we’ve been waiting for all year finally starts on the last weekend of November. Zagreb has won a new title – it is the best Christmas city-break destination 2026 according to European Best Destinations. Along with well-known attractions such as the Ice Park, Advent on Zrinjevac, Fuliranje and numerous other events, there are also novelties for the youngest on Mažuranac, and the entire Upper Town, as well as the Green Horseshoe of the Lower Town, become a unique Advent promenade. Run with Santa Claus, dance or skate in the parks, sing on the tram or just stop and enjoy.

if you’re the musical type…

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Soloists

Museum of the City of Zagreb, on the 3rd, 6th, 10th and 13th of December at 18:00

The Zagreb Soloists continue the tradition of Advent concerts at the Museum of the City of Zagreb. At each of the four concerts the Zagreb Soloists will be joined by a young musician.

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Chamber Orchestra

Church of St Joseph, Journalists’ House

Advent concerts of the Zagreb Chamber Orchestra in the city’s historical spaces. The Church of St Joseph is the location of the first concert on the 29th of November, followed by three more at the Journalists’ House on the 5th 13th and 19th of December with performances by renowned Croatian and international soloists.

Advent concerts of the Chamber Choir “Ivan Filipović” – Zagreb Voices

Church of St John the Baptist 29 Nov, Basilica of St Anthony of Padua on the 13th of December, the Church of St Francis of Assisi on the 29th of December

Concerts of the Chamber Choir “Ivan Filipović” – Zagreb Voices bring a combination of classical music, choral compositions and Croatian traditional Advent and Christmas songs. Contemporary choral arrangements of Croatian musical heritage are performed for the first time.

Music in St Mark’s Church

St Mark’s Church, on the 13th 20th and 24th of December (Midnight Mass)

Advent tradition, performances of classical and sacred music that echo within the historical walls of the Church of St Mark. Admission is free.

Advent with the Opera of the Croatian National Theatre in Zagreb

Republic of Croatia Square, balcony of the CNT, the 5th of December at 17:30 and the 7th of December at 19:00

From the balcony of the Zagreb CNT, young soloists accompanied by piano perform opera and Advent compositions. Two half-hour concerts for residents and guests alike will fill the space in front of the theatre with holiday melodies.

seasonal music

Boska i Kreso/TZGZ

From Christmas balconies to Zagreb

Balcony at the Stone Gate, balcony at Tkalčićeva 33, balcony of the CNT



Christmas melodies from Zagreb balconies performed by the six-member brass ensemble Ad gloriam brass. A unique musical experience of European flair and classical music, film themes and Christmas songs.

Festival of Advent and Christmas songs

Society of University Teachers and Other Scientists, Greek Catholic Co-Cathedral of Sts Cyril and Methodius, Church of St Peter the Apostle, Church of St Mark, Church of St Blaise, Stone Gate, terrace of Cravaticum – the Tie Museum



The Festival of Advent and Christmas songs brings festive concerts of Advent-Christmas music of different genres and eras. From classical to klapa and holiday pop songs at the 11th edition of the festival at six city locations. A children’s concert will also be held as part of the festival.

Zagreb Advent postcards

Oktogon, Neboder, Baković Sisters Passage



The vocal quartet Vox in the heart of Zagreb performs Advent compositions from Croatian and world musical heritage. With pop-up concerts, short performances without prior announcement, they will surprise random passers-by with the musical magic of Advent.

Advent under the lantern

Lotrščak Tower



Join the lamp-lighter and singers every Wednesday, Thursday and Friday until Christmas Eve at Lotrščak Tower. Light the gas lamps while singing kolende at Advent under the lantern in the Upper Town.

Advent symphony of the city

Radićeva – Tomićeva – Stone Gate – Bloody Bridge – Mažuranić Square



An Advent walk through Zagreb accompanied by Christmas songs performed by the Musical-Artistic Atelier Kralj. The Advent symphony of the city from 19:00 to 20:30 at various locations in the heart of Zagreb.

Musical control – Zagreb promenade

Ljubljanica depot, Zrinjevac Park



The Musical Control of the Zagreb ZET Orchestra on Saturday morning will surprise passengers at selected locations in the city. The ride starts at 10:00 from Ljubljanica and ends in Zrinjevac Park.

‘Flash mob’ on the tram

Zagreb trams



Surprise flash-mob concerts on Zagreb trams are a Christmas tradition. Sing along with the choir during the ride through the Lower Town.

single day events

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

Advent Run

Zagreb streets, 6th of December at 12:00



Zagreb Advent Run, a costume race for the whole family through the city, again has a humanitarian character this year. It is run as part of the Croatian national campaign for early detection of high cholesterol and blood pressure. You can choose to run five or ten kilometres.

Broadcast of the ballet The Nutcracker

Republic of Croatia Square, in front of the CNT, on the 19th of December 2026 at 18:00



Broadcast of the most performed classical ballet in the world in front of the Croatian National Theatre on 19 December from 18:00. The beloved Nutcracker in the ambitious version of the famous Russian ballet dancer Rudolf Nureyev.

Choirs on Christmas Eve – Midday Advent Melodies

Ban Josip Jelačić Square, 24th of December at 11:00



This year again on Ban Jelačić Square Zagreb choirs bring Christmas magic with a joint performance of fairy-tale evergreens. Enjoy the harmonious polyphony of the choirs accompanied by guitar and piano.

workshops and activities

Ernest Mazarekic/TZGZ

Christmas story at the Ethnographic Museum

Mažuranić Square 14



The Christmas programme at the Ethnographic Museum brings an exhibition of Pannonian nativity scenes from Burgenland and an exhibition dedicated to 30 years of exhibiting Croatian Christmas nativity scenes in Rome and the Vatican. You can also make your own Christmas nativity scenes from cornhusks and wool.

Advent at the Museum of the City of Zagreb

Opatička 20



The Advent programme of the Museum of the City of Zagreb brings an exhibition of Advent cards and objects “Christmas Story”, tours “Forgotten Holidays” and creative workshops for making Advent wreaths. For children there are theatre performances on the occasion of the feast of St Nicholas, and for quiz lovers a special edition of KviZG.

Advent at the Croatian Natural History Museum

Demetrova 1



The Croatian Natural History Museum uniquely connects science, art, music and entertainment. There are lectures and projections about the secrets of the universe, interactive scientific and creative workshops, as well as theatre performances and Advent concerts in the museum atrium.

Advent in the Crafts Passage

Ilica 49



A Christmas fairy tale at the Croatian Crafts Matrix in Ilica. There are hand-made souvenirs and appropriate workshops by the greatest masters. All accompanied by concerts of Christmas songs on the gallery of the Croatian Crafts Matrix.

for the kids

Samir Ceric Kovacevic/TZGZ

Teatrino klincolino

Antun, Ivan and Vladimir Mažuranić Square



The children’s puppet theatre at this year’s Advent performs more than thirty performances of popular and lesser-known children’s stories. Creative puppets perform on Mažuranić Square.

Living Christmas nativity scene

Opatovina Park, 19th to the 23rd of December, 26th to the 30th of December, 1st and the 6th of January

Traditional staging of the living nativity scene at Opatovina. Young people from the Cenacolo Community designed the entire performance themselves and perform it with the help of parents and friends. Performances are held at 16:00, 17:00 and 19:00.

The Magic Within

Marko Marulić Square



The projection runs from the 18th of December to the 1st of January on the building of the Croatian State Archives, which turns into a stylised Christmas house. Together with the neighbouring buildings of FKIT and PMF it will create a visual whole of recognisable architecture.

Very Merry Square

Ban Josip Jelačić Square



The Christmas tree on Ban Jelačić Square is the central symbol of the Christmas holidays in the city. Surrounded by snow-covered pines and sparkling lights, the Square becomes a real winter fairy tale with Manduševac as the most beautiful Advent wreath.

LumiLicious

Antun, Ivan and Vladimir Mažuranić Square from the 6th of December to the 1st of January



Mažuranac comes alive with Christmas magic. Walk through snowy pine forests and discover a world of imagination among oversized Christmas decorations. There are LUMI and LICI, an interactive audiovisual installation that invites children to bring two cute digital characters to life.

HNK – Layers of Christmas

Republic of Croatia Square



This Advent the building of the Croatian National Theatre will be wrapped in Christmas attire. Republic of Croatia Square becomes a glowing forest which is absolutely perfect for photos.

Let It Glow

Flower Square (Cvjetni trg)

The popular Flower Square, through lavish decorations, sparkling installations and interactive elements, combines the charm of old Zagreb with a modern Christmas atmosphere. A special photo point is the perfect place for unforgettable holiday moments.

Advent Open House Zagreb

9th and and the 16th of December

Advent Open House Zagreb opens the doors of normally inaccessible, most attractive architectural works in the city centre with expert guidance in Croatian and English. The festival encourages reflection on the values of the city. Click here to register.

Bells in the Oktogon

Oktogon, from the 13th to the 29th of December

In Zagreb’s Oktogon you will find a sound installation of 24 bells that every full hour perform an atmospheric version of the composition “Imagine”.

Polar Worlds

Grič Tunnel

A true polar dream in the Grič Tunnel – new scenes inspired by glaciers and crystal formations that transform it into an imaginary landscape of polar worlds. Experience the Grič Tunnel in a new edition.

Moon Garden

King Béla IV Park

Step into the magical Moon Garden in King Béla IV Park. Make a special wish on the Moon with an unforgettable view of the city.

Winter Nocturne

Grič Park, Strossmayer Promenade

Winter Nocturne brings a winter atmosphere to Grič Park, inspired by the stars and Chopin’s nocturnes. The benches are free throughout Advent.

Bells and Bell Towers of Croatia: Symphony of Peace and Togetherness

Palace of the Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts (HAZU), Nikola Šubić Zrinski Square 11

Saša Šekoranja presents drawings and video installations of bell towers from all over Croatia in the HAZU Palace. Their sounds create a unique Advent symphony of togetherness, love and holiday joy.

ADVENT IN HOTELS

Julien Duval/TZGZ

Hilton Hotels

Hilton Hotels: DoubleTree, Garden Inn, Canopy



Festive decorations, a warm atmosphere, signature cocktails and special offers at Hilton Hotels Zagreb.

Hotel Jägerhorn

Ilica 14



A small but idyllic Advent is hidden in the passage of Hotel Jägerhorn, the oldest in the city.

Advent Bachata Congress

Hotel Diplomat, Zrinjevac



An international dance congress from the 11th to the 14th of December gathers hundreds of bachata and salsa dancers from all over the world. Free dance programme on Zrinjevac on the 13th of December from 16:00 to 19:00.

Fuliranje

Hotel Esplanade



The Fuliranje – Christmas Station is a new edition of the popular Zagreb Advent project. The Oleander terrace of Hotel Esplanade turns into a unique Christmas destination. There is an impressive covered and heated greenhouse, a Christmas living room that in the evening turns into a large Christmas Disco Club.

LOCATIONS IN THE CITY CENTRE

Julien Duval/TZGZ

EU Advent

European Square



EU Advent on European Square brings a new theme – The City that Loves. Through performances by female vocalists, DJ programmes and stand-up evenings, European Square becomes a place of meetings, music, laughter, tastes and togetherness.

Baš Naš Vremeplov

Ban Josip Jelačić Square

January, Ban Josip Jelačić Square will beecome a place where the past and the present meet until January the 7th, 2027. Baš Naš Vremeplov (Our Time Machine) invites all generations to gather in the very heart of Zagreb.

Advent on Zrinjevac

Zrinjevac Park



Thousands of sparkling lights, music from the pavilion, the scents of winter delicacies and charming Advent houses – Zrinjevac once again opens the doors to the most beautiful holiday moments! This year it becomes a magical poetry promenade. Verses of Croatian poets about love, Christmas and Zagreb come to life among the century-old plane trees.

Fuliranje

Strossmayer Square



Until the 7th of January, Fuliranje on Josip Juraj Strossmayer Square brings an open-air winter living room. Creative workshops, children’s and family programmes, musical performances, theatrical and educational content, as well as top gastronomic offerings.

Ice Park

King Tomislav Square



In the heart of Zagreb, against the magnificent backdrop of the Art Pavilion and the glow of thousands of lights, the Ice Park once again becomes a favourite place for winter gatherings. From the first steps on the ice to evening get-togethers with music and favourite winter delicacies. The most beautiful outdoor winter stage is once again adorned by the Nutcracker on Ice performance.

Caffe de Matoš – Advent in the Upper Town

Strossmayer Promenade and Gradec Plateau



On Strossmayer Promenade, Caffe de Matoš offers a daily musical programme of young bands in cooperation with the Music House. A photo point with the best view of Zagreb. On the nearby Gradec Plateau, Caffe de Matoš revives the spirit of old Zagreb in a special holiday edition. Thousands of lanterns, red houses and a magical forest, with an unforgettable view of illuminated Zagreb.

The Great ZbiGatsby on Stross

Strossmayer Promenade – west



On Zagreb’s most romantic promenade, feel a touch of old Zagreb. Tak imam te rad – The Great ZbiGatsby on Stross brings the warmth of holiday gatherings with the charm and elegance of the 1920s and 1930s.

World.title: New Croatian Tourism Law: Different Deadlines for Landlords to Re-Categorise Apartments
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – A new Croatian tourism law could mean that private landlords end up having different deadlines to re-categorise their apartments. Some will get five years, others will be given ten.

The mandatory re-categorisation of apartments every ten years, registration numbers for advertising accommodation via online platforms, stricter inspection supervision and higher penalties for illegal operations are some of the changes envisaged by the final proposal of the new Hospitality Activity Act, which the Croatian Parliament discussed on Thursday. Poslovni reports that although the government is announcing more order on the tourist market and an increase in the quality of service, small landlords are warning of additional obligations and uncertainty about future operating conditions.

State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport Monika Udovičić, president of the association Spasimo male obiteljske iznajmljivače (SMOi) Vedran Tomić, and president of the Guild of Hospitality and Tourism Workers of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts Hrvoje Margan all spoke about the new rules.

different deadlines for different landlords

According to the final proposal of the law, rooms, apartments and holiday homes will in future have to undergo re-categorisation every ten years. However, different transitional deadlines are envisaged for existing landlords, depending on when their approval decision was issued. According to Article 80 of the final proposal of the law, landlords whose decision was issued by the 31st of December 2015 will have to align their operations and obtain a new decision within five years of the entry into force of the relevant ordinance.

For those whose decision was issued as of the 1st of January 2016, a deadline of ten years from the entry into force of the ordinance is envisaged. This means that the deadlines do not automatically start running from the beginning of 2027, but from the day the new ordinance defining the conditions enters into force. After alignment, periodic checks will follow every ten years, which the competent administrative bodies will carry out ex officio. If it is established that the facility no longer meets the prescribed conditions, its type or category may be changed, and in certain cases the decision may be revoked.

the new rules aren’t “anti-landlord”, the powers that be claim

It was explained that hotels and campsites have so far undergone re-categorisation every four years, while the new law extends that period to five years. For small landlords, re-categorisation every ten years is envisaged. The reason for introducing the new checks, according to her, is the fact that there are facilities on the market that were categorised more than 20 years ago and whose compliance with standards has not been re-checked since then.

“This new rule isn’t directed against landlords,” the State Secretary said. She added that those who meet the prescribed conditions need not fear losing their decision. She also emphasised that the goal of the new ordinances is not to prevent existing landlords from operating, but to align standards with modern requirements.

possible consequences…

SMOi president Vedran Tomić questions the need for new categorisation, considering that online platforms and guest reviews have already become an important indicator of accommodation quality. He referred to an analysis of more than 1.6 million reviews according to which, he claims, Croatian private accommodation was rated better than hotel accommodation. Tomić believes that the entire reform is aimed at reducing the share of private accommodation and increasing hotel capacities.

Udovičić rejects such claims and stresses that the Ministry wants to protect family accommodation, but also to distinguish landlords for whom this is a traditional activity from pure rentierism, especially in residential buildings. According to her, Croatia has been receiving approximately ten thousand new beds in private accommodation year after year, while demand has not grown at the same pace, which has also affected occupancy rates.

The Ministry is therefore seeking to further encourage the quality and recognisability of family accommodation. Tomić, however, believes that the market, and not the state, should decide on the further growth of accommodation capacities.

a new rule from may the 1st, 2027

Another important change concerns all landlords who advertise their accommodation units via online platforms for short-term rental. Each such unit will have to have a unique registration number that will be submitted to the platform and displayed in the . Udovičić announced that the issuance of this number will be free of charge, and the procedure digital, via a system available through e-Citizens. According to the final proposal of the law, the provisions on registration numbers and data exchange with platforms should start to apply on the 1st of May 2027. The goal is to link accommodation data with the competent authorities and more effectively suppress unregistered renting. Unlike the registration numbers, most of the other provisions of the new law, if adopted in the proposed form, should enter into force on the 1st of January 2027.

support for more transparency and digitalisation

Hrvoje Margan, president of the Guild of Hospitality and Tourism Workers of the Croatian Chamber of Trades and Crafts, welcomed the adoption of the new law and the announced digitalisation of administrative procedures. Nevertheless, he warned that it is necessary to carefully regulate the minimum technical conditions so that the new ordinances do not become an additional administrative burden for hospitality operators. “We don’t want the ordinances to become a cleansing mechanism for hospitality operators,” he said. Udovičić replied that neither the law nor the future ordinances are conceived as a way of abolishing existing decisions, but as an instrument for modernising the system and raising quality.

The final proposal of the new Hospitality Activity Act has passed parliamentary debate, but still has to be voted on. Until its adoption and the entry into force of the new ordinances, landlords continue to operate according to the current regulations.

World.title: Continental Croatian Tourism up 60%, Million-Euro Incentives in 2027
World.content:
November the 14th, 2026 – Continental Croatian tourism is up by 60%, with new million-euro incentives coming in 2027 aimed at less developed inland regions.

The Croatian National Tourist Board recently launched a new cycle of public tenders for 2027, focused on the development of continental and less developed tourist regions and the promotion of events. Zrinka Gabelica Toplek reports for Poslovni that the decision to announce the tenders was made by the HTZ Tourism Council at its 9th session, and funding is secured through dedicated resources from the Fund for Touristically Underdeveloped Areas and the Mainland and the Fund for Associated Tourist Boards.

big increases for continental croatia

The adopted Open Call for Expressions of Interest aims at cooperation with organisers of “TOP events” of national significance and other events in the segments of eno-gastronomy, nautical tourism, culture, sport, entertainment, MICE and health tourism. In addition, tenders have been announced for regional tourist boards in underdeveloped areas and for projects of associated tourist boards.

“By announcing new tenders for 2027 through the HTZ funds, we are continuing with concrete measures by which we encourage more balanced development of Croatian tourism, while at the same time continuing cooperation with organisers of events and top events that contribute to the attractiveness of our destinations and the attraction of guests throughout the year,” said Minister of Tourism and Sport Tonči Glavina. He emphasised that since 2021, 51.6 million euros have been secured from these funds for more than 2,000 projects.

“The results are also visible in tourist traffic, which in the continental counties has increased by 60 percent in arrivals and 58 percent in overnight stays over the past ten years, while according to the latest TOMAS research, the average daily expenditure of tourists in continental Croatia has increased by 21 percent compared to 2022.

These are indicators of the growing importance of continental tourism in the overall development of Croatian tourism, and our goal is to continue this positive trend, further strengthen the tourist offer and enable local communities across Croatia to feel the benefits of tourism even more strongly,” Glavina emphasised.

encouraging cooperation

HTZ director Kristjan Staničić stressed that with these calls they want to further encourage the development of quality events that have the potential to become a reason for the arrival of domestic and foreign guests.

“We place special emphasis on touristically underdeveloped areas and the mainland, where events can play an exceptionally important role in creating the recognisability of destinations, activating local potentials and a more even distribution of tourist traffic,” Staničić said, adding that their goal is to support events that, through quality, content and organisation, can position themselves at the national level, create additional value for the destination and encourage cooperation between tourist boards, local stakeholders and the economy.

World.title: Estonia to close border crossings with Russia after GRU-linked sabotage attacks
World.content:
Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) has requested that the "necessary steps" be taken to close Estonia's eastern border with Russia after an attempted arson attack on Saturday morning, which has been attributed to the Russian intellegence services. Road borders will close in December.

Eight Latvian citizens were detained after an attempt to break into Threod Systems' property in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, on Saturday (November 14) morning. The group was aiming to cause an explosion and set the building on fire. The company produces long-range reconnaissance and attack drones, among other things.

The Estonian Internal Security Service (KAPO) said the attack was carried out on the orders of Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU.

This is the second attempted arson attack on a defense industry company since August, when Milrem Robotics, which is based in Tallinn, was targeted.

In a statement issued on Sunday, Michal said he had discussed the possibility of closing the Estonian-Russian border with Minister of the Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) and had asked the minister and the Government Office to "prepare the necessary steps".

"If Russia continues its hybrid operations in Estonia, and we know that Russian intelligence services exploit border crossings to exert influence over people, we must be prepared to reduce the risks we face," he said.

On the night of 14 November, GRU-ordered sabotage attempt targeted Estonian defence company Threod Systems. Extensive damage was averted thanks to heightened security measures and a swift reaction by law enforcement. The attackers have been detained. This is part of Russia's broader hybrid war against Europe, with the aim of decreasing support to Ukraine and pressure on Russia. We will not be intimidated. Estonia is preparing for the possibility of closing its border with Russia to reduce the risks to our people and national security. — Kristen Michal (@KristenMichalPM) November 15, 2026

"Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia's defence industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable."

The prime minister said Russia is aiming to "make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine. Estonia's response is the opposite."

"Estonia is safe and secure. Our state institutions are vigilant, and our people and businesses know how to respond. We will not be intimidated," Michal added.

Road borders to be closed in December

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs clarified that Estonia will close road border crossing points with Russia on December 1.

Estonia has three open road border crossings with Russia in Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula, which admit pedestrians and freight goods. They operate for 12 hours a day from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.

The crossing at Narva is particularly busy during summer and the New Year period, as it is one of the only land crossings with Russia still open to travelers in Europe after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Taro said the government will discuss next week closing all Estonia-Russia road border crossing points from the beginning of December.

Interior Minister Igor Taro (Eesti 200). Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"Estonia has already significantly restricted traffic to and from Russia at our border crossing points, warning each time that further escalation could result in a complete closure of traffic. Now that moment has arrived – following discussions with the prime minister, I will propose to the government that all Estonia-Russia road border crossing points be closed to both pedestrians and vehicles from the beginning of December," Taro said.

The government will discuss in the coming days whether the decision will be temporary or indefinite, he added.

Estonian residents and truck drivers who have traveled to Russia will be able to return home over the next two weeks.

"After that, the journey home could become long and complicated. With this step, we will further mitigate risks related to security and sanctions violations and send a message to the aggressor state that hostile actions have both consequences and a price," Taro said.

Estonia also has railway crossings with Russia in Narva and Koidula.

The Estonian-Russian border runs through Lake Peipus. Border crossing points are highlighted on the map. Source: Helen Wright/ERR/OSM

World.title: 8 detained after GRU-linked arson at Estonian drone company Threod Systems
World.content:
Eight Latvian citizens have been detained after an attempted arson at Estonian drone manufacturer Threod Systems, which Estonia's domestic intellegence service has attributed to Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU. Estonia is planning to close its eastern border in response.

Prosecutor General Astrid Asi said at a press conference on Sunday that there was an attempt to break into Threod Systems' property in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, to start a fire at 3.06 a.m. on Saturday (November 14).

The incident was thwarted thanks to the intervention of Threod's security team, Asi added.

Internal Security Service (KAPO) Director General Margo Palloson said counterintelligence had confirmed that Russia was behind the attempted attack and that it was coordinated by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU.

"This was yet another attempt by Russia to carry out an act of sabotage in Estonia," he told the assembled media.

The attackers attempted to break the building's windows and pour flammable liquids inside to set the building on fire and cause an explosion, Palloson said. "We assess that if this attack had succeeded in the way the attackers planned, it would have caused very significant damage to the company," he said.

Margo Palloson and the Prosecutor's Office. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Palloson said no one was injured in the incident. The company did not suffer any significant damage, and the production and delivery capabilities were not affected, he added.

Eight detained, five arrested

Eight people have been detained, all residents of Latvia, by the Estonian Internal Security Service (KAPO) and the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA).

"The Prosecutor's Office submitted an application to the court for the arrest of five suspects. The task of the criminal proceedings now is to establish the circumstances surrounding the organization of the attack, the roles of those involved and possible links to other individuals," Asi added.

Palloson said Latvia's State Security Service (VDD) and Prosecutor's Office have contributed significantly to establishing the circumstances surrounding the case.

Threod Systems produces both long-range reconnaissance and attack drones.

This is the second known attempted arson attack on an Estonian defense company this year.

Astrid Asi. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

In August, a fire was reported at defense contractor Milrem's office in Tallinn's Lasnamäe district, which KAPO also attributed to the Russian special services. Several Latvian citizens were also arrested in connection with the case.

Several other defense industry companies across Europe have also been targeted in recent months.

KAPO has said Russia is aiming to sow fear in society and among businesses, disrupt and weaken defense industry companies' production and technological development, and prevent defense industry products and technology from reaching Ukraine.

Palloson explained that one of the GRU's methods is to recruit European Union residents who can move freely within the EU's Schengen Area to carry out physical attacks and acts of sabotage.

Perpetrators are recruited from criminal circles and among people in difficult socioeconomic circumstances, he said.

Estonia preparing to close Russian border

Kristen Michal and Igor Taro. Source: Jürgen Randma/Government Office.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) on Sunday requested that the "necessary steps" be taken to close Estonia's eastern border with Russia in response to the attacks.

"Closing the border would reduce the threat to people in Estonia and send a clear message that attacks on Estonia's defence industry and defense capabilities are unacceptable," he said in a statement.

Minister of the Interior Igor Taro (Eesti 200) said he will propose that all Estonia-Russia road border crossing points shut from the start of December.

"Estonia has already significantly restricted traffic to and from Russia at our border crossing points, warning each time that further escalation could result in a complete closure of traffic. Now that moment has arrived," he said.

Estonian citizens in Russia will have two weeks to return home, the minister added,

It is not yet known if the closure will be temporary or indefinite.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Estonia's road borders will close on December 1.

Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December. Russia's attempts to intimidate, destabilise, or undermine our security will come with a price. We will take every necessary step to protect Estonia's security. — Estonian MFA | #StandWithUkraine (@MFAestonia) November 15, 2026

This story was updated to add comments from Internal Security Service (KAPO) Director General Margo Palloson and additional details about the incident. Then, for a second time, to add comments from Kristen Michal and Igor Taro.

World.title: Estonia's first responders hold school drone attack drills
World.content:
Estonia's emergency services held a large-scale realistic crisis exercise at a high school in western Estonia to practice responding to a drone attack as the threat from unmanned aerial vehicles grows.

According to the scenario, a drone flew into the foyer of Kilingi-Nõmme High School in Pärnu County and exploded. The children were evacuated. Rescue services and ambulances arrived within minutes. However, injured students and a teacher were trapped in a third-floor classroom.

The scene there was disturbingly realistic, Saturday's "Aktuaalne kaamera" evening news show reported.

Kristjan Kaunissaar, field commander at the Western Rescue Center, said the school had provided approximately 20 simulated casualties for the exercise. In addition, personnel from the police, rescue services, ambulance services and bomb disposal teams were involved in the response.

Rescuers were tasked with evacuating the children from the third floor, while medical personnel carried out rapid triage. Young people wearing special effects makeup acted as the wounded pupils.

Aaron, a 12th-grade student at Kilingi-Nõmme High School, had been given a facial injury in the exercise. He described the exercise as exciting.

Lissa, a 12th-grade student at Kilingi-Nõmme Gymnasium, had been assigned more severe injuries, including shrapnel wounds to the legs and stomach. She considered the rescuers' work slow. "I think I should actually have been dead a long time ago," she told "Aktuaalne kaamera."

Arvi, a national defense teacher at the school, said he was satisfied with the rescue services. "We have practiced and dealt with similar situations in exercises before," he added.

Kilingi-Nõmme High School organized the exercise because the threat from drones is constantly present. During the exercise, the school tested whether its crisis plan would hold up in a situation more realistic than what is written on paper or a regular fire drill.

Harri Kramm, the school's facilities manager and the organizer of the exercise, said the exercise went well but there are always more lessons to be learned.

World.title: Estonia opens 4th honorary consulate in Greece
World.content:
Estonia opened its first honorary consulate on Rhodes last week, allowing Estonians visiting the Greek island to receive assistance locally if needed.

Kerli Veski, undersecretary for legal and consular affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, opened the consulate on the Greek island of Rhodes on November 12.

Stergos Leventis has been appointed honorary consul.

"His work will help raise awareness of Estonia, strengthen cultural and economic ties between our countries and assist Estonians who need help while travelling. We are very grateful to him for his willingness and commitment to representing Estonia," Veski said at the opening ceremony.

She stressed the good ties between the two countries, which are both members of the European Union and NATO. One practical example of cooperation is the mutual recognition of e-prescriptions, which makes travelling easier for people from both countries.

Greece is a popular travel destination among Estonians. In 2025, 33,600 Estonians travelled to Greece, while 17,500 Greeks visited Estonia.

The honorary consulate on Rhodes is Estonia's fourth in Greece, alongside those in Thessaloniki, Patras and Agios Nikolaos on the island of Crete.

World.title: Pavel Talankin: How a cage of Putinist propaganda was built on top of the Soviet cage in schools
World.content:
Teacher Pavel Talankin from the small Ural town of Karabash jokes that he has become the first film director in the world whose films have a 100 percent Oscar success rate. Admittedly, he has made only one film so far, the documentary "Mr. Nobody Against Putin" (2025). Talankin came to Tallinn to screen the film at Artis cinema and speak with viewers afterward. While the audience watched the movie, he reluctantly gave an interview to ERR.

The film shows how Russian schools changed after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, how state propaganda entered classrooms, and how militaristic events and lessons such as "Conversations about important things" became commonplace. It all unfolds through the example of an ordinary school in the small Ural town of Karabash, where the film's author worked as a teacher.

Before winning this year's Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature, the film had already received several awards at international film festivals, as well as a BAFTA.

ERR: You left Russia in 2024, so you have now spent two years as an émigré. Have you gotten used to your new life?

Pavel Talankin: The easiest thing would be to say "in exile." I do not really like it when people say "in exile." Am I an emigrant? Yes, a forced emigrant. There is no ready-made formula for getting used to it. Everyone adapts in their own way. In some respects it has been easier for me because I was not disconnected from the process of making the film (which was edited in Denmark -A.A.), nor from the work that followed its release. We travel to festivals, speak at lectures and present the film. So I have remained busy.

At the moment, it seems your whole life revolves around this film. You already have all the awards, even an Oscar. What comes next? A Nobel Prize?

Yes! That is what I will work on now!

In what field?

Physics. So that everyone back at school completely loses their minds.

By the way, what subject does the film's main antagonist, teacher Abdulmanov, teach?

History and civics. And physics too, because there are not enough teachers. There was a year when he taught physics to students.

What grade did you get in physics?

I got a C.

And yet your goal is the Nobel Prize?

Why not? Einstein got a C too.

But right now your life revolves around the film. You have the fame of an Oscar winner. What happens when that fame fades? Are you afraid of that?

No, there is no fear. Maybe it only looks that way from your perspective: Oscar, BAFTA, Sundance! I do not see myself that way. I am the same person I was before. I understand that if I start putting myself on some pedestal now, it will hurt when I eventually fall back into ordinary life. So I never really left ordinary life. It feels as though we are speaking two different languages. You say Oscar, BAFTA, fame. I sit here thinking: who are you talking about?

Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

At the beginning of the war, Ukrainian documentaries dominated the spotlight. Mstyslav Chernov's "20 Days in Mariupol" won an Oscar in 2024. Two years later, the Academy chose a film about the other side of the conflict. Why do you think that happened?

That is really a question for the members of the Academy. I do not know. They are the ones who vote. It is probably better to ask them.

How does a film even end up at the Oscars? What has to happen?

First, we took part in various film festivals. Then we submitted Oscar applications. There were two submissions. One was for Best International Feature on behalf of Denmark, since the film is a Danish-Czech production. Their system works similarly to the Oscars. They choose among three films, and eventually selected "Mr. Nobody Against Putin." The second submission was in the documentary category. Then the process unfolds in stages. First, members of the documentary branch watch the films and vote. Then they vote again. Then again. In the final stage, everyone votes.

So for the first three rounds only documentary filmmakers vote?

Exactly. Long list, short list, nominations. Then all Academy members watch the nominated films.

Do you still keep in touch with Karabash and your former students? In one interview you said the graduates featured in the film wrote your speeches for award ceremonies.

They write my speeches.

What do you mean?

Well, when you win an Oscar you have to go on stage and say something. That little statement is your speech.

But that is only a minute, maybe less.

A minute? I wrote to my students and said: "Listen, if we actually get called up, if we actually win, what would you want to say?"

They sent me an enormous wall of text with everything they wanted to share. They got together, wrote a speech and sent it to me.

Then we were sitting at the Oscars, and our interpreter Robin asked me: "If you get called up, what are you going to say? I am nervous because not all words translate directly. You have to understand the context." I told her I would read what the students wrote. She said: "Show me, so I know how to translate it."

I showed it to her, and she said: "Have you completely lost your mind?"

In the documentary category, you only get 45 seconds. Since I share the time with David, the film's producer David Borenstein, I am left with about 20 seconds. Since I have an interpreter, that time is cut in half again. So I had about 10 seconds.

We had to compress everything the students wrote while preserving the meaning.

Did any of your students watch the ceremony?

Of course. All of them did.

And what did they say afterward?

They congratulated me.

None of them felt you had put them in danger with the film? I mean the students and teachers who appear on screen.

No. They have not suffered because of it, and they are not angry with me.

What about the teachers? When I watched the film, I found the students likable, but the teachers...

Well, the history teacher Abdulmanov gave an interview to Andrey Malakhov (well-known Russian TV presenter – ed.), where he said he liked how he was portrayed. He said I made him look even more patriotic and even more devoted to Russia...

...than he actually is?

Apparently. So he is delighted. What happened in Karabash is a genuine phenomenon. People there say bad things about me, but not about the film.

Pavel Talankin in Tallinn. Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

Have many people in Karabash seen it?

Everyone!

That is strange. The students like it, the people of Karabash like it, audiences here like it, teacher Abdulmanov likes it, yet Putin's government labeled Pavel Talankin a foreign agent. Why do you think that is?

You should ask him!

Oh, by the way, you just got a WhatsApp message.

And who is writing?

Some Maria Zakharova...

That is the Telegram channel of Maria Zakharova, the official spokesperson of the Russian Foreign Ministry. I have to follow it for work. So, back to Putin?

Look, a lot of things ordinary people like are things the president of the Russian Federation does not like. People generally like living according to the law. He does not. People generally value human life and health. He does not. People generally respect the territorial integrity of neighboring countries and do not spend their time thinking about war. He does not. He is a deeply disturbed person. Only God knows what he likes and dislikes.

After receiving the Oscar, you had the statuette blessed in a church in Paris by the well-known Russian priest Alexey Uminsky. Why?

We will come back to Uminsky later. I had it blessed by someone who did not support Russia's war crimes, who did not support the invasion of Ukraine, who was expelled from the Russian Orthodox Church and forced to leave Russia.

That answers why you chose him. But why bless the Oscar at all?

In the film, Putin quotes a phrase that is not actually his: "Wars are won not by generals but by schoolteachers." The full quote is: "Wars are won not by generals but by schoolteachers and priests." When you hold that Oscar in your hands, you immediately understand that there are schoolteachers and priests who oppose the war. And that means he will never win this war. That is all.

So you believe teacher Talankin and priest Uminsky are stronger than Putin?

Yes. I do.

The film covers the first two years of the war and shows how the propaganda machine gathered momentum. I was born in 1971, attended a Soviet school and was a Pioneer. We had our own versions of "Conversations about important things" and all that patriotic education, but by then nobody really believed in it anymore. Do children today believe what they are told, especially by the film's main antagonist, Abdulmanov?

Listen, adults believe it. Grown adults believe it. People with multiple university degrees and doctoral degrees believe it. So of course children can. The historian and writer Edward Radzinsky once quoted a phrase attributed to Stalin. I do not know whether Stalin actually said it: "After my death, garbage will be piled on my grave, but the ruthless wind of history will sweep it away." Putin is that ruthless wind of history right now. Because when these schoolchildren grow up, they may say: "Actually, things were better under Putin." And that is the most frightening thing that could happen.

This film will continue to be watched and shown. It is not a one-time documentary product. After we won the BAFTA, a well-known educator said something remarkable: "At first, it becomes routine. Nobody wants to do it, neither the teachers nor the children. Then it becomes culture, part of everyday life, like waking up and having coffee. And then it becomes a cage from which there is no escape."

This film shows how quickly teachers stepped into that cage once again.

There was already a Soviet cage, and no one ever seriously examined what had happened. No one said: "Friends, you were all indoctrinated." Nobody crushed that cage with a tank. Nobody flattened it with a steamroller. Nobody dissolved it with acid. Instead, another cage simply grew on top of it, the cage of Putinist propaganda.

People's minds are a complete mess, and getting them out of that cage will have to be done one person at a time. People do not like admitting they have been deceived.

Autor/allikas: Siim Lõvi / ERR

But among your students, are there some who have not been indoctrinated? One wants to believe so...

There are. At least I hope there are. The effect is different for everyone. There is no universal recipe for avoiding it.

(A long pause.)

Some students support Putin and the war. Some do not. A great deal depends on the family. If parents tell their child: "Try not to listen too closely to what your teacher is saying. Look out the window. Draw something. Think about something pleasant," then the child develops a kind of immunity to war. You can see such children in the film.

When soldiers are displaying grenades, some children simply refuse to touch the weapons. Compare the number of children who were forced to sit through lectures by Wagner Group mercenaries with the much smaller number who stayed afterward to take photographs with them.

The film has also faced criticism. Some people have accused you of constantly creating an atmosphere of secrecy around your activities, yet you appear on camera so often that someone must have been filming you. Who was the cameraman?

Let's just say God helped.

You spend a lot of time meeting audiences. Do foreigners ask different questions than Russians?

The questions are different. To really understand the difference, you would have to travel with me to various countries. There have been so many questions that I cannot remember them all. But there is one notable distinction.

People from Russia, Ukraine and Belarus usually say, "Thank you for the film."

People from other countries usually say, "Congratulations on the film."

You have said you want to return to Russia. Why?

Because it is necessary.

Even if you do not want to, you will have to pack your bags and go back to Russia when the regime falls. We will need to dismantle both cages that people are trapped in now, the first one and the second one, and tell people that they were deceived. People do not like admitting they have been deceived, and they will have to be led out of those cages one by one.

It will be individual work. And there will be a great deal of it.

--

World.title: Political parties looking to reduce Riigikogu members' salaries
World.content:
Political parties are discussing MPs' salaries, with both the coalition and opposition looking to make cuts in the next Riigikogu after the 2027 election.

Since April 1, 2026, the monthly salary of a Riigikogu member has been €6,655.81. MPs can claim reimbursement for work-related expenses of up to 25 percent of their salary.

Isamaa Chairman Urmas Reinsalu said that in recent years, salary increases for other senior state officials have been relatively smaller in line with austerity policy. But "this has not been applied to parliament," he said.

At the moment, it is still possible to set MPs' salaries for the next composition of the Riigikogu, which will be elected in March 2027.

Reinsalu said Isamaa has drawn up legislation to make the change, and the proposal has two parts.

Urmas Reinsalu Source: Siim Lõvi / ERR

"The first part is to reduce MPs' base salaries by roughly 10 percent to restore the previous proportion with other senior state officials, which has now shifted out of balance," he explained.

"And also, when it comes to their salary increases, to move to a more gradual system, which the government proposed introducing for the coming years," the chairman added.

Reinsalu claimed this would lead to savings of around €10 million over four years. He said the issue has not yet been discussed with other political parties but hoped Isamaa's initiative would find support.

Reform: Subject already under discussion

Reform Party parliamentary group chair Õnne Pillak told ERR that Isamaa is pushing at an open door. The government is already in the process of amending the Salaries of Higher State Servants Act.

"The plan to similarly reduce the rate of salary increases for Riigikogu members has certainly been under discussion among us. The question is what that percentage should be. There are different alternatives, but we should first wait for the bill to reach the Riigikogu," she said.

Õnne Pillak. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Pillak said Reform supports the principle that Riigikogu members, like government ministers, should receive smaller salary increases.

"But for me, what matters is not who submitted the bill. What matters to me is that the necessary decision gets made. Isamaa also knew that this bill would be coming to the Riigikogu from the government. So we can make all the necessary decisions within the framework of that bill," Pillak added.

She said there is no competition between the submitted bills, but Isamaa's proposal is incomplete.

"If the government said several weeks ago that such a bill would be submitted to the Riigikogu, then it makes sense to decide everything within the framework of a single bill. Isamaa can also come and support it, and it is not ruled out that, if the solutions are similar in substance, Isamaa's bill could also be merged with it. There is no need to do the same thing through several different bills," Pillak added.

World.title: Shift changes at Tallinn hospitals may lead to staff shortages
World.content:
The decision by two Tallinn hospitals to abandon 24-hour shifts is unpopular with nurses and care workers. The Estonian Nurses Union said the new rules make it difficult to work additional shifts elsewhere.

West Tallinn Central Hospital (Lääne-Tallinna keskhaigla) and North Estonia Medical Center (PERH) will no longer allow care workers and nurses to work 24-hour shifts, citing patient safety.

PERH's director of nursing, Katre Zirel, said studies confirm that employees become tired after eight hours of very intensive work, and when shifts extend to 24 hours, mistakes occur.

One PERH care worker said what bothers her most is that the hospital is not interested in how the new shift schedule suits employees.

If she has to travel to work four or five times a week, it takes more time and money, the single mother writes. She is also upset that doctors can continue working 24-hour shifts.

Difficulties organizing family life

A midwife working at West Tallinn Central Hospital said she is being forced to look for a new job because it is difficult to manage shorter shifts in a family where both parents are medical professionals. Kindergartens are also not open until late in the evening.

Estonian Nurses Union head Kätlin Lillemaa said the union supports reducing shift times, but the reasons why 24-hour shifts were introduced must be addressed.

"Nurses also point out that consecutive 12-hour shifts are exhausting," she told Saturday's "Aktuaalne kaamera."

Additionally, it may be difficult to get home as public transport runs on a limited schedule at night.

Lillemaa said that working at multiple workplaces is the most pressing problem, with one in five nurses taking shifts at more than one workplace.

"If we now move to shorter working days, the second workplace will be left short of helping hands, meaning the workload of those who remain will increase significantly," she explained.

Smaller hospitals unable to cover shifts

Lillemaa said this may lead to a situation in smaller hospitals where they are unable to cover all shifts.

East Tallinn Central Hospital (Ida-Tallinna keskhaigla) is continuing with 24-hour shifts, and nurses' interest in working there has increased slightly.

The hospital's head of nursing, Kätlin Pallo, said the shift issue is not new. "They have also been reduced or eliminated, but for certain reasons, institutions have returned to their previous working arrangements," she said.

Pallo added that the reason is often the evident shortage of healthcare workers.

Standardized rules could apply across Estonia, but this would require an agreement between hospitals, she said.
