This was later revised to 2021, although progress was slow with some of the remaining work being re-awarded, including one as late as October 2025.

On the 120-km Goa section of the NH-66 project, the stretch from the Maharashtra border to Panaji is complete, which means that once work on the pending 8 km on the other side is finished, the highway will link the two state capitals.

Flyover construction work at Indapur on the Mumbai-Goa highway. (Express photo By Narendra Vaskar) Flyover construction work at Indapur on the Mumbai-Goa highway. (Express photo By Narendra Vaskar)

The reasons for the continuing delays in Maharashtra range from cash flow issues and loan defaults to issues over land acquisition and local protests, officials and contractors said. Speaking to The Indian Express, V Umashankar, Secretary, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH), said: “In the last two years, a lot of work was done on stalled stretches and 99% of the highway is through now. All pending work will be completed by April next year.”



So far, the overall cost estimate of the Maharashtra section has ballooned by around 44 per cent, from Rs 12,532 crore to over Rs 18,100 crore. The overrun was primarily because of land acquisition, change of scope in work due to site constraints and construction of additional underpasses following demands from local residents, MoRTH officials said.

A senior official of MoRTH, which is the main implementing agency for the project along with the state PWD, described the situation as “a showpiece example of what can go wrong in a major highway project”.

Flyover construction work at Indapur on the Mumbai-Goa highway. (Express photo By Narendra Vaskar) Flyover construction work at Indapur on the Mumbai-Goa highway. (Express photo By Narendra Vaskar)

“We have now mandated that the pre-construction activities, like environment and forest clearances, should be complete before inviting the tender. At least 90% of land acquisition should be completed before the project is awarded to contractors,” the official said.

Asked about action taken, the official said, “We are now terminating such contractors. We have also fixed cost limits on the ministry’s projects to state PWDs.”



What progress reports show: 89% to 98.5%

This newspaper tracked the five delayed packages — and found that the completion rate ranged from 89 per cent to 98.5 per cent. Consider this:

1&2: Panvel to Indapur: 2 sections, 84.6 km, 97.75% complete

Status: Implemented by NHAI. Contract awarded in 2011, completion deadline 2020, re-awarded 2022-23.

Delay: Cash flow issues, loan default, land acquisition.

Contractors: Consortium including Supreme Infrastructure, which was on RBI’s top-100 bank defaulters list in 2019; contract terminated, balance work re-awarded to firm owned by J M Mhatre, a businessman under probe by Enforcement Directorate (ED).

Bottomline: Original cost Rs 943 crore, cost settlement currently in arbitration.



Two packages, Panvel to Kasu and Kasu to Indapur, were awarded to a consortium led by Supreme Infrastructure India, a listed company. The consortium included its subsidiary Supreme Infrastructure BOT Pvt Ltd (64 per cent share together), City Universe Ltd, a subsidiary of China State Construction Engineering (Hong Kong) Ltd, and Mahavir Roads and Infrastructure.

The entire 84-km section was first awarded as a BOT (Build-Operate-Transfer) project and the contractors completed 36 km by 2017. Subsequently, Supreme Infrastructure defaulted on bank loans and figured among RBI’s top-100 bank defaulters in 2019. Under a restructuring plan backed by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) in March 2025, the debt fell from Rs 2,200 crore to Rs 464 crore. Supreme Infrastructure BOT Pvt Ltd later went into liquidation. The consortium’s contract was terminated in 2021.

Panvel to Kasu: Awarded to J M Mhatre Infra Pvt Ltd in March 2023. The Panvel-based firm belongs to politician and businessman J M Mhatre, who is under ED investigation for alleged fraud involving forest land. Mhatre, who was associated with Peasants and Workers Party, joined BJP in 2025. He holds over 17 per cent share in the company, with the remainder held by family members. The company reported profits of Rs 5.08 crore in FY 2024-25.

Kasu to Indapur: Awarded in November 2022 to Kalyan Toll Infrastructure Ltd, an Indore-based company belonging to the Kalyan group. The company reported a profit of Rs 141 crore in FY 2024-25.



Mhatre, his company and Kalyan Toll did not respond to emails and calls from The Indian Express. Officials said land acquisition and utility shifting issues were resolved but Supreme Infra faced financial issues.

Flyover construction work at Indapur on the Mumbai-Goa highway. (Express photo By Narendra Vaskar) Flyover construction work at Indapur on the Mumbai-Goa highway. (Express photo By Narendra Vaskar)

3. Indapur to Wadpale: 26.75 km, 89% complete

Status: Implemented by MoRTH. Contract awarded in December 2017, completion deadline 2021, contractors terminated; balance work re-awarded in October 2025.

Delay: Forest clearances, shifting of utilities, land acquisition and pre-construction activities.

Contractors: Joint venture of Chetak Enterprises and APCO Infratech. Chetak is owned by Udai Lal Anjana, a Congress leader and former Rajasthan minister of co-operatives between 2018 and 2023. Contract terminated in 2025, remaining work awarded to Jaipur-based LNA Infraprojects.

Bottomline: Cost escalated from Rs 1,203 crore to Rs 1,657 crore.



The section was awarded in 2017 to a joint venture of Udaipur-based Chetak Enterprises and APCO Infratech. Records filed with the Registrar of Companies (ROC) show that Congress leader Udai Lal

Anjana holds over 40 per cent share in Chetak Enterprises, and close to 87 per cent with his family members. The company made a profit of Rs 32.46 crore in FY25. Lucknow-based APCO Infratech is run by Anil Kumar Singh, an industrialist from UP, who holds over 37 per cent stake. The company made a profit of Rs 738 crore in FY25.

Due to multiple delays, the ministry terminated the contractors in June 2025. The balance work of 10.6 km for the Indapur and Mangaon bypasses was awarded in October 2025 to Jaipur-based LNA Infraprojects. The work is scheduled to be completed by March 2027.

Udai Lal Anjana could not be reached for comment. His brother Manohar Lal Anjana, who holds 26.66 per cent stake in the company, said, “I know that we have two sections in the project but I am not aware of its status.” APCO Infratech did not respond to an emailed request for comment.



4: Parashuram Ghat to Arawali: 34.45 km, 98.50% complete

Status: Implemented by MoRTH. Contract awarded in December 2017, completion deadline 2021, 1.8-km Chiplun flyover pending.

Contractors: Joint venture of Chetak Enterprises, owned by Congress leader Udai Lal Anjana, and Eagle Infra India Ltd.

Delay: Land acquisition, court cases.

Bottomline: Cost has escalated from Rs 983 crore to Rs 2,226 crore.

Chetak Enterprises, whose services were terminated in the Indapur-Wadpale section for delays, was awarded a second section in a joint venture with Thane-based Eagle Infra India Ltd in December 2017. That, too, is yet to be completed.



Eagle Infra India, a major road contractor in Maharashtra, is run by the Rupchandani family, with Udhav Rupchandani serving as CEO and managing director of the company. The Rs 929-crore company registered a profit of Rs 253 crore in FY25.

The section is scheduled to be opened for commercial operation in November 2026, with the completion of the 1.8-km flyover in Chiplun. Eagle Infra did not respond to an emailed request from The Indian Express for comment.

5. Arawali to Kante: 39.24 km, 95% complete

Status: Implemented by MoRTH. Contract awarded in November 2017, completion deadline 2021; original contractor in insolvency, work re-awarded in 2024.

Delay: Local demands of high compensation and protests, cash flow, loan default.

Contractors: Hazoor Infra Projects Pvt Ltd, a subsidiary of Hazoor Multi Projects Ltd, a listed company. The chairman and managing director of Hazoor Multi Projects, Radheshyam Mopalwar, is a former vice chairman and MD of Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation, who helmed the Samruddhi Mahamarg Expressway project.

Bottomline: Cost rose from Rs 1,102 crore to Rs 1,443 crore.

The other delayed section, Arawali to Kante, was awarded in 2017 to a joint venture of MEP Infrastructures Developers Ltd and San Jose India Infrastructure & Constructions Pvt Ltd. Incorporated in 2002, MEP is a listed company with majority share held by Mumbai’s Mhaiskar family and Jayant D Mhaiskar as its chairman and managing director. San Jose India is a subsidiary of a Spanish group.

The work was delayed and MEP defaulted on a loan of Rs 128 crore from Intec Capital Ltd. Following this, the NCLT initiated the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) against MEP in March 2024. This necessitated the ministry re-inviting the tender for both sections. The project was awarded in 2024 to Hazoor Infra Projects Pvt Ltd. ROC records show Hazoor Infra, incorporated in October 2023 as a special purpose vehicle (SPV) for the NH-66 section, registered a profit of around Rs 12 crore in FY25.

Work on the Sangameshwar bridge approach and hill cutting at four locations (Kurdhunda, Kolambe, Wandri and Kante, 1.5 km) is yet to be completed in this section.

A top executive of Hazoor Infra said, “The remaining section will be done in a month. Since the section passes through populated areas, there was a problem in blasting and there were acquisition problems regarding a Railway section, a temple and a crematorium.”

Jayant Mhaiskar, chairman and managing director of MEP Infrastructure Developers, said, “Since the project has not been with us for the last five years, we would not be able to comment. The company is still under CIRP.”

World.title: The AI boom needs data centres. But why don’t people want them?
World.content:
Two interlinked events earlier this month indicate rising scepticism about the future growth of data centres — facilities central to the expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) technology.

First came the US midterm elections for electing members of the legislature and several state governors. The Democratic Party swept the polls, which triggered the second event: a sell-off in tech and AI stocks, including Amazon and Google’s parent company, Alphabet. Around $2.5 trillion was wiped off the Nasdaq.

The sell-off came from the expectation that Democrats will not be as pro-AI as President Donald Trump’s Republican Party. Voters also responded to specific policy proposals on the ballot for their constituencies. Of 47 measures on data centres, 46 saw a rejection of their expansion or approvals for greater scrutiny, according to an analysis by the website Ballotpedia.



The disapproval is not just an American phenomenon. Closer to home, Adani Enterprises and Google announced plans last October to develop India’s largest AI data centre campus in Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh, for $15 billion. Several cases have been filed in courts, challenging the project on grounds including the environmental clearance process and land allocation.

VS Krishna, Coordination Committee Member at the Human Rights Forum, one of the organisations challenging the project, told The Indian Express that the manner of approval was of “deep concern”, with limited gains for the locals. Similar opposition has been raised to such projects ranging from Finland to Kenya.

What exactly is a data centre?

With technological improvements, accessing the internet is now seamless, done at the touch of a finger or press of a button on sleek devices. But the vast amount of information and data being exchanged still needs to be contained and managed at a physical location.

A data centre is a facility that houses the physical infrastructure needed to store, process and manage data, and provide the computing services that underpin much of the internet. Such a centre can include servers, computers, hard drives and cooling systems to manage the heat generated by electrical systems.



Half-filled racks at a data centre. (Wikimedia Commons) Half-filled racks at a data centre. (Wikimedia Commons)

Shane Greenstein, professor of business administration at Harvard Business School, told The Indian Express that data centres are of various types. “India already has many data centres within its borders, and these play a well-established functional role. They serve as cloud providers for India’s massive IT industry, offering computing, storage, and related software services.”

“Typically, they need to be nearby to deliver services without delays (what is termed “latency”). An Indian business could access such services in Europe or the US, but users would notice delays from the distance the electronic signals travel, or from congestion along the way,” he said.

Data centres for training Large Language Models (LLMs) like ChatGPT initially did not need to be located nearby, Greenstein added. However, the growing use of these models for everyday applications has increased demand for inference — the computing required to generate responses to user prompts. Some applications also retrieve information from external databases or the internet, adding to their computational requirements. Newer-generation data centres typically use Nvidia’s Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), which can carry out complex calculations and support running applications and programmes.

AI data centres thus tend to be larger and consume much more electricity. Adarsh Ranjan, research analyst at Carnegie India, said the scale has risen substantially. “Data centres are sometimes measured in terms of power, say a 10 megawatt data centre, referring to what it needs to run.” But now, he said, companies are treating bigger facilities as the baseline. According to the International Energy Agency, “A typical AI-focused data centre consumes as much electricity as 100,000 households, but the largest ones under construction today will consume 20 times as much.”



“AI adoption at the enterprise level is still not very high. Companies are still trying to devise how to make their operations more productive with it. LLMs, however, are being increasingly used, resulting in more data centres,” Ranjan told The Indian Express.

The other argument for expanding data centres concerns data sovereignty, he said. “The country in which the data centre is located will essentially determine the laws governing it — including how secure it is and who gets to access it. Imagine the data centre is located in a country that you don’t have friendly ties with; that would lead to worries about the data, especially if it’s critical and sensitive, like health.” Currently, the United States leads globally, housing nearly half of all data centres.

What explains the backlash against data centres?

AI is among the most rapidly adopted technologies of the modern age, and the companies driving its growth have painted this pace as somewhat inevitable. An Adani-Google data centre media release says that its development “will create a powerful engine for economic growth in Visakhapatnam… and thereafter the entire nation by driving digital inclusivity and creating tens of thousands of jobs in technology, construction and clean energy.” An associated energy project is planned not only to “support the data centre’s operations but also enhance the resilience and capacity of India’s electricity grid.”

India’s data centre capacity. (MeitY data via PIB, generated with AI assistance) India’s data centre capacity. (MeitY data via PIB, generated with AI assistance)

But for all their promised benefits, data centres have increasingly acquired a negative reputation, seen as guzzlers of water and electricity, with questionable benefits.



India’s 2025-26 Economic Survey, for instance, stated that “Despite generating nearly 20 per cent of the world’s data, India hosts only about 3 per cent of global data centres.” In the same paragraph, it described the facilities as “double-edged swords”. It further quoted Mark P Mills, senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute, from a Congressional testimony: “In moonshot terms: the amount of energy used to launch a rocket is consumed every day by just one AI-infused datacenter.”

Water is used in data centres primarily to remove the heat generated by servers and processors. Traditional cooling systems often use evaporative cooling, in which water is evaporated to dissipate heat. Newer approaches, including direct-to-chip cooling, circulate coolant through cold plates attached to processors. While these can improve cooling efficiency, they do not necessarily eliminate water consumption, since the heat still has to be dissipated elsewhere in the facility.

“People are generally wary of potable water being used, and how this could impact local community access to water. Over time, companies themselves have realised that this would be a major issue moving forward. They traditionally employed evaporative cooling, releasing water into the air to lower temperatures. It would consume vast amounts of water, which led to methods like direct-to-chip cooling that use significantly less water,” Ranjan said.

Data centres additionally require large and reliable electricity supplies. While companies do procure renewable energy, electricity may also come from grids that rely heavily on fossil fuels. The additional demand and load on the ground could ultimately be passed on to other electricity consumers.



Greenstein said there was also a clearer cost issue on frontier AI. “Some opposition worries about whether society is using its resources well. Consider a 150MW facility, a scale that marked the AI frontier last year. Constructing the shell — land, connectivity, cooling, electricity, racks, etc. — can cost roughly $2 billion to $4 billion. Filling it with servers and associated hardware can add $3 billion, and easily several times that, with the frontier chips driving expenses high above that minimum. Operating it can cost more than $500 million a year, depending on location and weather. Hardware replacement adds another recurring bill measured in billions.”

“Such a build creates many jobs during construction, with thousands working on it for a year. After construction, the number of newly created jobs is modest, maybe just a bit more than 100 employees,” he added.

VS Krishna of the HRF added that jobs were a major factor for the people of Visakhapatnam, too: “Say if 1 lakh jobs were expected to be created, the people would not have opposed the project so vehemently.”

In Visakhapatnam, he said that the environmental clearance process was not based on informed public debate. “The clearance was given despite sustained and well-founded objections from concerned citizens, environmental experts and civil society organisations who have repeatedly warned of the serious ecological, hydrological and social consequences of permitting a project of this scale in an environmentally sensitive area linked to the Mudasarlova reservoir catchment and the Kambalakonda Wildlife Sanctuary,” said an HRF press release.



How are data centres being regulated?

Ranjan said that globally, the conversation is focused on two areas. “Countries recognise the need to bring in investment and establish facilities to support their domestic ecosystem. The second part is to ensure that the environmental fallout does not impact local communities.”

The Economic Survey suggests that since investment in AI infrastructure competes directly with other sources of demand, such as households and industries, a stronger case can be made for “smaller, task-specific (AI) models that can run on limited hardware and decentralised compute networks.” These would require fewer resources.

National data centre-specific policies have generally been lacking, although states have formulated their own, including in India and the US. “Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Telangana have their own policies, but these largely look at attracting investments,” he said. In the absence of a national policy, states could engage in a kind of race to the bottom to offer the most cost-cutting alternatives to companies.

Experts say that better resource utilisation is achievable, including with more green technology and energy-efficient methods. Ranjan said whether companies and governments move towards mandating them is more a question of political will.



But there is also a bigger fundamental question at the heart of the opposition — discomfort, scepticism and even anger, over the technology itself. Krishna said, “It has been billed as a gamechanger, but it’s also indirect. It’s a rudimentary example, but say, a hospital was being built instead. People will have direct use for it; it will result in lodging and food facilities coming up nearby, but that’s not the case here.”

Greenstein added that data centres face an “inescapable issue”: “The benefits go to users and businesses, who are distant and dispersed, while many of the costs are conspicuously local. That also creates opportunities for NIMBY (not in my backyard) opposition. Locals have no reason to care.”

“LLMs today are doing all sorts of things — writing music, writing books, helping people do things like draft emails, which can be a drag as part of your job. But for the amount of hype around it, we don’t yet have a very clear sense of how that’s going to add value for people,” said Ranjan. In such an atmosphere, building trust was key, he added. Mandates could be specified for water and energy use, with the local communities made aware of the kind of costs associated with such projects before approvals are sought. Ultimately, the debate is about whether such projects justify their costs, and if they do, what can be done to ensure they are accepted by the very communities they could impact most directly.

World.title: Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia touches off echoes, sparks questions
World.content:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, the American tech giant at the heart of the global AI revolution, has raised questions extending far beyond Silicon Valley. For one, can exceptional achievement place a business leader above the established standards of accountability? Employees and investors demanding the return of Nvidia’s visionary founder insist that the company cannot thrive without him. But dependence on one individual reveals a failure of corporate governance, doesn’t justify its suspension. Technological genius and shareholder wealth should confer neither immunity nor permanent entitlement to leadership. Fairness towards Huang is equally important. Allegations of possible links to Chinese intelligence must be investigated thoroughly, without presuming guilt.

The controversy has also raised uncomfortable questions within the American political class about US President Donald Trump’s close relationship with Silicon Valley. Has his administration become too comfortable with the “tech bros”, and allowed their commercial interests to override national security concerns? The immediate focus is Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that bought advanced Nvidia chips and is suspected of diverting them to China in violation of American export controls. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has publicly questioned Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s failure to restrict Megaspeed’s access to American technology. The US Congress is all set to grill Lutnick in the coming weeks. The controversy comes as Trump prepares for another meeting with Xi Jinping and exposes the inherent tension in the US’s China policy. Silicon Valley wants access to the enormous Chinese market; national security officials worry about strengthening China’s military and intelligence capabilities and Beijing’s ability to close the technological gap with Washington. The growing pressure from China hawks in both parties — Democratic and Republican — could complicate Trump’s search for a personalised and transactional engagement with Beijing.

World.title: Sooji vs oats for breakfast: A nutritionist breaks down the difference
World.content:
Choosing the right breakfast can set the tone for your entire day, and with so many options available, it can be challenging to decide what’s best for your health. Among the popular choices, sooji (semolina) and oats are often compared for their nutritional benefits and versatility in the kitchen.

While both have their own set of advantages, the debate over which is the better breakfast option continues. Kanikka Malhotra, consultant dietician and certified diabetes educator, tells indianexpress.com, “Oats and sooji (semolina) are whole grains, although they have different nutritional profiles. Oats are the ultimate dietary fibre source because they are high in soluble fibre, specifically beta-glucan. This kind of fibre supports healthy digestion, lowers cholesterol, and controls blood sugar. While sooji contains some fibre, the quantity is significantly lower compared to oats.”

World.title: Asif hopeful of consensus on new provinces, says it will bring 'progressive' change in political landscape
World.content:
Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Sunday said the country’s political landscape would change in a progressive way if a consensus was reached on the matter of creating new provinces.

The defence minister made the remarks in an interview on Geo News programme ‘Naya Pakistan’ with Shahzad Iqbal. He was asked about reports that discussions were taking place on generating a broader consensus for creating new provinces, referring to two recent high-level meetings involving the president.

Asif replied that he had no inside information on the matter and “even if there was, obviously I cannot spill it on a show”. However, he said his personal assessment was that all the consultations were heading in the direction suggested by the anchor — consensus on new provinces.

“Consensus is being developed on the issue,” the minister said, adding that the process had been ongoing for the past several weeks.

“In my opinion, the political landscape will change very progressively if this consensus is built and these [new] provinces are created,” he added.

On Thursday night, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had called on President Asif Ali Zardari, who then met Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Saturday. The Presidency had refuted reports that President Zardari and Naqvi spoke about matters related to provinces.

While an official statement from the meeting between the president and premier said the country’s political situation came under discussion, official sources privy to the development told Dawn that both leaders agreed to “strictly adhere to constitutional provisions” governing the creation of new provinces or administrative units.

The sources said President Zardari and PM Shehbaz also held a brief one-on-one meeting to discuss a message reportedly conveyed to the president by Naqvi during his Nawabshah visit.

Speaking on Sunday, Asif said he believed it would not take long to reach a consensus and the process was “moving towards culmination”.

He added that he did not know the method of this culmination, declining to comment on whether there was likely to be a referendum on the subject in the National Assembly as it could create “complications”.

According to sources, President Zardari and PM Shehbaz have agreed that the Parliament could not be bypassed in deciding whether a referendum should be held and what questions should be put to the public. Naqvi, who ignited the political storm on new provinces in July, has termed holding a referendum as the solution to the debate.

Asked about impressions that the push for new provinces was coming from certain quarters, Asif stated that this was not true as far as his advocacy for new provinces was concerned.

“I have been saying for years that there should be a robust local governance system,” he said. “How long will we avoid this?”

He added, “I think this will be good for all provinces, for Pakistan […] this is a very healthy thing. In all changes that have come before (in previous governments), there was never so much effort to build consensus on major changes.”

On the lack of clarity regarding the situation, he added that until a direction on several matters was indicated, he did not want to share the details in the public realm.

He also expressed his personal opinion that “the new year will see the new system, God-willing”, adding that the process will “take some shape in 2026”.

‘Space can be given to create consensus’

Asif further remarked that there was “no need for anyone to feel politically threatened” by the idea of new provinces, as political ethos was not static and continued to change.

He further regretted that the changes brought by the 18th Amendment regarding local governments had not been implemented.

The PPP leadership has appeared unwilling to soften its position on new provinces, particularly in Sindh. The party has consistently invoked a unanimous resolution passed by the Sindh Assembly opposing the province’s division, maintaining that it reinforces its position against any such move.

Commenting on this, Asif gave his opinion that consensus was still being developed on the situation and it should not be cast in a negative light.

He also said that space would be given in minor matters to political parties in order to create this consensus in a “quid pro quo” sense and no one would have the decision “forced” on them.

Asked whether such an effort was being made for PTI founder Imran Khan, Asif alluded to the possibility that, if he were to agree to the new system, the developments could create a “window of opportunity” for the jailed ex-PM to return to mainstream politics afterwards.

Providing his “political advice”, the PML-N leader said Imran should not resist the idea as he did not have any “fundamental objection” to new provinces.

Sindh Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah has voiced opposition to the division of Sindh into smaller provinces — although, he said on Wednesday, the PPP had no objection to the creation of new provinces in other parts of the country if their people so desired.

He stated that the division of Sindh was “neither legally nor politically acceptable, as the people of the province had repeatedly rejected the idea through their elected representatives”.

The defence minister recently argued that Pakistan could have as many as 12 provinces if the exercise was guided by administrative requirements rather than linguistic, ethnic or political considerations.

He maintained that the country’s growing population necessitated smaller administrative units capable of delivering public services more efficiently.

However, the PML-N has so far refrained from articulating a formal policy, saying it will present its position when the matter comes before Parliament.

World.title: In call with Fazl, Bilawal condemns 'govt actions, political vengeance' against JUI-F
World.content:
SWABI/CHARSADDA: PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on Sunday spoke to Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman and condemned the “government’s actions” against him.

The telephone conversation comes as tensions have remained high between the JUI-F chief and the PML-N-led federal government over the past month. On Sunday, Fazl’s party also held street protests in several cities of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa against “propaganda” directed toward the party and its leadership.

According to a statement issued by PPP, Bilawal and Fazl exchanged views on the country’s political situation.

The Bhutto scion — whose PPP is an ally of the ruling coalition — “condemned the government’s actions and political vengeance” targeting the JUI-F.

“The government should tolerate the opposition’s criticism,” Bilawal was quoted as saying in the statement. He highlighted that the opposition had an “extremely important role in democracy and a parliamentary system”.

Speaking to Fazl, Bilawal said the “government should refrain from such actions that weaken democracy and the Parliament”.

The PPP chairman has recently been calling for political unity in the country, urging the prime minister to take measures to build trust with the government’s allies and the opposition.

“Via this reset, political parties will have to work together instead of fighting,” he said on Nov 10, days after he urged the federal government to engage all political and social stakeholders rather than “fighting everyone”, including Fazl.

The past month has witnessed exchanges of harsh remarks between Fazl and federal ministers, after the JUI-F chief accused the Centre of depriving the provinces of their rights.

These developments came after Fazl joined the opposition in criticising the Centre’s imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in the PTI-ruled KP. He also accused the Centre of reneging on its commitments amid his efforts to mediate between the federal and KP governments.

On its part, the Centre has repeatedly cited the KP government’s “deliberate disengagement” from the counterterrorism fight for its decision, following which the PPP’s governor now heads the provincial administration.

On Oct 16, without naming anyone, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi had claimed that a “head of a party” was “extremely upset over being denied a role in the new setup in KP and not getting the governorship”.

The next day, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif and State Minister for Interior Tallal Chaudhry rebuked Fazl directly, who later clarified his criticism was aimed at policies, not state institutions.

The row played out in the Parliament as well, where Fazl questioned Asif’s absence and Naqvi’s presence at a meeting of the Makkah pact countries and Iran in Tehran.

In his response the next day, the interior minister explained his participation and went on to assail the JUI-F for “continuously crossing the line” and accused it of “extracting wealth from the state”.

JUI-F holds protests across KP

JUI-F has decried “baseless and fake propaganda” against Fazl, accused the federal government of resorting to cheap tactics, and questioned actions being taken as part of the anti-encroachment drive in KP.

To protest the actions, the party took to the streets in various KP cities, sharing purported videos of its gatherings in Peshawar, Lower Dir, Shangla, Hangu, Swabi, Battagram and Lakki Marwat.

In Swabi, JUI-F workers staged a protest at Karnal Sher Khan Chowk despite a fresh ban on gatherings imposed under Section 144 across the district.

JUI-F district leader Maulana Fazal Ali contended that the ban was imposed by the district administration soon after midnight to scuttle the party’s plan to hold the planned protest demonstrations.

“We demand from the government that Maulana Fazlur Rehman, our beloved leader, madressahs and religious individuals should not be targeted. The browbeating tactics used by the government should be immediately given up,” he stressed.

A demonstration also took place at Maulana Hassan Jan Shaheed Chowk in Charsadda, where local party leaders alleged that drone surveillance was being carried out of Fazl’s residence.

The demonstration was attended by party workers and local leaders. However, the absence of the district leadership from the protest also became a subject of discussion among participants.

JUI Charsadda tehsil president Maulana Hashim, Maulana Tahmeedullah and other leaders addressed the gathering.

Late last month, the Directorate of Building Control (City) of the Capital Development Authority issued a warning notice to remove the guards’ room set up outside Fazl’s residence in Islamabad’s G-6 sector within 15 days.

Fazl’s son Asad Mehmood claimed the notice was retaliatory and expressed concern over the “transformation of political differences into personal revenge”.

Earlier this month, the National Accountability Bureau (NAB) summoned Mehmood, a former federal minister for communication, for alleged irregularities in 4,252 appointments at Pakistan Post during his 2022-23 term. Mehmood skipped two NAB summons notices and did not appear before its investigation team.

On Nov 6, the JUI-F staged protests in different parts of Sindh and Balochistan, decrying what it called a “coordinated character assassination campaign” against its chief.

World.title: Islamabad hosts foreign dignitaries for two-day ECO ministerial meeting
World.content:
Foreign dignitaries arrived in Islamabad on Sunday as Pakistan hosts the two-day 30th meeting of the Economic Cooperation Organisation (ECO) Council of Ministers, starting today.

Currently, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Tajikistan, Iran, Turkiye, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyz Republic and Uzbekistan are part of the ECO.

Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar hosted a welcome dinner in honour of the foreign ministers and heads of delegations of the member states in Islamabad ahead of the meeting, the Foreign Office (FO) said on social media.

He warmly welcomed the delegates and wished them productive deliberations while highlighting the close bonds among ECO member states, the FO said.

Addressing the gathering, DPM Dar also reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to “regional cooperation and advancing shared aspirations for peace, progress and prosperity”.

Alongside the visiting delegations, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, Parliamentary Minister Dr Tariq Fazal Chaudhary, representatives of the ECO secretariat, members of the diplomatic corps, and senior officials of the foreign ministry were also in attendance, FO added.

Shanghai Cooperation Organisation Deputy Secretary General Ahmad Saidmurodzoda, Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Secretary General Ismail Ould Cheikh Ahmed, Turkish Deputy Foreign Minister Musa Kulaklikaya, and Kyrgyz Republic’s Deputy FM Kairat Erkinovich Tursunkulov are among those in Islamabad for the meeting.

Azeri Deputy FM Elnur Mammadov, Kazakh Deputy FM Arman Issagaliyev, and Turkmenistan’s FM Rashid Meredov also arrived in the federal capital today.

At night, Iran’s FM Abbas Araghchi also landed in Islamabad for the moot, Iran’s state media reported.

Upon his arrival, Meredov, who is also the deputy chairman of Turkmenistan’s cabinet of ministers, was received by Pakistan’s Ambassador to Turkmenistan and other officials, the FO said.

The foreign minister of Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, Tahsin Ertugruloglu, had landed in Pakistan on Saturday for the meeting.

According to APP, incumbent ECO Secretary General Asad Majeed Khan chaired a meeting on the draft agenda of the 30th ECO-COM.

This gathering of senior officials from ECO member states was set to review the organisation’s activities and programmes, assess the work of its subsidiary bodies and finalise the agenda and draft outcome documents for consideration by the ministers.

Monday’s ministerial meeting will be chaired by DPM Dar and attended by foreign ministers and heads of delegations from ECO member states, along with representatives of the organisation’s secretariat and subsidiary bodies.

Pakistan, which holds the ECO chairmanship for 2026-27, will seek to advance the organisation’s objectives under the theme “Reviving Regionalism for a Resilient ECO”, the FO said in a statement on Saturday.

It said Pakistan’s chairmanship would focus on strengthening regional connectivity and integration, deepening partnerships and promoting collective efforts for economic prosperity and sustainable development.

The chairmanship would also provide an opportunity to strengthen the ECO’s role as a platform for regional cooperation, dialogue and economic collaboration, it added.

According to the FO, Pakistan also aims to position itself as a regional connectivity hub, facilitate logistics supply chains and help shape the agenda for regional trade.

The efforts would help unlock the region’s economic potential and translate the benefits of regional cooperation into tangible improvements in the lives of people in ECO member states, the statement said.

Dar meets ECO, OIC, CICA heads

On the sidelines of the meeting, DPM Dar met Ambassador Majeed, FO said.

Dar underscored the importance of strengthening “regional cooperation, connectivity and economic integration” within the ECO region. He reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to hosting the ECO Summit in 2027, the FO said.

He also appreciated the ECO secretariat’s efforts in advancing the agenda of the organisation, and its support for Pakistan’s priorities during its chairmanship.

“The secretary general appreciated Pakistan’s excellent arrangements, hospitality and coordination for the 30th ECO-COM and congratulated Pakistan on its upcoming chairmanship and hosting of the ECO-COM and ECO Summit in 2027, reflecting the importance Pakistan attaches to regionalism and multilateral cooperation,” the statement said.

It added that both sides reaffirmed the importance of close coordination during Pakistan’s chairmanship “to ensure effective implementation of agreed initiatives and advance shared goals of regional development and prosperity”.

DPM Dar also held a meeting with the OIC secretary general, welcoming him on his first visit to Islamabad since assuming office this year, the FO said.

He “reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to strengthening the OIC as a unified and effective voice of the Muslim Ummah” and assured Ahmed of Pakistan’s continued support and cooperation in advancing the OIC’s objectives.

“The secretary general appreciated Pakistan’s diplomatic efforts during the Iran-US conflict to promote peace and stability in the region. He also commended Pakistan’s active role in the OIC, including its contributions through COMSTECH to promoting scientific and technological cooperation among member states,” the FO said.

Both sides agreed to maintain close cooperation within the OIC, while also reiterating “their steadfast support for the peoples of Palestine and Jammu and Kashmir and the realisation of their right to self-determination”, it added.

The deputy premier also met with the secretary general of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), Ambassador Sultan Hajiyev, where he reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for CICA and its efforts to promote peace, security and stability in Asia through dialogue and confidence-building measures.

Hajiyev appreciated Pakistan’s constructive efforts in promoting dialogue and de-escalation. He also thanked Pakistan “for its warm hospitality and excellent arrangements” for the council meeting, the FO said.

Separately, the ECO secretary general also met Deputy FM Tursunkulov to discuss Kyrgyzstan’s “contributions and ECO’s work in a range of areas including trade, energy, industry and tourism cooperation”, he said.

World.title: Trump admin warns US air travellers of another messy day
World.content:
The Trump administration said on Sunday that the air travel havoc triggered by a no-takeoff order could drag on for another day, pushing back its timetable for a return to normal.

Hundreds more flights were cancelled and questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world’s largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess.

Officials blame Friday’s huge snafu on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables.

United States President Donald Trump on Sunday ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor Joe Biden for the debacle.

Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party has controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America’s outdated air traffic control system.

“The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster,” Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration.

“Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began,” Trump asserted.

FAA chief Bryan Bedford had said on Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday. He also apologised for the disruption, adding that the system remains stable.

But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday morning it will actually take longer to get planes, crews and travellers to where they need to be.

“So, in the airspace, we’re going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow,” Duffy said on ABC News.

“We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that.”

‘I’m the secretary’

Duffy also flatly rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure, such as, he said, radar equipment that dates back to the 1960s.

“So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I’m the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me,” Duffy said in an interview on CNN.

As of Sunday morning, 1,460 flights within, into or out of the United States had been cancelled, according to the travel monitor site FlightAware.

The Trump administration has blamed Friday’s ground stop — meaning no planes can take off — on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.

Friday’s disruption was only the second time such a ground stop had been issued in US airspace, which is among the busiest in the world, since the 9/11 attacks.

The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos, but it also raised serious concerns about the country’s ageing infrastructure.

Cancellations and chaos

As of 9:35pm on Saturday ET (7:35am Sunday PKT), airlines had cancelled more than 6,400 US flights and delayed more than 8,000, according to FlightAware, an aviation website.

That followed about 9,200 flights cancelled and 7,500 delayed on Friday after the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop because of disruptions to air traffic communications.

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Friday that halted nearly all departing flights for almost five hours. It was the longest nationwide halt to air travel since the attacks of Sept 11, 2001, and one of the single worst US travel days ever.

The issue prompted the White House to convene an emergency meeting in the Situation Room on Friday and federal agencies to scramble to determine if it was a cyberattack. But the problem was traced to FAA contractor L3Harris’ installation of at least one new router at a remote facility, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Saturday.

“We’re working to determine whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error or installer error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router? We haven’t determined what the fault was,” Duffy said at a press conference.

The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists, a union representing FAA safety employees, said the issue was isolated to two routers that were updated on Friday. An official told Reuters it was believed the routers were in Arkansas and Texas.

An FAA official said the agency conducted a safety assessment before the work. The union said PASS-represented technicians were not involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

L3Harris said it took the issue seriously and is supporting the FAA in its investigation. Its shares last traded down about four per cent after hours on Friday.

The Trump administration previously blamed the mess on a botched replacement of old copper wire communication lines.

Though the FAA lifted the ground stop — meaning no planes can take off — on Friday evening, the disruption for passengers was far from over, with tens of thousands of people stranded in airports. Airlines were trying to get flight crews and other personnel in position to resume flights.

It sparked widespread chaos and left hundreds of thousands of passengers in limbo, with some pulled off planes moments before they were due to depart by airline staff who appeared in the dark about unfolding events.

“Tired. Exhausted. Frustrated. Yeah, you know, it’s just a mess, right?” Lisa Beraid, 48, who works for an insurance company, told AFP as she waited for a flight on Saturday morning at New York’s La Guardia airport.

Duffy said Friday’s four-hour ground stop was declared after maintenance work to upgrade an old copper wire to a high-speed fibre cable had caused “issues” with communication with airplanes and radar feeds.

“Either through contractor error or a faulty piece of equipment… it started flooding other routers in our air traffic control system,” Duffy told reporters.

In another embarrassment, Saturday’s news conference — where administration officials also appealed for more funds to upgrade outdated systems — was delayed due to technical problems with the audio feed.

Overloaded communications centres

Duffy said the trouble began on Friday afternoon, when air traffic control centres experienced instability in radar and communications systems. The router issue led to data overloading other communications centres, officials said.

“We had over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, and what that did was [it] gave us issues with our communication with airplanes, and it also caused some disruption with our radar,” Duffy added.

The issue affected communications at 17 of the FAA’s 22 en route centres, which control aircraft during the cruise portion of a flight.

Bedford said the FAA ordered the ground stop in case a centre lost all communications. “No facilities went dark. Nothing was fully lost,” Bedford added.

The FAA said it was doing additional testing with L3Harris to see if there are any additional risks.

Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and American Airlines all cancelled about 25pc of their flights on Saturday, while JetBlue cancelled nearly 45pc. Airlines have issued travel waivers allowing passengers to rebook flights for later dates without cost.

Funds sought to fix system strain

Friday’s disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by ageing technology, equipment and communications problems and a shortage of several thousand controllers.

Duffy called on Friday for $50 billion in funding to upgrade air traffic control systems, up from his earlier request of $30bn after Congress approved $12.5bn last year.

House Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Saturday that he supports approving more funding for air traffic this year. Johnson’s Republicans control Congress until next year, when Democrats will take over because of their gains in the Nov 3 midterm elections.

US Representatives Rick Larsen and Andre Carson, Democrats slated next year to chair the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and aviation subcommittee, respectively, said in a joint statement Saturday that their panels will “hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again.”

Since receiving $12.5bn last year, the Transportation Department has awarded contracts worth $4.3bn but only spent $1bn, Larsen and Carson said.

Responding to Duffy’s appeal for funds, Illinois state governor and prominent Democrat, JB Pritzker, retorted, “Cut the crap”.

He wrote on X, “Trump and Republicans have controlled Congress and could have funded the system.”

New York Governor Kathy Hochul called on Duffy to resign or be fired by Trump, writing on X: “We’re fortunate no lives were lost.”

US lawmakers called for investigations into what caused the massive disruption and whether the country is adequately secure from cyber criminality.

“If today proves anything, it’s that we need to update our air traffic control system and rebuild our airport infrastructure,” Republican Senator Eric Schmitt said on X.

World.title: FIA books 8 Pakistanis deported from Turkiye for violating immigration laws
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) said on Sunday it has registered a case against eight Pakistanis deported from Turkiye for allegedly violating immigration laws.

FIA Islamabad registered the case against the eight deportees, who had travelled to Turkiye on work visas but allegedly started working elsewhere illegally instead of joining the companies concerned. Turkish police arrested them, took them to jail and later deported them to Pakistan.

The case has been registered under Sections 3 and 4 of the Passport Act, 1974. The involvement of other individuals or agents, if any, will be determined during the investigation.

The FIA Islamabad Zone reiterated its resolve to continue action against those involved in human smuggling and violations of immigration laws.

Separately, the FIA Anti-Human Trafficking Circle Rawalpindi recovered Rs3.8 million allegedly defrauded from a citizen on the pretext of providing a work permit in Portugal.

According to the FIA, the action was taken after complainant Wajid Hussain alleged that the suspect had taken €12,000 (approximately Rs3.8m) from him on the promise of arranging employment and a work permit in Portugal but failed to fulfil the commitment.

FIA said the full amount was recovered during the inquiry and handed over to the complainant. The inquiry was conducted by Sub-Inspector Ansa Tayyaba, under whose supervision the legal and departmental proceedings were completed.

The agency added that action against visa agents and those involved in human smuggling was continuing without delay and interruptions on the directions of Islamabad Zone Director Syed Shehzad Nadeem Bokhari.

World.title: GB police register case as PPP protests alleged malpractice in Diamer repolling
World.content:
GILGIT: Re-polling was held at three polling stations in Gilgit-Baltistan’s GBA-16 (Diamer-II) on Sunday, with PPP staging protests in Diamer’s Chilas, as well as Gilgit, against alleged electoral malpractice by the Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party (IPP).

PPP’s Attaullah Shah and IPP’s Imam Malik are the main contenders vying for the seat in the partial repolling, held after an election tribunal accepted Malik’s plea and suspended Shah’s assembly membership.

The electoral process began at 8am and continued until 5pm, with voters present within the polling station premises at that time allowed to cast their votes. A total of 2,780 registered voters were eligible.

However, after polling concluded, supporters of Shah took to the streets in Diamer district’s Chilas and Gilgit against the alleged removal of ballot boxes from a women’s polling station in Thore Valley.

Protesters block Shahrah Quaid-i-Azam near GB Assembly in Gilgit by burning tyres, on Nov 15, 2026. — Jamil Nagri

In a statement, the GB Police spokesperson said legal action has been initiated against those who “took away polling material” from the Wara polling station, and a first information report (FIR) under terrorism charges has been registered.

The case invoked sections 34 (common intention), 147 (punishment for rioting), 149 (every member of unlawful assembly guilty of offence), 186 (obstructing public servant), 353 (criminal force to deter public servant from duty) and 392 (punishment for robbery) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), as well as sections 6 and 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA).

“The situation is peaceful in the remaining two polling stations,” the police statement affirmed.

It warned that strict action under the law will be taken against those who take the law into their hands and block the highways, noting that some of those were already wanted by the police.

When contacted, GB Chief Election Commissioner Raja Shahbaz Khan told Dawn that an investigation was under way into the allegations.

He noted that foolproof security was provided at the stations, urging people not to take the law into their hands. The election commissioner affirmed that the matter will be resolved.

The PPP supporters staged demonstrations on the Karakoram Highway near Chilas, as well as outside the GB Assembly hall in Gilgit, and vowed not to let the public mandate be stolen.

Outside the assembly, demonstrators burnt tyres to block the road. One of the protesters, Rehman Deralo, claimed that Malik and others accompanying him entered a polling station and took away ballot boxes and other polling material.

PPP workers also staged a protest at Gilgit’s Etihad Chowk, chanting slogans and burning tyres to block the routes.

Imtiaz Gilgiti from People’s Youth Organisation, the PPP’s youth wing, said Shah had secured votes from the rival candidate’s hometown and therefore, Malik allegedly stole ballot boxes.

Addressing protesters in Gilgit, local PPP leader Shahzad Agha claimed Shah was winning in the polls, but his opponent violated the law and stole the ballot boxes.

The former GB minister also termed it negligence by the relevant administration and polling security. “Even if re-polling is conducted 10 times in Diamer, Attaullah will emerge victorious,” Agha contended.

Earlier during the day, a source told Dawn that IPP’s Malik had allegedly slapped Polling Officer Dr Maria at the Sarai polling station, adding that the overall polling process remained largely peaceful despite minor unpleasant incidents.

Electoral dispute

Among the two candidates, Malik had contested the June elections in Gilgit-Baltistan as an independent candidate, but had later joined the IPP.

Initially, the Election Commission had declared him the returned candidate for GBA-16 (Diamer-II), but his membership was suspended in September after Shah filed a petition before an election tribunal. The plea contended that the returning officer (RO) had issued Form-49 without counting the postal ballots.

In its order on Sept 11, the tribunal directed the relevant RO to complete the verification and counting of postal ballot papers by September 16 and, meanwhile, suspended Malik’s membership.

Subsequently, the counting and verification of postal ballots for GBA-16 (Diamer-II) was held and Shah was declared the winner on Sept 14. According to the revi­sed consolidated results issued by the GB Election Com­mission on Form-49, Shah secured 6,618 votes, defeating Malik by a margin of just 13 votes.

But then, Malik had challenged the tribunal’s decision before the GB Supreme Appellate Court.

On Sept 19, the appellate court dismissed his appeal against the suspension of his membership and upheld the tribunal’s decision declaring Shah the returned candidate.

Malik later again challenged the results at three polling stations and petitioned the election tribunal to order re-polling.

The tribunal accepted his plea and suspended Shah’s membership and directed the chief election commissioner to conduct re-polling at the three polling stations within 12 days of Nov 6.

World.title: Authorities ban gatherings in five districts of KP for 30 days, citing law and order situation
World.content:
BANNU/BAJAUR/LAKKI MARWAT/SWABI: The district administrations of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s Bannu, Bajaur, Lakki Marwat, Swabi and Tank on Sunday imposed Section 144 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) for a month, banning public gatherings and several other activities amid the prevailing law and order situation.

Three of the five districts — Bannu, Bajaur and Tank — are among the 12 districts that were deemed to face intense security challenges and special emergency measures were imposed there.

In Bajaur, the district administration prohibited all kinds of political gatherings, “hate speech” against the state and the display of arms and weapons for 30 days.

The notification formalising the restriction, seen by Dawn, said Bajaur Deputy Commissioner (DC) Adnan Farid Afridi approved the restrictions in view of the law and order situation, citing the need for additional measures to safeguard public life and property and maintain peace.

The notification further stated that law enforcement agencies were required to remain more vigilant to avert any “unpleasant mishaps” while also enhancing security at the district’s entry and exit points and discouraging and disallowing “unauthorised gatherings” in public places.

“Sufficient grounds exist to believe that immediate preventive measures are required to be taken,” the notification added.

The notification stated that the order would come into force on Nov 15 (Sunday) and remain in effect until Dec 15, unless modified or withdrawn.

It warned that anyone found violating the order would be punished under Section 188 (disobedience to order duly promulgated by public servant) of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC).

In October, authorities banned pillion riding in Bajaur for 10 days, citing the security situation back then as well.

Bannu ban includes tinted vehicle windows

Section 144 was also imposed in Bannu for the same period of time, according to a separate notification.

Bannu DC Ziaur Rehman imposed various restrictions across the district, including pillion riding, use of tinted vehicle windows, display of weapons, protest gatherings, use of loudspeakers on roads, and setting up tents or creating obstructions on public roads and other public places.

According to the notification, the order was similarly imposed “in view of the prevailing law and order situation in the area”. It noted that “public gatherings and processions are likely to disturb the free movement of the general public, disrupt traffic, peace, tranquillity, and affect the maintenance of law and order”.

JUI-F protest defies Swabi ban

Meanwhile, in Swabi, DC Nasrullah Khan imposed a ban on public gatherings, assemblies, processions, rallies, marches and demonstrations for one month with immediate effect.

The order, dated Sunday, said the preventive measures had become “imperative” to maintain public order and safeguard the lives, safety and security of the general public.

It contended that such gatherings “may expose the general public to serious security risks, endanger human lives and public property, and create opportunities for untoward incidents, thereby disrupting public peace and tranquillity”.

“It is, therefore, necessary to impose appropriate preventive restrictions in the larger public interest to avert any potential threat to human life and property,” the order read. It added that such activities would not be allowed without prior permission of the DC.

Despite the imposition of the ban, workers of the Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam-Fazl (JUI-F) staged a protest at Karnal Sher Khan Chowk against “propaganda” aimed at the party leadership.

Pillion riding also barred in Lakki Marwat

In Lakki Marwat, DC Shahid Rafique imposed a month-long ban on public gatherings, processions, rallies, assemblies and marches within the district’s territorial limits.

The order, a copy of which is available with Dawn, also prohibited the display, carrying and possession of all kinds of weapons, pillion riding, and setting up tents or temporary structures and other obstructions on public roads and highways in a manner likely to disturb traffic and public movement.

According to the order, the restrictions were imposed at the request of the district police officer, who had apprehended that such activities could obstruct public movement, disrupt public services and traffic, and disturb peace and tranquillity.

The restrictions will remain in force until Dec 13, unless withdrawn or modified. The notification warned that violators would be dealt with “sternly” under the law.

Tank ban; exams postponed in North Waziristan

In Tank, DC Jamshed Khan issued a notification announcing the restrictions on public gatherings, rallies, and processions, according to state broadcaster Associated Press of Pakistan (APP).

“A ban has also been imposed on pillion riding on motorcycles and the display of weapons,” APP reported, adding that legal action would be taken against anyone found violating the restrictions.

Additionally, the Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (BISE) in Bannu has postponed the Intermediate Annual-II Examinations 2026 across North Waziristan on the directions of the DC, also citing the prevailing law and order situation. According to the board’s notification, a revised examination schedule will be announced later.

However, examinations at centres located along Miranshah Road in Bakakhel will continue as per the original schedule.

KP has been witnessing terrorist attacks and security challenges for a long time.

Last month, a police officer was martyred after terrorists attacked a police post in KP’s Bajaur.

On Friday, the military’s media affairs wing said 74 terrorists had been killed in intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in KP and Balochistan. It said 43 terrorists were killed during operations conducted over 48 hours in KP, including 35 in North Waziristan’s Mir Ali and eight in Orakzai district. Another 31 terrorists were killed in Balochistan during an operation launched on Nov 3.

World.title: PM Shehbaz, CDF Munir share top spot in list of world’s 500 most influential Muslims
World.content:
Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir have shared the top spot in the latest edition of the world’s 500 most influential Muslims, alongside the Saudi king and crown prince and the Turkish president.

The rankings have been compiled by the Royal Islamic Strategic Studies Centre (RISSC), a research institute based in Amman, Jordan. It has been publishing an annual report titled “The 500 Most Influential Muslims” since 2009, recognising and highlighting individuals who have made significant contributions to Muslim communities.

This is the first time that the list features multiple names for the top rank, recognising the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, according to the edition.

“While this unified top spot features five individuals, it is actually divided into three shared entries that represent a massive shift in how Muslim nations are working together to protect one another. The main reason for this historic decision is the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement,” the edition said.

It added, “This mutual-defence pact unites the immense wealth of Saudi Arabia, the advanced tech and manufacturing of Turkiye, and the powerful military strength of Pakistan into a collective alliance.

“Modelled on a ‘one for all, all for one’ approach to security, this pact has completely reshaped regional politics.”

The report also acknowledged that “over the past year, Pakistan has navigated an intricate set of economic stabilisation challenges, regional security pressures, and major-power diplomatic balancing acts”.

It noted that Islamabad engaged in “regional shuttle diplomacy” in the Middle East to advocate for de-escalation, “even as domestic energy markets faced immediate pressures via elevated import costs and emergency fuel conservation measures”.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar posted about the development on X, saying, “A moment of gratitude for every Pakistani.”

He added, “From Marka-i-Haq to global diplomacy, they walked this journey together. This honour is a tribute to the sacrifices of our martyrs and the unity of our nation.”

Following the leaders of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, at the fourth and fifth place in the list are Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and Jordan’s King Abdullah II, respectively.

Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani is ranked at number six while United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al-Nahyan has been ranked at number 12. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah Saeed El-Sisi is at number 22.

Pakistani Scholar Sheikh Muhammad Taqi Usmani has been listed as the seventh most influential Muslim, while Scholar Maulana Tariq Jamil is ranked at 32.

Footballer Mohamed Salah is ranked at 39.

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas is listed at number 45, followed by Syrian Interim President Ahmed Al-Sharaa at the 46th place.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is listed as the 49th most influential Muslim in the list.

Honourable mentions in politics include Hamas Chief Khalil Al-Hayya, former prime minister Imran Khan, London Mayor Sadiq Khan and American Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed.

Similarly, honourable mentions in the “Social Issues, Science, Arts & Culture, Media and Sports” category include Jordan’s Queen Rania Al-Abdullah, British composer Sami Yusuf, Palestinian journalist Bisan Owda, British-American broadcaster and journalist Mehdi Hasan and Egyptian comedian Bassem Youssef.

Every year, the RISSC also names two people as Man of the Year and Woman of the Year.

This year, Palestinian paediatrician Dr Hussam Abu Safiya has been named as the Man of the Year. He is described as “a doctor who refused to abandon his patients, buried his son and returned to the wards, and has now spent more than six hundred days in Israeli custody without charge or trial”.

Under Israel’s invasion of Gaza, he documented attacks on medical facilities and appealed to the international community to protect Gaza’s health infrastructure. “A man with no army, no office and no freedom has done more than most governments to remind the world what courage and integrity look like,” the report says.

Minab school attack survivor Fatemeh Zahra Sheikhabadi has been honoured as the Woman of the Year.

On Feb 28, a US missile struck an elementary girls school in Iran’s Minab, killing over 150 people, including over 100 children.

After surviving the US strikes on her school, Sheikhabadi travelled to Geneva and addressed the UN Human Rights Council, urging world leaders to “hear the voices of the children of Minab”, the report says.

“She is honoured not as a symbol of a war, but as herself: a girl who lost her friends and her teachers on an ordinary morning, and who lived to tell their story so that it would not be lost with them,” the report added.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times.
