World.title: ‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019249/‘Sisters, Stand Up!’ A Bar’s Urinals for Women Make a Splash in China
World.content:
“Sisters, stand up!” reads a slogan written in pink on the mirror above three pink-and-white urinals. Alongside each sits a stack of disposable paper funnels, waiting for those willing to heed the call.

The scene, reportedly captured in the women’s restroom of a bar in China’s eastern city of Wuxi, began circulating online last week, sparking debate and prompting a related hashtag to garner over 54 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Tuesday.

“I stood there in disbelief for two minutes, thinking I’d walked into the wrong restroom,” one user wrote on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, attaching photos of the urinals. “I kept checking until a cleaner confirmed it was indeed the women’s restroom.”

The user, a Wuxi resident in her 30s surnamed Shi, told domestic media she was unsure how to use the urinals as there were no instructions nearby. She said she eventually opted for a traditional squat toilet in the same restroom instead because she worried about making a mess or soiling her clothes.

“I’d actually love to try this,” one commenter wrote. “In winter, it’s a hassle to squat with all those thick, long layers on, especially when you’re also carrying a bag.”

“Better yet, let the brothers sit down,” read another comment, which received nearly 1,400 likes.

On Tuesday, a woman surnamed Tang, who runs Gungun Folk Theater, the bar where the urinals were reportedly installed, told domestic media that they were intended for women who find it difficult to squat, including those wearing long dresses or with limited mobility. “We just wanted to make things easier and give women another option,” she said.

Studies suggest that standing to urinate may be easier for pregnant women and those with knee osteoarthritis, while standing, crouching, and sitting have been found to make no significant difference to bladder emptying in healthy women.

Standing urinals are increasingly common worldwide at music festivals to save space and reduce restroom queues, and at outdoor activities where toilets are scarce.

In China, efforts to introduce standing urinals for women reportedly date back to 2004. At that time, Ye Ganlin, a retired senior engineer, spent 10,000 yuan ($1,400) developing a portable standing urinal for all genders, and offered free disposable funnels to female users. She said the idea grew out of her own experience with a spinal condition that made squatting increasingly difficult as she aged.

Her toilet was tested in busy public areas of neighboring cities Xi’an and Xianyang, in the northwestern Shaanxi province, and reportedly drew around 200 users a day. However, women were in the minority, Ye said.

In 2010, Shaanxi Normal University, also in Xi’an, installed six standing urinals for women, an initiative championed by professor Qu Yajun to conserve water. Female students welcomed the idea but said it would take practice to get used to the fixtures.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Urinals installed in a women’s restroom at a bar in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

World.title: Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019251/Collage: Robots, Health and New Tech at China Expo
World.content:
SHANGHAI — The ninth China International Import Expo ran from Nov. 5 to 10, with 4,142 overseas exhibitors from 162 countries, regions and international organizations.

More than 480 exhibits made global, Asian or Chinese debuts. Qualcomm brought a 6G terminal prototype out of the lab. Medtronic’s China-developed Kanghui orthopedic surgical robot had its world premiere. And a rare type of durian tree fruit, the Malaysian white durian, made its global debut.

Robots at the expo could be found working hotel front desks, taking photos for visitors, and running booth demos on their own — visibly more advanced than in past years. In place of the mechanical arm designed to play ping-pong featured last year, at this year’s expo, a company debuted an entire humanoid robot playing the sport. At the forum held alongside the expo, Xiong Jijun, Vice Minister of Industry and Information Technology, said humanoid robots must be upgraded from performing simple actions to being “able to think and work.”

Sixth Tone photographers spent the week in the halls, capturing the new products, technologies and services on display.

(Header image: CIIE attendees play table tennis against a robotic opponent, Shanghai, Nov. 9, 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.title: From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019240/From 6G to Aerospace, New Tech Takes the Stage at CIIE
World.content:
The ninth China International Import Expo (CIIE) closed in Shanghai on Tuesday after showcasing cutting-edge technologies in artificial intelligence, commercial aerospace, and innovative drugs.

The six-day event drew exhibitors from a record 162 countries, regions, and international organizations. A total of 4,142 overseas companies took part — also a record high — with more than 480 representative products making their global, Asian, or China debut.

U.S. wireless chipmaker Qualcomm exhibited the world’s first 6G terminal prototype — the first time the device has been shown publicly outside the lab. The prototype has been used in joint tests with China Mobile, China’s largest telecom operator, and Chinese telecom equipment manufacturer ZTE. The prototype will provide the foundation for 6G chips and support the technology’s commercial rollout.

The event featured an expanded medical devices and health care exhibition area, acting as the stage for the China debut of pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca’s new hypertension medication baxdrostat. The oral medication works by inhibiting the enzyme aldosterone synthase, which helps synthesize the blood pressure-regulating hormone aldosterone, and was approved in the U.S. in May.

German optical giant Zeiss also made its global debut of its new non-spherical lens PT Lunana, designed for myopia correction. Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical company, showcased ianalumab, a drug used for treating the autoimmune illness Sjögren’s disease — also a China debut.

American electric vehicle company Tesla presented its Cybercab autonomous vehicle. Lacking a steering wheel or pedals, the vehicle relies on cameras and AI to drive. Hexagon — a global digital reality and metrology tech company — also displayed its industrial humanoid robot AEON.

Aerospace technology was also present, including the Zhuque-3 rocket developed by Chinese commercial aerospace company LandSpace. The rocket’s reusable booster, which uses liquid oxygen and methane as fuel, can land vertically, first achieved by the company in August.

Beyond showcasing new tech, the expo held its first exhibition area for 100 long-established, reputable international brands — from Canadian shoe companies to Spanish wineries — as well as hosted a trade and investment “matchmaking” conference, where companies and buyers met to sign cooperation agreements. The latter conference attracted more than 600 exhibitors and over 2,000 buyers from 59 countries and regions.

The deals reached at this year’s expo are projected to be worth a total of $85.45 billion over the coming year, up 2.3% from last year and a record high.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A view of the China International Import Expo in Shanghai, Nov. 6, 2026. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.

The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.

During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

World.title: ASEAN opens ‘progress-based’ path for Myanmar’s return, but keeps restrictions
World.content:
RETREAT. Leaders and representatives gather for the 49th ASEAN Summit retreat session at the Coconut Palace in Pasay City on November 15, 2026.

‘We want to see how Myanmar responds,’ says Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, as ASEAN weighs restoring Myanmar’s political representation based on its adherence to the bloc’s peace plan

MANILA, Philippines – Leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) have opened a path to a possible “step-by-step” return of Myanmar’s political representatives to high-level meetings, although this remains conditional on Myanmar demonstrating concrete progress in implementing the bloc’s peace plan.

In their review and decision on the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus (5PC), ASEAN leaders agreed to pursue “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar through a “phased and progress-based approach.”

“Subject to sustained and concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” said the document adopted on Sunday, November 15, the first day of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits in Manila.

In the same document, ASEAN leaders also reitered their “deep concern over the insufficient progress in the implementation of the 5PC.”

The regional bloc has previously left the door open for Myanmar’s political return. But the decision makes the possibility of a gradual restoration more explicit, even as leaders maintained existing restrictions.

In 2021, Myanmar’s military launched a coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and plunged the country into a bloody civil war. Since then, ASEAN has barred Myanmar’s political leaders from attending ASEAN summits and foreign ministers’ meetings, allowing only non-political representatives to participate.

The decision comes amid calls from some member countries, particularly Thailand, to re-engage Myanmar’s military-backed government following elections held under military rule. The elections remain contentious, however, with ASEAN leaders only saying they “noted the conclusion of the three phases of Myanmar’s general elections,” without explicitly endorsing its validity.

Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, who also serves as ASEAN’s special envoy on Myanmar, explained that the step-by-step approach would depend on whether Myanmar follows the peace plan.

“The step-by-step approach is adherence to the Five-Point Consensus. So, for example, the first one is cessation of hostilities,” Lazaro said in a press briefing on Sunday evening.

“We want to see how Myanmar responds to that because right now, there’s still certain bombings and displacement of Myanmar people. So step-by-step, we give it to them, how they’re going to tackle this issue, and we monitor that,” she added. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] ASEAN digital deal needs a Philippine dividend
World.content:
Easier commercial transactions are the real test through which ASEAN’s diplomatic achievement on DEFA must eventually enter the Philippine economy

ASEAN’s new digital trade pact promises smoother cross-border commerce, yet the real test for Manila lies in proving that local merchants, exporters, and consumers actually capture the financial gains. To turn diplomatic momentum into measurable economic dividends, the Philippine government must close the treaty scrutiny gap, track hard commercial benchmarks, and address foundational infrastructure bottlenecks before declaring victory.

The Philippines has helped deliver a regional digital agreement, but its harder assignment is proving that a Filipino merchant will pay less to collect an overseas sale, an exporter will clear documents faster, and a consumer cheated across borders will have somewhere effective to turn.

Those everyday commercial transactions are the real test through which ASEAN’s diplomatic achievement must eventually enter the Philippine economy.

Economic ministers signed the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, or DEFA, in Manila on Saturday, November 14, ahead of the leaders’ summit, a milestone confirmed by the ASEAN Secretariat.

Play Video

Signing gives participating governments a concrete diplomatic achievement to claim, yet businesses still need clarity on when specific obligations become effective, what domestic rules must change, and how compliance will be enforced across borders.

Singapore’s official factsheet describes DEFA as a legally binding agreement covering digital trade, cross-border payments, data protection, competition, and cybersecurity. According to the factsheet, the agreement enters into force 180 days after signing, with the full legal text scheduled for publication on ASEAN’s website in early 2027. That publication timetable leaves an immediate scrutiny gap.

Screenshot from Singapore Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry

Before endorsing sweeping claims about investor protection or regulatory constraints, businesses, legal analysts, and lawmakers need to examine the actual provisions, national exceptions, and dispute settlement mechanisms.

Still, the underlying economic case deserves a fair hearing. Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong acknowledged during the rollout that ASEAN member-states negotiated from vastly different levels of digital readiness, identifying interoperable payments, digital identities, and electronic trade documents among priority implementation projects. Making national systems work together could spare a small exporter the recurring expense of repeatedly proving its identity, reproducing physical paperwork, or arranging separate payment channels for each regional market.

Cutting red tape

Consider a Philippine manufacturer selling specialty food products to a regional distributor. Electronic customs and trade documentation could cut administrative overhead, while faster cross-border settlement could shorten the lag between shipping an order and receiving cash.

That efficiency would improve working capital without forcing the business to take on additional debt. This scenario illustrates the agreement’s potential benefit, however, rather than proving that DEFA has already delivered those savings.

To avoid confusion between diplomatic promise and commercial reality, the Philippine government should establish a clear baseline before claiming an economic dividend. Agencies should measure the total cost of receiving a cross-border payment—including foreign-exchange spreads and intermediary fees—alongside document rejection rates, average settlement times, and the number of smaller firms completing repeat export orders.

Publishing these benchmarks regularly will matter. A digital trade pact earns economic credibility only when businesses can identify which expense disappeared and how much cash they retained. Industry groups should help select those indicators so the scorecard reflects genuine commercial experience; otherwise, agencies risk counting websites launched, meetings held, and memoranda signed while leaving the cost of trading across borders unchanged for smaller firms.

Investors should likewise ask who ultimately captures the efficiency gains. A payment provider or digital platform could gain customers and transaction volume while merchants see little reduction in fees.

Alternatively, seamless connections between providers could intensify competition and force transaction charges down. Neither outcome follows automatically from the signing ceremony. Valuing banks, fintech firms, or logistics operators on the assumption of an immediate regional windfall would run well ahead of demonstrated implementation and commercial results.

Consumer protection

Consumer protection belongs squarely inside that calculation. If a cross-border transaction fails or turns fraudulent, the customer needs to know which institution must investigate, what digital evidence can be obtained, and who carries the financial loss. Policymakers should explain how Philippine regulators will cooperate with foreign counterparts, preserve access to transaction records, and resolve cross-border complaints.

Raising these questions is part of sound implementation and treaty scrutiny, not an argument that the agreement has weakened existing domestic safeguards.

At the same time, there is a legitimate objection to excessive regulatory caution: fragmented national requirements often insulate established incumbents and make regional expansion prohibitively expensive for smaller competitors. Preserving every local procedure intact would defeat the purpose of integration.

The practical answer is to distinguish essential consumer and security safeguards from duplicative compliance, then demonstrate that the resulting framework preserves clear accountability. Easier transactions and effective supervision must be designed together, with institutional responsibilities settled before customers encounter a problem.

Financing is beginning to accompany the policy commitments. On Saturday, the Asian Development Bank announced that its regional platform for artificial intelligence and the digital economy aims to mobilize up to US$5 billion in public and private financing by 2030 to support DEFA implementation across infrastructure, payments, digital identification, cybersecurity, and related reforms. Importantly, this represents a multi-year financing target across the entire region, not US$5 billion already disbursed or earmarked for the Philippines.

Play Video

For Manila, the next useful disclosure is a concrete project pipeline identifying Philippine beneficiaries, financing terms, lead implementing agencies, and target completion dates. A broad regional envelope tells investors little about which domestic bottlenecks will actually be removed.

Project preparation also matters: an attractive headline figure cannot substitute for disciplined procurement, technical capacity, and clear accountability when delivery slips. Any public borrowing tied to digital infrastructure must be judged against measurable productivity gains and ongoing operating costs.

The Philippines must also resist treating regional digital rules as a substitute for domestic competitiveness. An exporter still relies on dependable broadband connectivity, reliable electricity, and efficient physical logistics, alongside workers trained to operate digital systems.

If those foundational constraints remain unresolved, regional integration could make it easier for better-prepared foreign competitors to serve Philippine consumers than for Philippine firms to expand abroad—a risk that must be tested against actual investment and export data.

Ultimately, DEFA gives the Philippine ASEAN chairship a substantive policy result, and dismissing it as mere ceremony would ignore the real value of lowering regional barriers. The administration should now publish its agency implementation responsibilities, explain the treaty’s legal safeguards once the text is released, and commit to tracking hard business outcomes.

The strongest claim Manila could eventually make is straightforward: Philippine firms kept more of every sale, reached more regional customers, and recovered their money when something went wrong. Until that evidence arrives, the signing remains a promising achievement awaiting its economic accounting. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] A fellowship for the planet
World.content:
'I am going to Batangas to stay at a marine station with scientists working to bring citizen science closer to the public'

Hello! I cover environmental issues for Rappler, and this year my focus for the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) lies on the ocean.

With Australia as co-president of the summit, Pacific priorities are high on the agenda. The summit is billed as the “Blue COP,” with an Antalya ocean declaration in the works.

The ocean is the world’s largest carbon sink. Being front and center of the climate negotiations has been a long time coming.

I am joining seven other journalists from around the world to cover COP31 remotely through the ocean lens. Among the big questions we hope to shed light on: How will countries integrate ocean solutions in the complex architecture of the global climate regime? This question brings with it a host of other issues such as funding sources.

On a personal level, the fellowship’s focus on oceans provides relief, giving me a single angle to latch on. Climate negotiations have their own language. Coverage of COPs requires dealing with a broad array of issues, such as poverty, displacement, hunger, waste, capitalism, wars, and even genocide. It requires a perspective that thinks in the big picture.

An example is the sobering reminder from Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during the leaders’ summit: “Today, one cannot speak of the future of the planet without speaking of the wars that target soil, water, air, natural resources, and human lives.”

The summit, despite its own language, does not happen in a silo. In the backdrop of COP31 is the global fuel crisis and the war in Iran, the ecocide in Gaza, the El Niño that threatens fishers and farmers — and, in our own backyard, the hectic preparations for the ASEAN Summit.

In every coverage we have always thought of ways to bring the COP to our readers. To deal with the local stories. This year, we are giving regular updates through our Muni chat app, making space for environmental advocates in our social and newsletter spaces. We mean to make conversations because this is where understanding starts (a fellowship of sorts).

We are also recording (probably as you read this) another The Green Report podcast episode to wrap the developments of the week. Something to listen to on your commute home.

In early November, as part of my fellowship, I visited a group of volunteer divers in Batangas who monitor coral bleaching in a marine reserve.

Next week, I am going back to Batangas, in a different town, to stay at a marine station with scientists working to bring citizen science closer to the public. Their dream? That the ordinary fisherman learns to watch the waters, the changes in colors of the coral reef.

The COP is much about these communities on the ground as it is about the negotiators who deal in high-level, closed door meetings. We aim to report the stories from this broad spectrum to light. For starters, you can join our Muni chat here, or follow the COP stories from this page. – Rappler.com

World.title: Police arrest anti-Pax Silica protesters as ASEAN Summit opens in Manila
World.content:
PAX SILICA PROTEST. Militants gather at Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila on November 15, 2026, to protest the proposed Pax Silica initiative and US President Donald Trump’s visit to the 49th ASEAN Summit.

At least 11 protesters were arrested by police within the freedom park, according to Manila Police District Spokesperson Philip Ines

MANILA, Philippines – Police clashed with protesters at Liwasang Bonifacio on Sunday morning, November 15, as activists opposing Pax Silica and US President Donald Trump tried to march toward the ASEAN Summit venue.

The protesters were trying to reach the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC), the venue of the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Police blocked the protesters from proceeding to the summit venue. Some of the protesters managed to slip through several layers of policemen armed with shields. The cops, however, managed to block the protesters again.

ASEAN PROTEST. Protesters scuffle with police officers in Manila on November 15, 2026, during a protest against US President Donald Trump’s upcoming visit and participation in the 49th ASEAN Summit.

Kilusang Mayo Uno (KMU) President Jerome Adonis said police told them they could not hold a street protest because they did not have a permit.

After nearly an hour of attempts to march to PICC, the protesters retreated to Liwasang Bonifacio. Despite this, at least 11 protesters were arrested by police within freedom park, according to Manila Police District Spokesperson Philip Ines.

Ines said at least 16 personnel from the Manila Police District were injured.

Cops dragged protesters into a police vehicle. Some officers were seen slapping, kicking, and punching one activist as they took him away.

Adonis questioned the legality of the arrests, saying they were made inside a freedom park.

ASEAN PROTEST. Police arrest a protester in Liwasang Bonifacio on the opening of the ASEAN Summit in Manila, on Sunday, November 15. Photo by Patrick Cruz/Rappler

“Ang gulo ho nanggaling sa pulis. Hindi po galing sa amin. Nagdedepensa lang kami ng hanay namin,” he added. (The trouble started with the police, not us. We were only defending our ranks.)

Rappler asked the Manila Police District why the protesters were arrested, but it had yet to respond as of writing.

Under the Revised Penal Code, a person arrested without a warrant should be brought to court within a maximum of 36 hours, and that is for grave violations.

Police also towed the truck that protesters had used as a makeshift stage. Adonis accused police of puncturing their vehicles with nails.

In Liwasang Bonifacio, where the protesters plan to camp out, human manure was scattered in front of the statue of Andres Bonifacio, the “father of the Philippine revolution.”

ASEAN PROTEST. Personnel from the Manila Department of Environment and Public Service clean the human manure scattered in front of the statue of Andres Bonifacio, in Liwasang Bonifacio in Manila, on Sunday, November 15. Photo by Patrick Cruz/Rappler

Bayan Muna Chairperson Teddy Casiño, who was also at the protest, claimed that the police were behind this.

“Isang malaking ka-hipokrituhan ang ginagawa ng gobyerno. Nagpapakita ng hospitality sa mga dayuhan pero binabastos ang kanyang mga mamamayan,” Casiño said. (The government’s actions are widely hypocritical. It shows hospitality to foreign visitors while disrespecting its own people.)

Personnel from the Manila Department of Environment and Public Service later cleaned the human manure.

Concerns over Pax Silica

Protesters have raised concerns that Pax Silica could displace Indigenous peoples and farming communities in the planned 4,000-acre industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac.

Pax Silica is a US-led initiative that seeks to strengthen supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors through partnerships with other countries. The signing of the Pax Silica agreement had reportedly been targeted for November, coinciding with Trump’s visit to the Philippines for the ASEAN Summit.

Trump is expected to arrive in Manila on Tuesday, November 17, for the Special ASEAN-US Summit.

However, Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo clarified that the Philippines would not sign the agreement during the 49th ASEAN Summit.

“We do not want to distract attention or take away attention from the regional initiatives that ASEAN and the Philippines are proposing,” Rodolfo told reporters on Tuesday, November 10.

Despite the delay, the Philippines eyes to sign the deal with the US before the year ends, Rodolfo said.

Amid the protests, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro appealed to the public to reconsider holding demonstrations during the summit.

“Whatever their demands may be, I hope these are not pursued through protests, although I recognize that this is their right. In these times, however, it would be better to have more in-depth discussions about whatever concerns the students may have,” Castro said during a press briefing on Saturday, November 14.

Prior to the Sunday protest, thousands of students also protested against Pax Silica. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why Gabby Lopez wants Rockwell as ABS-CBN struggles
World.content:
Part 1 | The Lopez heirs who ran Rockwell but never controlled it

When Eugenio “Gabby” Lopez III sold his family’s shares in the main Lopez holding company in August, he said the move would allow his family to “channel our family’s resources into businesses aligned with our personal mission,” adding that more announcements would come in due time.

Three months later, his new game plan is clear. It centers on two companies that serve everyday Filipinos: ABS-CBN and Rockwell Land.

On Thursday, November 12, First Philippine Holdings Corporation (FPH), led by Gabby’s cousin, Federico “Piki” Lopez, agreed to sell its 90.74% voting stake in Rockwell Land. The buyer is Gabby’s and his siblings’ private firm, Crème Investment Corporation, and the price tag is P15.92 billion.

This completes a 94-day asset swap that began on August 10. Back then, Crème sold its 25.68% share in Lopez Inc. to San Miguel boss Ramon S. Ang for about P11 billion. Lopez Inc. was originally built as the untouchable top holding company meant to protect the family empire from outside takeovers. (READ: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN)

THEN…The Rockwell property with the old Meralco power plant (upper right) in Makati City. Rappler/Rockwell brand rap file image

For decades, Rockwell Land has been the Lopez Group’s luxury lifestyle and consumer jewel. Started in 1995 on the site of an old Meralco power plant in Makati, Rockwell turned an industrial lot into Rockwell Center, which is now home to Power Plant Mall, high-end condos, serviced apartments, and offices.

…AND NOW. Bird’s eye view of Rockwell Makati with Power Plant Mall at the center. Courtesy of Rockwell Land

This focus on everyday consumers is a natural fit for Gabby who spent his career in TV, entertainment, and public-facing brands. Just two days after the August sale, Gabby and his cousins pledged P2.2 billion of their own money to help rebuild ABS-CBN. He explained why: “ABS-CBN has been part of this family for generations. The mission our family set out to pursue remains the heartbeat of this family—to be in the service of the Filipino. We are putting our own money behind this conviction.” (READ: Gabby Lopez: Man on a mission)

This is a sharp contrast from Piki Lopez’s world at FPH and First Gen, an ascetic, heavy-infrastructure universe of geothermal steam fields, gas turbines, and pumped-storage hydropower projects that require tens of billions of pesos and years, sometimes decades, of engineering before they make money. At the 2026 annual stockholders’ meetings of FPH and First Gen, Piki repeatedly framed his leadership around the “compounding” value of long-term choices, and that “direction over speed” matters more. In other words, a slow-and-steady approach built for power grids rather than quick profits.

Gabby does not seem to be retreating from the family business. Instead, he is separating the group’s lifestyle and media brands from FPH’s power business and bringing them under his own control.

BOSS. Ambassador Manuel “Manolo” Lopez speaks at a corporate event following Rockwell Land Corp.’s listing on May 12, 2012, in Rockwell Power Plant Mall’s premises in Makati City. Courtesy of Rockwell Land FB

Rockwell also has deep ties to Gabby’s late uncle, Manuel “Manolo” Lopez. Manolo ran Meralco for over 30 years and was deeply disappointed when the family and business group, both led then by his older brother Oscar, the father of Piki, forced FPH to let go of Meralco in 2009 to pay off First Gen’s geothermal debts. Manolo was quoted then saying, “Meralco would have been my parents’ legacy.” In March and April 2026, Manolo’s children joined Gabby and other cousins in publicly challenging Piki’s leadership. Buying Rockwell brings a business closely linked to Manolo’s side of the family under Crème’s direct control.

Beyond family history and culture, this deal solves a major money problem for Gabby’s branch: ABS-CBN needs cash, and Rockwell makes it.

In 2025, Rockwell earned P4.73 billion. ABS-CBN lost P4.72 billion. Crème has already pledged P766.7 million to ABS-CBN’s P6-billion fundraising drive. Buying Rockwell gives Gabby’s family an established, profitable company that brings in its own money. (READ: Why ABS-CBN is still retrenching 200 employees with P6 billion on the way)

CASH COW. Rockwell Land’s 2025 earnings. Courtesy of Rockwell Land website

Where the dividends went

Before losing its broadcast franchise in 2020, ABS-CBN was a reliable cash machine for its parent firm, Lopez Holdings, former Benpres Holdings and one level below Lopez Inc in the Lopez group shareholder tree. ABS-CBN paid Lopez Holdings P447 million in dividends in 2018 and P269 million in 2019. Once the network went off the air, those payouts vanished. From 2020 to 2025, ABS-CBN racked up about P45.5 billion in losses. (READ: ABS-CBN is now 84% content — and still losing money. Can P6 billion fix it?)

With ABS-CBN out of cash, Lopez Holdings had to lean almost completely on FPH, which owns the group’s power and property businesses. From 2021 to 2025, FPH paid Lopez Holdings a flat P567 million a year in dividends. After Lopez Holdings paid its bills and shared profits with public stockholders, only about P247 million actually reached Lopez, Inc. in 2025.

FPH’s own financial records show where that money came from. In 2025, subsidiary Rockwell paid FPH roughly P630 million in dividends. Meralco—where FPH still owns a 3.95% stake—paid another P1.115 billion. Together, those two companies gave FPH P1.75 billion in cash dividends. That is more than triple the P567 million FPH sent up to Lopez Holdings.

FPH didn’t just hoard the extra cash. As a public company, it had debts, operating costs, outside shareholders, and massive power projects to pay for. First Gen and its subsidiary, Energy Development Corporation, were pouring money into geothermal drilling, hydropower, and battery storage while paying off loans. First Gen President and COO Giles Puno noted at this year’s annual meeting that while the company aims to pay out 30% of its yearly recurring profit, those payouts depend on spending needs, growth plans, and debt payments. To save cash, First Gen cut how much it paid as yearly dividend to its parent FPH from P0.90 per share in 2024 to P0.80 in 2025.

So most of the Piki-led power group’s profits stayed locked inside the operating companies. For family members at the very top of the corporate ladder, including Gabby and the heirs of Manolo, that meant waiting years for bigger payouts. Buying Rockwell lets Crème skip all those corporate middlemen. Instead of waiting for cash to trickle up through FPH, Lopez Holdings, and Lopez, Inc., Gabby’s firm can soon collect dividends straight from the source as Rockwell’s main owner.

What Rockwell brings Gabby

Rockwell’s net profit for parent shareholders climbed from P3.11 billion in 2023 to P3.71 billion in 2024, reaching P4.73 billion in 2025. The 2025 number got a boost from a one-time gain after buying Alabang Commercial Corporation. Even without that extra boost, Rockwell still earned about P4.1 billion.

Its cash flow has grown right along with its profits. Rockwell brought in P2 billion in cash from daily operations in 2025, up sharply from P144 million in 2024, even though real estate requires heavy upfront spending on land and construction. Its regular dividends grew steadily too, rising from P0.0752 per share in 2023 to P0.1018 in 2024, and hitting P0.1212 in 2025. Renting out commercial spaces gives Rockwell a steady safety net beyond just selling condos. Power Plant Mall in Makati, its office buildings, and its December 2025 purchase of Alabang Commercial Corporation—which added Alabang Town Center and a nearby office tower—bring in reliable rental cash.

Of course, Rockwell has big bills of its own. Its P21.6-billion Alabang deal is being paid in installments through December 2027, and it raised P10 billion in retail bonds in March 2026 to fund active projects. It can’t pay dividend to its owners every single peso it makes. Still, it gives Gabby a healthy business that makes money rather than drains it.

Rockwell’s ties to ABS-CBN

Rockwell and ABS-CBN share more than just the Lopez family name. Over the last four years, Rockwell has been one of the main buyers of the real estate ABS-CBN sold to raise cash.

In 2022, Rockwell bought properties from ABS-CBN for P786 million, followed by another P733 million deal in 2023. Those sales gave the network profit gains of P246 million and P232 million. In 2024, Rockwell bought more ABS-CBN land for about P679 million—booking a P223.1-million gain for the broadcaster—and agreed to buy ABS-CBN’s Iloilo property for P91.4 million. Later company filings showed even more property deals between the two firms.

Their shared history goes back even further. Before Rockwell went public in 2012, its housing arm built the 53 Benitez condos in Quezon City on the site of an old movie studio. Lopez Holdings, then known as Benpres Holdings, also owned 24.5% of Rockwell directly before selling it to FPH in August 2009.

Smaller day-to-day ties are still in place. ABS-CBN Holdings Corporation, which handles the network’s depository receipts, keeps its main office at Rockwell Business Center Sheridan in Mandaluyong. Lopez Holdings also pays office rent to Rockwell.

No merger or money-sharing plan between Rockwell and ABS-CBN has been announced, and they remain completely separate companies. Still, Rockwell has repeatedly stepped in to buy the properties ABS-CBN needed to sell, and now Gabby is taking over Rockwell itself.

From minority shareholder to controlling owner

Until August, Crème’s 25.68% share in Lopez Inc. gave Gabby’s family a small, indirect piece of several businesses, but very little control over dividend payouts.

Under the P15.92-billion deal approved by FPH on November 12, Crème will buy 86.58% of Rockwell’s common shares, plus voting preferred shares that raise its total voting power to 90.74%. Once regulators approve the deal and Crème makes a required buyout offer to the remaining public stockholders, it becomes the controlling owner. That gives Crème a direct say over Rockwell’s board and dividend payouts, within the limits of corporate law, loan rules, and minority shareholder rights.

If Rockwell keeps paying its 2025 dividend rate of P0.1212 per share, Crème’s incoming block of 5.30 billion common shares would bring in about P642 million a year before taxes. Future payouts aren’t guaranteed—they will depend on Rockwell’s profits, spending needs, and board votes.

Three months after leaving Lopez, Inc., Gabby Lopez’s new game plan is clear. He has fresh cash for ABS-CBN, the network he spent his life building, and direct control of Rockwell Land, a profitable lifestyle developer that already makes money. – Rappler.com

Lala Rimando wrote about Philippine business, and managed newsrooms, including Newsbreak, ABS-CBN, Rappler, and Forbes, for over 25 years. She’s now based in La Union, taking care of her mom with dementia, and working on the multimedia biography of the late John Gokongwei.

World.title: Maria Ressa speaks at 2026 ASEAN Business and Investment Summit
World.content:
Artificial intelligence can reproduce ‘the worst of who we are,’ says Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa

MANILA, Philippines – Rappler CEO and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa warned that artificial intelligence deployment by the private sector has outpaced regulation and control by the government.

Ressa delivered a keynote speech and joined a fireside chat on “Trust in the Age of AI,” at the ASEAN Business and Investment Summit in Parañaque City on Sunday, November 15.

She noted that because AI models scrape training material from the internet, it can reproduce “the worst of who we are.”

“It can work for you the same way social media works for content creators, but it is a Faustian bargain if you do not look at the design,” Ressa said during the fireside chat, hosted by veteran journalist Karen Davila.

The two-day business summit, happening on the sidelines of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits, ends on Sunday. – Rappler.com

World.title: DENR urges protection of rare Atimonan Spikemoss in Quezon
World.content:
.

LUCENA CITY — The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) has urged the public to help protect the Atimonan Spikemoss (Selaginella atimonanensis), a rare plant species found exclusively in the Quezon Protected Landscape (QPL) in Quezon province.

Spikemoss grows on steep limestone cliffs deep within the QPL.

“Every plant in our protected areas plays a role in keeping our ecosystems resilient,” the DENR in Calabarzon said.

Article continues after this 

“This particular species is endemic to Calabarzon — meaning it exists naturally right here in our region and nowhere else on Earth,” it added.

READ: Rare, endemic plant rediscovered in Masungi after 130 years

Although it resembles ordinary moss, “spikemosses are actually ancient vascular plants related to ferns that have survived for hundreds of millions of years,” according to the agency.

The DENR credited botanists Benito Tan and Clive Jermy with discovering the species. The botanical journal Fern Gazette published their findings on Nov. 10, 1981.

The plant is classified as a specialized lithophyte, meaning it grows on or within rock surfaces.

Article continues after this 

“It inhabits forest ecosystems over limestone substrates, typically at elevations of 250-430 meters above sea level. Its presence serves as a bioindicator of stable microclimatic conditions, high humidity, and the ecological health of karst ecosystems,” the DENR explained.

The QPL covers 983 hectares and was established as a forest reservation through Proclamation No. 740 in 1934 and Proclamation No. 594 in 1940. It was later incorporated into the National Integrated Protected Areas System (NIPAS) under Republic Act No. 7586, or the NIPAS Act of 1992.

Article continues after this 

The protected landscape extends across portions of Atimonan, Pagbilao, and Padre Burgos, including sections of the well-known zigzag road in Quezon province. /mcm

World.title: Puerto Princesa bishop raises alarm over mining in Palawan
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The Apostolic Vicar of Puerto Princesa has warned of continuing mining activities in southern Palawan, saying forests and mountains are showing signs of environmental degradation despite a provincial moratorium on endorsements for new mining applications.

In a pastoral letter dated Nov. 15, Bishop Socrates Mesiona called on government authorities, local communities, and residents to demand transparency and accountability from mining companies and government agencies.

Mesiona said the provincial government passed an ordinance more than a year ago imposing a moratorium on endorsements for new mining applications, describing it as a significant step toward protecting Palawan’s natural resources.

Article continues after this 

However, he questioned what had happened since its passage, noting that mining remained a pressing concern in southern Palawan, where mountains were being altered and trees continued to be cut.

READ: Palawan town vice mayor bares alleged violations of mining firm

“The forests that should be protected are gradually losing their natural cover,” the bishop said, warning that environmental changes were already visible even without comprehensive scientific studies.

He also expressed concern that mineral resources might be extracted and sold without sufficient public disclosure of the full composition of mineral deposits, including potentially more valuable minerals that might not have been thoroughly assessed.

The bishop called for clear answers on how much mining contributed to the national and provincial economies and, more importantly, who benefited from the extraction of Palawan’s mineral resources.

Article continues after this 

He acknowledged the efforts of local governments, civil society organizations, religious groups, Indigenous communities and other residents who had opposed the opening or operation of additional mining areas in the province.

Mesiona also questioned whether existing laws and government policies adequately protected local communities and the environment, saying these appeared to favor powerful interests over ordinary citizens.

Article continues after this 

“When people speak together with courage and perseverance, their voices become more powerful and can no longer be easily ignored,” he said, urging authorities to listen to the concerns of communities.

World.title: Pangasinan cops seek identity of man who died after Bued Bridge jump
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALASIAO, Pangasinan — An unidentified man died after jumping from the Bued Bridge in Sison town and falling about 100 meters onto the rocky riverbed on Friday afternoon, Nov. 13.

Mercedes Esmeralda, 49, a resident of Barangay Dungon in Sison, told investigators that she saw the man climb onto the bridge’s concrete railing along the southbound lane and balance himself before suddenly jumping.

The bridge connects Pangasinan and La Union provinces.

Article continues after this 

READ: Man reported to have jumped from San Juanico Bridge found dead

Responding police officers and firefighters rushed the victim to the Pozorrubio Community Hospital, where attending physician Dr. Jeff Jordan Regacho declared him dead on arrival.

The victim sustained severe injuries to his head and other parts of his body from the fall.

Police said the man remained unidentified as of the latest report. He was wearing blue shorts and a blue T-shirt bearing the word “PARIS.”

The Sison police are continuing their investigation to establish the man’s identity and determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. /mcm

World.title: No LPA, cyclone expected to form in PH in 3 days
World.content:
GRAPHICS BY INQUIRER

MANILA, Philippines — No low-pressure area (LPA) or tropical cyclone was expected to form inside or outside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) in the next three days, the state weather bureau said on Monday.

According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa), the shear line and easterlies are the weather systems currently affecting the country.

“Based on our data and analysis, no LPA or tropical cyclone will form in the next three days,” Pagasa weather specialist Aldczar Aurelio said in a morning forecast.

Article continues after this 

READ: ‘Very strong’ El Niño now active in tropical Pacific, says Pagasa

Aurelio noted that the shear line, where cool and warm winds converge, is forecast to bring cloudy skies with scattered rains and isolated thunderstorms over Batanes on Monday.

Meanwhile, the easterlies—or warm winds coming from the Pacific Ocean—will bring cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms over the Caraga and Davao regions.

READ: Puerto Princesa heat index to hit 45°C Monday

Metro Manila and the rest of the country are expected to experience fair weather, except for possible isolated rain showers or thunderstorms caused by localized thunderstorms.

No gale warning is currently in effect in any of the country’s seaboards. /mcm

World.title: El Niño threat forces Mansalay to cancel Mangyan Festival
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Mansalay has canceled most secular and civic activities for its Mangyan Festival and 98th Foundation Day celebrations due to the threat posed by Super El Niño.

In Memorandum Order No. 227, series of 2026, the local government said activities scheduled for Nov. 22, 23 and 25 for the Mangyan Festival, as well as those set for Dec. 8 to 11 for the town’s Foundation Day, would no longer push through.

READ: El Niño impact on PH growth may be minimal–Balisacan

Article continues after this 

The cancellation also covers the Bancathon, a local boat race originally included in the celebrations.

Instead, the municipality will focus on Catholic activities commemorating the feast of Mansalay’s patron saint, St. Catherine of Alexandria, on Nov. 24 and 25.

The local government said funds originally allocated for the Mangyan Festival and Foundation Day celebrations would be redirected to preparedness and response measures against the anticipated impacts of Super El Niño. /mcm

World.title: Occidental Mindoro declares Nov. 16 holiday for 76th anniversary
World.content:
.

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has declared Monday, Nov. 16, a special non-working day in Occidental Mindoro to allow residents to celebrate the province’s 76th founding anniversary.

Proclamation No. 1512, signed by Acting Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, was issued following a request from Gov. Eduardo Gadiano.

The provincial government will mark the anniversary at the Provincial Capitol Complex in Mamburao under the theme “Nagkakaisang Bayan Tungo sa Maunlad na Lalawigan” (United Communities Toward a Progressive Province).

Article continues after this 

Nov. 15 is the province’s actual founding anniversary, but it falls on a Sunday this year, prompting the government to move the celebration to Monday.

READ: PH town among 14 new Unesco biosphere reserves worldwide

The anniversary activities will begin with a motorcade at 6 a.m., followed by a thanksgiving Mass at 7 a.m.

The formal program at 8 a.m. will include the entrance of colors, an ecumenical prayer, the national anthem, and a drum and lyre exhibition by Occidental Mindoro National High School and Mamburao Central School.

The provincial government will also formally mark the 76th founding anniversary and hold a ceremonial dove release.

Article continues after this 

A highlight of the celebration will be the ceremonial signing of the province’s Children’s Protection and Welfare Code, aimed at strengthening the protection and welfare of children.

The provincial government will also hold the “Ganadong Serbisyo Caravan,” offering various public services, including a job fair, National Bureau of Investigation services, Philippine Statistics Authority assistance, anti-rabies vaccination, vegetable seed distribution, and livelihood assistance.

Article continues after this 

Other services include distributing vitamins to children and senior citizens, assisting farmers’ cooperatives and associations with agricultural machinery applications, providing dental services, and offering social welfare assistance.

The provincial government will also distribute checks to local government units recognized under the Seal of Good Local Governance and award the winners of a tourism video-making contest.

World.title: Hold your breath: Mucolytic may treat solvent addiction
World.content:
INQUIRER.net stock images

MANILA, Philippines — An over-the-counter drug commonly used to loosen mucus may help reverse brain changes and drug-seeking behavior caused by solvent addiction, according to a study by researchers from the University of the Philippines National Institutes of Health (UP-NIH).

A research team led by neuroscientist Dr. Rohani Cena-Navarro found that N-acetylcysteine (NAC), a drug typically prescribed as a mucolytic, eliminated drug-seeking behavior and reversed solvent-induced brain changes in rats exposed to toluene.

Toluene, the addictive chemical found in many solvents, is a clear, colorless liquid commonly used in industrial products such as paints, paint thinners, adhesives, gasoline and nail polish.

Article continues after this 

Solvent ranked as the fifth most commonly abused substance in the Philippines in 2024, according to data from the Dangerous Drugs Board.

READ: WATCH: ‘Solvent kids’ steal cash from jeepney driver in Manila

Last year, Cena-Navarro’s team developed a rat model of inhalant addiction, demonstrating that repeated solvent exposure could trigger persistent drug-seeking behavior.

“We are excited to find that NAC was able to reverse the harmful effects of solvents in the brain, confirming that addiction is a treatable brain disorder,” Cena-Navarro said on Friday.

The findings were published in the international scientific journal Neuropharmacology in October this year.

Article continues after this 

READ: Gangs threaten stores to supply them solvents

The researchers said the study was the first in the world to examine the long-term effects of solvent exposure on brain activity and the first rodent neuroscience paper of its kind from the Philippines.

Article continues after this 

The findings underscore how solvent exposure can have lasting neurological consequences, with behavioral changes potentially persisting even after the substance has left the body.

The researchers said NAC is believed to help regulate glutamate, a chemical messenger involved in learning and memory that may also play a role in addiction-related behavior.

However, the researchers clarified that they did not directly measure glutamate levels in their experiment.

The team also said the experiment did not establish whether the improvements would last after the NAC treatment was discontinued or whether the affected brain circuits could fully return to their original state.

Cena-Navarro said longer-term treatment may be necessary and could potentially be combined with other therapies, similar to maintenance medications used for chronic conditions such as heart disease and diabetes.

The research team stressed that further studies and clinical evidence are needed before NAC can be considered an established treatment for solvent addiction in humans.

World.title: Chinese fish cage operators move cages from Pangasinan shoal
World.content:
RESTRICTED ZONE Fish cages are seen at Calpay Shoal in Sual, Pangasinan, a traditional fishing ground for local fishers where Chinese operators set up cages outside the designated mariculture zone as seen in this photo taken on Oct. 26 —Contributed photo

SUAL, PANGASINAN, Philippines — Chinese fish cage operators in this coastal town began moving their cages out of Calpay Shoal, a traditional fishing ground for local small-scale fishers, on Nov. 11, following an Inquirer report on their presence in the area.

“After the media exposé, the operators were alarmed and immediately started pulling their cages from the site, although they were given by the local government officials up to Nov. 30 to remove their cages and put them back to the mariculture zone,” said Nicasio Abata, leader of the Small Fisherfolk and Stakeholders of Cabalitian, an island barangay in the town.

But complaining fishermen who inspected the area said several fishing cages were just transferred to areas still inside the Calpay Shoal “so they are still occupying spaces that are restricted from mariculture activities.”

Article continues after this 

“It’s a continuous violation by the Chinese operators of the fishery laws. This is not acceptable at all. But even if they will bring back their cages to the mariculture zone, they are still answerable to the Philippine laws for violations of the fishery laws and we hope this issue will be investigated by the authorities,” Abata told the Inquirer in a text message.

READ: Chinese-run fish cages blamed for displaced Pangasinan fisherfolk

Records from the local government unit showed that there are 1,207 fish cages granted fishery privilege permits as of 2024, but one company reportedly stopped operating its 50 cages in December 2023.

Stoppage order

Of the total, 257 are owned allegedly by Chinese companies, two of which moved around 150 cages to Calpay Shoal starting last May, allegedly because of undesirable water conditions inside the mariculture zone that causes fish fatalities.

Last May, 99 cages were first transferred to Calpay Bay, followed by another 33 cages. The municipal government issued a cease-and-desist order last Sept. 21, but instead of removing the cages, the Chinese operators relocated seven more cages on Sept. 29 and 11 on Nov. 5, Abata said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Solar power to operate aeration systems for bangus in Pangasinan

“We could not understand how these Chinese could blatantly disregard local officials’ orders. They do not appear during hearings of the Sangguniang Bayan and merely send a secretary to the hearings,” Abata said.

Article continues after this 

The mariculture zone that occupies Baquioen Bay along barangays Cabalitian, Pangascasan and Baquioen was meant to host only 750 cages.

A local fish cage operator said Chinese operators have also “invaded” coastal areas in different provinces like Quezon where they put up fish cages.

“The bangus (milkfish) industry is suffering from the high cost of inputs like feeds, and low prices for the fish. But the Chinese operators seemingly are not affected by these issues. There are only such number of cages with fishery privilege permits, but there much more cages than the official list,” the operator said.

He added that residents in the town know about the presence of the Chinese but feel they cannot do anything about it, thinking “someone powerful up there is coddling them.”

“Ask a boatman and he would say, ‘There are many of them (Chinese),’” the local operator said.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: ASEAN Should Accept Myanmar Back at Diplomat Level: Bangkok
World.content:
BANGKOK—Myanmar’s foreign minister should be allowed back into meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional bloc, Thailand’s top diplomat said on Thursday after a visit to the war-torn country.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said his meetings with regime leader Min Aung Hlaing and others had revealed “a desire on the part of Myanmar to engage, to return to ASEAN.” But he said there was no talk of specific steps.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level meetings of the 11-nation ASEAN since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize ties since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president earlier this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

“For Thailand, we believe that the next step is to have the foreign minister of Myanmar participate in the ASEAN meetings at the level of foreign minister,” Sihasak told reporters.

His comments came ahead of a meeting of ASEAN leaders starting Sunday in the Philippines.

Sihasak said he had also raised the “very urgent problem” of water pollution among tributaries of the Mekong River, which straddles five Southeast Asian countries and China, saying a working group would meet later this month.

Last week, authorities in northern Thailand suspended tap water production after arsenic levels at the waterworks intake was found to be 30 times higher than the safety standard. More than a dozen villages were affected by the suspension.

A subsequent field sample from the nearby Sai River measured arsenic at 25 times the safety standard, the government said.

Thai officials previously pinned the toxic sediment on wastewater from mining activity upstream in Myanmar.

Sihasak said he also raised the issue of a spillover of violence into Thailand.

World.title: Myanmar Faces Year of Blackouts as Regime Admits 30% Power Shortfall
World.content:
Myanmar’s rotating power cuts will remain in place through 2027, with generation expected to meet only 70 percent of national demand, Deputy Energy Minister Aye Kyaw announced Wednesday.

Addressing the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament, he said next summer’s 24-hour electricity demand is forecast at 5,010 MW, while generation capacity is only 3,540 MW.

“That’s why we need to continue the load shedding measures,” he said.

Despite having the poorest electricity access in the region, Myanmar made significant progress in grid connectivity under the National League for Democracy’s 15-year National Electrification Plan in 2015. By 2020, more than half of households had electricity access, and the NLD’s World Bank-backed plan aimed to achieve nationwide electrification by 2030.

However, the plan was scrapped after the 2021 coup, and regime mismanagement has since triggered rolling power outages across the country.

The World Bank says reliable supply has dropped sharply since the military takeover, affecting nearly half of connected households — with 41.6 percent receiving only enough electricity for basic lighting and phone charging, and 9.1 percent getting no electricity at all.

It blames the deepening generation crisis on the suspension of LNG power plants, declining domestic gas production, hydropower stress, infrastructure damage, and stalled investment.

In response, the regime reintroduced nationwide rolling blackouts, leaving residents in even major cities struggling to manage households and livelihoods.

“We have to be ready to fill up the water, cook meals, and iron our clothes the moment the power comes back on,” Ko Thant Zin from Insein Township in the suburbs of Yangon told the Irrawaddy.

He said the electricity supply rotates between four hours on and four hours off.

“Under the civilian government, the roads were bright with lights. Now, I have to open my eyes wide to see the way ahead while driving at night,” he commented.

The deputy energy minister told citizens to install solar panels if they want a reliable supply. However, import curbs and surging prices have put solar options out of reach for most urban residents.

“Forget about solar panels, most people can’t even afford a portable power pack,” a resident of downtown Yangong’s Botahtaung Township told The Irrawaddy. “Prices have been skyrocketing because of import restrictions.”

He added that power cuts would cause major suffering during the El Niño heatwave forecast for November through January.

“I can’t imagine how we will get through next summer,” he said, reacting to the rationing announcement. “It will be especially tough for young children and the elderly.”

Demand driven by outages has seen the price of solar panels surge to a record high. Yangon residents said a household solar power system now costs at least 10 million kyats (around US $4,760), putting it beyond the reach of ordinary families.

Last month, Yangon City authorities mandated that all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar power systems to operate elevators and emergency lighting, as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

The World Bank says chronic power shortages remain one of the main constraints on Myanmar’s economy, limiting its recovery and keeping poverty persistently high.

The deputy energy minister also announced plans to develop two 55 MW small-modular-reactors in cooperation with Russia’s atomic agency, ROSATOM, starting in fiscal 2028-29. The project is slated for completion in fiscal 2035-36 but locations have yet to be announced.

World.title: Three Years After Operation 1027, Hopang Transformed Under Wa Rule
World.content:
Friday marks three years since Hopang in the Wa Self-Administered Zone experienced its first taste of the joint ethnic offensive known as Operation 1027, when drones deployed by the Brotherhood Alliance bombed a monastery sheltering retreating Myanmar military personnel from nearby Kunlong base.

For the Myanmar military, which had controlled Hopang for decades, the drone strike was an early warning that its grip on the town was nearing an end. For the United Wa State Army (UWSA), it presented an opportunity to gain one of the most important towns in Wa territory without firing a shot.

Less than two months after the Nov. 13 drone attack, forces of the Brotherhood Alliance—which grouped the Arakan Army, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)—and allied groups entered Hopang with little resistance. Rather than holding the town themselves, they quickly handed it over to their ally, the UWSA.

Operation 1027, which inflicted one of the most devastating military setbacks in the Myanmar military’s history, had begun on Oct. 27, 2023, in Chinshwehaw, a border town just 8 km from Hopang. Just 19 km away, Kunlong, a key town on a China-Myanmar trade route, also fell after sustained drone attacks by alliance forces.

As Kunlong collapsed, its commander, officers and wounded soldiers fled to Hopang.

“A battalion commander and a soldier entered the monastery building and pleaded for shelter,” recalled a witness who was in the compound. “They told the abbot they had been under drone attacks for four days, and had only managed to retreat after receiving supporting fire.”

That same night, drones struck the monastery.

For Hopang residents, who had watched the fighting around Kunlong from hilltop pagodas, the attack on the monastery signaled that war was coming closer. By the next morning, many were fleeing the town, leaving their homes and shops behind.

Some local drivers found themselves ferrying displaced families back and forth, while others stayed behind to guard their properties. Residents feared not only a potential urban battle similar to the fighting in Kunlong, but also the prospect of Myanmar military airstrikes.

One restaurant owner recalled watching looters load crates of beer from his shop onto vehicles through CCTV cameras while he was fleeing.

Among those who fled were a monk who was injured in the November 13 drone attack, as well as health workers from a public hospital in Hopang.

Hopang was home to a military battalion and a police station, but all the surrounding towns including Kunlong and Chinshwehaw were controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance. At this point, Hopang was effectively isolated.

When MNDAA troops entered Hopang in early January 2024, the remaining military and police units reportedly surrendered with little resistance. Under a prior arrangement between the MNDAA and the UWSA, control of the town was then transferred to the Wa army.

Unlike Lashio, Laukkai, Chinshwehaw or Kunlong, Hopang largely escaped major battle damage. Yet residents say the town has since undergone a different kind of transformation, one increasingly shaped by Chinese capital and Wa administration.

The ethnically diverse town, home to Shan, Wa, Bamar, Kachin, Ta’ang and other communities, was once known for its Buddhist, Christian and traditional ethnic festivals. Today, residents say casinos, bars, hotels, massage parlors and prostitution-related businesses funded by Chinese investors have proliferated.

Some residents also complain of heavy taxation and a justice system that includes public executions, practices rarely seen under previous administrations.

The yuan now dominates much of the local economy, with residents increasingly pricing goods in the Chinese currency rather than kyats. In the healthcare arena, expensive Chinese-run private hospitals have emerged alongside the only public hospital.

Over the past three years, rumors have repeatedly surfaced that the UWSA will return Hopang to the regime. Residents say they see no sign that this is imminent, however.

The town, which participated in the 2010, 2015 and 2020 elections, did not take part in the regime-organized 2025 poll and is absent from the list of constituencies scheduled to be put to a vote in additional elections scheduled for April 2027.

Recently, regime Defense Minister and peace negotiator Lieutenant General Yar Pyae visited Panghsang, the UWSA headquarters. There was no indication that Hopang’s status was discussed during his meetings with Wa leaders, however.

While the UWSA remained officially neutral during Operation 1027, it emerged among the campaign’s biggest beneficiaries. Without openly joining the offensive, it gained full control of Hopang and Panlong, while also securing partial control along with the Myanmar military over Tangyan, a strategically important town on the route to Lashio, the largest town in northern Shan.

Three years after the first drone bombs fell on Hopang, the town has changed beyond recognition for longtime residents.

During Operation 1027, the MNDAA and TNLA went on to seize almost the whole of northern Shan State including the capital Lashio and all vital trade routes with China.

However, under strong Chinese pressure, in 2025 the ethnic armies were forced to halt fighting the Myanmar military and hand back several liberated towns to the regime.

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.
