The possible restrictions Kaladze mentioned suggest a shift towards a stricter transport policy aimed at curbing the growth in the number of cars in Tbilisi. However, the mayor has yet to specify when the measures might take effect or how the authorities plan to implement them.



Possible traffic restrictions in Tbilisi

World.title: Why has Abkhazia been unable to resolve its waste crisis for 20 years?
World.content:
Waste crisis in Abkhazia

The history of the waste crisis in Abkhazia resembles an endless, absurdist tragicomedy: the problem is clear, experts have worked out technical solutions, yet for years the authorities have directed their efforts towards the wrong measures and on an insufficient scale.

Presidents and mayors come and go, expert commissions are convened, but each time another fire breaks out at an illegal rubbish dump or residents take to the streets to protest against the unbearable stench, the authorities are forced to revisit the issue. And each time, it emerges that the problem has only grown worse.

Timeline of waste protests

Public debate over Abkhazia’s waste problem intensified following a protest in the village of Alakhadzy, near the resort town of Pitsunda, when it became clear that the authorities’ assurances that they had the situation “under control” were far from reality.

On 27 October, residents of Alakhadzy blocked access to a rubbish dump. They were driven to take action by persistent smoke from burning waste, an unbearable stench and the risk of a major fire. Nearly 1,000 people signed a petition calling for the dump to be closed.

The head of the district administration, Yury Khagush, arrived at the scene, along with members of the district assembly, local officials, police officers and even representatives of the State Security Service. The protesters dispersed after being promised that the issue would be resolved.

This was far from the first such incident. The history of “waste protests” in Abkhazia dates back to July 2007, when residents of the Mayak neighbourhood in Sukhum first blocked rubbish trucks from entering a municipal landfill located within the city limits.

In the years that followed, the landfill continued to catch fire repeatedly, engulfing Sukhum in toxic smoke. In August 2011, city authorities promised to bring the site up to an “acceptable standard” by November that year.

However, nothing had changed by November, and in December, then-President Alexander Ankvab openly acknowledged that the republic was facing a waste crisis.

“We need to find the courage either to reach agreements with investors or to make savings elsewhere and build at least two large waste-processing plants ourselves,” Ankvab said at the time.

Two years later, he described purchasing Italian equipment as the most cost-effective option. However, the plans never materialised.

From one landfill to another

In 2018, the landfill in the Mayak neighbourhood was finally closed. However, the problem did not disappear – it was simply relocated. Waste from the capital began to be transported daily to a landfill in the village of Shashakuara, in Gali district, 72km away, resulting in significant costs and wear and tear on vehicles.

“The Sukhum landfill contains hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of waste. But most of that volume is air. Only 15% consists of solid and liquid waste, while 85% is air. So these trucks keep driving back and forth, transporting air and burning fuel,” Russian hydraulic engineer Alexander Tsekhovoy explained to specialists in Sukhum in 2019.

According to his calculations, rather than endlessly transporting waste between landfills, each district should establish special compaction stations capable of compressing waste four- to fivefold. This would reduce the number of trips to the central landfill to just four truckloads a day.

However, instead of introducing these technologies, the authorities have continued simply transporting waste from one district to another.

Costly and pointless landfill in Katsikyt

A new waste management complex in the village of Katsikyt, in Gulripshi district, was supposed to provide a breakthrough solution to the waste problem.

The 5.5-hectare site was equipped with a waste disposal pit featuring a multilayer insulating base, treatment facilities and a conveyor belt for sorting waste. Construction proved extremely challenging, both technically and financially, with the project costing more than 150m roubles [$1.81m].

However, by the time the facility was nearly complete, it turned out that nobody wanted it.

Sukhum refused to use the complex, while the authorities in Gulripshi district were also reluctant to take responsibility for it. Security personnel were soon withdrawn from the site, which has since been effectively abandoned and remains unused.

Waste processing complex in the village of Katsikyt

The landfill in the village of Katsikyt was intended to be a financially sustainable facility. During its construction, Timur Agrba, then head of the Capital Construction Department and now mayor of Sukhum, said the facility could become self-financing by sorting, compacting and selling recyclable materials, including plastic, paper and metal.

According to Agrba, if properly managed, the facility could not only cover its operating costs but also generate revenue for further development.

However, in practice, the main obstacle is the tariff for household waste disposal.

“The current tariff policy does not reflect the realities or the costs incurred by our companies. International practice shows that waste collection and transportation should be funded through payments made by the residents who generate that waste,” Beslan Eshba, then head of the Sukhum city administration, explained back in 2014.

He promised that city authorities would seek to introduce relevant amendments to a new housing code. However, 12 years later, the new code has still not been adopted.

The current waste collection fee in Abkhazia is 27 roubles [$0.33] per person per month, a relatively modest amount. Yet most urban residents do not even pay this, as there is no clearly established system for collecting utility payments.

To obtain an objective assessment of the situation, Abkhazia’s Public Chamber held a series of meetings with Russian specialists, local environmental experts and representatives of district administrations.

As a result, an expert report was drawn up, providing a comprehensive assessment of the entire household waste management system. The report has already been submitted to the president, parliament, executive authorities and the Institute of Ecology.

For now, however, it represents little more than another faint glimmer of hope on the horizon. No tangible progress has been made towards resolving the problem.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Проблема мусора в Абхази

World.title: Special forces officers convicted of assaulting protesters jailed for five years each
World.content:
Special forces officers jailed for assaults

A court has sentenced special forces officers convicted of physically assaulting journalist Guram Rogava and protester Zviad Maisashvili during demonstrations in November and December 2024 to five years in prison each.

The special forces officer convicted of assaulting Guram Rogava, a journalist with Formula TV, was also banned from professional duties for three years. Lasha Gamkrelidze, the new prosecutor in the case, informed the journalist of the verdict by telephone.

According to Formula, Rogava had expected to testify as a victim during the trial. However, the prosecutor explained that his testimony was unnecessary because the court and the defence had accepted the charges as undisputed. Rogava himself believes that the person who directly assaulted him remains at large.

Two other special forces officers arrested in connection with the assault on Zviad Maisashvili were each sentenced to five years in prison. Lawyer Dimitri Mchedlishvili confirmed the information to Tabula.

On 30 November 2024, at around 06:30, special forces officers kicked Zviad Maisashvili in the face during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, causing him to lose consciousness. Footage of the assault circulated on social media.

On 7 May 2026, Georgia’s Prosecutor’s Office announced that it had identified and detained five people in connection with assaults on Rogava, Maisashvili and opposition politician Levan Khabeishvili.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office, four of those detained were current or former special forces officers, while the fifth was a serving officer with the Interior Ministry’s Security Police Department. Two of the suspects were already serving prison sentences at the time of their arrest.

Prosecutors said that on 29 November 2024, during a protest on Rustaveli Avenue, an officer from the Interior Ministry’s Special Tasks Department assaulted Guram Rogava while the journalist was carrying out his professional duties.

The detainees were charged under Article 333(3) of the Criminal Code with abuse of official powers involving violence. The officer detained in connection with the assault on Rogava also faced an additional charge of unlawfully obstructing a journalist’s professional activities.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office’s initial statement, the charges carried prison sentences of five to eight years.

Maisashvili said both special forces officers detained over the assault on him had admitted their guilt and apologised to him.

Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili

Background

The assaults on Guram Rogava and Zviad Maisashvili were among several high-profile incidents of police violence during pro-European protests in Tbilisi in November and December 2024.

The protests began on 28 November 2024, after Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that the government would take the issue of opening EU accession talks off the agenda until the end of 2028.

In the following days, law enforcement officers used water cannon, tear gas and other crowd-control measures against protesters on Rustaveli Avenue and near the parliament building. Numerous incidents of physical violence against demonstrators, journalists and human rights defenders were documented.

Both protesters and members of the media sustained injuries during the demonstrations. The assault on journalist Guram Rogava attracted particular attention. On 29 November 2024, a special forces officer attacked Rogava while he was reporting live from Rustaveli Avenue, leaving him seriously injured.

Media representatives and human rights organisations called for investigations into these incidents. On 30 November 2024, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) said the police’s use of water cannon, pepper spray and batons, including against peaceful demonstrators and journalists, had been disproportionate.

According to Georgia’s Public Defender’s 2024 report, the ombudsman and his representatives visited 624 people who had been detained or injured during protests between 15 April 2024 and 1 March 2025. Of those, 360 reported ill-treatment.

The report also noted that no police officers had been held accountable for violence committed by law enforcement personnel during that period.

According to the Prosecutor’s Office statement of 7 May 2026, more than 550 witnesses were questioned and thousands of investigative and procedural actions were carried out as part of the investigations into the cases involving Zviad Maisashvili, Levan Khabeishvili and Guram Rogava.

The Prosecutor’s Office said the investigations would continue to identify other possible perpetrators and bring them to justice.

World.title: Dayhanbank accounts for 40.2% of ATM cash withdrawals in Turkmenistan
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Dayhanbank SCBT accounted for 40.2% of total ATM cash withdrawal volume in Turkmenistan in January-September 2026.

This was calculated by Trend based on data published by the Central Bank of Turkmenistan.

According to the calculations, Turkmenistan State Commercial Bank (SCBT) followed, accounting for 27.4% of the total volume of these transactions.

Meanwhile, Turkmenbashi JSCB and Halkbank accounted for 12.2% and 11.4%, respectively, while Senagat JSCB held a 4.5% share.

The remaining banks - Rysgal JSCB, the State Bank for Foreign Economic Affairs, Turkmen-Turkish JSCB, and the Central Bank of Turkmenistan - jointly accounted for less than 5%, according to Trend's calculations.

For reference, the Central Bank of Turkmenistan launched cashless payments in 2001 with the introduction of the domestic Altyn Asyr card scheme. While the initial infrastructure was developed in the 2000s, broader adoption gained momentum in the mid-2010s as part of government efforts to digitalize the economy.

In August 2020, the government announced the launch of the Halkbank Terminal mobile application, developed by JSCB Halkbank to allow merchants to accept cashless payments directly through NFC-enabled smartphones, replacing traditional POS terminals. The initiative was presented as a step toward expanding cashless payments and introducing contactless payment technologies across the country.

Alongside payment terminals, Turkmen banks have expanded digital banking services, including Internet Banking, Mobile Banking, e-commerce payment platforms and specialized applications such as Senagat Töleg, while continuing to develop the national Altyn Asyr bank card payment system. These services enable customers to pay for utilities, telecommunications, transport, taxes and other public services electronically.

World.title: Turkmenistan Railways announces international tender for freight wagon spare parts
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Turkmenistan Railways Open Joint Stock Company has announced an open international tender for the procurement of spare parts for freight wagons from manufacturers.

The tender is No. DÝ/AGPJ-055. Interested companies should submit a written application indicating their full name, legal status and details, accompanied by registration and charter documents, a power of attorney and a copy of the applicant representative’s passport.

Applicants must obtain the lot specifications, technical requirements and tender documentation, and pay a fee of $200, including VAT, per lot. Bank account details for payment will be provided upon submission of the written application. Tender proposals will be considered only after the funds have been received by Turkmenistan Railways OJSC.

Companies registered in or holding bank accounts in offshore jurisdictions are not eligible to participate.

Tender documents must be submitted in two separate packages containing the technical and commercial proposals. They will be accepted at Turkmenistan Railways OJSC’s office No. 305, third floor, from 9:00 to 18:00 local time.

The proposals will be considered until December 24.

Additional information:

Phone: +993 12 38-31-03, +993 12 38-34-78

Fax: +993 12 38-40-27

Address: 7 Beyik Saparmurat Turkmenbashi Avenue, Ashgabat, Turkmenistan

World.title: Central Bank of Azerbaijan boosts note auctions, its portfolio reaches $1B
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. The Central Bank of Azerbaijan (CBA) increased note auctions, and its portfolio reached 1.7 billion manat ($1 billion).

According to CBA’s data on monetary indicators, from January through September 2026, the CBA actively continued note auctions and deposit operations to manage excess liquidity in the banking sector. As a result, the total volume of the CBA's note portfolio reached 1.7 billion manat at the end of September, up 1.4 billion manat ($823.5 million) compared to the end of last year.

During the reporting period, the CBA's monetary operations were aimed at regulating liquidity in the banking system and ensuring that short-term interest rates in the money market remained within the target range.

To this end, open market operations and standing facilities were actively used, taking into account changes in liquidity conditions. The parameters of monetary operations were adjusted in line with liquidity dynamics in the banking sector.

Banking sector liquidity surplus rises to 6.2 billion manat ($3.65 billion)

According to the CBA, the banking sector operated under excess liquidity conditions during the reporting period. Specifically, the structural liquidity surplus, calculated excluding required reserves, reached 6.2 billion manat at the end of September 2026.

This figure was 2.2 times higher than in December last year.

The structural liquidity surplus represents the difference between the CBA's liabilities to the banking system and its claims on the banking system.

The report notes that the existing liquidity conditions not only support banks in meeting their current obligations on time but also indicate their strong lending capacity.

146 note auctions held in nine months

To manage excess liquidity, the CBA continued auctions for the placement of notes with various maturities as part of its open market operations.

A total of 146 note auctions were held from January through September 2026. Of these, 37 involved 28-day notes, 36 involved 84-day notes, 37 involved 168-day notes, and 36 involved 252-day notes.

Taking into account the maturity structure of excess liquidity, the CBA increased the offered amounts at note auctions starting in July this year. As a result, by the end of September, the total volume of the institution's note portfolio had risen to 1.7 billion manat.

For comparison, this figure stood at around 300 million manat ($176.5 million) at the end of last year. Thus, the note portfolio increased by 1.4 billion manat ($823.5 million) over the nine-month period.

Note yields decline across all maturities

During the reporting period, yields on the Central Bank's notes also declined. Yields recorded at the latest auctions held in September 2026 were lower across all maturities compared to the end of last year.

Specifically, the yield on 28-day notes fell from 6.75% to 6.50%, while that on 84-day notes declined from 6.68% to 6.56%.

Yields on 168-day notes decreased from 6.80% to 6.60%, while those on 252-day notes fell from 6.85% to 6.67%.

Thus, note yields declined across all maturities, with the largest decrease recorded in 28-day notes.

Average deposit auction volume reaches 2 billion manat ($1.2 billion)

The CBA also actively used seven-day deposit operations to manage excess liquidity in the banking system during the reporting period.

According to the institution, 62 deposit auctions were held during the first nine months of this year, with the average transaction volume amounting to 2 billion manat.

These operations helped effectively manage excess liquidity, neutralize the impact of autonomous factors on monetary conditions, and keep the AZIR index on a trajectory close to the policy rate.

Banks were also observed to have primarily used sterilization-oriented instruments among the standing facilities. While the overnight deposit standing facility was used on every business day, the overnight reverse repo standing facility was used on only 2% of business days.

Required reserve requirements exceeded

During the reporting period, the continued application of the averaging regime for required reserves enabled banks to manage their liquidity more flexibly.

According to the results of the CBA's monitoring, the average balances held by banks in their correspondent accounts with the institution, in both national and foreign currencies, exceeded the amounts required to be maintained as mandatory reserves over the respective periods.

These indicators confirm that the banking sector has sufficient liquid funds.

Overall, during the first nine months of 2026, the Central Bank's monetary operations primarily focused on managing excess liquidity in the banking system, keeping short-term interest rates within the target range, and supporting stability in the money market. The increase in the note portfolio to 1.7 billion manat, the holding of 146 note auctions, and the active use of deposit operations were among the key indicators of the measures implemented in this regard.

World.title: Azerbaijan's Kenan Nasibov wins gold at Zagreb Grand Prix
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. Azerbaijani judoka Kenan Nasibov (over 100 kg) has won the gold medal at the Grand Prix tournament held in Zagreb, the capital of Croatia.

In the final bout, Nasibov defeated Germany's Losseni Kone.

The Azerbaijani athlete secured four victories on his way to the title, successfully defending the championship he won last year. Three of his bouts went into overtime and were decided by golden score.

In the semifinals, Nasibov defeated seeded Georgian judoka Saba Inaneishvili by ippon.

This victory marks the third World Tour title of Nasibov's career. His head-to-head record against Losseni Kone now stands at 2–1.

Another Azerbaijani judoka, Ushangi Kokauri, was unable to compete in the bronze medal match due to an injury sustained in the semifinals. He therefore finished the tournament in fifth place.

World.title: A century of radio, 70 years of television: "Jubilee Night" held at Heydar Aliyev Palace (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 16. A concert program titled "Jubilee Night" was held at Heydar Aliyev Palace on November 15 to mark the 100th anniversary of Azerbaijani Radio and the 70th anniversary of Azerbaijani Television.

Arzu Aliyeva, head of the Baku Media Center, attended the concert.

The event opened with the national anthem of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

Rovshan Mammadov, chairman of the Azerbaijan Television and Radio Broadcasting Closed Joint-Stock Company, delivered a speech and read out a congratulatory letter from President Ilham Aliyev marking the anniversaries.

Renowned Azerbaijani artists and musical ensembles performed during the concert. People's Artists, Honored Artists, and the Rast group presented musical performances, while the Azerbaijan State Dance Ensemble added a distinctive touch to the evening. Latvian singer Laima Vaikule also performed at the jubilee concert.

Prominent Azerbaijani television presenters shared their memories of the history of Azerbaijani radio and television.

Films produced using AzTV's rich archival materials were screened during the event. Scenes from well-known television plays that have remained in viewers' memories were also shown.

The jubilee evening concluded with performances by the 100-member choir of Azerbaijani Television and People's Artist Zeynab Khanlarova.

World.title: Jury hung in trial exploring dark chapter of Sydney's criminal history
World.content:
A jury has been unable to reach a verdict for a second time in the Bilal Hamze murder trial.

The man accused of killing gangster Hamze in the Sydney CBD five years ago, Samuel John Rokomaqisa, now faces the prospect of a rare third murder trial in the Supreme Court.

Rokomaqisa was facing trial as either the gunman who took out Hamze or the getaway driver fleeing with the hitman from the scene on June 17, 2021.

Hamze died in a hail of bullets after his killer fired on him from a car as he left Kid Kyoto restaurant near Bridge Street with a sex worker.

Dashcam vision captured the moment Mr Hamze's killer circled back to look at his lifeless body before fleeing. (Supplied)

Graphic CCTV footage played to the jury showed the gunman shoot Hamze, circle back and fire again before pulling up a third time to the curb near his lifeless body.

On Friday, after deliberating for 11 days, the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict on the charge of murder and were discharged.

However, Rokomaqisa was found guilty over a failed attempt to kill Hamze's brother Ibrahem Hamze at North Sydney months later in November 2021.

Deadly chapter comes to a close

Mr Hamze's funeral, which was followed by the burials of three more of his family. (AAP)

The three-month trial explored one of the deadliest chapters in Sydney's criminal history.

Hamze's death was one of seven in 18 months of violence at the height of the Alameddine crime family's war with the Hamzys.

The two gangs had been locked in a feud over control of Sydney's drug trade at the time.

Police had deployed rarely used non-association powers, dubbed Serious Crime Prevention Orders, to calm the bloodshed between the two clans.

Mr Hamze inside Kid Kyoto restaurant before he was shot dead. (Supplied)

But Hamze would be followed to the grave by relatives Salim Hamze, Toufik Hamze and Ghassan Amoun during a wave of violence that plagued the city.

Hamze, the cousin of notorious SuperMax prisoner Bassam Hamzy, was targeted due to his standing in the family's crime network headed by the former Brothers 4 Life boss.

Rokomaqisa's case is the fifth stemming from the seven gangland assassinations attributed to the Hamzy-Alameddine war.

In his first trial last year the jury deliberated for four weeks before being unable to reach a verdict.

Key witness quizzed for days over underworld associations

The woman waiting to meet Bilal Hamze the night he died. (Supplied)

The sex worker seen with Hamze that night, who cannot legally be named, spent days being quizzed by Rokomaqisa's defence barrister over her links to Hamze's enemies.

Hamze's dinner date would tell the jury hundreds of times that she could not remember key details of what led up to her meal with the married underworld figure.

In opening their case to the jury Rokomaqisa's defence team argued: "[The woman] may have been used by others to get to Bilal Hamze that evening."

"How did the shooters know exactly where Bilal Hamze was going to be at 10:20pm on 17 June 2021?" defence barrister Nicole Carroll said.

Ms Carroll laid out how the Hamzy crime network was also at war with Sydney's Haouchar family and the Comanchero bikie gang at the time, not just the Alameddines.

Rokomaqisa's barrister had zeroed in on her partying with Lone Wolf bikie gang boss Eric 'The Wolf' Keskin and Comanchero sergeant-at-arms Tarek Zahed.

The jury were read messages showing the woman was requested for a threesome with Tarek Zahed and his wife before Mr Hamze was killed.

Comanchero boss Mr Zahed, who is not accused of any invovlement in the Hamze murder. (Supplied)

Mr Zahed is not accused of having any involvement in Bilal Hamze's murder.

"You know who Tarek Zahed is though, don't you?" defence barrister Ms Carroll asked.

"No," the woman replied.

"Are you telling the truth?" Ms Carroll asked.

"Yes," the woman answered.

In closing Rokomaqisa's defence, his lawyers told the jury the woman either "knowingly or unwittingly" led Hamze to his killers through other violent underworld figures she knew.

Gang associations and a jailhouse boast

The moment the first shot was fired by a gunman at Bilal Hamze as he crossed a CBD street. (Supplied)

Crown prosecutor Kate Ratcliffe outlined how Rokomaqisa was allegedly a member of the KVT, a street gang of Fijian-Australians used by the Alameddine family as muscle.

The jury heard while in custody Rokomaqisa joked on a call that his name was "Samu Alameddine" and boasted of his involvement in the hit on Hamze.

In opening the Crown case, Ms Ratcliffe said Rokomaqisa committed the murder to gain the trust of the Alameddine family and to "demonstrate his loyalty".

Hamze runs after being shot in the CBD, before dying from his injuries. (Supplied)

Evidence obtained by police and presented to the jury detailed how Rokomaqisa allegedly told an associate he and his cousin "did the job", referring to the Bilal Hamze murder.

In one series of surveillance device recordings, Rokomaqisa could allegedly be heard laughing and mimicking gunshot noises as news of another Hamzy being shot was played on a TV.

The jury also heard other covert recordings from inside the home of Alameddine crime family boss Masood Zakaria as senior members game-planned a strategy in the war against the Hamzy's.

The failed hit

Underworld figure Ibrahem Hamze, with other members of the Hamzy clan. (Supplied)

Rokomaqisa was also on trial for, and found guilty of, a failed attempt to kill Bilal Hamze's younger brother Ibrahem months after the gangster's death.

That attempt on Ibrahem Hamze's life was only thwarted when Highway Patrol officers spotted his would-be killers stopped in a no-parking zone near his North Sydney home.

That murder plot was botched after Rokomaqisa and another hired assassin then blew a tyre fleeing from police before car-jacking an elderly man at gunpoint in their getaway.

Loading...

CCTV footage played to the jury showed how Ibrahem Hamze missed the killers in the same car with cloned number plates weeks prior.

The vision depicted Hamze exiting an elevator to the apartment block's underground car park just seconds before the vehicle failed to breach its entry gates.

Rokomaqisa will remain in custody to await sentencing later this year.

World.title: Police charge 14-year-old boy over crash of allegedly stolen car
World.content:
A 14-year-old boy has been charged over a two-vehicle crash in Brisbane's south-east involving an allegedly stolen car that left three other teenagers in hospital.

Emergency services were called to the intersection of Wynnum and Hemmant Tingalpa Roads just before 4pm on Sunday following reports a white Toyota Corolla had collided with another vehicle and crashed into a power pole.

Police allege the white Toyota had been reported stolen from Wynnum earlier in the day.

The alleged driver of the vehicle, a 14-year-old boy and three passengers in the car, two 15-year-old girls and a 16-year-old boy, were transported to hospital.

One of the girls remains in a critical condition.

The occupants of the other vehicle were physically uninjured. (ABC News)

The occupants of the other vehicle were not physically injured.

The crash knocked out power for more than 1,200 households in the area for several hours.

The 14-year-old boy has been charged with three counts of dangerous operation of a motor vehicle causing death or grievous bodily harm, enter premises and commit indictable offence, driving of a motor vehicle without a licence and proceeding through a red traffic light.

He is expected to face the Brisbane Children's Court today.

Police are asking any witnesses or anyone with vision of the incident to come forward.

World.title: Woolworths apologises after customers report drained gift card balances
World.content:
Dozens of Woolworths customers say they've lost hundreds of dollars after discovering their digital gift cards were drained by transactions they did not authorise.

The ABC has been contacted by customers across Australia who say their Everyday WISH gift cards, purchased through the Everyday Rewards website or app, were spent by someone else.

Some customers have reported losing up to $500, with transactions appearing at stores in different states from where the cards were purchased.

Woolworths has acknowledged an issue affecting "a number of" customer e-gift cards, apologising to those affected and saying it is investigating the reports as a priority.

"We recognise the concern this has caused affected customers and we apologise to customers impacted," a spokesperson said.

Complaints first appeared on Australian bargain-sharing website OzBargain last week, with similar reports subsequently emerging across Facebook and Reddit.

All of the customers who contacted the ABC appear to have purchased their gift cards during a promotional offer through Everyday Gifting that advertised a 4 per cent discount.

Everyday WISH gift cards can be redeemed in store and online at participating Woolworths Group retailers and partners, including Big W, BWS, Dan Murphy's and Cellarmasters.

The complaints reported to the ABC so far involve Everyday WISH cards purchased digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app. (Supplied)

Deborah Kellie, from Brisbane, said she lost $500 after purchasing an Everyday WISH card last Monday.

"I have been an Everyday Rewards customer for ages, and I usually buy my rewards cards through the RACQ," she said.

But Ms Kellie said a promotional email from Everyday Gifting advertised a "great deal", offering an extra 1 per cent discount on WISH gift cards compared with RACQ.

"So I thought I've got to go shopping next week, I'll get one from them [Everyday Gifting] instead."

Two days later, she discovered the entire balance had been spent at a Big W store in Doncaster, Victoria, despite never having used the card or shared its details.

In Sydney, Michael Bennett said he had also switched from buying the WISH gift card through the NRMA app after seeing the 4 per cent discount offer in the Everyday Rewards app.

He said he purchased a $400 WISH gift card through the app on November 9. But when he attempted to use it at a Woolworths store in Hornsby on November 14, the card had disappeared from his digital wallet.

Deborah Kellie says her gift card was drained in another state two days after she purchased it. (Supplied)

After checking the balance through a link in his email, he discovered the money had been spent.

The transaction history showed $400 had been spent at a Big W store in Pagewood, in Sydney's east, on November 12.

Mr Bennett said he had not shared the gift card details, his mobile phone had remained in his possession, and his Everyday Rewards account was protected by a complex password and two-factor authentication.

He also said the gift card had never been physically printed.

"Woolworths warn customers to treat gift cards like cash," Mr Bennett said.

" It turns out they [gift cards] are much less secure than cash as key information can be stolen remotely. "

Suspecting a cybersecurity breach, Ms Kellie said she cancelled her Visa card as a precaution.

She said she made three attempts to contact Woolworths customer service, but was unable to speak to anyone despite waiting for more than an hour on the phone the first two times.

On her third attempt, Ms Kellie said an automated message advised the company was receiving an increasing number of calls before disconnecting her.

She subsequently emailed Woolworths screenshots and details of the transactions and lodged a report with cybersecurity authorities.

The report has since been referred to Queensland Police for assessment in correspondence seen by the ABC.

Following ABC enquiries, a Woolworths spokesperson advised customers who notice an unrecognised transaction to contact its Gift Card Support team at giftcard@customerservice.woolworths.com.au.

Customers can also log into the Everyday Gifting website and register their details on the homepage.

"Our team will work directly with customers to determine the appropriate next steps, including issuing replacement e-gift cards for customers impacted," the spokesperson said.

How does gift card fraud happen?

The complaints reported to the ABC so far involve Everyday WISH gift cards purchased digitally through the Everyday Rewards website or app.

Woolworths has not said how the affected gift cards were accessed or whether a security vulnerability or data breach is suspected.

The digital purchases make traditional in-store gift card tampering less likely. In that form of fraud, criminals steal card details from products displayed in stores before they are purchased and activated.

Gift card fraud in Australian supermarkets An ABC investigation discovers gift cards that have been tampered with are being sold by Australia's biggest supermarkets, with charges even being laid over the issue.

An ABC investigation earlier this year uncovered tampered Apple gift cards being sold by Australia's biggest supermarkets, including Woolworths, with criminal charges subsequently laid over the issue.

Other forms of gift card fraud involve criminals impersonating individuals or organisations and tricking victims into purchasing cards and handing over the codes.

But customers who have contacted the ABC say they did not share their card details or knowingly authorise the transactions.

It remains unclear how the gift card details were obtained or how the unauthorised transactions could occur.

World.title: Stranded turtle's 16-hour road trip to recovery
World.content:
An animal lover has made a 16-hour round trip across southern Western Australia to play taxi driver for a stranded baby turtle.

After spotting an urgent late-night call-out for a volunteer driver, Letesha Heslewood drove nearly 700 kilometres from Bunbury to Esperance to collect the tiny patient and bring him back to the South West city for rehabilitation.

The juvenile loggerhead, nicknamed Shaggy for the thick green algae covering his shell, was spotted floating in seaweed off the Esperance coast and brought to the local wildlife hospital early last week.

Loggerheads are a tropical species, meaning the chilly southern waters leave them dangerously cold and dehydrated, making a fast transfer to specialised care critical.

Letesha Heslewood drove almost 700km to Esperance to bring the turtle back to Bunbury for care. (Supplied: Dolphin Discovery Centre)

By the time Ms Heslewood arrived in Esperance, staff were cleaning the algae off the turtle's shell to get him ready for transport.

"When I collected him, he looked picture perfect. He was gorgeous; the colouring on him was outstanding," she said.

The return trip to Bunbury was punctuated by a number of pit stops.

"They wanted me to pull over every couple of hours for rest and to give him a little bit of a splashdown," she said.

"They gave me some really clean water in a jar to splash over his eyes and his back every couple of hours to keep him comfortable, and he absolutely loved that.

Shaggy received routine water breaks on his Esperance-Bunbury road trip. (Supplied: Letesha Heslewood)

"He really responded to the water touching him, which was just the cutest thing I've ever seen in my life."

A retail worker who rarely gets to spend time with wildlife, the marathon rescue mission was one Ms Heslewood won't soon forget.

She now hopes to repeat the experience, officially registering as a volunteer wildlife transport officer.

"I knew I was going to enjoy doing it, but it filled something in my heart that I didn't know was missing," she said.

Colder detour not unusual for turtles

Shaggy is now recovering in a heated tank at Bunbury's Dolphin Discovery Centre, the second loggerhead to come into the team's care in recent weeks.

The turtle is being cared for at Bunbury's Dolphin Discovery Centre. (ABC News: Amelia Searson)

A centre spokesperson said that while they regularly see rescued turtles from nearby beaches like Binningup and Peppermint Grove, finding them as far south as Esperance was rarer.

But Marine Scientist Scott Whiting, from WA's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions, said the turtles' most routine nesting grounds were around Ningaloo and Shark Bay.

But he said there were a number of natural factors in play behind them turning up along WA's southern coast.

Ms Heslewood now hopes to register as an official volunteer wildlife transport officer. (Supplied: Letesha Heslewood)

"It's not uncommon for turtles to wash up; they get sick like every other animal and humans as well," he said.

"Sometimes they could have a shark wound they're trying to recover from, or sometimes they might even come in closer to shore because it's warmer water, there's less wave action, it's calmer, and they can recover."

Shaggy will remain in care in Bunbury until April next year, when staff plan to transport him north to Exmouth for release off the Ningaloo coast.

World.title: Looking for a summer job? Here's what to consider
World.content:
If you're looking for a few extra hours of work or desperately trying to save before university begins, a summer job could be the right fit for you.

These seasonal roles can simply be about earning extra cash, but it could help you discover what you love (or hate) doing for work.

It could even help with starting a new career.

Ben Walker was 16 when he got a casual job at his local supermarket in Sale, in regional Victoria.

Ben Walker's first casual job led to ongoing part-time work. (Supplied: Ben Walker)

The 21-year-old says that led to the part-time job that now supports him while studying game design at university.

In the beginning, Ben says he learnt a lot from interactions with people outside of school and cricket.

"The people skills, I think, are massive," he says.

Why summer is a good time to get a job

There is an influx of roles in hospitality, retail and tourism ahead of Christmas and summer, says Blair Chapman, the chief economist at employment service Seek.

"In Australia we get the double dose of Christmas and summer," he says.

Loading...

Retail picks up from early November (because of Black Friday sales), and online shopping has led to an increase in warehouse or "pick-packer roles" too, Dr Chapman says.

And given cost-of-living pressures and airfare prices, more Australians are likely to holiday closer to home this summer, he says.

"That sort of domestic-driven tourism might pick up because people can't afford to go overseas."

Dr Chapman says there is also "a bit of an evolution" in who is looking for summer jobs.

"There's a cost-of-living crunch and people are looking for that second job to help supplement their income," he says.

What are the benefits (other than pay)?

Grozdana Manalo says her first job as a barista began a "love affair" with coffee and helped her build confidence and communication skills.

"It also showed me just how hard and long some people work and made me really appreciate being a uni student," she says.

She's now a career services manager at the University of Sydney's Business School.

"Summer jobs can also help students discover what they enjoy, and just as importantly, what they don't," Ms Manalo says.

Seasonal and casual roles can also help young people develop professional skills, she says.

"Teamwork, communication, problem solving and time management — all important skills no matter what job or career you pick in the future."

Thinking strategically when applying for jobs

Irma Mooi-Reci is a professor of sociology at the University of Melbourne and the CEO of a company specialising in workforce data and skill gaps.

She would like young people to think "more strategically" about summer employment.

"Is it because you want to pay your bills? Is it because you want to have that experience or get a reference? Or is it because you want to get that first permanent job?" she asks.

Economic report dubs 2026 'year of AI' A new economic report by consultancy firm Deloitte says the AI "winners" will be organisations that combine human and machine strengths, with recruiters saying human judgement will still be key.

It's worth looking for a job that complements your career goals and whether an employer will see the experience as relevant, Professor Mooi-Reci says.

"Find something that you like doing, that you feel passionate about and learn as much as possible."

Professor Mooi-Reci says young people can become overwhelmed by information and fearmongering about the job market, the value of their degree and artificial intelligence.

"Don't be afraid, but think strategically," she adds.

How to find a summer job (and avoid exploitation)

If you're after seasonal work, Ms Manalo recommends looking for roles advertised on social media and job boards, or simply walking into local businesses and asking if there are positions available.

She says there are also "hidden job markets", which is why so many positions are filled before they're advertised.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

"This is all about leveraging your personal networks and making it known that you're looking for work," she says.

If you're young or have never been employed before, understanding workplace rights and responsibilities is very important, Ms Manalo says.

But Professor Mooi-Reci says it can be tricky for some people to resist jobs that have low pay and poor conditions.

Avoid jobs that seem exploitative and look for other options, she adds.

Ms Manalo says it's also important to keep records of the hours you've worked.

"Review your pay slips, and ask questions if something doesn't seem right," she says.

She recommends the Fair Work Ombudsman website for information and assistance regarding your rights and entitlements.

World.title: Walsh 'disappointed' after seeing Aussie fans cheering against Kangaroos
World.content:
Reece Walsh has taken aim at Australia "supporters" who wanted the team to lose the World Cup final, while launching an impassioned defence of the Kangaroos team culture.

The 24-year-old starred in the 32-12 final win over New Zealand at Lang Park on Sunday. In the dressing sheds former skipper Darren Lockyer presented him with the Harry Sunderland Medal, judged by Australia selectors and given to the team's best player of the tournament.

He was also presented with the Kangaroos players' player award for the World Cup by current number six Cameron Munster, who won it during last year's Ashes tour.

Walsh, who takes a keen interest in social media, has been irked by those who downplay Australia's "culture" as compared to other nations at the World Cup.

"I can see the culture and I can feel it," he said.

"I have seen it multiple times on social media, people disrespecting us and saying, 'I hope Australia loses just to make the game better.' No. If you are an Aussie you need to support and be proud of that.

"You would never see … a Tongan fan saying, 'I hope Tonga loses.' Social media is a big thing and I was a little bit disappointed in seeing some people come out in Australia and saying they didn't want to see us win.

"That was why I got so emotional [during the national anthem], seeing my family and knowing how much they care and how much Aussies care.

" I think that is an area we can get a lot better at … getting behind each other. "

Walsh said there were those outside the team's four walls that underplayed how much the players cared about their country and the badge they wore. He highlighted team captain Isaah Yeo as a great example.

"Isaah Yeo has had a torn pec and he has played five weeks of extra football for this badge, for this team, for us boys, for this country. That's culture," Walsh said.

"We love this country. We love winning. Culture is not just about cheering. It is about winning, being connected and turning up for your mate."

Walsh said the Australian team had players of other heritages, including himself and prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, who still united for the Kangaroos.

Kangaroos star Tino Fa'asuamaleaui (centre) represents Australia despite his Samoan heritage. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

"Tino is of Samoan heritage and I know he is so proud of that. He sat us down two weeks and … said how much he loves the jersey and wants to go out here and do Australia proud and us proud," Walsh said.

"I am the same. I am a proud Maori too. My mum is from there. I know when I pull on this jersey how much it means to me and how much my family care.

"My old man raised five kids as a single dad. That is what he done for me to be able to represent my old man and our last name and wear [the jersey] with pride."

Walsh did not have his best year at Brisbane but finished with a bang and justified his Kangaroos selection.

"It has been a tough year for myself and there were probably a lot of people that thought and said I shouldn't be here," he said.

"Having the support of the boys and the coaching staff and everyone behind me gave me the strength and confidence to go out there and do my job. The only thing that matters is winning and that is what we did."

AAP

World.title: Solomon Islands opposition accuses Australia of 'chequebook diplomacy'
World.content:
The Solomon Islands opposition has accused Australia of "chequebook diplomacy" after Prime Minister Matthew Wale funnelled budget support from Canberra into constituency funds for government MPs as the two countries wrapped up negotiations on a high-profile treaty due to be signed next week.

Government documents seen by the ABC show that multiple parliamentarians in Mr Wale's 31-strong GREAT Coalition received "discretionary grants" of up to $SBD1 million (about $180,000) per MP in their constituency accounts in October and November.

The payments were made from a bank account labelled AusAID — the name previously used by the Australian government's aid agency before it was wrapped into DFAT in 2013 — which initially drew accusations of direct foreign interference from the opposition.

But the ABC has established that the bank account is not an Australian government one and belongs to the Solomon Islands government instead.

The money seems to have been drawn from a larger $SBD200 million ($35 million) package of budget support announced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in June this year when Mr Wale visited Canberra.

At the time, Mr Wale's government said the money would "assist Solomon Islands in responding to Tropical Cyclone Maila and addressing the impacts of global energy shocks".

The use of constituency development funds (CDFs) has long drawn scrutiny and controversy in the Pacific Island nation, and Mr Wale's actions are not unprecedented.

Manasseh Sogavare has taken aim at Matthew Wale. (Reuters: Eduardo Munoz)

Politics in Solomon Islands is fluid and transactional, and previous Solomon Islands governments have also funnelled money from donors — including from both Taiwan and China — into CDFs for MPs, helping them to shore up their sometimes-wobbly coalitions in parliament.

But Solomon Islands opposition leader and former prime minister Manasseh Sogavare, who has a vexed history with Australia, has taken aim at Mr Wale, while accusing the federal government of meddling and hypocrisy.

"If Australia is channelling money to members of parliament through the Prime Minister's Office while it negotiates a 'comprehensive treaty', that is chequebook diplomacy," he said.

"It puts Australian aid at the centre of our domestic politics. Australia has rightly criticised other countries for doing exactly this in the Pacific.

"It should hold itself to the same standard."

Mr Sogavare also said money from Australian taxpayers was being used to "reward political loyalty", unfairly excluding the opposition.

"The people who lose are not opposition MPs. They are the villages, schools and clinics in the constituencies left out," he said.

"Aid should go to people according to need, not according to how their member votes."

Mr Wale's office declined to comment on the documents.

A federal government spokesperson denied any wrongdoing, saying "all of Australia's development assistance is based on the priorities of partner countries, subject to robust accountability and transparency guidelines, and complies with the OECD development guidelines."

Australia has never paid money directly to Solomon Islands MPs, and the money from budget support was provided to the Ministry of Finance and Treasury in Honiara.

The federal government has denied any wrongdoing in regards to Australia's development assistance. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

One federal government source also emphasised that Mr Wale and his ministers, and not the Australian government, ultimately made the decisions about how to spend budget support.

But the opposition's accusation is still politically dangerous, as it comes just nine days before Mr Wale is expected to visit Canberra to sign a sweeping new "comprehensive" treaty between the two nations, less than six months since negotiations began.

In September, the ABC revealed that Australia was planning to substantially ramp up contributions to constituency development funds under that treaty. None of that funding has yet been provided.

In a leaked text message, Australian High Commissioner Jeff Roach laid out new commitments totalling more than $980 million under the agreement, while emphasising that both governments were hoping to lock in the pact before the end of this year.

In his statement, Mr Sogavare again criticised the timing of that text message, saying it was sent just before Mr Wale was due to face a looming no-confidence vote in parliament, and suggesting Australia was trying to prop up the prime minister's leadership to secure the treaty.

"The motion was withdrawn days later. Solomon Islanders are entitled to ask whether that is a coincidence," he said.

"Both governments should answer openly."

But his accusations are likely to rankle with Canberra, given Mr Sogavare was himself accused of using CDFs to bolster his political position when facing parliamentary challenges as prime minister.

For example, in 2021 Mr Wale — then in opposition — complained when Mr Sogavare channelled money from China into CDFs for 39 government and crossbench MPs, saying the prime minister had deliberately excluded his political enemies.

Kerryn Baker from the Australian National University's Department of Pacific Affairs said while the optics of Mr Wale's payments were not ideal, it was "definitely not the first time that opposition MPs have complained their access to funds is blocked or restricted".

"There are always problems with fairness, even if funds are going equally to every MP, because the size of constituencies in Solomon Islands varies wildly — you have some with a few thousand voters and some with tens of thousands," she said.

"So the system isn't perfect, even before you get into political games."

There has long been a debate around the effectiveness of constituency development funds, with some development experts warning they are a vector for corruption and that they encourage patronage politics.

But Dr Baker said while there was a "risk" in contributing to CDFs, it was "probably a risk worth taking", and that the funding mechanism was "definitely more than a slush fund".

"CDFs are hugely important for development. It's a way to ensure funds reach the grassroots and can be spent on what communities need," she said.

"It's definitely not the ideal system, but Australia has poured in a huge amount of money in the past trying to strengthen central government institutions, and that hasn't been super successful.

Manasseh Sogavare was himself accused of previously using constituency development funds to bolster his political position. (Reuters: Joe Armao/Pool)

"So trying things a different way, to try to make sure money for development reaches the people that need it, isn't necessarily a bad thing."

The Wale government has also tried to tighten up the way that some of the payments have been made to local constituencies through CDFs.

Documents obtained by the ABC, which lay out the rules for MPs who receive money through the CDFs by the prime minister's grants, make it clear that parliamentarians have to acquit the funds spent.

The documents say that using funds for "private enrichment" or "political campaigning" is expressly forbidden, and that funded projects must deliver a clear development benefit.

Dr Baker said there was "always the risk of politicisation" with the scheme, but said "that risk exists with all government budget processes".

"There's been a lot of work in recent years to regulate CDFs and provide more transparency and accountability," she said.

"And they are popular with voters. People worry about fairness, but there isn't a huge popular drive to get rid of them altogether."

World.title: ‘Stop the delays’: Wong, counterparts blast Israel over Gaza humanitarian crisis
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Stop the delays’: Wong, counterparts blast Israel over Gaza humanitarian crisis Matthew Knott November 16, 2026 — 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Australia has united with Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom to urge Israel to allow a rapid expansion of aid and essential supplies into Gaza, as cold weather and heavy rains exacerbate an already desperate humanitarian situation. Images of flooded tent cities and reports of young Palestinian children dying in recent days have sparked renewed international attention on Gaza a year after a supposed ceasefire between Israel and Hamas came into effect. Foreign Minister Penny Wong and her three counterparts said in a statement on Monday that “the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire” as winter takes hold in Gaza. Foreign Minister Penny Wong says Israel must do more to allow the entry of crucial supplies into Gaza. Alex Ellinghausen “People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance. Yet 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza,” the foreign ministers said.



“This situation is entirely reversible – and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in.” The foreign ministers called for the Israeli government “to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza”. “The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in,” they said. “Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late.” Displaced Palestinian children repair tents damaged by heavy rain in Gaza City earlier this month. AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi The Israeli embassy in Canberra was approached for comment.



The fresh international focus on Gaza comes as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu tries to remain in office despite his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, receiving a mandate to try to form a governing coalition following last month’s elections. The European Union earlier called for Israel to allow more supplies to enter Gaza, declaring that severe flooding and cold weather “are further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering”. A Palestinian woman with a water container during heavy rainfall. Bloomberg Israel’s foreign ministry responded by labelling the European statement “completely unbalanced” and saying Hamas, which governs much of the strip, must be held responsible for refusing to disarm and cede control of Gaza. Asmahan Abdalraheem, a 25-year-old Palestinian accounting graduate in Gaza, said: “Winter is coming and we are drowning in tents.”



Three children aged between four and eight were killed with their mother when a dune collapsed on their tent in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, after heavy rainfall, UNICEF, the United Nations children’s fund, reported last week. Related Article Updated

World elections The Israeli elections have produced a deadlock. Here’s what happens now “Families are living without the most basic conditions for their safety, health and dignity,” UNICEF executive director Catherine Russell said. “More children could die without proper shelter, working water and sanitation systems, and the equipment needed to restore essential services. The worst of winter is yet to come.” An estimated 65 per cent of Gaza’s population, about 1.4 million people, live in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN’s aid co-ordination office



The Board of Peace, created by US President Donald Trump, last week called on Israel to allow the entry of essential materials for temporary shelter, water and sanitation infrastructure, waste management, drainage and sewage removal. The Board of Peace said the threat posed by cold and unsafe conditions represented “an immediate humanitarian emergency”, labelling Israel’s efforts to allow the entry of supplies into Gaza “insufficient” and calling for Hamas to disarm. An Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza last week killed six people and attracted renewed international criticism. Israel said it was targeting a top Hamas brigade commander who is believed to have survived the strike. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Weapons seized, hundreds arrested during statewide DV blitz
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Weapons seized, hundreds arrested during statewide DV blitz Jack Gramenz Updated November 16, 2026 — 11:47am ,first published November 16, 2026 — 8:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Hundreds of people have been arrested during a three-day blitz targeting alleged domestic violence offending in the state as police seize weapons and crack down on people allegedly breaching court orders from jail. The NSW Police Operation Amarok, targeting high-risk domestic violence offenders, led to 681 arrests and 1594 charges being laid. Police checked compliance with 11,375 apprehended domestic violence orders, finding 283 breaches. A 38-year-old man is arrested during a NSW Police Operation Amarok blitz targeting alleged domestic violence offences. NSW Police NSW Police Assistant Commissioner Peter McKenna said a number of people accused of breaching the orders were already in jail. “Just because someone’s in custody doesn’t mean they’re also out of our sights,” McKenna said on Monday.



“We actually shut down the [Metropolitan Remand and Reception Centre at Silverwater] with their cooperation and identified a number of persons in custody who were breaching AVOs … there’s nowhere to hide.” Officers also seized 73 firearms and 21 other weapons during the blitz between Thursday and Saturday last week. Police regularly seize weapons during Operation Amarok activities. A knife found by police during Operation Amarok was among 73 firearms and 21 other weapons seized during the three-day blitz. NSW Police “We do tend to find those during these operations because we are going after the most high-risk offenders,” McKenna said.



“The most high-risk DV offenders don’t just commit domestic violence, they’re usually caught up in all sorts of crime.” Among the arrests, a 39-year-old man accused of breaching bail and an apprehended domestic violence order when allegedly assaulting and choking a 26-year-old woman while armed with a pistol as he detained her at a Coraki home in the NSW Northern Rivers earlier this month. He was arrested at a Goonellabah home on Friday afternoon. In Sydney’s west at Harris Park, a 38-year-old man was arrested on Saturday afternoon and charged with domestic violence-related common assault and carrying out a sexual act without consent. Operation Amarok is an ongoing, intelligence-led program which began in 2023, aimed at addressing domestic and family violence. Police Minister Yasmin Catley said domestic and family violence was a blight on society that officers were working hard to address.



Related Article Updated

Domestic violence Meta reinstates page dedicated to tracking the murder of women in Australia “But they’re responding at the crisis end,” she said. “We need a whole-of-community effort to call out this vile offending and help prevent it before it occurs.” McKenna said anyone experiencing domestic and family violence, or those concerned for a loved one’s safety, should contact police for support. “Our message is clear: domestic and family violence will not be tolerated, and offenders can expect to be identified, targeted and brought before the courts,” McKenna said.



“Domestic violence is and will remain our number one priority, and we don’t shy away from that because we understand that when we don’t get it right, people can die,” McKenna said. National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). Get alerts on breaking news as it happens.

World.title: I’m an air traffic controller and can explain the US shutdown better than the White House
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAviation Opinion I’m an air traffic controller and can explain the US shutdown better than the White House Geoff Fairless Aviation safety specialist November 16, 2026 — 11:43am

November 16, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For only the second time since 9/11, last Saturday saw the temporary suspension of all flight departures in the United States, something we in the trade call a “ground stop”. It makes sensational headlines when it happens on such a scale, but a ground stop actually occurred at Brisbane Airport last Wednesday, when severe thunderstorms held aircraft on the ground in other locations around Australia so as not to create unsafe congestion in the air. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin praised Donald Trump while providing an update on the cause of the shutdown. AP Photo/Alex Brandon A ground stop is a relatively simple mechanism that can be used by Air Traffic Control (ATC) to immediately take pressure off the controllers dealing with aircraft in the air. Ground stops happen all over the world from time to time. Airservices Australia, our equivalent of the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), routinely uses a ground-stop at Sydney Airport when the tower assesses that the airport will break the 70 aircraft movements an hour imposed by the federal government. Arrivals continue, but departures stop until the clock ticks over to the next hour. Facts are scarce, so conspiracy theories are flourishing, aided by the big Microsoft outage on the same day, an increase in cyberattacks and the general panic around AI. On Friday the 13th of all days! I’m here to call for calm. Essentially, the nationwide ground stop was called because the routine communication systems that connect the air traffic control centres failed. When the back-ups also failed, it was time to act.



The US has 20 ATC centres, not counting Alaska and Hawaii, compared to just two that we have in Australia – in Brisbane and Melbourne. If the controllers were handling aircraft movements but unable to communicate with colleagues, unable to hand-off aircraft from centre to centre, and potentially not able to trust their radar screens, then fast and effective action was required. A ground-stop coupled with immediate landing instructions to all aircraft is the best and safest course of action for the travelling public. Related Article Aviation An old copper wire in the bush: why the US had to shut down its airspace Information from reliable sources shows that work was being conducted by L3 Systems, a well-known provider of ATC systems. It is reported they were in the process of replacing an outdated copper wire system with newer fibre-optic material when the failure occurred. The notion that such an upgrade should have happened at a less busy time ignores that fact that, unlike the curfews imposed in some of Australia’s eastern seaboard airports, the US aviation system is 24-hour operation. Sadly, in Trumpian times, the public has lost trust in any narrative emanating from the White House briefing room. Trump only has himself to blame for that. But when Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy begin their press conference with, “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like by the organisation and team he’s put together”, it politicises a process that is, for all intents and purposes, purely an aviation event. Little wonder that people become suspicious.



Accused of not doing enough to upgrade the system during his time in charge, the previous transportation secretary under Democrat President Joe Biden, Pete Buttigieg said, “this should not be about politics” and that “when we had an outage, I didn’t stand there complaining about the Trump administration ... we got to work … I’m certain that that’s what career officials and the career day-to-day employees at FAA and USDOT [US Department of Transport] are doing.” Buttigieg called for transparency and said that he did not know why back-up systems did not operate, but the very “dedicated public servants” of the FAA will be working hard on the problem and we should wait for the officials to tell us what happened. Good advice for us all. View post on X Some are speculating that very little money was spent on the system by Biden. Others say that Elon Musk and his DOGE cut all of the funds. Also in play is the theory that a new AI system called the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) had gone berserk. But political statements by presidential appointees blaming Congress for not providing enough money to keep things running do not make sense when the Congress is, or at least was until the midterms, controlled by the Republicans.



The state of US politics and suspicion of AI systems means the public is loath to believe that such a critical failure can be explained in simple terms. But I believe we should take all theories other than a systems upgrade gone wrong with a pinch of salt, and rely on the National Transportation Safety Board to eventually tell us what really occurred. Yes, eventually. I know no one likes to wait any more, but wait we must if we want to learn lessons rather than entrench mistakes. Geoff Fairless is a retired air traffic controller, a CASA aviation safety inspector and aviation safety and risk management specialist.
