World.title: The inner west Sydney suburb with the smallest gender pay gap – and the area men earn 50 per cent more than women
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPay The inner west Sydney suburb with the smallest gender pay gap – and the area men earn 50 per cent more than women Matt Wade and Craig Butt November 16, 2026 — 11:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Men earn 40 to 50 per cent more than women across a swath of Sydney suburbs from the city’s north shore to the outer south-west, but the male income premium narrows to single digits in one pocket of the inner west. Analysis of official personal income data by this masthead casts fresh light on differences in the earnings of men and women across Sydney. The biggest gender income gap was at Wollondilly in the city’s outer south-west, where the median male income of $78,055 a year was 52.5 per cent more than the female median of $51,191. The next biggest gender gap was in neighbouring Camden, where the male income premium was 46 per cent, while at Rouse Hill-McGraths Hill in the city’s north-west the male median income was 45.8 per cent higher than for women.



A lack of employment opportunities is a key reason for the yawning income gap between men and women in west and south-western Sydney. Alison Holloway, an economic geographer and partner at consultancy firm SGS Economics and Planning, said women in outer suburbs are often forced to take relatively low paid jobs, which they are overqualified for, so they can be close to home and available for caring and other domestic duties. “Those gender differences are largely because women are juggling work and caring responsibilities and that often limits how far they’re able to travel for employment,” she said. “Women are often just as qualified as men, but they don’t always have the same access to opportunities.”



Holloway’s research shows well-qualified women in outer suburbs often have job options at major employment hubs, such as the CBD, but do not take them because of the distance, the cost of travel and a lack of reliable transport options. “They just can’t risk not being able to get back for things like children’s pickups and their home responsibilities,” she said. Economists have described this effect as a “spatial leash” that suppresses the earnings of female workers because they are limited to jobs relatively close to their place of residence, which are often low paid. The median annual income for Sydney men is 27.4 per cent more than for women. Louie Douvis There are also substantial gender income gaps across affluent northern suburbs: in Pittwater the median male income was 43.6 per cent higher than for women; in Ku-ring-gai the male income premium was 42.4 per cent; and in Baulkham Hills the gap was 42.2 per cent.



KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said one reason for this pattern is mothers in those areas do not need to work as much because of high incomes of their male partners. Related Article Exclusive

Pay What do Sydneysiders in your area, and age group, earn? “In Sydney’s north shore and north-west many households can rely on the husband’s high wage to get by,” he said. Throughout Greater Sydney the median annual income for men was $70,343 and for women it was $55,209 – a gap of $15,134, or 27.4 per cent. The median is the middle value of all incomes so includes full-time and part-time workers. The analysis shows that in 10 of the 46 statistical districts that make up Greater Sydney, the median income for men is over 40 per cent more than for women.



However, Sydney’s gender income gap is smaller than some other capital cities – in Melbourne men enjoy a 31 per cent premium. Sydney’s smallest gender income gap was in Marrickville-Sydenham-Petersham where the median male income of $77,120 was only 7.7 per cent higher than the median female income of $71,649. “In that Marrickville-Sydenham-Petersham area you’ve got a lot of professional people working in sectors which pay roughly the same,” Rawnsley said. The narrowest gender income gap measured in dollars was in Auburn where the male median income was $4743 more than for women. In the Canterbury district the gender income gap was only a little bigger at $4782. The analysis also revealed how incomes vary by age and sex.



Male earnings rise sharply from the mid-30s, but for women, the increase at that stage of life is much more subdued. Among 25 to 34-year-olds there are two districts out of the 46 in Greater Sydney where the median income for men is more than 40 per cent that of women, but among 35-44 year-olds this rises to 28 districts. A key reason for this difference is a high share of part-time work among women with children. Holloway says the tendency for women to switch to part-time work, or leave the workforce, when their children are young has lasting financial consequences.



“Once you lose that time in employment when children are young – when you might be working part-time or less – you lose future earning capacity as well,” she said. The top three areas for female median income were Leichhardt, North Sydney-Mosman and Marrickville-Sydenham-Petersham. Gender income gaps also vary widely by age group and location. The biggest disparity was among those aged 45 to 54 years in the Manly area where the median income for men was 79.2 per cent – or $87,666 – more than for women. The narrowest gender income gap of any area and age group was in the 25 to 34-year-old cohort in Canterbury where the median male income was only 1.4 per cent – or $752 – more than for females.



Holloway said employment opportunities for women should be “front and centre” in urban planning decisions amid the rush to lift housing supply in Sydney. “If we can build a city where women are better able to match their skills with the right jobs, then that will be a benefit for the whole economy and for the whole city,” she said. The analysis draws on ABS personal income data for local area statistical districts; it does not include assets owned by individuals, such as housing and shares. Also, it doesn’t distinguish between part-time and full-time workers, which is one factor in the gap between men and women, since women are more likely to work part-time than men. The data is for 2022-23, the most recent year available. Throughout Greater Sydney the median annual income for all earners was $62,180.

World.title: The Jensen Huang affair is a tawdry story, but it’s laced with good news for us all
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAI Opinion The Jensen Huang affair is a tawdry story, but it’s laced with good news for us all Toby Ralph CEO at The Ad Department November 16, 2026 — 11:32am

November 16, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

CEO means chief executive officer. The job involves allocating capital, choosing people and making decisions that increase the value of a business. It does not ordinarily mean chief erotic officer, a position generally absent from the organisational chart, though not always from the organisation. Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has brought these competing job descriptions into unfortunate proximity. Having apologised for infidelity, he resigned amid reporting on relationships and questions about what he’d told company leaders. He seemingly misled senior colleagues about his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. Allegations that she worked for Chinese intelligence remain unproven; Beijing denies them, and they have not been independently verified. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang pictured at a Shanghai restaurant. If two consenting adults conduct a private relationship without coercion, favouritism, company money or business consequences, I struggle to see why shareholders expect visiting rights to the bedroom. What they do with their bits is quite literally their affair. The complications arrive when realms overlap. A relationship with a subordinate, which The New York Times is reporting Huang also indulged in, can affect promotions, complaints and whether anyone feels safe saying no. A relationship involving a suspected intelligence operative warrants scrutiny because secrets and security could be involved.



Related Article Executive shake-up ‘I don’t care’: Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO Nvidia is a curious word. Its name appears to draw on invidia – the Latin for envy. It isn’t actually an acronym, although “Net Value Implodes During Intimate Adventures” now suggests itself. A little cumbersome for the business cards, but admirably clear about the investment risks. The company’s market-value has been rooted too. Since its October 6 closing high it’s dropped more than $US1.8 trillion. That’s eighteen hundred billion dollars. That decline began before the scandal broke, however. Attributing the entire loss to Huang’s private activities would be accounting by gossip. Beneath public prurience sits a worthwhile question: how much of a chief executive does a company actually employ? Their judgment, certainly. Their working time, leadership and ability to distinguish a promising opportunity from an approaching catastrophe. Does it also employ their marriage? Their weekends? The entire troublesome acreage of their personality? If we insist that everyone managing a business must also be an exemplary spouse, we’ll substantially reduce the talent pool without necessarily improving the quarterly results. Sexual indiscretion and business proficiency are separate issues. People can be competent in one part of life and appalling in another. Anyone who has met a brilliant surgeon who can’t operate a dishwasher knows that ability isn’t distributed evenly. Nor is virtue. Plenty of devoted husbands have bankrupted companies without once taking off their wedding rings.



I don’t want my investment manager selected for their suitability to lead a church picnic. I want them to understand investment. Sure, it’d be nice if they’re pleasant to their spouse, but I wouldn’t authorise a management fee for checking. Related Article Updated

Executive shake-up Jensen Huang eyes shock Nvidia return: report The defence of privacy nevertheless has limits. A consensual affair outside work is one thing. A relationship with someone whose career you control, an undisclosed business conflict, or misleading your own company’s lawyers is another. Such questions belong in the boardroom because they concern power, judgment and whether anyone can believe what the boss tells them. A board can reasonably decide that someone who deceives it is no longer suitable to lead the business. It needn’t commission a theological inquiry into adultery. Then there’s the wonderfully inconsistent public tribunal. Donald Trump was found liable by a civil jury for sexually abusing and defaming E. Jean Carroll. He nevertheless returned to the presidency. It seems the public has different recruitment criteria for someone running a technology company and someone running the country with the codes to its nuclear weapons.



A board fears a scandal will damage the brand. A politician can make the scandal part of the brand, and sell more hats. This doesn’t excuse Huang. Trump’s conduct isn’t a transferable indemnity policy. The other car going faster doesn’t excuse a speeding ticket. But it does make the public solemnity rather difficult to swallow. Do we sometimes punish an available offender with extra enthusiasm because we’re frustrated by people who seem beyond punishment? I suspect we do. Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump Can Trump survive a Stormy sex scandal? Just ask Bill Clinton Nick Bryant Journalist and author Anger surrounding Jeffrey Epstein and demands for accountability don’t evaporate when institutions fail to satisfy them. Appetite remains, then a conspicuous executive supplies a face, a fortune and a sufficiently humiliating story. That suspicion isn’t proof of what motivates any particular board. Nor is being named in somebody’s address book proof of wrongdoing. We should remember both things before raising the gallows. Other executives will be nervous: those with undisclosed workplace relationships, boards that have avoided awkward questions, assistants whose calendars look like evidence registers. Some observers may privately envy the adventure. Others will simply be grateful their worst conference decision was karaoke. Meanwhile, corporate communications reaches for its emergency vocabulary. Deep disappointment. Personal reflection. A difficult decision. Commitment to values. No press release explains they thought they could ride this out until they saw the photos. Jensen Huang saw what was coming and, unusually, took a quick clean bullet. Having $145 billion in the bank made it easier. He can still afford Netflix.



I want chief executives judged on whether they can be trusted with the company: its money, its people, its information and its future. Private behaviour becomes the company’s business when it puts those things at risk. That’s a demanding standard. It should be. It’s also rather more useful than appointing the board to supervise the nation’s bedrooms. But good news lurks in this tawdry yarn. There’s no shortage of speculation about AI taking over the world, trashing employment as we know it and possibly eliminating Homo sapiens altogether should we prove too troublesome. Reassuringly its masters remain steadfastly human. Toby Ralph is CEO at The Ad Department, a marketer and market researcher specialising in persuasion who sits on a few boards. Contact him at toby@tobyralph.com.au

World.title: Back up and running: Cancelled collision sport gets green light from regulator
World.content:
Exclusive SportSporting rules Back up and running: Cancelled collision sport gets green light from regulator Frances Howe November 16, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

How do you legitimise a sport which involves two men running at each other at high speed, seeking to cause as much damage as possible to the other party? Which health experts have repeatedly warned could be life-threatening – and in one example was life-ending? For starters, you need a permit. Tremaine Fernandez, photographed in his office, founded Run Nation Championship after trying to acquire a backyard competition. Wolter Peeters Inside a complex of small warehouses in the inner-city Sydney suburb of Alexandria sit the Run Nation Championship (RNC) headquarters. In one of the units, Tremaine Fernandez is preparing for the competition’s next event, on November 28 – which will take place only after a court temporarily prevented it being held. Fernandez appeared in September as a witness in a case he brought against the state regulator for combat sport in the NSW Supreme Court, in a bid to overturn its decision to cancel the fourth edition of the competition. His case was unsuccessful.



But outside the court, Fernandez told reporters RNC wasn’t going anywhere, and instead vowed to work with the authority to gain a permit to hold the event. That has now been obtained, this masthead can reveal, and the Run Nation Championship is good to go. “I think a lot of outsiders looking in get brought in by the hysteria and some of the headlines, which is ‘sport to be banned’ or ‘unsafe’,” Fernandez said. “The Supreme Court hearing was about regulation, not about safety.” Former NRL player and RNC managing partner, Sandor Earle, and founder Tremaine Fernandez arrive at the NSW Supreme Court with their legal team. Dominic Lorrimer Fernandez, though, is not naive to the criticisms directed at RNC. Instead, he says, he shares many of the same concerns about unregulated, backyard versions of the sport, even though an event like it is what drew him into investing in the first place. Fernandez did not create the concept of two men running at each other. The internet trend known as “run it straight” started off as a backyard game across Australia and New Zealand, with videos gaining viral popularity.



When Fernandez tried to acquire the rights to a backyard competition, its founders opposed his vision of turning it into a global sport. “I wanted to institutionalise it,” he said. “Change up the rules completely, bring in the safety protocols that we’ve had since the start. Take it from a spectacle to a sport.” Tremaine Fernandez speaks to reporters outside the NSW Supreme Court next to Sandor Earl. They promise that RNC will return with a permit. Dominic Lorrimer As “run it straight” videos generated millions of views, critical comments started filling their comment sections, too. The backlash increased after the death of a 19-year-old man, Ryan Sattherwaite, in New Zealand after he and his friends participated in the trend at a birthday party in a park.



“The death in New Zealand was horrible,” Fernandez said. “From the best of my knowledge, I think it happened at a party or something like that. But it was from these guys who are running the backyard versions at a viral level. I disagree with how those events were run. It’s the reason I couldn’t get into business with them.” While Fernandez says he has enforced rigorous safety protocols since creating his own rule book in 2025, RNC hasn’t been without scares of its own. A clip from Run Nation Championship’s first event. Run Nation At his second event, a collision resulted in both participants being knocked unconscious. Footage of the two men lying on the running track was clipped and posted on Instagram, where it generated 37.5 million views. “We had a 20 per cent circa concussion rate,” Fernandez says of that event. “Too high. It was also a little bit sickening. I saw the footage and I said, ‘How many times could an athlete do this?’”



Fernandez said he consulted sports scientists who recommended shortening the distance each participant runs from to slow them at the point of collision. Fernandez claims this change, combined with safety protocols enforced by RNC organisers from the outset, have made RNC the safest “run it”-style competition in the country. It’s also why he’s not concerned about the potential for future lawsuits brought by RNC athletes that could replicate those in other codes in Australia and overseas. Tremaine Fernandez says Run Nation Championship has greater safety protocols than the NRL and AFL. Wolter Peeters He says the organisation is actively seeking to introduce more ways to test brain health, including mouth guards trialled by World Rugby which light up when there is heavy contact with the head, and has one of the most conservative concussion protocols in Australian sport. The return to play period after a concussion in RNC is 90 days (similar to professional boxing guidelines), compared to 11 days in the NRL and12 days in the AFL.



“Would I call it unsafe? I think every sport’s got risk, any contact sport has risk,” Fernandez said. “It’s how you handle it. What protocols do you have in place? And I think we are arguably the best in the country at doing it. “I don’t think the NRL does a better job than us, I don’t think boxing does a better job than us – or the AFL. We are using technology that is used in Formula One and the NFL which guys here are just starting to use, and we’re using it from day one.” At their last event, RNC3, of more than 80 individual runners, not a single athlete became concussed, Fernandez says. At a recent event in Queensland, he said there were no knockouts and one grade one concussion from illegal shoulder contact. “These are now professional athletes,” Fernandez says. “You shouldn’t be trying this at home. This is something that is regulated, it’s in a controlled arena, there’s a referee, and they’ve been having a 12-week camp to get to this moment.” On November 6, Fernandez received a permit from the Combat Sports Authority (CSA) to hold the RNC4 event.



His athletes and promoters will now be included on the CSA’s register, and subject to additional health checks including serology tests. CSA officials will also attend future events. Related Article Updated

Sporting rules Judge makes big call on what is a ‘combat sport’ Although Fernandez is excited about RNC becoming a regulated sport (“we want to set the bar so high that these backyard guys can’t get into it”), he said the existing legislation that governs combat sports in NSW needs to change to accommodate new sports. His view is shared by the NSW Office of Sport, which referred the legislation to a Parliamentary Inquiry. Its first hearings took place earlier this month. “We’re working with the authority at the moment and they are being fantastic,” he said. “There’s a really great relationship being formed. However, it’s really clear to us that a lot has to change in its current framework to accommodate us.”



Collision sports, including RNC, will be considered alongside other emerging combat sports including face-slapping and bare-knuckle boxing. But Fernandez believes his competition is worlds away from the others. “The rules in bare knuckle are to constantly deliver blows to the head and, even if you’re opponent looks unconscious, to keep going until the referee stops you,” he said. “We don’t have that in our sport. Our sport is built on trying to perfect a technique.” News, results and expert analysis from the week in sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘The obvious place’: Inside the push to turn Sydney ambulance depot into arts hub
World.content:
CultureArt & designCity life ‘The obvious place’: Inside the push to turn Sydney ambulance depot into arts hub Linda Morris November 16, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. An all-but-vacated ambulance depot in the corner of a 61-hectare inner-city heritage park could become a permanent visual arts centre under a community-led proposal to revive some of the parkland’s abandoned buildings. As demolition gets under way on nine neglected buildings at the heart of the historic Rozelle site, the Glebe Art Society – which runs an annual exhibition showcasing more than 200 local artists – has teamed up with social-impact architecture firm Vigilanti to reimagine the former depot as an arts precinct featuring a gallery, open studios and an outdoor sculpture garden. The Ambulance Depot at Callan Park reimagined as an arts centre. Vigilanti NSW Ambulance operated out of the six-building complex in the south-west corner of Callan Park for 40 years before relocating all but its call centre operations to Sydney Olympic Park. The site, on the corner of Balmain and Wharf roads, has sat largely unoccupied since, save for minor call centre operations. The unsolicited plan is backed by Greens MP for Balmain Kobi Shetty, the Inner West Creative Network and its 400 members, as well as Friends of Callan Park, which has received two briefings and given the plan its “strong support” and noted Writing NSW already occupies Garry Owen House, a heritage-listed Georgian manor inside Callan Park.



Vigilanti founder Eddie Ma said: “Right now, the former NSW Ambulance headquarters is a block of six buildings sitting empty, and it’s really a shame for this prime public land. “We could turn it quickly and efficiently into a community art gallery that showcases local artists and creative businesses. Outside that initial phase-one building, there are five other buildings that could be turned into artist-in-residence workshops, kids’ art classes, and other creative pursuits like glassmaking.” Artist Peter Griffen (centre) with Greens MP Kobi Shetty (left), Tim Stackpool and Jenny Grant. Jessica Hromas Abstract painter and Glebe Art Society president Peter Griffen has spent four years lobbying for a dedicated regional-style arts centre in the inner west, comparable to Lane Cove Gallery or Hazelhurst Arts Centre, after earlier pitches for the old Leichhardt Town Hall and White Bay Power Station failed. Despite the inner west boasting the highest per-capita concentration of creatives in NSW, Griffen said it lacked a central public exhibition hub. Volunteers would initially run the not-for-profit centre until external funding could be secured.



“Everybody agrees it’s a good idea, and when I say Callan Park, they say it’s the obvious place,” Griffen said. “It’s accessible, it’s on a main road, it has parking and a bus network. For a long time, this was a mental health facility, and art therapy has long been a standard way of treating people. Setting this up in Callan Park feels like a natural flow-on.” The pitch comes amid broader changes under the 10-year Callan Park Plan of Management, alongside works on a new tidal pool, a community football clubhouse and Bay Run upgrades. Under the Callan Park (Special Provisions) Act, the land cannot be sold, uses are restricted to health, community, or education, and development must stay within existing building footprints. Shetty, who brought the groups together, said she would press the Minns government to back the model. “There’s a desperate need for artist working spaces because we’re seeing more and more gentrification and the loss of light industrial spaces,” she said. “We want to make sure when Ambulance does vacate the site entirely that it is not just another building left with no purpose and left to demolition by neglect.” Vigilanti’s concept designs lay out a staged transformation across the six interlocking buildings around a central courtyard. The southern building facing Balmain Road would become the primary gallery opening onto a sculpture garden, the western wing would house open studios, residencies, and education rooms, and a northern training building would become classrooms.



Editor's pick Development Sydney’s answer to the Louvre? Battle brews over what to do with Victoria Barracks Ma estimated the complex could be stripped back and opened within six to 12 months, noting routine asbestos and lead paint hazards were manageable if addressed soon. “My greatest fear is that these buildings are left in a bureaucratic process and nothing happens for years – demolition by neglect,” Ma said. “The longer we leave it without proper care and maintenance, the more likely it becomes a hazard and more expensive to remediate later.” Planning and Public Spaces Minister Paul Scully and NSW Ambulance have been contacted for comment. World.title: Trump has lost the ‘podcast bros’, says Joe Rogan
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump Trump has lost the ‘podcast bros’, says Joe Rogan Alexandra Snow November 16, 2026 — 11:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Donald Trump has lost the backing of the “podcast bros”, Joe Rogan has said after young people fuelled the blue wave that swept through the US midterm elections. The world’s most-listened-to podcaster endorsed Trump for the 2024 election, but has remained relatively quiet about politics since Trump took office for a second term as US president. Joe Rogan has cooled on Donald Trump since his 2024 endorsement. AP In his show The Joe Rogan Experience, the podcaster blamed the Republicans’ midterms drubbing on the Iran war and hard-line immigration raids. “They didn’t just lose the podcast bros, they lost most of the country,” Rogan told listeners on Friday.



Related Article Trump's America ‘It’s all showbusiness’: Meet the publicist behind America’s political influencers He added that support for Trump had waned when the administration began “a war that no one wants to be in”. US Vice President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war for his party’s midterms defeat. Rogan has been uneasy about White House policies since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in March. “It just seems so insane,” Rogan said at the time. “He ran on no more wars: end these stupid, senseless wars. And then we have one.”



On Friday, the podcaster also attributed the midterm elections loss to the administration putting “militarised police in the streets wearing masks”, referring to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He said the ICE raids had targeted “nice, good people that are loved by the community, but they just don’t have the right paperwork”. Rogan says the conflict with Iran, following Trump’s 2024 pledge of no more foreign wars, has cost the Republicans dearly. AP Photo/Alex Brandon The “manosphere” world of podcasters helped Trump and his allies reach young male voters for the 2024 election. They touted the importance of preserving “biblically based” family values and male supremacy.



However, some podcasters have been left feeling alienated by the Trump administration and are providing the US president with less airtime. Related Article US midterms Midterms launch wave of historic firsts across the United States This resulted in the young, male Republican vote collapsing in the midterm elections. Men under 30 shifted nearly 40 points towards the Democrats, after a 23-point shift toward Republicans in the 2024 election. The swing back to blue has been pinned on grievances including inflation and the cost of living, the war in Iran and Republicans’ failure to prosecute those named in the Epstein files.



Young Latino men also swung sharply toward Democrats, as the hard line on immigration became increasingly contentious. Some of these men, who were previously enmeshed in the “podcast bro” world, now describe themselves as being “black-pilled” and see voting as pointless altogether. The “pill” metaphor originates from The Matrix, the 1999 sci-fi film, and has been adopted by online communities to describe stages of radicalisation. The concept of men being “black-pilled” refers to people moving past the belief that society is skewed against men into total nihilism, arguing that efforts to improve the world are completely futile. Following the devastating midterm losses, the Trump administration is trying to win back young male voters.

World.title: ‘Stop the delays’: Wong, counterparts blast Israel over Gaza humanitarian crisis
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Stop the delays’: Wong, counterparts blast Israel over Gaza humanitarian crisis Matthew Knott November 16, 2026 — 11:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Australia has united with Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom to urge Israel to allow a rapid expansion of aid and essential supplies into Gaza, as cold weather and heavy rains exacerbate an already desperate humanitarian situation. Images of flooded tent cities and reports of young Palestinian children dying in recent days have sparked renewed international attention on Gaza a year after a supposed ceasefire between Israel and Hamas came into effect. Foreign Minister Penny Wong and her three counterparts said in a statement on Monday that “the humanitarian situation on the ground is dire” as winter takes hold in Gaza. Foreign Minister Penny Wong says Israel must do more to allow the entry of crucial supplies into Gaza. Alex Ellinghausen “People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance. Yet 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border and prevented from entering Gaza,” the foreign ministers said.



“This situation is entirely reversible – and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in.” The foreign ministers called for the Israeli government “to stop the delays now and allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza”. “The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in,” they said. “Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late.” Displaced Palestinian children repair tents damaged by heavy rain in Gaza City earlier this month. AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi The Israeli embassy in Canberra was approached for comment.



The fresh international focus on Gaza comes as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu tries to remain in office despite his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, receiving a mandate to try to form a governing coalition following last month’s elections. The European Union earlier called for Israel to allow more supplies to enter Gaza, declaring that severe flooding and cold weather “are further aggravating the living conditions of an already exhausted population, exacerbating unsafe conditions and human suffering”. A Palestinian woman with a water container during heavy rainfall. Bloomberg Israel’s foreign ministry responded by labelling the European statement “completely unbalanced” and saying Hamas, which governs much of the strip, must be held responsible for refusing to disarm and cede control of Gaza. Asmahan Abdalraheem, a 25-year-old Palestinian accounting graduate in Gaza, said: “Winter is coming and we are drowning in tents.”



Three children aged between four and eight were killed with their mother when a dune collapsed on their tent in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, after heavy rainfall, UNICEF, the United Nations children’s fund, reported last week. Related Article Updated

World elections The Israeli elections have produced a deadlock. Here’s what happens now “Families are living without the most basic conditions for their safety, health and dignity,” UNICEF executive director Catherine Russell said. “More children could die without proper shelter, working water and sanitation systems, and the equipment needed to restore essential services. The worst of winter is yet to come.” An estimated 65 per cent of Gaza’s population, about 1.4 million people, live in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN’s aid co-ordination office



The Board of Peace, created by US President Donald Trump, last week called on Israel to allow the entry of essential materials for temporary shelter, water and sanitation infrastructure, waste management, drainage and sewage removal. The Board of Peace said the threat posed by cold and unsafe conditions represented “an immediate humanitarian emergency”, labelling Israel’s efforts to allow the entry of supplies into Gaza “insufficient” and calling for Hamas to disarm. An Israeli air strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza last week killed six people and attracted renewed international criticism. Israel said it was targeting a top Hamas brigade commander who is believed to have survived the strike. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Weapons seized, hundreds arrested during statewide DV blitz Jack Gramenz Updated November 16, 2026 — 11:47am ,first published November 16, 2026 — 8:28am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Hundreds of people have been arrested during a three-day blitz targeting alleged domestic violence offending in the state as police seize weapons and crack down on people allegedly breaching court orders from jail. The NSW Police Operation Amarok, targeting high-risk domestic violence offenders, led to 681 arrests and 1594 charges being laid. Police checked compliance with 11,375 apprehended domestic violence orders, finding 283 breaches. A 38-year-old man is arrested during a NSW Police Operation Amarok blitz targeting alleged domestic violence offences. NSW Police NSW Police Assistant Commissioner Peter McKenna said a number of people accused of breaching the orders were already in jail. “Just because someone’s in custody doesn’t mean they’re also out of our sights,” McKenna said on Monday.



“We actually shut down the [Metropolitan Remand and Reception Centre at Silverwater] with their cooperation and identified a number of persons in custody who were breaching AVOs … there’s nowhere to hide.” Officers also seized 73 firearms and 21 other weapons during the blitz between Thursday and Saturday last week. Police regularly seize weapons during Operation Amarok activities. A knife found by police during Operation Amarok was among 73 firearms and 21 other weapons seized during the three-day blitz. NSW Police “We do tend to find those during these operations because we are going after the most high-risk offenders,” McKenna said.



“The most high-risk DV offenders don’t just commit domestic violence, they’re usually caught up in all sorts of crime.” Among the arrests, a 39-year-old man accused of breaching bail and an apprehended domestic violence order when allegedly assaulting and choking a 26-year-old woman while armed with a pistol as he detained her at a Coraki home in the NSW Northern Rivers earlier this month. He was arrested at a Goonellabah home on Friday afternoon. In Sydney’s west at Harris Park, a 38-year-old man was arrested on Saturday afternoon and charged with domestic violence-related common assault and carrying out a sexual act without consent. Operation Amarok is an ongoing, intelligence-led program which began in 2023, aimed at addressing domestic and family violence. Police Minister Yasmin Catley said domestic and family violence was a blight on society that officers were working hard to address.



Related Article Updated

Domestic violence Meta reinstates page dedicated to tracking the murder of women in Australia “But they’re responding at the crisis end,” she said. “We need a whole-of-community effort to call out this vile offending and help prevent it before it occurs.” McKenna said anyone experiencing domestic and family violence, or those concerned for a loved one’s safety, should contact police for support. “Our message is clear: domestic and family violence will not be tolerated, and offenders can expect to be identified, targeted and brought before the courts,” McKenna said.



“Domestic violence is and will remain our number one priority, and we don’t shy away from that because we understand that when we don’t get it right, people can die,” McKenna said. World.title: I’m an air traffic controller and can explain the US shutdown better than the White House
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaAviation Opinion I’m an air traffic controller and can explain the US shutdown better than the White House Geoff Fairless Aviation safety specialist November 16, 2026 — 11:43am

November 16, 2026 — 11:43am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For only the second time since 9/11, last Saturday saw the temporary suspension of all flight departures in the United States, something we in the trade call a “ground stop”. It makes sensational headlines when it happens on such a scale, but a ground stop actually occurred at Brisbane Airport last Wednesday, when severe thunderstorms held aircraft on the ground in other locations around Australia so as not to create unsafe congestion in the air. Transport Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin praised Donald Trump while providing an update on the cause of the shutdown. AP Photo/Alex Brandon A ground stop is a relatively simple mechanism that can be used by Air Traffic Control (ATC) to immediately take pressure off the controllers dealing with aircraft in the air. Ground stops happen all over the world from time to time. Airservices Australia, our equivalent of the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), routinely uses a ground-stop at Sydney Airport when the tower assesses that the airport will break the 70 aircraft movements an hour imposed by the federal government. Arrivals continue, but departures stop until the clock ticks over to the next hour. Facts are scarce, so conspiracy theories are flourishing, aided by the big Microsoft outage on the same day, an increase in cyberattacks and the general panic around AI. On Friday the 13th of all days! I’m here to call for calm. Essentially, the nationwide ground stop was called because the routine communication systems that connect the air traffic control centres failed. When the back-ups also failed, it was time to act.



The US has 20 ATC centres, not counting Alaska and Hawaii, compared to just two that we have in Australia – in Brisbane and Melbourne. If the controllers were handling aircraft movements but unable to communicate with colleagues, unable to hand-off aircraft from centre to centre, and potentially not able to trust their radar screens, then fast and effective action was required. A ground-stop coupled with immediate landing instructions to all aircraft is the best and safest course of action for the travelling public. Related Article Aviation An old copper wire in the bush: why the US had to shut down its airspace Information from reliable sources shows that work was being conducted by L3 Systems, a well-known provider of ATC systems. It is reported they were in the process of replacing an outdated copper wire system with newer fibre-optic material when the failure occurred. The notion that such an upgrade should have happened at a less busy time ignores that fact that, unlike the curfews imposed in some of Australia’s eastern seaboard airports, the US aviation system is 24-hour operation. Sadly, in Trumpian times, the public has lost trust in any narrative emanating from the White House briefing room. Trump only has himself to blame for that. But when Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy begin their press conference with, “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like by the organisation and team he’s put together”, it politicises a process that is, for all intents and purposes, purely an aviation event. Little wonder that people become suspicious.



Accused of not doing enough to upgrade the system during his time in charge, the previous transportation secretary under Democrat President Joe Biden, Pete Buttigieg said, “this should not be about politics” and that “when we had an outage, I didn’t stand there complaining about the Trump administration ... we got to work … I’m certain that that’s what career officials and the career day-to-day employees at FAA and USDOT [US Department of Transport] are doing.” Buttigieg called for transparency and said that he did not know why back-up systems did not operate, but the very “dedicated public servants” of the FAA will be working hard on the problem and we should wait for the officials to tell us what happened. Good advice for us all. View post on X Some are speculating that very little money was spent on the system by Biden. Others say that Elon Musk and his DOGE cut all of the funds. Also in play is the theory that a new AI system called the Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) had gone berserk. But political statements by presidential appointees blaming Congress for not providing enough money to keep things running do not make sense when the Congress is, or at least was until the midterms, controlled by the Republicans.



The state of US politics and suspicion of AI systems means the public is loath to believe that such a critical failure can be explained in simple terms. But I believe we should take all theories other than a systems upgrade gone wrong with a pinch of salt, and rely on the National Transportation Safety Board to eventually tell us what really occurred. Yes, eventually. I know no one likes to wait any more, but wait we must if we want to learn lessons rather than entrench mistakes. Geoff Fairless is a retired air traffic controller, a CASA aviation safety inspector and aviation safety and risk management specialist. World.title: The inner west Sydney suburb with the smallest gender pay gap – and the area men earn 50 per cent more than women
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWPay The inner west Sydney suburb with the smallest gender pay gap – and the area men earn 50 per cent more than women Matt Wade and Craig Butt November 16, 2026 — 11:40am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Men earn 40 to 50 per cent more than women across a swath of Sydney suburbs from the city’s north shore to the outer south-west, but the male income premium narrows to single digits in one pocket of the inner west. Analysis of official personal income data by this masthead casts fresh light on differences in the earnings of men and women across Sydney. The biggest gender income gap was at Wollondilly in the city’s outer south-west, where the median male income of $78,055 a year was 52.5 per cent more than the female median of $51,191. The next biggest gender gap was in neighbouring Camden, where the male income premium was 46 per cent, while at Rouse Hill-McGraths Hill in the city’s north-west the male median income was 45.8 per cent higher than for women.



A lack of employment opportunities is a key reason for the yawning income gap between men and women in west and south-western Sydney. Alison Holloway, an economic geographer and partner at consultancy firm SGS Economics and Planning, said women in outer suburbs are often forced to take relatively low paid jobs, which they are overqualified for, so they can be close to home and available for caring and other domestic duties. “Those gender differences are largely because women are juggling work and caring responsibilities and that often limits how far they’re able to travel for employment,” she said. “Women are often just as qualified as men, but they don’t always have the same access to opportunities.”



Holloway’s research shows well-qualified women in outer suburbs often have job options at major employment hubs, such as the CBD, but do not take them because of the distance, the cost of travel and a lack of reliable transport options. “They just can’t risk not being able to get back for things like children’s pickups and their home responsibilities,” she said. Economists have described this effect as a “spatial leash” that suppresses the earnings of female workers because they are limited to jobs relatively close to their place of residence, which are often low paid. The median annual income for Sydney men is 27.4 per cent more than for women. Louie Douvis There are also substantial gender income gaps across affluent northern suburbs: in Pittwater the median male income was 43.6 per cent higher than for women; in Ku-ring-gai the male income premium was 42.4 per cent; and in Baulkham Hills the gap was 42.2 per cent.



KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley said one reason for this pattern is mothers in those areas do not need to work as much because of high incomes of their male partners. Related Article Exclusive

Pay What do Sydneysiders in your area, and age group, earn? “In Sydney’s north shore and north-west many households can rely on the husband’s high wage to get by,” he said. Throughout Greater Sydney the median annual income for men was $70,343 and for women it was $55,209 – a gap of $15,134, or 27.4 per cent. The median is the middle value of all incomes so includes full-time and part-time workers. The analysis shows that in 10 of the 46 statistical districts that make up Greater Sydney, the median income for men is over 40 per cent more than for women.



However, Sydney’s gender income gap is smaller than some other capital cities – in Melbourne men enjoy a 31 per cent premium. Sydney’s smallest gender income gap was in Marrickville-Sydenham-Petersham where the median male income of $77,120 was only 7.7 per cent higher than the median female income of $71,649. “In that Marrickville-Sydenham-Petersham area you’ve got a lot of professional people working in sectors which pay roughly the same,” Rawnsley said. The narrowest gender income gap measured in dollars was in Auburn where the male median income was $4743 more than for women. In the Canterbury district the gender income gap was only a little bigger at $4782. The analysis also revealed how incomes vary by age and sex.



Male earnings rise sharply from the mid-30s, but for women, the increase at that stage of life is much more subdued. Among 25 to 34-year-olds there are two districts out of the 46 in Greater Sydney where the median income for men is more than 40 per cent that of women, but among 35-44 year-olds this rises to 28 districts. A key reason for this difference is a high share of part-time work among women with children. Holloway says the tendency for women to switch to part-time work, or leave the workforce, when their children are young has lasting financial consequences.



“Once you lose that time in employment when children are young – when you might be working part-time or less – you lose future earning capacity as well,” she said. The top three areas for female median income were Leichhardt, North Sydney-Mosman and Marrickville-Sydenham-Petersham. Gender income gaps also vary widely by age group and location. The biggest disparity was among those aged 45 to 54 years in the Manly area where the median income for men was 79.2 per cent – or $87,666 – more than for women. The narrowest gender income gap of any area and age group was in the 25 to 34-year-old cohort in Canterbury where the median male income was only 1.4 per cent – or $752 – more than for females.



Holloway said employment opportunities for women should be “front and centre” in urban planning decisions amid the rush to lift housing supply in Sydney. “If we can build a city where women are better able to match their skills with the right jobs, then that will be a benefit for the whole economy and for the whole city,” she said. The analysis draws on ABS personal income data for local area statistical districts; it does not include assets owned by individuals, such as housing and shares. Also, it doesn’t distinguish between part-time and full-time workers, which is one factor in the gap between men and women, since women are more likely to work part-time than men. The data is for 2022-23, the most recent year available. Throughout Greater Sydney the median annual income for all earners was $62,180.

World.title: The Jensen Huang affair is a tawdry story, but it’s laced with good news for us all
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAI Opinion The Jensen Huang affair is a tawdry story, but it’s laced with good news for us all Toby Ralph CEO at The Ad Department November 16, 2026 — 11:32am

November 16, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

CEO means chief executive officer. The job involves allocating capital, choosing people and making decisions that increase the value of a business. It does not ordinarily mean chief erotic officer, a position generally absent from the organisational chart, though not always from the organisation. Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has brought these competing job descriptions into unfortunate proximity. Having apologised for infidelity, he resigned amid reporting on relationships and questions about what he’d told company leaders. He seemingly misled senior colleagues about his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang. Allegations that she worked for Chinese intelligence remain unproven; Beijing denies them, and they have not been independently verified. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang pictured at a Shanghai restaurant. If two consenting adults conduct a private relationship without coercion, favouritism, company money or business consequences, I struggle to see why shareholders expect visiting rights to the bedroom. What they do with their bits is quite literally their affair. The complications arrive when realms overlap. A relationship with a subordinate, which The New York Times is reporting Huang also indulged in, can affect promotions, complaints and whether anyone feels safe saying no. A relationship involving a suspected intelligence operative warrants scrutiny because secrets and security could be involved.



Related Article Executive shake-up ‘I don’t care’: Inside Jensen Huang’s last hours as Nvidia CEO Nvidia is a curious word. Its name appears to draw on invidia – the Latin for envy. It isn’t actually an acronym, although “Net Value Implodes During Intimate Adventures” now suggests itself. A little cumbersome for the business cards, but admirably clear about the investment risks. The company’s market-value has been rooted too. Since its October 6 closing high it’s dropped more than $US1.8 trillion. That’s eighteen hundred billion dollars. That decline began before the scandal broke, however. Attributing the entire loss to Huang’s private activities would be accounting by gossip. Beneath public prurience sits a worthwhile question: how much of a chief executive does a company actually employ? Their judgment, certainly. Their working time, leadership and ability to distinguish a promising opportunity from an approaching catastrophe. Does it also employ their marriage? Their weekends? The entire troublesome acreage of their personality? If we insist that everyone managing a business must also be an exemplary spouse, we’ll substantially reduce the talent pool without necessarily improving the quarterly results. Sexual indiscretion and business proficiency are separate issues. People can be competent in one part of life and appalling in another. Anyone who has met a brilliant surgeon who can’t operate a dishwasher knows that ability isn’t distributed evenly. Nor is virtue. Plenty of devoted husbands have bankrupted companies without once taking off their wedding rings.



I don’t want my investment manager selected for their suitability to lead a church picnic. I want them to understand investment. Sure, it’d be nice if they’re pleasant to their spouse, but I wouldn’t authorise a management fee for checking. Related Article Updated

Executive shake-up Jensen Huang eyes shock Nvidia return: report The defence of privacy nevertheless has limits. A consensual affair outside work is one thing. A relationship with someone whose career you control, an undisclosed business conflict, or misleading your own company’s lawyers is another. Such questions belong in the boardroom because they concern power, judgment and whether anyone can believe what the boss tells them. A board can reasonably decide that someone who deceives it is no longer suitable to lead the business. It needn’t commission a theological inquiry into adultery. Then there’s the wonderfully inconsistent public tribunal. Donald Trump was found liable by a civil jury for sexually abusing and defaming E. Jean Carroll. He nevertheless returned to the presidency. It seems the public has different recruitment criteria for someone running a technology company and someone running the country with the codes to its nuclear weapons.



A board fears a scandal will damage the brand. A politician can make the scandal part of the brand, and sell more hats. This doesn’t excuse Huang. Trump’s conduct isn’t a transferable indemnity policy. The other car going faster doesn’t excuse a speeding ticket. But it does make the public solemnity rather difficult to swallow. Do we sometimes punish an available offender with extra enthusiasm because we’re frustrated by people who seem beyond punishment? I suspect we do. Related Article Opinion

Donald Trump Can Trump survive a Stormy sex scandal? Just ask Bill Clinton Nick Bryant Journalist and author Anger surrounding Jeffrey Epstein and demands for accountability don’t evaporate when institutions fail to satisfy them. Appetite remains, then a conspicuous executive supplies a face, a fortune and a sufficiently humiliating story. That suspicion isn’t proof of what motivates any particular board. Nor is being named in somebody’s address book proof of wrongdoing. We should remember both things before raising the gallows. Other executives will be nervous: those with undisclosed workplace relationships, boards that have avoided awkward questions, assistants whose calendars look like evidence registers. Some observers may privately envy the adventure. Others will simply be grateful their worst conference decision was karaoke. Meanwhile, corporate communications reaches for its emergency vocabulary. Deep disappointment. Personal reflection. A difficult decision. Commitment to values. No press release explains they thought they could ride this out until they saw the photos. Jensen Huang saw what was coming and, unusually, took a quick clean bullet. Having $145 billion in the bank made it easier. He can still afford Netflix.



I want chief executives judged on whether they can be trusted with the company: its money, its people, its information and its future. Private behaviour becomes the company’s business when it puts those things at risk. That’s a demanding standard. It should be. It’s also rather more useful than appointing the board to supervise the nation’s bedrooms. But good news lurks in this tawdry yarn. There’s no shortage of speculation about AI taking over the world, trashing employment as we know it and possibly eliminating Homo sapiens altogether should we prove too troublesome. Reassuringly its masters remain steadfastly human. Toby Ralph is CEO at The Ad Department, a marketer and market researcher specialising in persuasion who sits on a few boards. Contact him at toby@tobyralph.com.au

World.title: Back up and running: Cancelled collision sport gets green light from regulator
World.content:
Exclusive SportSporting rules Back up and running: Cancelled collision sport gets green light from regulator Frances Howe November 16, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

How do you legitimise a sport which involves two men running at each other at high speed, seeking to cause as much damage as possible to the other party? Which health experts have repeatedly warned could be life-threatening – and in one example was life-ending? For starters, you need a permit. Tremaine Fernandez, photographed in his office, founded Run Nation Championship after trying to acquire a backyard competition. Wolter Peeters Inside a complex of small warehouses in the inner-city Sydney suburb of Alexandria sit the Run Nation Championship (RNC) headquarters. In one of the units, Tremaine Fernandez is preparing for the competition’s next event, on November 28 – which will take place only after a court temporarily prevented it being held. Fernandez appeared in September as a witness in a case he brought against the state regulator for combat sport in the NSW Supreme Court, in a bid to overturn its decision to cancel the fourth edition of the competition. His case was unsuccessful.



But outside the court, Fernandez told reporters RNC wasn’t going anywhere, and instead vowed to work with the authority to gain a permit to hold the event. That has now been obtained, this masthead can reveal, and the Run Nation Championship is good to go. “I think a lot of outsiders looking in get brought in by the hysteria and some of the headlines, which is ‘sport to be banned’ or ‘unsafe’,” Fernandez said. “The Supreme Court hearing was about regulation, not about safety.” Former NRL player and RNC managing partner, Sandor Earle, and founder Tremaine Fernandez arrive at the NSW Supreme Court with their legal team. Dominic Lorrimer Fernandez, though, is not naive to the criticisms directed at RNC. Instead, he says, he shares many of the same concerns about unregulated, backyard versions of the sport, even though an event like it is what drew him into investing in the first place. Fernandez did not create the concept of two men running at each other. The internet trend known as “run it straight” started off as a backyard game across Australia and New Zealand, with videos gaining viral popularity.



When Fernandez tried to acquire the rights to a backyard competition, its founders opposed his vision of turning it into a global sport. “I wanted to institutionalise it,” he said. “Change up the rules completely, bring in the safety protocols that we’ve had since the start. Take it from a spectacle to a sport.” Tremaine Fernandez speaks to reporters outside the NSW Supreme Court next to Sandor Earl. They promise that RNC will return with a permit. Dominic Lorrimer As “run it straight” videos generated millions of views, critical comments started filling their comment sections, too. The backlash increased after the death of a 19-year-old man, Ryan Sattherwaite, in New Zealand after he and his friends participated in the trend at a birthday party in a park.



“The death in New Zealand was horrible,” Fernandez said. “From the best of my knowledge, I think it happened at a party or something like that. But it was from these guys who are running the backyard versions at a viral level. I disagree with how those events were run. It’s the reason I couldn’t get into business with them.” While Fernandez says he has enforced rigorous safety protocols since creating his own rule book in 2025, RNC hasn’t been without scares of its own. A clip from Run Nation Championship’s first event. Run Nation At his second event, a collision resulted in both participants being knocked unconscious. Footage of the two men lying on the running track was clipped and posted on Instagram, where it generated 37.5 million views. “We had a 20 per cent circa concussion rate,” Fernandez says of that event. “Too high. It was also a little bit sickening. I saw the footage and I said, ‘How many times could an athlete do this?’”



Fernandez said he consulted sports scientists who recommended shortening the distance each participant runs from to slow them at the point of collision. Fernandez claims this change, combined with safety protocols enforced by RNC organisers from the outset, have made RNC the safest “run it”-style competition in the country. It’s also why he’s not concerned about the potential for future lawsuits brought by RNC athletes that could replicate those in other codes in Australia and overseas. Tremaine Fernandez says Run Nation Championship has greater safety protocols than the NRL and AFL. Wolter Peeters He says the organisation is actively seeking to introduce more ways to test brain health, including mouth guards trialled by World Rugby which light up when there is heavy contact with the head, and has one of the most conservative concussion protocols in Australian sport. The return to play period after a concussion in RNC is 90 days (similar to professional boxing guidelines), compared to 11 days in the NRL and12 days in the AFL.



“Would I call it unsafe? I think every sport’s got risk, any contact sport has risk,” Fernandez said. “It’s how you handle it. What protocols do you have in place? And I think we are arguably the best in the country at doing it. “I don’t think the NRL does a better job than us, I don’t think boxing does a better job than us – or the AFL. We are using technology that is used in Formula One and the NFL which guys here are just starting to use, and we’re using it from day one.” At their last event, RNC3, of more than 80 individual runners, not a single athlete became concussed, Fernandez says. At a recent event in Queensland, he said there were no knockouts and one grade one concussion from illegal shoulder contact. “These are now professional athletes,” Fernandez says. “You shouldn’t be trying this at home. This is something that is regulated, it’s in a controlled arena, there’s a referee, and they’ve been having a 12-week camp to get to this moment.” On November 6, Fernandez received a permit from the Combat Sports Authority (CSA) to hold the RNC4 event.



His athletes and promoters will now be included on the CSA’s register, and subject to additional health checks including serology tests. CSA officials will also attend future events. Related Article Updated

Sporting rules Judge makes big call on what is a ‘combat sport’ Although Fernandez is excited about RNC becoming a regulated sport (“we want to set the bar so high that these backyard guys can’t get into it”), he said the existing legislation that governs combat sports in NSW needs to change to accommodate new sports. His view is shared by the NSW Office of Sport, which referred the legislation to a Parliamentary Inquiry. Its first hearings took place earlier this month. “We’re working with the authority at the moment and they are being fantastic,” he said. “There’s a really great relationship being formed. However, it’s really clear to us that a lot has to change in its current framework to accommodate us.”



Collision sports, including RNC, will be considered alongside other emerging combat sports including face-slapping and bare-knuckle boxing. But Fernandez believes his competition is worlds away from the others. “The rules in bare knuckle are to constantly deliver blows to the head and, even if you’re opponent looks unconscious, to keep going until the referee stops you,” he said. “We don’t have that in our sport. Our sport is built on trying to perfect a technique.” News, results and expert analysis from the week in sport sent every Friday.

World.title: ‘The obvious place’: Inside the push to turn Sydney ambulance depot into arts hub
World.content:
CultureArt & designCity life ‘The obvious place’: Inside the push to turn Sydney ambulance depot into arts hub Linda Morris November 16, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

An all-but-vacated ambulance depot in the corner of a 61-hectare inner-city heritage park could become a permanent visual arts centre under a community-led proposal to revive some of the parkland’s abandoned buildings. As demolition gets under way on nine neglected buildings at the heart of the historic Rozelle site, the Glebe Art Society – which runs an annual exhibition showcasing more than 200 local artists – has teamed up with social-impact architecture firm Vigilanti to reimagine the former depot as an arts precinct featuring a gallery, open studios and an outdoor sculpture garden. The Ambulance Depot at Callan Park reimagined as an arts centre. Vigilanti NSW Ambulance operated out of the six-building complex in the south-west corner of Callan Park for 40 years before relocating all but its call centre operations to Sydney Olympic Park. The site, on the corner of Balmain and Wharf roads, has sat largely unoccupied since, save for minor call centre operations. The unsolicited plan is backed by Greens MP for Balmain Kobi Shetty, the Inner West Creative Network and its 400 members, as well as Friends of Callan Park, which has received two briefings and given the plan its “strong support” and noted Writing NSW already occupies Garry Owen House, a heritage-listed Georgian manor inside Callan Park.



Vigilanti founder Eddie Ma said: “Right now, the former NSW Ambulance headquarters is a block of six buildings sitting empty, and it’s really a shame for this prime public land. “We could turn it quickly and efficiently into a community art gallery that showcases local artists and creative businesses. Outside that initial phase-one building, there are five other buildings that could be turned into artist-in-residence workshops, kids’ art classes, and other creative pursuits like glassmaking.” Artist Peter Griffen (centre) with Greens MP Kobi Shetty (left), Tim Stackpool and Jenny Grant. Jessica Hromas Abstract painter and Glebe Art Society president Peter Griffen has spent four years lobbying for a dedicated regional-style arts centre in the inner west, comparable to Lane Cove Gallery or Hazelhurst Arts Centre, after earlier pitches for the old Leichhardt Town Hall and White Bay Power Station failed. Despite the inner west boasting the highest per-capita concentration of creatives in NSW, Griffen said it lacked a central public exhibition hub. Volunteers would initially run the not-for-profit centre until external funding could be secured.



“Everybody agrees it’s a good idea, and when I say Callan Park, they say it’s the obvious place,” Griffen said. “It’s accessible, it’s on a main road, it has parking and a bus network. For a long time, this was a mental health facility, and art therapy has long been a standard way of treating people. Setting this up in Callan Park feels like a natural flow-on.” The pitch comes amid broader changes under the 10-year Callan Park Plan of Management, alongside works on a new tidal pool, a community football clubhouse and Bay Run upgrades. Under the Callan Park (Special Provisions) Act, the land cannot be sold, uses are restricted to health, community, or education, and development must stay within existing building footprints. Shetty, who brought the groups together, said she would press the Minns government to back the model. “There’s a desperate need for artist working spaces because we’re seeing more and more gentrification and the loss of light industrial spaces,” she said. “We want to make sure when Ambulance does vacate the site entirely that it is not just another building left with no purpose and left to demolition by neglect.” Vigilanti’s concept designs lay out a staged transformation across the six interlocking buildings around a central courtyard. The southern building facing Balmain Road would become the primary gallery opening onto a sculpture garden, the western wing would house open studios, residencies, and education rooms, and a northern training building would become classrooms.



Editor's pick Development Sydney’s answer to the Louvre? Battle brews over what to do with Victoria Barracks Ma estimated the complex could be stripped back and opened within six to 12 months, noting routine asbestos and lead paint hazards were manageable if addressed soon. “My greatest fear is that these buildings are left in a bureaucratic process and nothing happens for years – demolition by neglect,” Ma said. “The longer we leave it without proper care and maintenance, the more likely it becomes a hazard and more expensive to remediate later.” Planning and Public Spaces Minister Paul Scully and NSW Ambulance have been contacted for comment. World.title: Trump has lost the ‘podcast bros’, says Joe Rogan
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump Trump has lost the ‘podcast bros’, says Joe Rogan Alexandra Snow November 16, 2026 — 11:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Donald Trump has lost the backing of the “podcast bros”, Joe Rogan has said after young people fuelled the blue wave that swept through the US midterm elections. The world’s most-listened-to podcaster endorsed Trump for the 2024 election, but has remained relatively quiet about politics since Trump took office for a second term as US president. Joe Rogan has cooled on Donald Trump since his 2024 endorsement. AP In his show The Joe Rogan Experience, the podcaster blamed the Republicans’ midterms drubbing on the Iran war and hard-line immigration raids. “They didn’t just lose the podcast bros, they lost most of the country,” Rogan told listeners on Friday.



Related Article Trump's America ‘It’s all showbusiness’: Meet the publicist behind America’s political influencers He added that support for Trump had waned when the administration began “a war that no one wants to be in”. US Vice President JD Vance has also blamed the Iran war for his party’s midterms defeat. Rogan has been uneasy about White House policies since the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in March. “It just seems so insane,” Rogan said at the time. “He ran on no more wars: end these stupid, senseless wars. And then we have one.”



On Friday, the podcaster also attributed the midterm elections loss to the administration putting “militarised police in the streets wearing masks”, referring to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He said the ICE raids had targeted “nice, good people that are loved by the community, but they just don’t have the right paperwork”. Rogan says the conflict with Iran, following Trump’s 2024 pledge of no more foreign wars, has cost the Republicans dearly. AP Photo/Alex Brandon The “manosphere” world of podcasters helped Trump and his allies reach young male voters for the 2024 election. They touted the importance of preserving “biblically based” family values and male supremacy.



However, some podcasters have been left feeling alienated by the Trump administration and are providing the US president with less airtime. Related Article US midterms Midterms launch wave of historic firsts across the United States This resulted in the young, male Republican vote collapsing in the midterm elections. Men under 30 shifted nearly 40 points towards the Democrats, after a 23-point shift toward Republicans in the 2024 election. The swing back to blue has been pinned on grievances including inflation and the cost of living, the war in Iran and Republicans’ failure to prosecute those named in the Epstein files.



Young Latino men also swung sharply toward Democrats, as the hard line on immigration became increasingly contentious. Some of these men, who were previously enmeshed in the “podcast bro” world, now describe themselves as being “black-pilled” and see voting as pointless altogether. The “pill” metaphor originates from The Matrix, the 1999 sci-fi film, and has been adopted by online communities to describe stages of radicalisation. The concept of men being “black-pilled” refers to people moving past the belief that society is skewed against men into total nihilism, arguing that efforts to improve the world are completely futile. Following the devastating midterm losses, the Trump administration is trying to win back young male voters.
