World.title: TVNZ proposes news team changes 'less tied to a broadcasting schedule'
World.content:
A TVNZ spokesperson says they are proposing changes to their news teams to be less tied to a broadcasting schedule.

Staff had been meeting this morning to discuss a proposal for how its news team could operate and structure itself.

A staffer told RNZ the meeting was causing considerable anxiety.

TVNZ earlier said it expected to report a loss in the 2027 year as it completes its two-year investment programme, before returning to profitability in 2028.

The spokesperson said the proposal would give them more capacity to deliver news throughout the day.

World.title: Services activity hits 3.5-year high
World.content:
The BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Services Index rose 0.8 points to 51.7 in October.

That's the fifth month in a row above 50, the line seperating growth and contraction, and the best result in more than three and a half years.

BusinessNZ chief executive Katherine Rich said it was a welcome sign heading into summer.

"Many businesses were clearly holding off decisions in the lead-up to the election and with a new government hopefully being formed soon, there's a chance some of that deferred spending and investment starts to come through," she said.

"It's definitely a positive number and moving in the right direction. I wouldn't call it strong, though. I think that would be a stretch," BNZ senior economist Doug Steel said.

New orders (53.0) and activity/sales (52.6) were the strongest sub-indexes.

Employment was the only one below 50, at 49.9.

Steel said the new orders number suggests more activity and sales growth to come.

Respondents still worried about fuel prices, the cost of living, interest rates and election uncertainty, but the lead-in to summer, Christmas bookings and returning tourists were cited as positives.

Negative comments eased to 57.9 percent from 59.9 percent in September.

Steel said there was a clear theme: sectors linked to exports are doing better.

Accommodation, cafes and restaurants were among the strongest, which Steel said ties in with strong international tourism growth.

"These things all have that sort of external association, and the export sector is going pretty well," he said.

By contrast, discretionary and domestically focused sectors were more subdued, with cultural, recreational and personal services falling sharply and retail staying subdued despite the school holidays.

All regions are growing, with the South still well ahead, but Steel said it was encouraging to see the North push above 50 for the first time in a while.

"It gives a sense of the recovery broadening, not only by industry, but also, as we suggest, by region," he said.

Steel said the PSI and the even stronger manufacturing PMI together point to annual growth of around 2 percent, in line with BNZ's forecast for 2026.

More encouraging, he said, was services starting to move after a long period of weakness.

World.title: Kiribati vice president Dr Teuea Toatu dies
World.content:
Dr Teuea Toatu, the vice president of Kiribati since 2019, has died.

Dr Toatu also served as Kiribati Finance and Economic Development Minister since 2016.

His passing was announced by Cabinet colleague Ruth Cross Kwansing on Sunday night.

In a social media post, Cross Kwansing wrote that his life had defined in service to Kiribati.

"We are so devastated that he is gone. Personally, I looked up to and admired him so much for his reassuring leadership, his wisdom, guidance and unmatched work ethic," she wrote.

"He sacrificed tirelessly not only for Kiribati, but also to serve our wider Blue Pacific family."

The Chinese embassy in Kiribati also paid tribute, praising Dr Toatu's "significant contributions to the strengthening of the bilateral relationship between China and Kiribati".

"His dedication and efforts throughout his life will serve as a source of inspiration for the friendship and cooperation between our two countries."

Dr Toatu, an economist by trade, earned his PhD from the Australian National University in 2001.

He spent seven years at the Commonwealth as Head of the Project Management and Referal unit until 2011, and led the Phoenix Islands Protected Area (PIPA) Conservation Trust before becoming a Minister in 2016.

World.title: The 16 MPs (likely) voted out of Parliament
World.content:
Even as Parliament looks likely to grow to 131 MPs, several who have been there for the last term have been saying goodbye this week.

Because they were involuntarily ejected by voters, these 16 departing MPs probably won't get the chance to deliver valedictory speeches - so this will have to do for now.

National

Nicola Willis, the deputy leader and finance minister who also championed National's economic growth and social investment strategies, is the highest-profile exit, and one of National's hardest-working and most effective ministers.

She had worked as a staffer for both John Key and Bill English, and built a reputation as a fierce debater, going on to be a general manager at Fonterra and a director at the New Zealand Initiative, before returning to Parliament as an MP in 2018 on National's list, after the resignation of Steven Joyce.

After previously attempting campaigns in traditionally left-leaning Wellington electorates - against Grant Robertson in Wellington Central in 2017 and 2020, and Ōhāriu's Greg O'Connor in 2023 - she chose not to contest an electorate this time, ending up a victim of National's overhang.

Paul Goldsmith and Nicola Willis were key members of Christopher Luxon's cabinet. Fiona Goodall/Getty Images

At third on the list, Chris Bishop is another victim of National's electorate success, after conceding Hutt South to Labour's Ginny Andersen on election night and acknowledging his chances of returning in the final count were "extremely unlikely".

A former lobbyist for Philip Morris, and staffer for Gerry Brownlee and Steven Joyce, Bishop entered Parliament in 2014 on National's list, claimed Hutt South in 2017 after the departure of Labour's Trevor Mallard and lost it to Andersen in the 2020 'red wave' election, before winning it back in 2023.

Another of National's hard-working front bench, Bishop has led National's revision and replacement of Labour's Resource Management Act reforms, housing, infrastructure and transport, and became Attorney-General this year, while losing his role as National campaign chair in April, after rumours of an attempted leadership spill.

With National's low polling in 2026, Paul Goldsmith shifted from the one-tick strategy he'd run in Epsom against a succession of ACT leaders since 2011 to an explicit two-tick campaign against David Seymour, but appears to have fallen short, winning 30.5 percent of electorate votes on the night, compared to Seymour's 36.8.

A historian, biographer, pianist and taekwondo black belt, the trusted Luxon loyalist ended up with 10 portfolios (with GCSB and NZSIS being one combined role) - believed to be the most held by a minister this century - after Chris Penk's August attempt to topple the leader and sudden exit.

After being an Auckland councillor criticised for attempts to have homeless people removed from the CBD, he went on to become a National minister under John Key, had a stint as finance spokesperson under Judith Collins, and under Luxon, has led broadcasting, electoral and justice changes, including the move-on orders and removal of same-day voter enrolment.

Gerry Brownlee leaves Parliament as the father of the House - the longest continuously serving male MP - and Parliament's Speaker.

Gerry Brownlee leaves Parliament as father of the House. VNP / Phil Smith

He became MP for Ilam in the first MMP election of 1996, after unsuccessfully challenging Jim Anderton in '93, holding the seat until the red wave of 2020. He was deputy leader under both Don Brash and Judith Collins, and was a Leader of the House, defence minister, foreign minister, transport minister and led the response to the Canterbury earthquakes under Key.

His past life as a woodwork teacher stood him in good stead in the Speaker's chair, but whether his family's Olympic rowing history had much impact is unclear.

Nancy Lu was National's highest-ranked new MP in 2023, after Andrew Bayly's by-election win in Port Waikato saw him move to an electorate seat, freeing up a spot for a list seat.

Born in Guangzhou, China, she moved to Auckland at age 10 and became a chartered accountant, before becoming the party's only Chinese-heritage candidate in 2020.

Melissa Lee was the first Korean elected to Parliament - and the first Korean-born woman to enter a country's Parliament outside Korea - when she came in on National's list in 2008. She came close to unseating Labour's Helen White from Mt Albert in 2023, falling short by just 18 votes in a judicial recount.

After being a journalist for 23 years, including writing for the NZ Herald and the Listener, she was replaced as media and communications minister, and dumped out of Cabinet in Luxon's first reshuffle in 2024.

Carlos Cheung will hope special votes tip his way in Mt Roskill, with just 262 votes separating him and Michael Wood, who was dumped from cabinet in 2023 for repeatedly failing to declare shares and lost the previously safe Labour seat, as the red tide swept back out.

Cheung was born in Hong Kong and moved to New Zealand as a teenager, he has a PhD in diabetes and cardiac disease, and made it a point of pride to visit every junior, intermediate, secondary and special school in his electorate.

Vanessa Weenink had probably the most explosive comments of any departing MP, saying she would not miss the abuse from members of the public and expressing frustration at National's rightward shift.

A general practitioner for 20 years and an army medical officer for 22 - including deployments to Afghanistan and East Timor - Weenink was a Labour member, until the NZ Medical Association she chaired was disestablished in 2022, after which she joined National, narrowly taking Banks Peninsula in '23, before losing it again to Labour's Tracey McLellan.

Vanessa Weenink was a Labour member, until the NZ Medical Association she chaired was disestablished in 2022, after which she joined National. VNP/Phil Smith

Labour

Deborah Russell was first elected in 2017, as MP for New Lynn, replacing former leader David Cunliffe, but after two terms, had to return on the list in 2023, after losing to Paulo Garcia.

An academic with a PhD in philosophy and co-writer of a book on tax fairness, she was minister of statistics and the Earthquake Commission under Chris Hipkins, and occasionally landed in hot water for expressing tax views out of line with the party's.

Rachel Boyack was an organiser for First Union, before reclaiming the Nelson electorate in the 2020 red wave from National's Nick Smith, who had held the seat since 1996, and narrowly held it in '23 by just 26 votes against National's Blair Cameron, before losing it to him by more than 1200 votes this election.

National sought to reverse her Plain Language Bill - which aimed to make government documents easier to understand - last term, but the repeal did not reach a second reading before the election.

Dan Rosewarne was an army mechanic, who attained the rank of captain - with two deployments to Afghanistan, one to Solomon Islands and one responding to the Kaikōura earthquake - and survived leukaemia, before entering Parliament in 2022 on the list, after Kris Faafoi's retirement.

He was ejected again, after losing Waimakariri to National's Matt Doocey in '23, but returned to Parliament briefly this year, after the resignation of Peeni Henare in March.

Georgie Dansey entered Parliament on Labour's list, after Adrian Rurawhe's resignation in February, before the former Speaker's death in September.

Georgie Dansey's stay in Parliament may be brief, unless special votes save her seat. VNP / Phil Smith

She had lost the Hamilton West by-election, caused by Gaurav Sharma's resignation, to National's Tama Potaka in 2022, and fell short in Hamilton East in '23 and '26, but with just 456 votes separating her and incumbent Ryan Hamilton, she'll hope special votes land in her favour.

Green

At 19th on the Greens list in 2023, Mike Davidson never really expected to be an MP, but entered in October 2025, after the resignation of Benjamin Doyle capped off a now well-traversed string of MP replacements for the party in the last term.

A former Christchurch City Councillor who advocated for cycleways and public transport, his 2026 list placing at 20th means a return to Parliament seems very unlikely - almost as unlikely as the first time.

NZ First

Jamie Arbuckle controversially stayed on as a Marlborough district councillor - a role he'd held since 2010 - after coming to Parliament on New Zealand First's list in 2023.

He's 13th on the list - so, next in line - after placing behind rising stars Craig Stobo and Taine Randall, and former National MPs like Alfred Ngaro, Harete Hipango-Brownlie and Michael Laws. He could yet return, if Laws is eventually dumped and the party doesn't lose support in special votes.

Independents

Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Tākuta Ferris were both removed from Te Pāti Māori during its internal ructions a year ago.

Kapa-Kingi - who had helped develop iwi health services, and worked in homelessness and suicide prevention - had defeated Labour deputy Kelvin Davis and was later re-instated to Te Pāti Māori, after a court battle.

Mariameno Kapa-Kingi's term was tumultuous, after she was banished from and then re-instated to Te Pāti Māori. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

However, she ultimately stood under the banner of her own Te Tai Tokerau party for the election, losing to Te Pāti Māori's Aperahama Edwards.

Ferris - nicknamed 'Doc' (Tākuta means 'doctor', he was named for the man who saved his and his mother's life during a difficult birth) never sought a court battle to return to the fold and ran as an independent this year.

An expert in Māori art and design, and mātauranga Māori, he was considered an outside chance to defeat Labour's Rino Tirikatene, who had beat him in 2020, but won in 2023 with a 2800-vote margin, after a campaign where he went toe to toe with the likes of Winston Peters and David Seymour in The Press leaders debate.

Pre-election exits

Lest we forget, some honourable mentions for the MPs that chose to leave on their own terms, resigning within the final six months, so as to not trigger by-elections.

World.title: Rare 1941 plane returns to Nelson skies
World.content:
Audio player for " Rare Lockheed Electra returns to Nelson skies " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/regions/2618241%2Frare-1941-plane-returns-to-nelson-skies

Rare Lockheed Electra returns to Nelson skies Morning Report Download MP3 3m

A plane that once provided Nelson's only air service during World War II has returned to the city's skies.

The restored 1941 Lockheed 10A Electra - named Kuaka - drew a crowd during a special visit to Nelson Airport.

The rare art deco airliner, with its blindingly bright polished aluminium exterior, was last seen in Nelson when Trans Island Airways stopped its scheduled flights between Nelson and Christchurch in 1959.

The plane is one of only two still flying in the world, with the other in the Czech Republic.

Aviation historian Richard Waugh said the Lockheed Electra was a "very sophisticated, fast aircraft" that played a pioneering role in New Zealand's aviation history.

"They were the first monoplane all metal aircraft in New Zealand and, with a tailwind, capable of say 200 miles an hour, which was faster than anything the Air Force had in the late 1930s."

Aviation historian Richard Waugh and his wife Jane St George-Waugh. RNZ / Samantha Gee

During World War II, they were the only planes servicing Nelson.

"In 1937-1938 it pioneered most of the airline schedule routes in New Zealand, particularly Auckland to Dunedin, and then from 10 November 1939, it did the airline service to Nelson."

He said the Lockheed Electra was remarkably comfortable and relatively quiet, with an interior as spectacular as the exterior.

The aircraft was involved in New Zealand's first fatal accident involving passengers on a scheduled flight, when ZK-AFE 'Kereru' crashed near the summit of Mt Richmond on a flight from Wellington to Nelson on 7 May 1942.

Five occupants were killed, with the tragedy commemorated on a plaque at Nelson Airport.

There are only two Lockheed 10A Electra planes still flying in the world. RNZ / Samantha Gee

A restoration decades in the making

Kuaka is owned by Rob Mackley, who saw it advertised in the Trade-A-Plane magazine in 1996.

"I thought, wow, that's quite rare. It was an Alaskan number, so I rang them, and I said, 'is it a Lockheed 10?' And they said, 'yes, sir, it is'."

It was being sold by a museum and was not in a flyable condition, but Mackley flew to Alaska that night to take a look at it.

The restored Lockheed Electra plane, Kuaka RNZ / Samantha Gee

He said because they rarely came up for sale there was no benchmark for its worth, and despite being "young and naive" he decided to put an offer in.

"It was a sealed bid tender, so you had to just write what you wanted to pay, put it in an envelope, take it to the reception of the museum, put it in their mahogany box."

About two weeks later, to his surprise, he got a fax saying, "come and get your aeroplane".

He said it was a mission to get the plane to New Zealand, it almost didn't happen. A restoration job he thought would take three years, took almost 30.

"It's just been one of those restorations where we've tried to be as faithful on everything as we can, and that's led to multiple years more and obviously more money, and I never added it up.

Inside the 10-seater Lockheed Electra, which has been painstakingly restored. RNZ / Samantha Gee

His wife Caroline is also a pilot and Mackley said the pair loved taking people out on the plane.

"You can fly it with one, but I opt to fly it with my wife, because she's actually more qualified than me so she's always co-pilot, and then there's room for 10 passengers.

"It's not a hangar queen, we do use it, it's neat for people to be able to come and see what aviation used to be like."

No. 23 Squadron air cadet Tayla McLean said flying in the Electra was 'very cool'. RNZ / Samantha Gee

On Saturday, one of those lucky passengers was No. 23 Squadron air cadet Tayla McLean.

"It was very cool, [the flight] was way longer than I thought and the inside is very nicely decorated and we've got to go over Kaiteri and Tahuna area and circle around Nelson."

Nelson Airport chief executive Brendan Cook said the rare plane drew quite a crowd, with people young and old turning up to get a closer look at it.

"It's an absolutely amazing aircraft, only two of its kind flying in the world with a long history of aviation in Nelson through its flying career back in the 40s and 50s."

Nelson Airport chief executive Brendan Cook. RNZ / Samantha Gee

He said travelling on it offered a "bit of a look back in time as to what flying would have been like" then.

"It was unbelievably smooth and quiet, it would have been the sight of luxury back in the day."

World.title: Pacific tuna stocks at centre of regional fisheries talks in Port Vila
World.content:
The adoption of key tuna fisheries management measures on the table for this year's 23rd Regular Session of the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC), scheduled to take place in Port Vila, Vanuatu, from 30 November, is critical for the sustainability of tuna fisheries in the region.

Niue's Josie Tamate, who is the WCPFC chair, told RNZ Pacific this week that all measures that are being discussed and that would be tabled at the meeting, are focused on ensuring that tuna stocks remain healthy, and that small island developing states that rely largely on their fisheries for income, are not negatively affected.

She said the big decisions for the Commission would be the adoption of the implementing measure for the South Pacific albacore, and also the bigeye management procedure.

Tamate, who is also finishing off as chair at the Port Vila meeting, said they would also be monitoring the COP31 meeting in Turkey, especially on the decisions on the oceans.

The WCPFC adopted a resolution on climate change in 2019, and there was also decision for climate change to be a standing agenda item at the Commission meeting.

"It is a challenge because, you know, we're managing and then you also have these conditions, the changing conditions due to climate change, so we will continue to have a conversation on the impact of climate change," Tamate said.

"I like to see what will be the outcomes from the COP31, and how do we weave those in as part of an overall conversation that we need to have at the commission, so we're not just doing things in isolation.

"We don't work in a bubble, but we're working with all these issues that has an impact on the fisheries, and especially on the distribution of tuna and movement.

"There's some information that says that there's a movement of the distribution from the west to the east. Again, those are implications that the Commission will be looking into because it does come with a whole lot of implications."

Niue's Josie Tamate is the WCPFC chair. Western & Central Pacific Fisheries Commission (WCPFC)

Critical measures

On the decisions around management procedures and measures, Tamate reiterated that in 2022 the interim skipjack management procedure was adopted while the commission adopted the South Pacific Albacore Management Procedure last year in Manila.

"So, this year, on our schedule, the commission is expected to adopt the the implementing measure for the South Pacific albacore and the management procedure for bigeye tuna," she said.

"In addition to that, maybe the the yellowfin management procedure as well and there's some expectation to adopt the the Pacific blue fin tuna management procedure. This Pacific blue fin is work that is led by the Northern Committee, and they will be presenting that for adoption at the WCPFC.

"We continue the ongoing discussions on the work of the Commission and the tasking, but the key one for me, critical for this meeting, would be decision on the implementing measure for the South Pacific Albacore, and also the decision on the Big Eye management procedure."

Tamate said all these measures and procedures have been discussed over the past few years, with science also involved in the decision-making.

She said the special science commission meeting prior to the full Commission meeting is a significant one, and is the first to be held as part of the annual gathering.

"That's a layer we never had before, but the the special science committee is important because of the the advice from the science is built into the to the decision making process by the commission the following week.

"I think there's we've done everything that we can. It's going to be a lot of negotiation that's going to take place."

Challenges

Tamate said time and implementation are two major individual challenges.

She said since taking over as WCPFC chair three years ago, there were a lot more issues and alot more work to be done.

"I think it's time," she said. "We only have five days at the commission meeting to make substantial decisions with respect to the management of our tuna fisheries, but the work has been undertaken throughout the year.

"For me timing and also just the opportunity to be able to address some of this complex discussions because there are other features and issues that comes on top of that as well.

"The different interests that are at play, the interests of fishing states, interests of coastal states and trying to find a pathway on a lot of the important issues that it will be before the commissions, and it's ongoing discussion."

She said there are two important phase of the discussions.

The first focused on the negotiation of the conservation management measure, which is the measure to be adopted.

The second part is the actual implementation of those into making sure that there is compliance.

"So, I think that's the other big challenge, the compliance," she said.

"Those will be ongoing challenges, and the commission has been working very hard to address those, to make sure that there is clarity and also transparency in the way that we do the work.

"So I think for me it is the time, and it's just finding the balance, finding a way forward, and also the making sure that when we adopt measures, that there is obligations followed through.

"But it would also be understanding the capacities of the members and the participatory territories in the commission to implement a lot of these measures that has been adopted by the commission."

Highlights

On a personal note, Tamate said the adoption of special tuna fisheries measures over the last three years and those that would be adopted in Port Vila would be the highlights of her leadership term.

She said being WCPFC chair from a small island state like Niue was challenging and daunting in an important sector like tuna fisheries, but having commission members agree to take critical steps together for the betterment of the tuna fisheries had been exciting.

"For me the highlight has been the adoption of some of the critical decisions that have been made by the commission," she said.

"We've been able to progress a lot of this work, and this is due mainly to the support by the the commission members, but also the work with the secretariat as well, and the work that was undertaken by the the regional organisations, such as the Forum Fisheries Agency, the Pacific Community (SPC) and other stakeholders and partners.

"There is a lot of work and a lot of interest in making sure that the the health of the the key tuna stocks continue to be healthy, so that we're still in green."

She said all key tuna species under the Commission's mandate "is still in the green", meaning the stocks are still healthy.

"For me that's a highlight in terms of the work and the contribution that I made into the the work of the commission to spearhead a lot of the discussions and that we maintain that green status of our key stocks," she said.

"I'm also very proud of the the work that's been undertaken by the Commission in terms of the harvest strategies and it's important to build the capacity of everybody, especially those where the fishery is important for their livelihoods.

"I'm proud of all the work that has been undertaken by all the members, the SIDS, and all the. The 33 members of the commission, they continue to come with the willingness to find positive ways forward, because it is the livelihood of the fishery, which is the livelihood for a lot of people, not only for the Pacific Islands but also those who operate in the Western and Central Pacific Ocean.

"It's highly important that we need to sustain the fishery and keeping the health of the tuna species that we have, especially when they're in the interface of climate change and all these other discussion that that will have an impact on the way we work going forward."

Forum Fisheries take

Meanwhile, the Forum Fisheries Agency (FFA) said its 17 members will push for a landmark management procedure for bigeye tuna at the upcoming meeting.

The FFA said in a statement the proposal is among several fisheries management priorities formally submitted to the Commission following the 22nd Management Options Consultation (MOC22), a weeklong series of meetings involving FFA Members, partners and stakeholders on key regional fisheries management issues.

If adopted, the proposed bigeye tuna measure would be the Commission's first management procedure covering both purse seine and longline fisheries, two major fishing methods used to catch tuna.

The FFA said it would be an important step towards strengthening the management of the world's largest bigeye tuna stock, which accounts for approximately 40 percent of global bigeye tuna catches and, according to the latest stock assessment, has never been overfished.

Managing bigeye tuna remains a challenge because both purse seine and longline fisheries catch the same stock. Existing restrictions on purse seine fishing help protect bigeye tuna but also reduce fishing opportunities and potential revenue for Pacific Island countries, while benefiting longline fisheries.

FFA said members are seeking a more balanced approach that protects bigeye tuna while recognising the economic interests of Pacific Island countries and ensuring that conservation responsibilities are shared more fairly between the two fishing methods.

Other proposals submitted by FFA members include new arrangements for managing South Pacific Albacore, stronger fisheries reporting and monitoring and stronger management of transhipment activities.

The FFA members are also calling for stronger fisheries monitoring and compliance, including a prohibition on transferring fish between vessels on the high seas until the Commission adopts clear guidelines.

Other priorities include improving fisheries data reporting and protecting Pacific Island countries' fishing rights and economic interests as climate change affects tuna distribution.

World.title: What went wrong for the Kiwis in their Rugby League World Cup final defeat?
World.content:
A terrible start, unforced errors and a lack of possession undid the New Zealand men in the Rugby League World Cup final, according to former Kiwis forward Monty Betham.

The Kiwis were trounced 32-12 by defending champions Australia in the title decider in Brisbane, with the Kangaroos claiming their fourth straight World Cup crown.

New Zealand were on the back foot from the kick off as Jamayne Isaako sent the ball bouncing over the dead ball line to concede a penalty inside the opening seconds.

Kangaroos players celebrate. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

The Kangaroos took full advantage with Liam Martin scoring inside 90 seconds, the fastest try in a RLWC final.

Betham said expectations were high among the Kiwis and their fans after an impressive win over Tonga in the semi-finals.

However, he said the way the Kiwis started would have eroded that confidence.

"To kick the ball out on the full and then to have your first chance to repel them and turn them away, to let them score first up early, it just wasn't the ideal start for any sort of match, especially Australia," Betham told RNZ's Morning Report.

Monty Betham Anthony Au-Yeung

Betham said he had faith that if the Kiwis started to get some possession for sustained periods then they would fight their way back into the match.

He said by halftime, with Australia leading 24-6, that faith was beginning to waver.

"It just got to be worse and worse in terms of chasing the scoreboard, no possession, getting a lot of fatigue in their legs and in their body, which means that when they finally got the ball at the right end of the field, they just weren't able to go forward with any impetus or any real potency."

A dejected Jamayne Isaako of New Zealand with his children after losing the Rugby League World Cup final, 2026. Andrew Cornaga/www.photosport.nz

Betham said the result was all the more disappointing given just how strong this Kiwis side was on paper, with the team studded with NRL stars.

He said the Kiwis big name players didn't fire a shot.

Kalyn Ponga Bradley Kanaris

"A lot of people were making noise that this is the best Kiwi side ever assembled, definitely the forward pack," Betham said.

"That was a really good forward pack and a lot of talented players across the board and it was hoped that he (Ponga) could be the one that provided t X-factor, but unfortunately he never really got the chance to get into game."

The Jillaroos were too strong for the Kiwi Ferns in Brisbane. Bradley Kanaris/Getty Images

Betham believes the Kiwi Ferns, who were beaten 34-10 by the Jillaroos in the women's final in Brisbane, had similar struggles to the New Zealand men.

He said they New Zealand women were outclassed by their Australian opposites.

"14 of the Jillaroos players that had won NRLW titles and there was five that had won eight Dally M awards amongst them, so it was always going to be tough.

World.title: Our Changing World: What the 'complex' Kaikōura earthquake taught scientists
World.content:
Follow Our Changing World on Apple, Spotify, iHeartRadio or wherever you listen to your podcasts

Just after midnight on 14 November 2016 a 7.8 magnitude earthquake struck Kaikōura and the surrounding areas.

Starting near the North Canterbury town of Waiau on the Humps Fault, the activity spread north and north east - over 20 different faults ruptured in what is regarded as a globally unprecedented complex earthquake.

The full earthquake event lasted just two minutes, but the energy released resulted in loss of life, damage to houses and properties, landslides that took out road and rail networks and a structural change to about 120 km of the Kaikōura coastline.

A decade on, what has the Kaikōura earthquake taught us?

Audio player for " Earthquake research a decade after Kaikōura " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2627067%2Four-changing-world-what-the-complex-kaikoura-earthquake-taught-scientists

Earthquake research a decade after Kaikōura Our Changing World Download MP3 26m

Complexity

If the Kaikōura earthquake were to be summed up in one word, that word would be 'complex'.

And though scientists knew about the potential of complex earthquakes to occur, this one did some very unexpected things, says Dr Anna Kaiser.

"It really jumped from faults in North Canterbury, kind of up to faults in Marlborough, which is kind of jumping across different geological regimes, if you like."

GNS scientists in the Kekerengu Fault which was one of 20 faults to rupture on the Kaikōura earthquake. RNZ / Tracy Neal

Anna is the chief scientist of earthquake hazards at Earth Sciences New Zealand. In the days, weeks, months, and years since the quake, observations flowed in on how the faults had slipped and what the impacts had been.

Kaikōura peninsula was uplifted by about a metre, whilst north of there the coastal reef jumped by about six metres. The ground shifted sideways along the Kekerengu fault by around 10 to 12 metres along more than an 80 km stretch, while the Leader Fault shot up vertically by three metres, creating a scarp dubbed the 'Wall of Waiau'. Tens of thousands of landslides were triggered in the process, including underwater landslides in the deep canyons offshore.

Earthquake damage on Henry Pinckney's farm. RNZ / Maja Burry

As well as the local effects, Anna and her team were keen to understand what the findings meant for New Zealand earthquake hazards in general and to incorporate this into the National Seismic Hazard model - the science-based estimate of the likelihood and strength of earthquake shaking throughout New Zealand.

In 2022, this model was revised to incorporate a wider range of earthquakes that could happen, taking into account more complicated ruptures.

The earthquake also drew attention to the impacts of ground shaking, particularly in Wellington.

Another look at what lies beneath Wellington

Although it was over 80 km away from the earthquake, areas of Wellington city experienced intense shaking which resulted in severe damage to some buildings.

That, Anna says, is due to the 3D shape and make-up of the ground under parts of the city.

"We had an earthquake that started in North Canterbury and ruptured through to the Cook Strait and kind of directed a lot of its energy northwards. And then because of the way that it ruptured and travelled towards Wellington, you had a soft sedimentary basin in Wellington, which further sort of amplified the ground motions there."

Damage to Wellington port from earthquake RNZ / Phil Pennington

It wasn't that scientists weren't aware of the sedimentary basin under Wellington, or the potential for it to amplify ground shaking.

The basin had been mapped by a gravity survey in 1967, and events like the 1985 Mexico City earthquake had made it clear the potentially devastating impacts of combining a distant earthquake with a city built on a sedimentary basin.

Because it is underground, the basin structure can only be inferred from modelling. Small differences in the shape, angle and depth of the basin can have significant impacts on how the ground shaking gets amplified, and which buildings are most badly affected. After the Kaikōura earthquake New Zealand researchers once again looked to model the shape of the basin, using updated techniques.

Emeritus Professor Tim Stern and then Masters student Alistair Stronach decided to use the gravity survey method again, but with the latest equipment.

Alistair Stronach and Emeritus Professor Tim Stern at Clyde Quay Wellington Claire Concannon / RNZ

Alistair explains that it is a method that measures the variation of gravity strength from place to place - "Gravity is not the same everywhere in the world. It only varies by very, very small amount. But if you have a very precise instrument, you can measure that."

The difference in rocks beneath your feet is one thing that impacts gravity, and is what Alistair set out to map.

That helped them model the shape and depth of the basin, which they then checked using a seismic reflection method.

Their results indicated a slightly different basin shape to that modelled by others post-earthquake, including a maximum depth of over twice as deep in an area near the stadium.

Both Tim and Alistair hope that this more 'granular' modelling of the basin shape will help prepare the city for future earthquakes.

Audio player for " Earthquake research a decade after Kaikōura " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2627067%2Four-changing-world-what-the-complex-kaikoura-earthquake-taught-scientists

Earthquake research a decade after Kaikōura Our Changing World Download MP3 26m

A new configuration

On a sunny spring day, University of Canterbury Professor David Schiel stands on the grey-white rock of Wairepo reef towards the end of the Kaikōura peninsula.

Professor David Schiel stands on Wairepo reef in Kaikōura. Claire Concannon / RNZ

Once this large flat reef area was an important study site for dozens of marine science postgraduate students that David supervised. They had been investigating the diverse life that had made a home in the sea, under the Neptune's necklace seaweed canopy, and the impacts that tourism was having on the reef.

When Our Changing World visited just two weeks after the earthquake the seaweed was already drying out and dying. The flat reef platform had been lifted close to a metre, and the changes in tide height and temperature had made it unsuitable habitat now for Neptune's necklace.

Dead seaweed litters the rocky coastal reef around the Kaikōura Peninsula, which has been left high and dry since being uplifted by a metre. RNZ / Alison Ballance

Now a decade on, all life has gone from the rock, with remnants of what was once there hanging out in tidal cracks closer to the water's edge.

The Neptune's necklace still exists, explains David, just in much lower quantities than before.

"What's happened is that this massive reef that was covered with it is now compressed into a zone... maybe twenty centimetres of tidal height. So the species are still here, but just in nowhere near the abundance they used to be."

Audio player for " The Kaikōura coast 10 years post earthquake " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/environment/2627067%2Four-changing-world-what-the-complex-kaikoura-earthquake-taught-scientists

The Kaikōura coast 10 years post earthquake Our Changing World Download MP3 42m

In the wake of the earthquake David and some of his students established study sites along the coast to assess the changes and monitor the recovery. Though recovery, David says, is a relative term - "It's a new configuration".

Professor David Schiel Supplied

Extra stressors such as a marine heatwave in the summer of 2017/2018, and large amounts of sediment washing into the ocean from the earthquake-damaged catchments, meant important species like bull kelp, durvillaea, struggled to return after the earthquake.

"That was lost pretty much entirely. That species was lost over the one hundred and thirty kilometres of coastline."

The crumbling reef

With the uplift of the reef and the loss of its key seaweed inhabitants, something unusual began to happen to the rock, says David.

"Within the months after the earthquake, we'd be standing on a little promontory like that, and the whole thing would just shear off and go into powder, and literally you'd be on a rock, and the next thing you'd be on on your backside."

Measuring this change was Professor Wayne Stephenson of the University of Otago.

The coastline around Kaikōura peninsula experienced uplift during the earthquake, changing the reef ecology and erosion rates. Claire Concannon / RNZ

He and his predecessor, Professor Bob Kirk, had been interested in reef platform erosion because as the reefs get worn down more wave energy reaches the base of the cliffs, causing erosion there. The study began in 1973 and the observations continued post earthquake, but with remarkable differences says Wayne.

"The platforms that had been eroding at one millimetre per year before the earthquake were suddenly eroding at two to two point five millimetres per year."

The impact was especially noticeable for the mudstone reefs, he says.

"They began to crumble really rapidly after being lifted out of the tide. They got a chance to dry out completely and just sort of fell apart."

This means that the coastal uplift, which does protect the cliffs from erosion, hasn't bought as much time as they first hoped.

"If you account for the erosion rates, the subsidence and the sea level rise, instead of having, we thought initially maybe five or six or seven hundred years of protection, we've actually got less than two hundred."

The pāua rollercoaster

Another key concern in the aftermath of the earthquake was the impact to pāua populations, as the uplift along the coast had left thousands of pāua stranded.

That's what Dr Shawn Gerrity set out to investigate for his PhD research with Professor David Schiel.

Dr Shawn Gerrity holds a wandering anemone. Claire Concannon / RNZ

The government moved quickly to close the fishery as the concern was that the hit on the adult pāua numbers, coupled with the disruption of a key habitat for their lifecycle, would lead to long-lasting impacts on the population and slow recovery.

However, Shawn says, something remarkable happened the day after the earthquake struck.

"Abalone are known to spawn when there's natural disasters; earthquakes, tsunamis. We've seen it in Japan. And after the Kaikōura earthquake, we observed a spawning event in November, which is sort of atypical. So it was sort of like a response mechanism to a disaster... I think they kind of realized this could be it. Let's see if we can get our propagules out. We saw a synchronised spawning event all up and down the coast."

Three years later, with the fishery still closed, the results of this spawning event were clear, says Shawn.

"The abundance of juvenile pāua at every one of our twenty six sites up and down the coast was unlike anything I've ever seen. It was just every rock you turned over."

Pāua need sub and inter-tidal areas in the reef for the juvenile stage of their lifecycle. Claire Concannon / RNZ

The fishery reopened for three months in the summer of 2021/2022 but evidence and estimates suggest that the recreational catch during that time far exceeded the five tonne allowance.

"Lessons were learned" says Dr Shawn Gerrity. "We realized that it is actually quite vulnerable to overfishing in that sort of a gold rush type environment."

"In those areas where we had good pāua next to those parking areas, the harvest rates were up to ninety two percent of the legal size."

"We did some modeling... Population size was probably contracting about fourteen percent a year, which is really significant and unsustainable even over the short term."

The Kaikōura coast 10 years post earthquake Our Changing World Download MP3 42m

In 2023, the fishery reopened with different recreational catch rules, including a larger minimum size, and a reduced bag limit of three pāua per person.

Since 2024, Shawn has been a member of the Kaikōura Marine Guardians group, His role is to liaise with the Minister for Conservation on behalf of the Guardians and, he says, the new rules seem to be working well.

The subtidal zone at Wairepo reef where Neptune neckace seaweed still grows. It once covered the entire flat reef expanse. Claire Concannon / RNZ

The key lesson for him, after a decade of studying this coast and its life, is that it's a pretty resilient place.

"It's healthy. You've got the deep sea trench. It's wave exposed. The water's cold. And we've learned that it can handle some really serious stressors; heat waves, earthquakes, coastal uplifts. What it doesn't handle so well is really intensive usage by humans. So that's the one thing we can manage."

World.title: Renshaw concerned about Khawaja's wellbeing amid sandpaper controversy
World.content:
Australian batter Matt Renshaw has checked in on the wellbeing of Usman Khawaja after Pat Cummins's stinging press conference rebuke of his ball tampering claims.

Cummins labelled some of the claims Khawaja made in his book, Sabr, "utter nonsense" in a 69-minute minute presser on Friday morning, casting some doubt on the pair's friendship moving forward.

Renshaw, who is also friends with Khawaja, reminded everyone of the human side of the ongoing saga after scoring 63 in Australia's 135-run loss to England in the second ODI on Sunday night in Adelaide.

"I have spoken to Usman, just checking in on him," Renshaw said.

"Haven't really spoken too much about what's going on, just sort of checking on him as a human — obviously there's a lot going on.

"I wasn't there in Cape Town when it happened so I have got no idea what was going on, so tough for me to comment on that.

"But yeah, I think everyone as humans, obviously everything is going on, but I think the biggest thing is making sure everyone's OK."

Khawaja has received support from David Warner on multiple occasions, while Chadd Sayers, who played one Test on the 2018 South Africa tour, also backed him on Sunday prior to the one day clash.

Despite the ongoing accounts from Khawaja, Warner and Sayers, Cricket Australia at this stage remains unwilling to re-open its investigation into the scandal.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Worrying signs as Wallabies leave it too late to fire in Scotland defeat
World.content:
It might be unfair to be overly critical about the Wallabies' latest defeat, this time to Scotland at Murrayfield.

Its narrow nature, 15-12, is one aspect.

The conditions too have to be considered.

Scotland beat Wallabies in desperate, dour Murrayfield arm-wrestle The Wallabies fall to a fourth straight defeat as Scotland claims a 15-12 victory in a dour display at Murrayfield.

Dank and grey, the lingering firework smoke above the playing surface was reminiscent of some primordial Celtic realm.

This was an afternoon of such monochrome dreariness that even Scotland couldn't muster much of their usual attacking verve.

It was far removed from the bright lights of Friday night in Paris or Saturday afternoon in Cardiff.

Opposing skippers Rory Darge and Harry Wilson both referred to the game as descending into an arm-wrestle, though at times the contest we witnessed was so bad that calling it as such would almost be cruel to practitioners of that maligned pastime.

But then again, autumnal Scottish afternoons are just not what the proponents of free-flowing, attacking rugby union had in mind as ideal conditions for their craft.

Les Kiss said as much to UK broadcaster ITV, describing the game as "turgid".

"I think [Gregor Townsend] and I both would have preferred some drier weather," he added.

Both teams struggled to hold the ball in cold and wet conditions. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Undoubtedly, the conditions were reflected in the Scottish play as the hosts produced a litany of errors, most of which were a by-product of a series of over-complicated running lines that looked perfect when drawn up in the dryness and warmth of the training rooms, but less so when countered by the freezing rain and fast-pressing Wallabies defence.

That defence is worth pointing out as a positive.

The Wallabies had conceded seven tries in each of their previous three games, letting 138 points be scored against them. Shipping just two against Scotland marked a huge improvement.

But neither side hit the attacking heights both are capable of — a familiar failing of this Wallabies team at present.

Where the Scots' limitations seemed a result of over complication, the Wallabies' attacking limits were self-imposed by the bland simplicity of their game plan.

Things started relatively well despite the tricky conditions.

Scotland barged up to the Wallabies line and spun the ball wide to an unmarked Matt Fagerson to open the scoring.

Matt Fagerson scored the opening try. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol)

The Wallabies went up the other end and hit back immediately, Harry Potter finishing a move started by Carter Gordon's driving surge.

This was what the Wallabies didn't have against England; the fly half taking charge, double-pumping the pass as he approached the line before releasing Jeremy Williams, Len Ikitau and finally Potter to score.

A solid move, well constructed, well finished.

It took the best part of an hour before we saw anything of the like again from the men in gold.

Between times, fans were subject to a dour attacking display whenever the Wallabies had the ball in hand, the visitors relentlessly forced to retreat back up field before either kicking the ball away or flat-out losing it.

One-out runners with no passing, no speed in the back line movement, no width, no use of the thrilling attacking talents at their disposal, no way through the walls of Scottish defenders.

One of the most desperate passages came with about a quarter of an hour remaining.

The Wallabies had forced a lineout just outside the Scotland 22, a rare attacking chance. But through 18 phases of bland hit ups with little to no imagination the Wallabies went backwards a handful of metres, and then lost the ball to a Scotland turnover.

A kind observation would have been that the Wallabies were being patient, taking their time to find an opening in a Scottish defence that had significantly tightened its leash.

A less kind one would be that it was clueless and uninventive, destined to fail.

The Wallabies struggled to make anything happen with the ball in hand. (AP Photo: Scott Heppell)

Neither side had anything like clean ball, a litany of errors plaguing the contest in the loose, with the chaotic breakdown simply adding to the confused display from both teams.

But the Wallabies showed they can attack when they want to, adding to the frustration of what had gone before.

Ben Donaldson came onto the field, shifting Gordon to centre, and immediately made an impact, passing wide and giving the visitors the impetus to attack.

With almost his first phase of play, Donaldson immediately looked to move the ball wide, moving laterally at pace to open the Scotland defence — perhaps running himself into a starters spot in Cardiff next week.

Later, Donaldson spun the ball wide to Williams, whose flick pass out the back of the hand released Jorgensen to scoot down the line and score.

As the clock ticked into the red, the ball was again spun wide, Tate McDermott and Harry Wilson releasing Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, almost a non-entity both this week and last in an attacking sense but finally running with the ball in hand.

Jorgensen and Tom Wright were both involved before the latter was bundled into touch, the gun-shy Wallabies now firing from the hip with alacrity.

Suaalii. Jorgensen. Wright. These names had barely been mentioned all game.

Tom Wright and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii were barely seen in an attacking sense. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Ian MacNicol)

By the time they were, it was far too late.

Again, perhaps it's unfair to judge the Wallabies too harshly for a sour outing in which both teams struggled to rouse themselves from their mutual stupor.

So attention should shift to Wales, which now awaits inside the Principality Stadium next Sunday (AEDT).

The roof in Cardiff means "conditions" is not an excuse that can be laid down in case of another attacking no-show.

But Wales's defence may yet be just as stingy as it was against the All Blacks, where the Welsh made a stunning 346 tackles.

For reference, Scotland (154) and the Wallabies (194) combined to make 348 at Murrayfield.

The Wallabies have one more chance to prove they are moving in the right direction.

They would do well to find a way to unleash their attacking weapons before it's too late.

World.title: Scotland beat Wallabies in desperate, dour Murrayfield arm-wrestle
World.content:
The Wallabies have delivered another woeful display on their spring tour, falling to a 15-12 defeat against Scotland at Murrayfield.

The defeat was the Wallabies' fourth in a row and piles the pressure on new coach Les Kiss after another display of limited attacking rugby.

A dour contest never really ignited was always destined to be close, with both teams struggling to get their attacks working on a freezing Edinburgh afternoon.

"I thought there were some really nice attacking moments from us," Les Kiss said post-match.

"Our defence definitely turned up.

"Our physicality overall was right up, which was pleasing.

"A couple of moments, that try in the corner with the maul, probably a couple of discipline moments that gave them easy yards just put us on the back foot.

"Full of fight, that's for sure. But you want to win those ones."

In the sort of dank, drizzly conditions that a Scottish autumn is famous for, the match descended into a gruelling arm-wrestle.

With the pre-match fireworks still hovering above the playing field, Matt Fagerson opened the scoring for the hosts inside the opening 10 minute, finishing off a spell of dominant possession in the corner.

The Wallabies hit back straight away, Harry Potter contorting himself to reach over and finish a rare flowing move sparked by the returning Carter Gordon in midfield.

Harry Potter scored for the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Nations Championship/Liam Chester)

That was the end of any real attacking impetus for the Wallabies for almost an hour though as the team fell into the habit of one-out hit ups and box kicks.

As the two sides grappled with close-contact battles, former Wallaby Jack Dempsey burrowed over to score, the last points before a 45-minute scoreless spell that stretched deep into the second half.

The Wallabies felt they had hit back just before half time when Ryan Canham dived over from a rolling maul, but it was bought back by the TMO for obstruction by Jeremy Williams.

"It was a tough one," Wilson said.

"They're really trying to crack down on that at the moment and that was probably a really big moment in the end, because 14-all at half time we might have had them there.

"We've got to be better at icing those big moments."

Former Wallaby Jack Dempsey scored for Scotland in the first half. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Neither side could get going in the second half, the Wallabies defence standing tall despite Billy Pollard sin binning just after the break.

A Russell penalty looked to have sealed the game for the Scots, before Max Jorgensen scored a brilliant try in the final minute, an attacking raid of such class it raised questions as to why there had been no go-forward before then.

The Wallabies even had one chance to win the game late when Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii made a line break and Tom Wright was freed down the right wing.

However, he was bundled into touch and the Scots held on.

The Wallabies next head to Cardiff to take on a Wales team buoyed by beating the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years.

Look back on how all the action unfolded from Murrayfield in our live blog.

World.title: Shark attack hero breaks through for Iron Series win
World.content:
An emotional Charlie Verco has described his journey from a shark-attack rescue to a maiden Iron Series win as a "roller coaster".

Five months after saving Leah Stewart at Coogee Beach, Verco claimed the third round of the series by prevailing in a sprint finish in Sunday's race at Thirroul Beach.

In June, the 25-year-old paddled towards the danger and pulled the unconscious woman from the surf.

This shark attack hero believes Olympic inclusion could save lives The top seed in this year's Iron Series, who made headlines by helping save a shark attack victim earlier this year at Coogee, says having surf life saving in the Brisbane Olympic Games would help raise the profile of the sport.

After 12 days in a critical condition in hospital and a series of surgeries to amputate her arm, Stewart woke from an induced coma and was reunited with her daughter.

"Being able to manage the ups and downs of it, like the stressful rescue with Leah — I'm so happy that she was able to be alright," Verco said.

"It meant that I was able to keep focused on what I love, which is the sport.

"But realistically, we all do this sport as part of surf lifesaving. It certainly doesn't feel like we were doing a race like that.

"It feels like we're all just really wanting to win and compete against each other.

"But I like that we have the skills to be able to go and help people when they need it."

Verco beat home Ethan Callaghan and Henry Simpson in a breakthrough victory, which comes after the 25-year-old had entered this year's Iron Series as the top seed following the legendary Ali Day's retirement.

"It is a step up to try and put yourself at the front of the race as opposed to just being happy that you're here," Verco said.

"And for so long that was my goal, was just to get here. It's all about confidence.

"I've spent a long time doing races trying to get myself comfortable being at the front and setting my own pace, and I think that definitely helps."

Naomi Scott took out the women's event, with the Northcliffe athlete pipping Emma Woods in a sprint up the beach.

Before the Iron Series heads to Newcastle in January, Scott will travel to South Africa next week to defend her global Ironwoman title at the world lifesaving championships.

World.title: Chapman hat-trick fires Jillaroos to Rugby League World Cup glory
World.content:
The Jillaroos have defended their Rugby League World Cup title, dominating New Zealand 34-10 in the tournament decider at Lang Park.

The victory was all but assured after a commanding first half, with winger Jaime Chapman crossing for a hat-trick in sweltering Brisbane heat.

The win saw Australia claim a fourth-straight crown in the fifth-consecutive final featuring the Trans-Tasman rivals.

Rugby League World Cup finals live: Look back on all the action in our blog.

Chapman, whose treble brought her World Cup tally to 13, told ABC Sport it was a dream afternoon for her side.

"I feel over the moon. There's no better feeling than winning a World Cup on your turf, against the Kiwis as well.

"We knew it was coming. It was a really hard, tough game in this heat and super proud of our team and proud of our girls."

Chapman scored a stunning treble in sweltering Brisbane heat. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Lessons seemingly learnt from a lethargic start to their semifinal win over Fiji, the Jillaroos were dominant from the first minute in the tournament decider.

It took Chapman just two minutes to score the first try of the day by breaking wide, stutter stepping and rampaging through the New Zealand defence, allowing for the recalled Jesse Southwell to nail a difficult conversion.

A spectacular dive and one-handed putdown saw Chapman cross for her second in the 14th minute, before the winger put on the afterburners to complete her treble with a scintillating breakaway effort.

By half-time, Australia had run in six tries to the Kiwi Ferns' one, with Shaylee Best, Jess Sergis and Tamika Upton having also registered four-pointers, and Southwell having nailed all but one of the conversions.

Sergis's effort came after a breathtaking breakaway, while Upton completed some neat interplay with Abbi Church to compound New Zealand's misery in the shadows of half-time.

Shannon Mato's 23rd-minute converted effort was the Kiwi Ferns' only contribution to a 34-6 half-time scoreline.

Only a try-saving tackle prevented the Jillaroos from going further ahead five minutes after the break, but the Australians struggled for any cut through in an energy-sapping second half in which the still taxing conditions restricted the quality of play.

New Zealand winger Mackenzie Wiki was denied a late score thanks to a try-saving Isabelle Kelly tackle, but proceeded to find the only points of the second period by diving over with the full-time siren seconds from sounding.

Their 4-0 second-half scoreline meant the Kiwi Ferns went the entire tournament without conceding a point after half-time.

World.title: After tragically losing a mate, Herbert is helping businesses with his shirt
World.content:
Golfer Lucas Herbert has returned to Australia on a mission to use his platform to help those struggling in the tough economic climate.

Herbert has played in this week's NSW Open at the Hunter Valley, finishing in a tie for third.

But Herbert, fresh off the collapse of LIV Golf, entered this week's tournament without something synonymous with professional sport: sponsorships.

The end of LIV Golf brought an end to many commercial arrangements Herbert had, meaning he entered this week's NSW Open with his clothing as a blank canvas.

But Herbert decided he wanted to use his platform to help, following the tragic death of a mate earlier this year.

The 30-year-old from Bendigo put a call out to small businesses in the lead-up to the tournament, offering to promote them on his clothing.

He said small business owners were doing it tough, and said he wanted to help out.

He told golf journalist Tom Hobbs earlier this week that he was inspired to help small Australian businesses following the passing of a friend.

"Just seeing local business getting destroyed over here makes me sad," he said.

"One of my good friends took his own life in January because he was a small business owner and couldn't take the pressures of working 60 hours a week to keep the lights on any longer.

"I thought it would be better than coming home wearing blank hats and clothes."

A mental health charity, electrical and a lawn care business were among the sponsors Herbert carried on his clothing this week.

Herbert will also be part of the Australian Open and Australian PGA Championship during this golf season.

World.title: Aussies crashes to record ODI loss against England after top order collapse
World.content:
Australia's top-order batters have crashed spectacularly as England romped to a record 135-run win to level their one-day international series 1-1.

England opener Tom Banton clubbed 121 runs from 99 balls as the tourists posted 6-355 — their highest ODI total in Australia — after being sent in at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

The hosts were bowled out for 220 in 44.3 overs as England achieved its biggest winning runs margin in an ODI in Australia.

Australia's run chase started horribly with three batters — Travis Head (7), Cooper Connolly (0) and captain Mitchell Marsh (2) — caught at slip in a six-ball span.

The rapid-fire dismissals left the hosts reeling at 3-13 after 3.2 overs as England set course to level the series ahead of Wednesday's decider in Hobart.

It could have been worse for the Australians, who were 4-29 before England dropped two regulation catching chances from the bats of Matthew Renshaw, on 27, and Cameron Green, on 7.

The reprieves allowed Renshaw (63 from 74 balls) and Green to pause the rot with a 98-run partnership.

Green top-scored with 64 from 82 balls but the early damage inflicted chiefly by England paceman Gus Atkinson, who snared 3-22 from his initial seven overs, was irreparable.

Atkinson finished with 4-28 from 10 overs, his best ODI figures, and Sam Curran (2-38) and spinner Liam Dawson (2-41) also claimed multiple wickets.

Earlier, Banton, Jordan Cox (67 from 49 balls), Joe Root (62 from 68) and Will Jacks (54 not out from 40) dominated.

Banton and Root took control with a 137-run partnership from 136 balls for the second wicket, taking England to a powerful position of 1-156 in the 28th over.

Somerset batter Banton, 28, reached his second ODI ton from 86 balls before Cox and Jacks combined for a 102-run stand in less than 12 overs as England accelerated to an imposing total.

Tom Banton led from the front as England posted 6-355 in its innings. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Mark Brake)

Paceman Xavier Bartlett (3-72 from 10 overs) was the only Australian to take multiple wickets before a crowd of 31,412, the fifth-highest ODI attendance at Adelaide Oval.

Australia rested paceman Mahli Beardman, two days after his stunning one-day international debut of 6-24 in a seven-wicket win in Perth.

Beardman was replaced by Riley Meredith, who was punished in taking 1-75 from 10 overs.

Bartlett, Meredith, Spencer Johnson (1-61 from eight overs) and Jack Edwards (0-73 from nine) all conceded more than seven runs per over.

AAP

World.title: Aussie quick says 'everyone knew' about sandpaper, as Warner doubles down
World.content:
Former Australian cricketer Chadd Sayers, who played his lone Test after Sandpapergate on the infamous 2018 South African tour, has said he is comfortable stating he believed everyone in the team knew about ball-tampering.

The notorious Cape Town Test match, where Cameron Bancroft was filmed using sandpaper on the cricket ball, was thrust into the spotlight this week after Usman Khawaja in his memoir, Sabr, claimed ball-tampering was commonplace and the entire team needed to take responsibility.

The memoir has caused a rift in Australian cricket.

David Warner, who was suspended with Cameron Bancroft and then-captain Steve Smith over the incident, backed Khawaja's account in Sabr, saying it was "100 per cent accurate".

Meanwhile, Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Sayers, who was part of the Australian touring squad in 2018, said ahead of Australia's second ODI against England in Adelaide on Sunday that he was comfortable saying every member of the team knew sandpaper was being used.

"I'm comfortable saying where I'm sitting now that everyone knew what was going on [in South Africa in 2018]," Sayers said on the SEN broadcast.

"It [sandpaper] was used in two Test matches and there were discussions in change rooms … I'm not taking sides; it's just my recollection of what took place."

Sayers also said there was a meeting held in the wake of the team being caught with sandpaper, which lasted between 60 and 90 minutes.

Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball during the Test match in Cape Town, with an investigation determining he, Smith and vice-captain Warner were responsible for the ball tampering.

The trio was suspended, while the bowlers in that Test have always denied knowledge that sandpaper was being used on the ball.

In his memoir, Khawaja claimed he knew sandpaper was being used on the ball and told Bancroft to be careful.

Khawaja also said ball-tampering was commonplace in cricket.

Test captain Pat Cummins, who was part of the infamous 2018 side, held a 70-minute press conference on Friday, again denying he had any knowledge of sandpaper being used and claiming Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

Cummins hits out at Khawaja Australian Test cricket captain Pat Cummins rubbishes Usman Khawaja's ball-tampering claims in a long and passionate press conference.

"When he says 'we all knew', if by that he means we knew sandpaper was going out on the field, he's 100 per cent wrong," Cummins said on Friday.

"I've said that consistently for the last eight years; I did not know that was happening.

"But I think Usman actually says things that are far more serious than that. He says that I and others were architects of a scheme to ball tamper with sandpaper; that's complete and utter nonsense.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper. That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman that has been part of the team that's helped rebuild the Australian cricket culture over the last eight years, and the Usman that would have stopped that from happening there and then.

"Usman's a friend, but friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations. In his book Ussie's been casual with my [life] and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell a story, 100 per cent. I'm really glad he feels like he can, but we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Warner doubles down on Cricket Australia on social media

David Warner has hit out at Cricket Australia as Sandpapergate continues to dominate headlines. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

David Warner has made another statement on social media, claiming he was not aware of all the facts before taking the brunt of punishment for Sandpapergate.

On Saturday, Warner accused Cricket Australia of a potential cover-up by claiming he believed the bowlers were not interviewed by the organisation about the incident.

Cape Town inquiry spoke to all Aussie bowlers, ABC understands Sources connected to the Australian bowling group say they all spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into Cape Town ball tampering, which runs counter to claims by David Warner.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation," he wrote on Instagram.

"If that's correct then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning … ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Multiple media outlets, including ABC Sport, have reported the bowlers were interviewed by Cricket Australia.

On Sunday, Warner then doubled down on his criticism of Cricket Australia and supported his previous post.

Loading Instagram content

"Just to clarify 'As far as I am aware' was the POINT," he wrote.

"I was never told the bowlers had been interviewed or provided statements.

"That information would've been pretty useful when I was forced to make decisions back in 2018.

"Why weren't we given all the evidence by CA?"

Tech.title: Listen to this: Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I open with this caveat: I haven’t had a ton of time to digest the surprise Armand Hammer record that dropped this week. Billy Woods and Elucid rarely miss, though, and my initial reaction is that Snakes & Ladders ranks among their best. It doesn’t have the seamless throughline production-wise that their collabs with Alchemist (Haram and Mercy) do, but it’s still clearly the singular vision of the two men at its center.

Ominous noises dance in the background, blasts of noise add dashes of industrial rage, bass lines throb, and saxophone bleats call out to the sky. Woods and Elucid have always had excellent taste in production, but here they seem to have brought out the best in collaborators like clipping, Kenny Segal, and Child Actor. They’ve also successfully rallied them around a specific sound palette that keeps the record from actually sounding like it has beats from 11 different producers.

Of course, what makes Armand Hammer stand out from many of their contemporaries is their unique and verbose flows. Their lyrical mastery even makes guest rappers like $ilkmoney, who you can practically hear stalking around the mic as he seethes on “Risk,” up their game.

On songs like “Gravity,” Billy Woods navigates burgeoning romance with shocking directness, while also acknowledging obliquely how hard it can be to say what you mean.

Get it off your chest or put it to the side

As a preface, all due respect, I suggest

‘Cause it’s nothing more precious than time

On “Vespers,” he references Siouxsie and the Banshees and says “My nightcap three fingers of Fernet,” which is probably the first time I’ve ever heard Fernet Branca get a shoutout in a rap song.

“Graveside” is another highlight where it’s Elucid’s turn to get vulnerable:

I see you in the grave, I see you in the dirt

Shouts and hollers every which way, hurting

Darkness chase light

Steel shut close curtain

In some ways, this record feels like a culmination of what Billy Woods and Elucid have been working towards on their non-Alchemist-produced Armand Hammer records like We Buy Diabetic Test Strips, but also their recent solo records like Golliwog and Revelator.

Armand Hammer’s Snakes & Ladders is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Qobuz, and Deezer.

Tech.title: Vulcan rocket fails, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon’s competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a small portion of the necessary satellites to challenge Starlink into orbit. Today’s launch was supposed to be the first of 38 flights Amazon purchased from ULA.

In a statement posted on X, ULA said, “Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.”

The company said it was currently unclear what caused the failure, but pledged transparency as it continues its investigation. Amazon projected confidence in its launch partner despite the failure, posting on X that, “ There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01. ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

Tech.title: Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.

Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.
